prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is a multiaccess network?
pairs.definition: A network that can have two or more end devices attempting to access the network simultaneously; Ethernet LANs and WLANs are examples.

pairs.term: What are the two basic access control methods for shared media?
pairs.definition: Contention-based access and controlled access.

pairs.term: What is contention-based access?
pairs.definition: In contention-based multiaccess networks, all nodes operate in half-duplex and compete for the use of the medium; only one device can send at a time. Examples include CSMA/CD (legacy bus Ethernet LANs) and CSMA/CA (wireless LANs).

pairs.term: What is controlled access?
pairs.definition: A method in which each node has its own time to use the medium; these deterministic legacy networks are inefficient because a device must wait its turn. Examples include legacy Token Ring and legacy ARCNET.

pairs.term: Do contention-based systems scale well under heavy media use?
pairs.definition: No. Contention-based systems, whether Ethernet LANs using hubs or WLANs, do not scale well under heavy media use.

pairs.term: Why do switched Ethernet LANs not use a contention-based system?
pairs.definition: Because the switch and the host NIC operate in full-duplex mode; today Ethernet networks operate in full-duplex and do not require an access method.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: In the CSMA/CD hub scenario, which device accepts the frame that the hub floods out all ports?
pairs.definition: Only PC3, the device whose destination data link address matches the frame; all other device NICs ignore the frame.

pairs.term: How is a collision detected in CSMA/CD?
pairs.definition: The NIC compares data transmitted with data received, or it recognizes that the signal amplitude is higher than normal on the media. In the event of a collision, the data sent by both devices is corrupted and needs to be re-sent.

pairs.term: Which device accepts a frame sent by a hub?
pairs.definition: All devices attached to the hub receive the frame, but because the frame has a destination data link address, only the device that matches that address accepts and copies in the entire frame; all other device NICs ignore it.

pairs.term: Where is CSMA/CD used?
pairs.definition: CSMA/CD is used on legacy bus topology Ethernet LANs and on legacy Ethernet LANs using a hub; WLANs use CSMA/CA.

pairs.term: What does a PC NIC do before sending a frame in the CSMA/CD process?
pairs.definition: The PC1 NIC determines whether any device is transmitting on the medium; if it does not detect a carrier signal, it assumes the network is available to send and sends the Ethernet frame.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What happens in a fragile environment?
pairs.definition: More controls are needed to ensure delivery; the header and trailer fields are larger as more control information is needed.

pairs.term: How is the Layer 3 PDU wrapped to form a Layer 2 frame?
pairs.definition: The Layer 3 PDU is wrapped with a header and a trailer to form the Layer 2 frame.

pairs.term: Why does a WLAN frame require additional control information compared to an Ethernet frame?
pairs.definition: Because a WLAN frame must include procedures for collision avoidance, which requires more control information than an Ethernet frame.

pairs.term: What are the three basic parts of every data link frame?
pairs.definition: Header, data, and trailer.

pairs.term: What is unique about the data link layer trailer?
pairs.definition: Unlike other encapsulation protocols, the data link layer protocols append information in the form of a trailer at the end of the frame.

pairs.term: What is encapsulated within the data field of a frame?
pairs.definition: The data from the network layer, which is usually an IPv4 or IPv6 packet. All data link layer protocols encapsulate the data within the data field.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is half-duplex communication?
pairs.definition: A mode in which two devices can transmit and receive on the medium but cannot do so simultaneously; only one device can send or receive at a time. WLANs and legacy bus topologies with Ethernet hubs use half-duplex.

pairs.term: What is full-duplex communication?
pairs.definition: A mode in which both devices can simultaneously transmit and receive on the shared medium; the data link layer assumes the medium is available for transmission for both nodes at any time. Ethernet switches operate in full-duplex mode by default.

pairs.term: What is a duplex mismatch?
pairs.definition: The condition that occurs when two interconnected interfaces, such as a host NIC and an Ethernet switch interface, do not operate using the same duplex mode; it creates inefficiency and latency on the link.

pairs.term: What duplex mode can an Ethernet switch operate in when connecting to an Ethernet hub?
pairs.definition: Ethernet switches operate in full-duplex mode by default, but they can operate in half-duplex if connecting to a device such as an Ethernet hub.

pairs.term: Why is it important that two interconnected interfaces operate using the same duplex mode?
pairs.definition: Because otherwise there is a duplex mismatch, which creates inefficiency and latency on the link.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What topologies are used to interconnect nodes in multiaccess LANs?
pairs.definition: Star or extended star topologies, in which end devices are connected to a central intermediary device, in this case an Ethernet switch.

pairs.term: What is a star topology?
pairs.definition: A topology in which end devices connect to a central intermediary device; it is easy to install, very scalable (easy to add and remove end devices), and easy to troubleshoot. Early star topologies interconnected end devices using Ethernet hubs.

pairs.term: What is an extended star topology?
pairs.definition: A topology that extends the star topology by interconnecting multiple Ethernet switches.

pairs.term: What is a bus topology?
pairs.definition: A legacy LAN topology in which all end systems are chained to each other and terminated in some form on each end; infrastructure devices such as switches are not required. Legacy Ethernet networks were often bus topologies using coax cables.

pairs.term: What is a ring topology?
pairs.definition: A legacy LAN topology in which end systems are connected to their respective neighbors, forming a ring; unlike a bus topology, the ring does not need to be terminated. Legacy FDDI and Token Ring networks used ring topologies.

pairs.term: Which early LAN technologies included the two legacy topologies of bus and ring?
pairs.definition: Early Ethernet and legacy Token Ring LAN technologies included bus and ring topologies.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Which devices can act as nodes that operate at the data link layer?
pairs.definition: NICs on computers as well as the interfaces on routers and Layer 2 switches.

pairs.term: Which protocols are used by wired LANs and WLANs?
pairs.definition: Ethernet protocols are used by wired LANs; wireless communications fall under WLAN protocols specified in IEEE 802.11, which were designed for multiaccess networks.

pairs.term: What WAN Layer 2 protocols have been common over the years?
pairs.definition: Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP), High-Level Data Link Control (HDLC), Frame Relay, Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM), and X.25.

pairs.term: What is happening to these WAN Layer 2 protocols?
pairs.definition: They are now being replaced in the WAN by Ethernet.

pairs.term: What determines the Layer 2 protocol used in a TCP/IP network?
pairs.definition: The Layer 2 protocol used depends on the logical topology and the physical media; each protocol performs media access control for specified Layer 2 logical topologies.

pairs.term: What determines the technology used to implement a network topology?
pairs.definition: The size of the network, in terms of the number of hosts and the geographic scope, as well as the services to be provided over the network.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: When are Layer 2 addresses used?
pairs.definition: Layer 2 addresses are only used to connect devices within the same shared medium on the same IP network; they have no meaning beyond the local network.

pairs.term: What happens to the IP packet and its frames at each hop as it travels to its destination?
pairs.definition: As the IP packet travels from host to router, router to router, and finally router to host, it is re-encapsulated in a new data link frame at each point; each frame contains the source and destination data link addresses of the NICs on that segment.

pairs.term: What is the scope difference between Layer 2 and Layer 3 addresses?
pairs.definition: The data link layer address is used only for local delivery and has no meaning beyond the local network; at Layer 3, addresses in the packet header are carried from the source host to the destination host regardless of the number of network hops.

pairs.term: In the host-to-router encapsulation example, what addresses does the source host place in the frame header?
pairs.definition: Its own Layer 2 address as the source and the Layer 2 address of R1 as the destination.

pairs.term: How do Layer 2 physical addresses differ from Layer 3 logical addresses?
pairs.definition: Unlike Layer 3 logical addresses, which are hierarchical, physical addresses do not indicate on what network a device is located; a physical address is unique to a specific device and stays the same even if the device moves to another network or subnet.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What do the delimiting bits provided by frame delimiting do?
pairs.definition: They provide synchronization between the transmitting and receiving nodes and help identify fields within a frame.

pairs.term: What does the MAC sublayer add to the packet delivered by the LLC?
pairs.definition: The LLC takes the network protocol data, typically an IPv4 or IPv6 packet, and adds Layer 2 control information to help deliver the packet to the destination node.

pairs.term: In which IEEE standards is the Media Access Control (MAC) sublayer specified?
What controls the NIC and other hardware responsible for sending and receiving data on the LAN/MAN medium?
pairs.definition: The MAC sublayer.

pairs.term: What is the Media Access Control (MAC) sublayer?
pairs.definition: A sublayer specified in IEEE 802.3, 802.11, and 802.15 that is implemented in hardware; it is responsible for data encapsulation and media access control, provides data link layer addressing, and is integrated with various physical layer technologies.

pairs.term: What does the MAC sublayer control?
pairs.definition: It controls the NIC and other hardware responsible for sending and receiving data on the wired or wireless LAN/MAN medium. The LLC sublayer takes the packet and adds Layer 2 control information to help deliver it.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Does adding intermediary physical connections change the logical topology?
pairs.definition: No. A source and destination may be indirectly connected over geographic distance using multiple intermediary devices, but the logical point-to-point connection remains the same.

pairs.term: What does a node do on a point-to-point circuit?
pairs.definition: The node places the frames on the media at one end, and the frames are taken from the media by the node at the other end of the point-to-point circuit.

pairs.term: In a physical point-to-point topology, do the two nodes share the media with other hosts?
pairs.definition: No. In a physical point-to-point topology, the two nodes directly connected do not have to share the media with other hosts.

pairs.term: Which serial communications protocol keeps logical data link protocols simple on a point-to-point connection?
pairs.definition: The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP).

pairs.term: Why can logical data link protocols be very simple on a physical point-to-point connection?
pairs.definition: The two nodes do not share the media with other hosts; with a serial protocol such as PPP, a node does not have to determine whether an incoming frame is destined for it, because all frames can only travel to or from the two nodes.

pairs.term: Does a point-to-point connection over Ethernet require determining whether an incoming frame is destined for this node?
pairs.definition: Yes. Unlike a serial point-to-point link, a point-to-point connection over Ethernet requires the device to determine if the incoming frame is destined for it.

topic: Purpose of the Data Link Layer
prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does the data link layer do to a corrupt frame it receives?
pairs.definition: It performs error detection and rejects any corrupt frame.

pairs.term: What does the data link layer (Layer 2) of the OSI model do?
pairs.definition: It prepares network data for the physical network and is responsible for network interface card (NIC)-to-NIC communications.

pairs.term: What is a node?
pairs.definition: A device that can receive, create, store, or forward data along a communications path; it can be an end device such as a laptop or mobile phone, or an intermediary device such as an Ethernet switch.

pairs.term: What would happen without the data link layer?
pairs.definition: Network layer protocols such as IP would have to make provisions for connecting to every type of media along a delivery path, and IP would have to adapt every time a new network technology or medium was developed.

pairs.term: How does the data link layer prepare a Layer 3 packet for transmission?
pairs.definition: It adds Layer 2 (Ethernet) destination and source NIC information to the packet and converts this information into a format supported by the physical layer (Layer 1).

pairs.term: What does the data link layer do with received encapsulated data?
pairs.definition: It receives the encapsulated data, usually Layer 3 packets, and directs the data to the proper upper-layer protocol.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the topology of a network?
pairs.definition: The arrangement, or the relationship, of the network devices and the interconnections between them.

pairs.term: What is a logical topology?
pairs.definition: It refers to the way a network transfers frames from one node to the next; it identifies virtual connections using device interfaces and Layer 3 IP addressing schemes.

pairs.term: Which topology does the data link layer see when controlling data access to the media?
pairs.definition: The logical topology, which influences the type of network framing and media access control used.

pairs.term: What does the logical topology identify?
pairs.definition: It identifies virtual connections using device interfaces and Layer 3 IP addressing schemes, and it refers to how a network transfers frames from one node to the next.

pairs.term: What must the data link layer know about a network in order to transfer frames from one device to another?
pairs.definition: It must know the logical topology of the network in order to determine what is needed to transfer frames.

pairs.term: What are the two types of topologies used when describing LAN and WAN networks?
pairs.definition: Physical topology and logical topology.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are the three common physical WAN topologies?
pairs.definition: Point-to-point, hub and spoke, and mesh.

pairs.term: What is a point-to-point WAN topology?
pairs.definition: The simplest and most common WAN topology; it consists of a permanent link between two endpoints.

pairs.term: What is a hub and spoke topology?
pairs.definition: A WAN version of the star topology in which a central site interconnects branch sites through point-to-point links; branch sites cannot exchange data with each other without going through the central site.

pairs.term: What is a mesh topology?
pairs.definition: A topology that provides high availability but requires every end system to be interconnected with every other system, so the administrative and physical costs can be significant.

pairs.term: What is a hybrid topology and a partial mesh?
pairs.definition: A hybrid topology is a variation or combination of any topologies; a partial mesh is a hybrid topology in which some, but not all, end devices are interconnected.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does the $schema property do in a JSON Schema document?
pairs.definition: It specifies the version of JSON Schema being used, allowing tools to know which rules to use when parsing the schema and validating data with it, e.g., "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema".

pairs.term: What does the required key do in JSON Schema?
pairs.definition: It references keys within the JSON document that are mandatory; they must be present for a JSON document to be considered valid, e.g., "required": ["hostname", "vlans", "nameservers"].

pairs.term: What does the properties key do in JSON Schema?
pairs.definition: It allows you to specify further constraints that should be applied to keys of an object, such as type, minLength/maxLength, items, minItems, uniqueItems, minimum/maximum, and nested required.

pairs.term: Can JSON Schema validate YAML data?
pairs.definition: Since YAML and JSON are close relatives, some tools allow you to seamlessly validate YAML data as if it were JSON, and it's usually possible to convert a YAML document to JSON so existing JSON-only tools can be used.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Is YANG a serialization format?
pairs.definition: No. YANG is not a serialization format like JSON or XML; you won't see YANG syntax in a packet capture. APIs that leverage YANG usually use XML (or JSON per RFC 7951) as the serialization format when sending data between a server and client.

pairs.term: What is a leaf in YANG?
pairs.definition: A core YANG primitive that defines a singular piece of data containing a single value with no children. It includes statements like type, mandatory, config, and description.

pairs.term: What is a leaf-list in YANG?
pairs.definition: A statement that models multiple instances of the same leaf (e.g., a list of configured DNS servers). It can use ordered-by to control whether element order is respected.

pairs.term: What is a container in YANG?
pairs.definition: A statement used to nest lists and leaves under a parent element, e.g., container vlans { list vlan { ... } } to model a parent <vlans> element containing multiple <vlan> children.

pairs.term: What is a typedef in YANG?
pairs.definition: A statement that defines a custom data type by name. It can inherit from a built-in type while enforcing constraints, e.g., typedef vlanid { type int16 { range "1 .. 4094"; } }.

pairs.term: What does the key statement do in a YANG list?
pairs.definition: It indicates which field should be used as a unique identifier for elements in the list, roughly analogous to a primary key in database terms, e.g., key "id";.

pairs.term: What is containerlab?
pairs.definition: Open-source tool for creating virtual network labs using containers. Launches containerized network devices (FRR, Arista cEOS, Cisco XRd, Nokia SR Linux) and connects them into topologies using Docker networks and bridges.

pairs.term: What is Vagrant?
pairs.definition: Tool for building and managing virtual machine environments. Uses a Vagrantfile (Ruby) to define VM configuration. Supports multiple providers (VirtualBox, VMware, KVM) and provisioners (shell, Ansible, Puppet).

pairs.term: What is VirtualBox?
pairs.definition: Free and open-source hypervisor for running virtual machines on desktop operating systems. Commonly used for network automation lab environments due to its broad OS support and Vagrant integration.

pairs.term: What is Make / Makefile?
pairs.definition: Build automation tool that executes commands defined in a Makefile based on dependency tracking. Target: prerequisites → recipe syntax. Useful in networking for automating test runs, config generation, and lab setup tasks.

pairs.term: What is dyff?
pairs.definition: A diff tool for YAML files that provides intelligent comparison output, showing additions, modifications, and deletions with colored formatting. Useful for comparing Kubernetes manifests and Ansible inventory changes.

pairs.term: What is the difference between a text editor and an IDE?
pairs.definition: Text editor (Vim, VS Code) is lightweight, fast, and extensible via plugins. IDE (PyCharm, GoLand) is more feature-rich with integrated debugging, refactoring, project management, and language-specific tooling, but is heavier and language-specific.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Why was the CLI built and what is its key limitation?
pairs.definition: The CLI was built for humans—put on devices to improve usability for human operators. It was not meant for machine-to-machine communication (network scripting and automation).

pairs.term: What is the nature of a CLI show command's output?
pairs.definition: Raw text with no structure, which requires custom screen-scraping logic (regular expressions or manual parsing) that is difficult to maintain because small output changes could break the parsing.

pairs.term: What is the biggest shift in network operations over the past decade and why?
pairs.definition: The migration from Telnet to SSH. It wasn't about operations but about security, ensuring communications to network devices were encrypted.

pairs.term: Is it impossible to automate with SSH/CLI?
pairs.definition: No. SSH/CLI doesn't make it impossible to automate; rather, it makes automation extremely error prone and tedious, which is why expect scripts and manual parsing have been used for decades.

pairs.term: What two components are required to use SNMP?
pairs.definition: An SNMP agent on a managed device, and a network management station, which is the device that functions as a server that monitors and/or controls the managed devices.

pairs.term: What are MIBs in SNMP?
pairs.definition: Management information bases: the set of data on a managed device that can be collected and configured via the SNMP agent. Only if an MIB is exposing a certain feature can it be monitored or managed.

pairs.term: What are SNMP GetRequests and SetRequests?
pairs.definition: GetRequests are used for monitoring (reading data), while SetRequests are used for manipulating objects and variables exposed through MIBs (making configuration changes via SNMP).

pairs.term: What is SNMP used for?
pairs.definition: A protocol widely deployed for over 25 years on network devices, commonly used for polling devices for information such as up/down status and CPU, memory, and interface utilization.

pairs.term: What does the FROM instruction do in a Dockerfile?
pairs.definition: Specifies the base image we want to build from. For example, FROM python:3.8-slim-buster comes with Python 3.8 already installed.

pairs.term: What does the COPY instruction do in a Dockerfile?
pairs.definition: Copies a file from the outside filesystem into the image itself (e.g., COPY requirements.txt requirements.txt copies the requirements file into the image).

pairs.term: What does the RUN instruction do in a Dockerfile?
pairs.definition: Executes a shell command to run inside the container image during the build (e.g., RUN pip3 install -r requirements.txt installs the Python requirements).

pairs.term: What does the CMD instruction do in a Dockerfile?

pairs.term: What is an EAP peer?
pairs.definition: The client computer that is attempting to access a network.

pairs.term: What is an EAP authenticator?
pairs.definition: An access point or NAS that requires EAP authentication prior to granting access to a network.

pairs.term: What is the EAP authentication server?
pairs.definition: A server computer that negotiates the use of a specific EAP method with an EAP peer, validates the EAP peer's credentials, and authorizes access to the network. Typically it is a RADIUS server.

pairs.term: What is the EAP pass-through mode?
pairs.definition: The mode in which the authentication server functions as a backend server that authenticates peers as a service to a number of EAP authenticators, and the EAP authenticator makes the decision of whether to grant access.

pairs.term: What is a supplicant in the EAP context?
pairs.definition: The software entity in the EAP peer that operates at the lower-level protocol (such as PPP or IEEE 802.1X) used to connect to the EAP authenticator.

pairs.term: What is successful authentication in the context of RFC 3748?
pairs.definition: An exchange of EAP messages as a result of which the authenticator decides to allow access by the peer, and the peer decides to use this access. The peer may authenticate successfully but still be denied access due to policy reasons.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does the EAP Data field contain?
pairs.definition: Information related to authentication. Typically it consists of a Type subfield, indicating the type of data carried, and a Type-Data field. The Success and Failure messages do not include a Data field.

pairs.term: What are the four EAP code values?
pairs.definition: Request (1), Response (2), Success (3), and Failure (4).

pairs.term: What is the purpose of the EAP Identifier field?
pairs.definition: It is used to match Responses with Requests.

pairs.term: What does the EAP Length field indicate?
pairs.definition: The length, in octets, of the EAP message, including the Code, Identifier, Length, and Data fields.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How do EIGRP neighbors initially exchange routes and what do they advertise afterward?
pairs.definition: EIGRP neighbors exchange the entire routing table when forming an adjacency, then advertise only incremental updates as topology changes occur.

pairs.term: What is the purpose of the EIGRP neighbor adjacency table?
pairs.definition: It is vital for tracking neighbor status and the updates sent to each neighbor.

pairs.term: When does EIGRP use unicast packets versus multicast?
pairs.definition: EIGRP uses multicast packets (224.0.0.10) where possible and unicast packets when necessary.

pairs.term: What parameters must match for an EIGRP adjacency to be established?
pairs.definition: The routers must be in the same AS, use compatible K values/metrics, and have matching authentication and timers on the shared interface.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What do the K values reference in the EIGRP metric formula?
pairs.definition: K1 and K2 both reference bandwidth, K3 references delay, and K4 and K5 reference reliability. A common misconception is that K values apply directly to bandwidth, load, delay, or reliability, but this is not accurate.

pairs.term: What happens when K5 is 0 in the EIGRP metric formula?
pairs.definition: RFC 7868 states that if K5 equals 0, the reliability quotient is defined to be 1.

pairs.term: What is the EIGRP classic metric formula?
pairs.definition: Metric = 256 * [(K1 * BW + (K2 * BW)/(256 - Load) + K3 * Delay) * (K5/(K4 + Reliability))], where K values define which factors the formula uses.

pairs.term: What are the default K values in EIGRP?
pairs.definition: By default, K1 and K3 have the value 1, and K2, K4, and K5 are set to 0. With defaults, the simplified formula is Metric = 256 * (10^7 / Min Bandwidth + Total Delay / 10).

pairs.term: How are bandwidth and delay defined in the EIGRP classic metric?
pairs.definition: Bandwidth is the slowest link in the path scaled to a 10 Gbps link (10^7), measured in kilobits per second. Delay is the total measure of delay in the path, measured in tens of microseconds.

pairs.term: What are the default EIGRP metrics for Serial, T1, Ethernet, FastEthernet, GigabitEthernet, and 10 GigabitEthernet interfaces?
pairs.definition: Serial 40,512,000; T1 2,170,031; Ethernet 281,600; FastEthernet 28,160; GigabitEthernet 2,816; and 10 GigabitEthernet 512 (with their respective delays).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What happens when a router receives a reply for every downstream query it sent?
pairs.definition: It completes the DUAL computation, changes the route to passive, and sends a reply packet to any upstream routers that sent a query packet to it.

pairs.term: What does the query packet for a route going active include?
pairs.definition: It includes the prefix with the delay set to infinity so that other routers are aware that the route has gone active.

pairs.term: When a link fails and EIGRP loses its successor, what happens if a feasible successor exists?
pairs.definition: The feasible successor instantly becomes the successor route, providing a backup route, and the router sends out an update packet for that path because of the new metrics.

pairs.term: When no feasible successor exists for a prefix, what does DUAL do?
pairs.definition: DUAL performs a new route calculation; the route state changes from passive (P) to active (A), and the router sends query packets to EIGRP neighbors with the prefix and the delay set to infinity.

pairs.term: What is a query boundary in EIGRP?
pairs.definition: A point in the network where a router receiving a query does not mark the prefix as active and instead responds that it has no route or replies with EIGRP attributes, stopping the query from propagating farther.

pairs.term: When does an EIGRP router complete its DUAL computation and set a route back to passive?
pairs.definition: When the router receives a reply for every downstream query it sent out, it completes DUAL, changes the route to passive, and sends a reply packet to any upstream routers that sent it a query.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What deficiencies of RIPv2 does EIGRP overcome?
pairs.definition: EIGRP overcomes the deficiencies of distance vector routing protocols like RIPv2 with features such as unequal-cost load balancing, support for networks 255 hops away, and rapid convergence features.

pairs.term: How was EIGRP standardized?
pairs.definition: EIGRP was initially a Cisco proprietary protocol but was released to the IETF through RFC 7868, ratified in May 2016.

pairs.term: What IP protocol number does EIGRP use?
pairs.definition: EIGRP uses IP protocol number 88 in the IP header.

pairs.term: What multicast address does EIGRP use when communicating with neighbors?
pairs.definition: EIGRP uses the multicast group address 224.0.0.10 (with multicast MAC 01:00:5E:00:00:0A) where possible and unicast packets when necessary.

pairs.term: What algorithm does EIGRP use to identify network paths?
pairs.definition: EIGRP uses the diffusing update algorithm (DUAL) to identify network paths and enable fast convergence using precalculated loop-free backup paths.

pairs.term: What is an EIGRP autonomous system?
pairs.definition: An EIGRP process operates under the context of an autonomous system, representing a common routing domain; routers in the same domain use the same metric calculation formula and exchange routes only with members of the same AS.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is an EIGRP successor route?
pairs.definition: The route with the lowest path metric to reach a destination.

pairs.term: What is an EIGRP successor?
pairs.definition: The first next-hop router for the successor route.

pairs.term: What is the feasible distance (FD)?
pairs.definition: The metric value for the lowest-metric path to reach a destination, calculated locally using the EIGRP metric formula.

pairs.term: What is the reported distance (RD)?
pairs.definition: The distance reported by a router to reach a destination; the reported distance value is the feasible distance for the advertising router.

pairs.term: What is the feasibility condition?
pairs.definition: The condition under which, for a route to be considered a backup route, the reported distance received for that route must be less than the feasible distance calculated locally; this guarantees a loop-free path.

pairs.term: What is a feasible successor?
pairs.definition: A route that satisfies the feasibility condition (its reported distance is less than the local feasible distance) and is maintained as a loop-free backup route.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are the default EIGRP hello timer values?
pairs.definition: The default hello timer is 5 seconds, but it is 60 seconds on slow-speed interfaces (T1 or lower).

pairs.term: What is the EIGRP hold time and its default values?
pairs.definition: The hold time is the amount of time EIGRP deems a router reachable and functioning; it defaults to 3 times the hello interval (15 seconds, and 180 seconds on slow-speed interfaces).

pairs.term: What happens when the EIGRP hold time reaches 0?
pairs.definition: EIGRP declares the neighbor unreachable and notifies DUAL of a topology change. The hold time resets and restarts the countdown upon receipt of each hello packet.

pairs.term: What is the secondary function of EIGRP hello packets?
pairs.definition: In addition to neighbor discovery, hello packets ensure that EIGRP neighbors are still healthy and available.

pairs.term: How does EIGRP use the hold time to detect a dead neighbor?
pairs.definition: The hold time is the maximum time EIGRP waits for a hello before declaring the neighbor down; when it expires, the neighbor is considered down and DUAL recalculates any affected routes.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is equal-cost multipathing (ECMP) in EIGRP?
pairs.definition: Installing multiple successor routes with the same metric into the RIB for the same prefix to load share across paths.

pairs.term: How does EIGRP perform unequal-cost load balancing?
pairs.definition: By changing the variance multiplier. The EIGRP variance value is the feasible distance multiplied by the variance multiplier; any feasible successor whose metric is below the variance value is installed into the RIB.

pairs.term: How is the EIGRP variance multiplier calculated?
pairs.definition: Divide the feasible successor metric by the successor route metric; the variance multiplier is a whole number, so remainders should always round up.

pairs.term: In the unequal-cost example, what traffic share counts are seen for the two paths?
pairs.definition: The 5376-metric path has a traffic share count of 149 and the 3328-metric path has a traffic share count of 240, correlating to the ratio of traffic sent across each path.

pairs.term: In the variance example, how is the variance multiplier determined for a successor metric of 3328 and a feasible successor metric of 5376?
pairs.definition: Divide the feasible successor metric by the successor route metric: 5376/3328 is approximately 1.6, which rounds up to a whole number, so a variance of at least 2 is needed to install the feasible successor.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does the Init neighbor state mean in EIGRP?
pairs.definition: It means the neighbor adjacency is beginning; the router has discovered a new EIGRP neighbor but the neighbor relationship is not fully established.

pairs.term: What does the Ready neighbor state mean in EIGRP?
pairs.definition: It means the neighbor relationship has been established and the neighbor is ready to exchange routing information.

pairs.term: What does the Down neighbor state mean in EIGRP?
pairs.definition: It means the neighbor is not communicating; this state is seen in show ip eigrp neighbors for neighbors configured statically or when a hello is not received within the hold time.

pairs.term: What are the three EIGRP neighbor states?
pairs.definition: Neighbors are in one of three states: Init, Ready, and Down.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: In the reference topology, what is R1's feasible distance (FD) for 10.4.4.0/24?
pairs.definition: The FD calculated by R1 for 10.4.4.0/24 is 3328 (that is, 256+256+2816).

pairs.term: What is R1's successor route and successor for 10.4.4.0/24 in the reference topology?
pairs.definition: The successor route is R1â†’R3â†’R4, and the successor (first next-hop router) is R3.

pairs.term: What reported distances do R3 and R4 advertise for 10.4.4.0/24?
pairs.definition: R3 advertises the prefix with an RD of 3072, and R4 advertises it with an RD of 2816.

pairs.term: Why is the R1â†’R4 path a feasible successor for 10.4.4.0/24?
pairs.definition: Because the reported distance (RD 2816) is lower than the feasible distance (FD 3328) for the R1â†’R3â†’R4 path, satisfying the feasibility condition.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What additional benefit does EIGRP summarization provide besides shrinking routing tables?
pairs.definition: Summarization creates a query boundary and shrinks the query domain when a route goes active during convergence.

pairs.term: In the summarization example, which routes does R2 summarize to 172.16.0.0/16?
pairs.definition: R2 summarizes 172.16.1.0/24, 172.16.3.0/24, 172.16.12.0/24, and 172.16.23.0/24 into the single summary route 172.16.0.0/16 advertised to R4.

pairs.term: How does the size of an EIGRP AS affect convergence and what is required for scaling?
pairs.definition: As the size of an EIGRP AS increases, convergence may take longer; scaling requires summarizing routes in a hierarchical fashion, and the scalability of the AS depends on summarization.

pairs.term: When is the EIGRP summary route advertised?
pairs.definition: The summary route is not advertised until one of the component routes matches the summary address range.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does an active (A) route state indicate in the EIGRP topology table?
pairs.definition: An active route means DUAL is computing a new path for that prefix during a topology change.

pairs.term: What is the format of a path entry in the show ip eigrp topology output?
pairs.definition: Each path shows the next-hop router and the format metric/RD (for example, via 10.13.1.3 (3328/3072), GigabitEthernet0/1), followed by the feasible distance for the prefix.

pairs.term: Which prefix in the example topology table has 2 successors?
pairs.definition: The 10.23.1.0/24 prefix has 2 successors (FD is 3072), demonstrating ECMP with two equal-metric paths.

pairs.term: What does a passive (P) route state indicate in the EIGRP topology table?
pairs.definition: A passive route means the topology is stable; the route is not undergoing a path computation.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the wide metrics backward-compatibility requirement?
pairs.definition: With wide metrics, K1 and K3 are set to 1 and K2, K4, K5, and K6 to 0; as long as K1 through K5 are the same and K6 is not set, classic and wide metric routers can form an adjacency, and EIGRP unscales the metric when peering with a classic router.

pairs.term: What does the additional K6 value in EIGRP wide metrics do?
pairs.definition: K6 adds an extended attribute to measure jitter, energy, or other future attributes.

pairs.term: Why were EIGRP wide metrics introduced?
pairs.definition: Because the classic metrics (delay in 10 microsecond units and bandwidth in kilobits per second) did not scale well with higher-speed interfaces; classic metrics cannot differentiate between an 11 Gbps link and a 50 Gbps link.

pairs.term: What maximum interface speed do EIGRP wide metrics support?
pairs.definition: Wide metrics support interface speeds up to 655 Tbps (65,536 x 10^7) without scalability issues.

pairs.term: How does EIGRP handle peering between classic and wide metric routers?
pairs.definition: EIGRP is able to detect when peering with a router using classic metrics and unscales the metric, allowing adjacency.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is DANE?
pairs.definition: DNS-based Authentication of Named Entities - a protocol (RFC 6698) allowing X.509 certificates, commonly used for TLS, to be bound to DNS names using DNSSEC, to authenticate TLS client and server entities without a certificate authority (CA).

pairs.term: What are the four fields of the TLSA RR?
pairs.definition: Certificate Usage (defines the usage model), Selector (whether the full certificate or just the public key is matched), Matching Type (exact match, SHA-256 hash, or SHA-512 hash), and Certificate Association Data (raw certificate data in hex format).

pairs.term: Which DANE usage models operate with and without public CAs?
pairs.definition: PKIX-TA and PKIX-EE are designed to co-exist with and strengthen the public CA system; DANE-TA and DANE-EE operate without the use of public CAs (self-issued chains not verified against a trusted root in the client).

pairs.term: dig _443._tcp.example.com TLSA
pairs.definition: Queries for the DANE TLSA resource record that specifies the TLS certificate association for port 443 at example.com; a client looks up this record and matches the TLSA data against the certificate presented during TLS negotiation.

pairs.term: dig _25._tcp.example.com TLSA
pairs.definition: Queries for the TLSA record for SMTP over TLS (port 25) at example.com, used with DANE to signal that encryption must be performed (preventing STARTTLS downgrade) and to authenticate the SMTP TLS certificate via DNSSEC.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does the DMARC p= tag do?
pairs.definition: The mandatory policy field with values none, quarantine, or reject: p=none recommends no specific action on mail that fails DMARC checks, p=quarantine treats failed mail as suspicious, p=reject rejects all failed mail, preferably at the SMTP transaction stage.

pairs.term: What does SP 800-177 recommend for DMARC rollout?
pairs.definition: A sending domain should begin by setting a DMARC policy of p=none so disposition of failing messages is determined by the receiver's local policy; as aggregate reports are collected, the sender can set p=reject indicating failing mail should be rejected.

pairs.term: dig TXT _dmarc.example.com
pairs.definition: Queries the DMARC policy TXT record at the _dmarc subdomain of example.com (e.g., v=DMARC1; p=reject; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com), which specifies how receivers should treat mail purporting to originate from the domain.

pairs.term: dig TXT _dmarc.example.com +short
pairs.definition: Returns only the raw DMARC TXT value(s) without DNS metadata, giving the DMARC policy (v=DMARC1; p=...; rua=...; pct=...) in compact form.

pairs.term: What is the organizational domain in DMARC?
pairs.definition: If no DMARC policy is found for a domain, the DMARC module determines the organizational domain and repeats the attempt to retrieve a policy from the DNS.

pairs.term: What problem does DMARC solve?
pairs.definition: Neither SPF nor DKIM tells receivers if SPF/DKIM are in use, nor provides feedback to senders about the effectiveness of anti-spam techniques; DMARC standardizes how receivers perform e-mail authentication using SPF and DKIM mechanisms and provides reporting.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: dig example.com A ; dig example.com AAAA
pairs.definition: Queries for the A (IPv4 host address) or AAAA (IPv6 address) resource records mapping a host name to its numerical address.

pairs.term: What is the Domain Name System (DNS)?
pairs.definition: A directory lookup service that provides a mapping between the name of a host on the Internet and its numeric IP address; essential to the functioning of the Internet and used by MUAs and MTAs to find the address of the next hop server for mail delivery.

pairs.term: What is the MX resource record?
pairs.definition: Mail Exchange RR - identifies the system(s) via which mail to the queried domain name should be relayed; sending MTAs query DNS for the MX RR of the recipient's domain to find the receiving MTA to contact.

pairs.term: What are the four new DNS resource records defined by RFC 4034 for DNSSEC?
pairs.definition: DNSKEY (contains a public key), RRSIG (a resource record digital signature), NSEC (authenticated denial of existence), and DS (Delegation Signer).

pairs.term: What is an RRset?
pairs.definition: The set of resource records that have the same label, class, and type; an RRSIG is associated with each RRset, and when a client requests data the RRset is returned together with the associated digital signature in an RRSIG record.

pairs.term: What is the DS resource record used for?
pairs.definition: The Delegation Signer record facilitates key signing and authentication between DNS zones to create an authentication chain, or trusted sequence of signed data, from the root of the DNS tree down to a specific domain name.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are the five MIME header fields?
pairs.definition: MIME-Version (must be 1.0), Content-Type, Content-Transfer-Encoding, Content-ID, and Content-Description. Implementations must support MIME-Version, Content-Type, and Content-Transfer-Encoding; Content-ID and Content-Description are optional.

pairs.term: What does the MIME-Version field do?
pairs.definition: It must have the parameter value 1.0 and indicates the message conforms to RFCs 2045 and 2046.

pairs.term: What does the MIME Content-Type field do?
pairs.definition: Describes the data contained in the body with sufficient detail that the receiving user agent can pick an appropriate agent or mechanism to represent the data to the user or otherwise deal with it.

pairs.term: What does the MIME Content-Transfer-Encoding field do?
pairs.definition: Indicates the type of transformation used to represent the body of the message in a way acceptable for mail transport.

pairs.term: What are the seven major MIME content types?
pairs.definition: Text, Multipart, Message, Image, Video, Audio, and Application; there are 15 subtypes in total. The content type declares the general type of data and the subtype specifies a particular format.

pairs.term: What are the text MIME subtypes?
pairs.definition: Plain (unformatted text, ASCII or ISO 8859) and Enriched (provides greater format flexibility).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What document provides a list of specific e-mail threats and mitigations?
pairs.definition: SP 800-177 (Trustworthy E-mail, September 2015), whose table lists threats such as unauthorized MTA sending, spoofed domains, forged addresses/phishing, modification in transit, disclosure, UBE/spam, and DoS/DDoS.

pairs.term: What is UBE?
pairs.definition: Unsolicited Bulk E-mail, i.e., spam; mitigated by techniques to address UBE, and its impact is magnified when the purported sender is spoofed.

pairs.term: What are phishing and spear phishing?
pairs.definition: E-mail sent using a forged sending address or e-mail address to lure users into divulging sensitive information or PII; mitigation includes domain-based authentication techniques and digital signatures over e-mail.

pairs.term: How is a DoS/DDoS attack against e-mail servers mitigated?
pairs.definition: By using multiple mail servers and cloud-based e-mail providers.

pairs.term: How is e-mail modification in transit or disclosure mitigated?
pairs.definition: By using TLS to encrypt e-mail transfer between servers and by using end-to-end e-mail encryption.

pairs.term: What security services does STARTTLS provide for SMTP?
pairs.definition: Authentication, integrity, non-repudiation (via digital signatures) and confidentiality (via encryption) for the entire SMTP message by running SMTP over TLS.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What do the SMTP reply codes 220, 250, 354, 221, and 550 indicate?
pairs.definition: 220 - service ready; 250 - OK/requested action completed; 354 - start mail input; 221 - closing transmission channel; 550 - no such user here (recipient mailbox unknown).

pairs.term: What is SUBMISSION?
pairs.definition: The currently preferred standard (RFC 6409, Message Submission for Mail) for MUA/MSA message transfer; it derives from SMTP but uses a separate TCP port and imposes distinct requirements such as access authorization.

pairs.term: What is IMAP?
pairs.definition: Internet Message Access Protocol - enables an e-mail client to access mail on a server using TCP port 143; it is more complex than POP3, provides stronger authentication, and provides other functions not supported by POP3.

pairs.term: What are the two fundamental worlds in the Internet mail architecture?
pairs.definition: The user world in the form of Message User Agents (MUA) and the transfer world in the form of the Message Handling Service (MHS), composed of Message Transfer Agents (MTA).

pairs.term: What is a Mail Submission Agent (MSA)?
pairs.definition: Accepts the message submitted by an MUA and enforces the policies of the hosting domain and the requirements of Internet standards; may be co-located with the MUA or separate, in which case SMTP is used between the MUA and MSA.

pairs.term: What is a Mail Delivery Agent (MDA)?
pairs.definition: Responsible for transferring the message from the Message Handling Service (MHS) to the Message Store (MS).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is SignerInfo in signedData?
pairs.definition: A block containing the signer's public-key certificate, an identifier of the message digest algorithm, an identifier of the algorithm used to encrypt the message digest, and the encrypted message digest.

pairs.term: What is S/MIME?
pairs.definition: Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extension - a security enhancement to the MIME e-mail format based on technology from RSA Data Security, providing authentication, confidentiality, compression, and e-mail compatibility.

pairs.term: What is RFC 5652 (CMS)?
pairs.definition: Cryptographic Message Syntax - the syntax used to digitally sign, digest, authenticate, or encrypt arbitrary message content; it defines the S/MIME content types Data, SignedData, EnvelopedData, and CompressedData.

pairs.term: What are the four principal services provided by S/MIME?
pairs.definition: Authentication (digital signature), confidentiality (encryption), compression, and e-mail compatibility (radix-64/base64 conversion).

pairs.term: How does S/MIME provide confidentiality?
pairs.definition: Most commonly AES-128 with CBC using a one-time content-encryption (session) key generated randomly per message; the message is encrypted with this key, and the key itself is encrypted with RSA using the recipient's public key and attached to the message.

pairs.term: What is a detached signature?
pairs.definition: A signature that is stored and transmitted separately from the message it signs; useful for signature logs, detecting virus infection of executable programs, and when multiple parties must each sign a document independently.

pairs.term: What problem does SPF address?
pairs.definition: With the current e-mail infrastructure, any host can use any domain name for the various identifiers in the mail header; this is a major obstacle to reducing UBE (spam) and concerns ADMDs about others using their domain names with malicious intent.

pairs.term: What are the SPF mechanisms?
pairs.definition: ip4 (IPv4 address/range of authorized senders), ip6 (IPv6 address/range), mx (hosts in the MX RRs are valid senders), include (looks in another domain's SPF RR for further senders; recursive), and all (matches every IP address not otherwise matched).

pairs.term: What are the SPF mechanism modifiers?
pairs.definition: + (mechanism check must pass - the default), - (mechanism is not allowed to send on behalf of the domain), ~ (in transition - accept but mark for closer inspection), and ? (the SPF RR states nothing; default behavior is to accept).

pairs.term: What is the SPF checking behavior on the receiver side?
pairs.definition: If no SPF TXT RR is returned, the default behavior is to accept the message; if the SPF TXT RR has formatting errors, the default behavior is to accept the message; otherwise the mechanisms and modifiers are used to determine disposition (pass/fail).

pairs.term: dig TXT example.com
pairs.definition: Queries the TXT records of example.com, which include the SPF record (e.g., v=spf1 ip4:192.168.0.1 -all) listing the IP addresses authorized to send mail for the domain.

pairs.term: dig TXT example.com +short
pairs.definition: Shows just the raw TXT records (including the SPF record) without DNS response metadata, useful for quickly inspecting the SPF policy of a sending domain.

pairs.term: PGP Services
pairs.definition: Five security services: 1. Authentication (digital signature). 2. Confidentiality (encryption). 3. Compression (ZIP). 4. Email compatibility (Radix-64 encoding). 5. Segmentation (RFC 1423 message format). Uses Web of Trust — no central CA.

pairs.term: S/MIME vs PGP
pairs.definition: S/MIME: uses PKI with X.509 certificates, centralized CA hierarchy. PGP: uses Web of Trust, decentralized. S/MIME: standard for enterprise/government. PGP: popular for personal use. Both provide encryption + signing. S/MIME certificate management more complex.

pairs.term: DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail)
pairs.definition: Email authentication standard (RFC 6376). Sender's domain signs outgoing mail with private key. Receiver verifies signature using public key in DNS TXT record. Prevents spoofing. Headers: DKIM-Signature (v, a, d, s, h, bh, b).

pairs.term: SPF (Sender Policy Framework)
pairs.definition: email authentication (RFC 7208). Domain publishes authorized sending IPs in DNS TXT record. Receiver checks if sender IP is authorized. Prevents sender forgery. Syntax: v=spf1 ip4:192.0.2.0/24 -all.

pairs.term: DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication)
pairs.definition: Policy framework (RFC 7489). Domain publishes policy in DNS TXT record (_dmarc.domain.com). Tells receivers what to do if SPF/DKIM fail. Policies: none (monitor), quarantine (spam), reject. Aggregates reports from receivers.

pairs.definition: Parses and checks the topology clab file, creates the lab directory and a docker network, then creates the containers and virtual wires connecting them to deploy the topology.

pairs.definition: A YAML-based file used by Containerlab to define a topology. It specifies the name of the topology, the nodes (with kind and image), optional startup-config, and links (endpoints) between nodes.

pairs.term: What is the 'name' field in a Containerlab clab file used for?
pairs.definition: It names the topology as a whole, allowing Containerlab to understand which nodes are in which topology - especially useful for running multiple topologies at once.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Why does the access layer need high-bandwidth connectivity even if endpoints rarely use full capacity?
pairs.definition: The ability to burst up to high bandwidths when required improves the quality of experience (QoE) and productivity of the end user.

pairs.term: Which devices extend the access layer one more layer out from the access switch?
pairs.definition: Wireless access points and IP phones are prime examples of devices that extend the access layer outward.

pairs.term: What wired and wireless access technologies does the access layer provide?
pairs.definition: Gigabit Ethernet and 802.11n, 802.11ac, and 802.11ax wireless; the ability to burst to high bandwidths when required improves quality of experience (QoE) and productivity.

pairs.term: What types of endpoints connect to the access layer?
pairs.definition: Personal computers (PCs), IP phones, printers, wireless access points, personal telepresence devices, and IP video surveillance cameras.

pairs.term: What is the access layer?
pairs.definition: The layer that gives endpoints and users direct access to the network. It is also commonly referred to as the network edge.

pairs.term: What types of devices connect to the access layer?
pairs.definition: PCs, IP phones, printers, wireless access points, personal telepresence devices, and IP video surveillance cameras, using wired and wireless technologies such as Gigabit Ethernet and 802.11n/ac/ax.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the core layer?
pairs.definition: The backbone and aggregation point for multiple networks; it provides scalability, high availability, and fast convergence.

pairs.term: When should a core layer be considered?
pairs.definition: When networks grow beyond three distribution layers in a single location.

pairs.term: What does the core layer connect?
pairs.definition: It provides interconnectivity between the end-user/endpoint campus access layer and other network blocks such as the data center, private cloud, public cloud, WAN, Internet edge, and network services.

pairs.term: How does the core layer reduce network complexity?
pairs.definition: It reduces the number of links from N x (N-1) to N links for N distributions.

pairs.term: Why is a core layer needed when multiple distribution layers must be interconnected?
pairs.definition: When multiple distribution layers need to be interconnected, it becomes necessary to use a core layer to interconnect the building blocks (PINs).

pairs.term: What properties does the core layer provide to the network?
pairs.definition: The core is the backbone and aggregation point for multiple networks and provides scalability, high availability, and fast convergence.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the primary function of the distribution layer?
pairs.definition: To aggregate access layer switches in a given building or campus and act as a services and control boundary between the access layer and the core layer.

pairs.term: What two key functions does the Layer 2/Layer 3 boundary at the distribution layer provide?
pairs.definition: On the Layer 2 side it creates a boundary for Spanning Tree Protocol (STP), limiting propagation of Layer 2 faults; on the Layer 3 side it provides a logical point to summarize IP routing information entering the core.

pairs.term: How are distribution layer switches deployed?
pairs.definition: In pairs for redundancy, and the pairs should be interconnected to each other using either a Layer 2 or Layer 3 link.

pairs.term: Why are multiple distribution layer switches sometimes placed in different buildings?
pairs.definition: When access layer switches are located in multiple geographically dispersed buildings, distribution switches in those buildings reduce the number of costly fiber-optic runs between buildings.

pairs.term: What is the benefit of route summarization at the distribution layer?
pairs.definition: It reduces IP routing tables for easier troubleshooting and reduces protocol overhead for faster recovery from failures.

pairs.term: How should distribution layer switch pairs be interconnected?
pairs.definition: Distribution layer switches are deployed in pairs for redundancy, and each pair should be interconnected to each other using either a Layer 2 or a Layer 3 link.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is a building block (place in the network, PIN)?
pairs.definition: A modular building block used in enterprise network design, such as WAN edge, data center, Internet edge, and network services blocks, each deployed using the hierarchical design model.

pairs.term: What types of endpoints does a campus network typically support?
pairs.definition: Laptops, PCs, mobile phones, IP phones, printers, and video conferencing systems, spanning workers and guest users.

pairs.term: What does modularity ensure in the hierarchical design regardless of how many layers are implemented?
pairs.definition: Each layer provides the same services and the same design methods at each geographic location.

pairs.term: What is the purpose of the core or backbone in large campus networks?
pairs.definition: It provides interconnectivity to other networks, such as the campus access, data center, private cloud, public cloud, WAN, and Internet edge.

pairs.term: How can a small campus network environment be described?
pairs.definition: It might span a single floor or a single building, while a larger campus might span a large group of buildings over an extended geographic area.

pairs.term: What does the hierarchical design allow in terms of placing components in and out of service?
pairs.definition: Network components can be placed or taken out of service with little or no impact to the rest of the network, facilitating troubleshooting, problem isolation, and network management.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is a GR-unaware router?
pairs.definition: A neighbor router that does not support Graceful Restart routing protocol extensions and is not GR-aware.

pairs.term: What does the term NSF in Cisco documentation and the IOS XE command line actually refer to?
pairs.definition: Graceful Restart. NSF (SSO/NSF) was the term initially used by Cisco to refer to Graceful Restart, and any NSF command or keyword refers to Graceful Restart; SSO/NSF is not configurable and is enabled by default when SSO is enabled.

pairs.term: What is Graceful Restart (GR)?
pairs.definition: A standards-based feature defined in RFC 4724 and the only high availability technology that interacts with neighbor routers. It requires GR routing protocol extensions on the neighbor routers to keep them forwarding traffic during the switchover.

pairs.term: What are the three categories of GR routers?
pairs.definition: SSO/NSF-capable router (dual RPs, preserves FIB through switchover, also GR-aware), GR-aware router (also called GR Helper or NSF-aware; a neighbor that continues forwarding without needing dual RPs), and GR-unaware router (does not support GR extensions).

pairs.term: What is the difference between SSO/NSF and Graceful Restart?
pairs.definition: SSO/NSF is an internal capability (checkpointing within the box), while Graceful Restart is an external capability that interacts with neighbor routers via routing protocol extensions.

pairs.term: What RFC defines Graceful Restart, and what does it interact with?
pairs.definition: GR is a standards-based feature defined in RFC 4724 and is the only one of the high availability combinations that interacts with neighbor routers.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the hierarchical LAN design model?
pairs.definition: It divides the enterprise network architecture into modular layers (access, distribution, core), each implementing specific functions. Layers can be replicated to simplify design, scale the network, and provide a consistent deployment method.

pairs.term: What are the three layers of the hierarchical LAN design model?
pairs.definition: Access layer, Distribution layer, and Core layer (also called the backbone).

pairs.term: What are the benefits of the hierarchical LAN design model?
pairs.definition: It improves performance, simplifies the design, increases scalability, and reduces troubleshooting time.

pairs.term: How does hierarchical design provide fault containment and resilience?
pairs.definition: It constrains network changes to a subset of the network, affecting fewer systems. In a flat fully meshed network, changes tend to affect a large number of systems, which is undesirable.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does the active RP handle in a router with redundant RPs?
pairs.definition: The control plane, the routing table (RIB), and, in centralized forwarding architectures, the Forwarding Information Base (FIB) and adjacency table; an active RP failure can cause routing adjacencies to go down, resulting in packet loss and instability.

pairs.term: What does high availability mean in networking?
pairs.definition: A resilient network that can operate with continuous uptime without failure for a given period of time to ensure business continuity.

pairs.term: In a router with redundant RPs, what are the roles of active and standby RPs?
pairs.definition: The active RP handles the control plane, routing table (RIB), and in centralized forwarding also the FIB and adjacency table; the standby RP takes over in case of an active RP failure.

pairs.term: What are the possible combinations of high availability technologies for RP switchover?
pairs.definition: SSO and NSF; SSO and NSF with GR; SSO and NSF with NSR; SSO and NSF with NSR and GR.

pairs.term: What happens to routing adjacencies when the active RP fails in a router with redundant RPs?
pairs.definition: An active RP failure can cause routing protocol adjacencies to go down, resulting in packet loss and network instability; high availability technologies allow the router to keep forwarding packets using current CEF entries in the FIB.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What happens when a VLAN spans multiple access layer switches in a looped topology?
pairs.definition: STP blocks links, which reduces the bandwidth available from the rest of the network and can cause slower network convergence.

pairs.term: How is a highly available IP gateway provided at the distribution layer in a Layer 2 access design?
pairs.definition: By configuring a pair of standalone distribution switches with first-hop redundancy protocols (FHRPs) such as HSRP, VRRP, or GLBP to provide hosts a consistent MAC and gateway IP per VLAN.

pairs.term: What is the downside of HSRP and VRRP at the distribution layer?
pairs.definition: They only allow hosts to send data out through a single active uplink, leaving one access-to-distribution uplink unutilized. Manual configuration is needed to load-balance (e.g., one distribution switch active for odd VLANs and the other for even VLANs).

pairs.term: What does Gateway Load Balancing Protocol (GLBP) provide?
pairs.definition: Greater uplink utilization by load balancing host traffic across multiple uplinks, but it works only on loop-free topologies.

pairs.term: Why do the redundancy protocols HSRP/VRRP/GLBP require fine-tuning of default settings?
pairs.definition: To allow for sub-second network convergence, which can impact switch CPU resources.

pairs.term: What is the trade-off of restricting a VLAN to a single access switch?
pairs.definition: It provides a loop-free design but reduces network flexibility because all hosts within a VLAN are restricted to a single access switch.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is a Layer 3 access layer (routed access) design?
pairs.definition: Layer 3 is extended all the way to the access layer switches, which act as full Layer 3 routed nodes; the access-to-distribution Layer 2 uplink trunks are replaced with Layer 3 point-to-point routed links.

pairs.term: What are the advantages of routed access over a Layer 2 access design?
pairs.definition: No FHRP required, no STP required, increased uplink utilization (both uplinks used), easier troubleshooting (ping and traceroute), and faster convergence using protocols such as EIGRP and OSPF.

pairs.term: What are the limitations of the routed access design?
pairs.definition: It does not support spanning VLANs across multiple access switches, and access layer switches with Layer 3 capability may cost more than Layer 2 switches.

pairs.term: Where is the Layer 2/Layer 3 demarcation point in a routed access design?
pairs.definition: It is moved from the distribution switch to the access switch.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is NSR's primary benefit over GR?
pairs.definition: It is a completely self-contained in-box high availability solution with no disruption to routing adjacencies, so the neighbor router does not need to be NSR-aware or GR-aware and it works with GR-unaware neighbors.

pairs.term: What is the downside of NSR?
pairs.definition: It increases the workload on the router due to the constant checkpointing of routing and forwarding information to the standby RP.

pairs.term: What is the recommendation for scaled deployments regarding GR and NSR?
pairs.definition: Use GR for neighbor routers that are GR-aware and NSR for peers that are GR-unaware.

pairs.term: What does the active RP constantly checkpoint to the standby RP with NSR?
pairs.definition: All relevant routing control plane information, including routing adjacencies and TCP sockets, so the new RP can maintain current adjacencies and recalculate the routing table without alerting the neighbor router.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is Stateful Switchover (SSO)?
pairs.definition: An internal router redundancy feature that checkpoints (synchronizes/mirrors) router configuration, line card operation, and Layer 2 protocol state information from the active RP to the standby RP.

pairs.term: What is Nonstop Forwarding (NSF)?
pairs.definition: An internal Layer 3 data forwarding plane redundancy feature that checkpoints and frequently updates the Forwarding Information Base (FIB) from the active RP to the standby RP.

pairs.term: Can NSF be configured separately?
pairs.definition: No. NSF is not a configurable feature; it is enabled when SSO is enabled, which is why they are typically referred to together as SSO/NSF.

pairs.term: What is the downside of using SSO and NSF without GR or NSR?
pairs.definition: When routing adjacencies go down during the RP switchover, neighbor routers only see the adjacencies going down and stop forwarding traffic to the failing router.

pairs.term: What information does SSO checkpoint from the active RP to the standby RP?
pairs.definition: The router configuration, line card operation, and Layer 2 protocol state information.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the simplified campus design?
pairs.definition: It relies on switch clustering technologies: VSS and StackWise Virtual (SWV) cluster two physical switches into a single logical switch, and StackWise stacks two or more switches into a single logical switch with a single management and control plane.

pairs.term: Which layers are StackWise and VSS/SWV targeted for?
pairs.definition: StackWise is supported on switches targeted for the access layer, whereas VSS and SWV are supported on switches targeted for the distribution and core layers.

pairs.term: What is a Multichassis EtherChannel (MEC)?
pairs.definition: An EtherChannel that spans across the two physical switches in a VSS or SWV cluster.

pairs.term: What is a cross-stack EtherChannel?
pairs.definition: An EtherChannel that can span across all the switches in a StackWise stack.

pairs.term: How is high availability achieved in a simplified campus design?
pairs.definition: Seamless traffic failover when one switch in the cluster fails, using interchassis SSO/NSF.

pairs.term: Is STP still required in a simplified campus Layer 2 access design?
pairs.definition: Yes, STP is still required as a failsafe in case multiple access switches are interconnected, though EtherChannel eliminates the need for STP blocking on the uplink bundles.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the data center/server room block?
pairs.definition: Where business-critical servers are placed to serve websites, corporate email, business applications, storage, big data processing, backup services, and e-commerce transactions.

pairs.term: What is the Internet edge block?
pairs.definition: The block used for regular Internet access, e-commerce, connection to remote branches, remote VPN access, and cloud provider connectivity that does not require dedicated interconnections.

pairs.term: What is the network services edge block?
pairs.definition: Where devices providing network services reside, such as wireless LAN controllers (WLCs), Cisco Identity Services Engine (ISE), Cisco TelePresence Manager, and Cisco Unified Communications Manager (CUCM).

pairs.term: What must be considered before selecting a two-tier collapsed core design?
pairs.definition: Future scale, expansion, and manageability factors need to be considered because the collapsed core pairs must handle both WAN/Internet/network services connectivity and LAN aggregation.

pairs.term: Which devices reside in the network services edge block?
pairs.definition: Wireless LAN controllers (WLCs), Cisco Identity Services Engine (ISE), Cisco TelePresence Manager, and Cisco Unified Communications Manager (CUCM).

pairs.term: What is a two-tier design (collapsed core)?
pairs.definition: A design where the core function is collapsed into the distribution layer, eliminating core layer devices. It is cost-effective for smaller campus environments while retaining most benefits of the three-tier model.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Default EtherChannel configuration
pairs.definition: Channel groups: none assigned. Port-channel logical interface: none defined. PAgP mode: no default. PAgP priority: 128 on all ports. LACP mode: no default. LACP port priority: 32768. LACP system priority: 32768.

pairs.term: Default EtherChannel load-balancing method
pairs.definition: Load distribution on the switch is based on the source MAC address of the incoming packet (src-mac).

pairs.term: Default PAgP/LACP learn method
pairs.definition: The default PAgP learn method and LACP learn method are aggregate-port learning on all ports.

pairs.term: LACP system ID
pairs.definition: The LACP system ID is the LACP system priority and the switch (or switch stack) MAC address.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: channel-group 1 mode on
pairs.definition: Assigns the member interfaces to EtherChannel 1 as a static EtherChannel with no aggregation protocol and no health check.

pairs.term: channel-group 1 mode active
pairs.definition: Assigns the member interfaces to EtherChannel 1 using LACP active mode, which initiates the EtherChannel and transmits LACP packets.

pairs.term: channel-group 1 mode passive
pairs.definition: Assigns the member interfaces to EtherChannel 1 using LACP passive mode, which only responds to LACP packets and does not initiate.

pairs.term: channel-group 2 mode desirable
pairs.definition: Assigns the member interfaces to EtherChannel 2 using PAgP desirable mode, which initiates the EtherChannel and transmits PAgP packets.

pairs.term: interface port-channel 1
pairs.definition: Enters the logical EtherChannel interface configuration mode where channel-level settings such as switchport mode trunk are configured.

pairs.term: lacp rate fast
pairs.definition: Configures the LACP packet rate to fast (1-second interval) on the member interfaces, allowing failed links to be detected and removed in 3 seconds.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is an EtherChannel bundle (port channel)?
pairs.definition: A logical link created by aggregating multiple physical links, defined in the IEEE 802.3AD link aggregation specification. The industry term is EtherChannel or port channel.

pairs.term: What are member interfaces in an EtherChannel?
pairs.definition: The physical interfaces that are used to assemble the logical EtherChannel.

pairs.term: How does STP view an EtherChannel?
pairs.definition: STP operates on the logical EtherChannel link and not on the individual physical member links.

pairs.term: For which forwarding types can EtherChannels be used?
pairs.definition: EtherChannels can be used for Layer 2 (access or trunk) or Layer 3 (routed) forwarding.

pairs.term: What are the primary benefits of using an EtherChannel?
pairs.definition: Increased bandwidth between devices by aggregating links, and a reduction in topology changes/convergence because a member link failure does not trigger STP or route calculations while one active member remains up.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What do the S and R flags mean for an EtherChannel?
pairs.definition: S means the EtherChannel interface is configured for Layer 2 switching; R means it is configured for Layer 3 routing.

pairs.term: What does the P flag mean for a member interface in show etherchannel summary?
pairs.definition: P means the interface is actively participating and forwarding traffic for the EtherChannel.

pairs.term: What does the H flag mean for a member interface in show etherchannel summary?
pairs.definition: H means the interface is a hot standby (LACP only); it participates in LACP with the remote peer but does not forward traffic because the maximum number of active interfaces is configured.

pairs.term: What does the I flag mean for a member interface in show etherchannel summary?
pairs.definition: I means the member interface has not detected any LACP activity on that interface and is treated as an individual (stand-alone).

pairs.term: What do the w, s, and u flags mean for member interfaces?
pairs.definition: w means there is time left to receive a packet from the neighbor to ensure it is still alive (waiting to be aggregated); s means the member interface is suspended; u means the interface is unsuitable for bundling.
