pairs.term: What are SD-WAN edge devices?
pairs.definition: Physical or virtual routers that deliver WAN, security, and multicloud capabilities and forward traffic across WAN transports between locations.

pairs.term: What is OMP?
pairs.definition: The Overlay Management Protocol, a proprietary routing protocol similar to BGP that advertises routes, next hops, keys, and policy information needed to establish and maintain the SD-WAN fabric.

pairs.term: How do SD-WAN routers connect to the fabric?
pairs.definition: Each router automatically establishes a secure DTLS connection with the vSmart controller and forms an OMP neighborship over the tunnel to exchange routing information, plus standard IPsec sessions with other SD-WAN routers.

pairs.term: What are vEdge and cEdge routers?
pairs.definition: vEdge routers are original Viptela hardware running a dedicated Viptela OS (legacy, no longer available for purchase); cEdge routers are Cisco IOS XE platform devices using a unified image starting with version 17.2.

pairs.term: What limitations do vEdge platforms have?
pairs.definition: URL filtering and IPS are not supported on vEdge platforms and may not be present on some cEdge platforms because they run outside the operating system in IOS XE containers.

pairs.term: Which standard routing features do SD-WAN edge devices support?
pairs.definition: OSPF, EIGRP, BGP, ACLs, QoS, and routing policies, in addition to the SD-WAN overlay control and data plane functions.

pairs.term: What is the most powerful component of Cisco SD-WAN?
pairs.definition: The ability to push a unified policy across the fabric; policy can modify the topology, influence traffic forwarding decisions, or filter traffic, and changes can be pushed to thousands of devices in minutes from vManage.

pairs.term: What is a local SD-WAN policy?
pairs.definition: Part of the configuration pushed to the edge device by vManage, including ACLs, QoS policies, routing policies, and the on-device security stack.

pairs.term: What is a centralized SD-WAN policy?
pairs.definition: Contains configuration changes to the vSmarts, where control plane functions are processed before OMP routes are advertised to edge devices; data plane functionality is transmitted to edge devices' volatile memory for enforcement.

pairs.term: What is Application-Aware Routing (AAR)?
pairs.definition: A data plane policy that enhances forwarding of packets on an application-by-application basis, using BFD probes in SD-WAN tunnels to track a tunnel's packet loss, latency, and jitter.

pairs.term: How is BFD used in SD-WAN?
pairs.definition: It detects path liveliness (up/down) and measures quality (loss/latency/jitter and IPsec tunnel MTU).

pairs.term: How does AAR select paths?
pairs.definition: It considers factors beyond standard routing (bandwidth, delay, hop count). If the preferred transport exceeds the defined loss/latency/jitter thresholds for an application, AAR forwards traffic across a different transport that meets the requirements.

pairs.term: What are the two models of underlay supported by SD-Access?
pairs.definition: Manual underlay (configured via CLI/API, allows customization such as changing the IGP to OSPF or running over legacy/third-party networks) and automated underlay (configured and managed by DNA Center LAN Automation).

pairs.term: What does the DNA Center LAN Automation feature do for an automated underlay?
pairs.definition: It creates an IS-IS routed access campus design and uses Cisco Network Plug and Play (PnP) to deploy unicast and multicast routing configuration, eliminating misconfigurations and simplifying underlay building.

pairs.term: What is a downside of an automated underlay?
pairs.definition: It does not allow manual customization for special design requirements.

pairs.term: What routing configuration does the LAN Automation feature deploy in the underlay?
pairs.definition: It creates an IS-IS routed access campus design and uses Cisco Network Plug and Play to deploy both unicast and multicast routing configuration in the underlay to improve traffic delivery efficiency for SD-Access.

pairs.term: What is the recommended underlay design for SD-Access?
pairs.definition: A Layer 3 routed access campus design using IS-IS as the IGP. A Layer 2 underlay running STP is possible but not recommended.

pairs.term: What operational advantages does IS-IS offer as the underlay IGP?
pairs.definition: Neighbor establishment without IP dependencies, peering using loopback addresses, and agnostic treatment of IPv4, IPv6, and non-IP traffic.

pairs.term: Distributed Forwarding
pairs.definition: When line cards have forwarding engines so they switch packets without RP intervention, it is a distributed forwarding architecture. Packets destined for another line card cross the switch fabric (backplane), bypassing the RP.

pairs.term: Distributed CEF (dCEF)
pairs.definition: In distributed platforms, CEF data structures are downloaded to forwarding ASICs and line card CPUs so they participate in packet switching, increasing packet throughput.

pairs.term: ASICs Versus NPUs
pairs.definition: ASICs allow very high packet rates but are hardwired to specific tasks. NPUs are programmable and their firmware can be changed, overcoming ASIC inflexibility.

pairs.term: Centralized Forwarding Flow
pairs.definition: In centralized forwarding, a packet received on the ingress line card is transmitted to the forwarding engine on the RP, which forwards it to the egress line card.

pairs.term: Distributed Forwarding Flow
pairs.definition: In distributed forwarding, the ingress line card forwards to its local forwarding engine. If the outbound interface is local, it forwards locally; otherwise, the packet crosses the switch fabric directly to the egress line card, bypassing the RP.

pairs.term: Distributed Forwarding Advantage
pairs.definition: The main advantage of distributed forwarding is that packet throughput is greatly improved by offloading packet switching responsibilities to the line cards.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Glean Adjacency
pairs.definition: When an IP packet has no valid FIB entry, CEF uses a glean adjacency, sending the packet to the CPU because CEF cannot handle it. Missing adjacency entries invoke ARP.

pairs.term: CEF Header Rewrite
pairs.definition: The router overwrites the destination MAC with the next-hop MAC from the adjacency table, overwrites the source MAC with the outbound interface MAC, decrements TTL, and recomputes the IP header checksum.

pairs.term: TTL
pairs.definition: TTL is a Layer 3 loop prevention mechanism that decrements the TTL by 1 per hop. A packet received with TTL 0 is discarded.

pairs.term: Forwarding Engines
pairs.definition: Forwarding engines provide the packet switching, forwarding, and route lookup capability to routers. On hardware-based routers they are implemented in specialized ASICs, TCAM, and NPUs.

pairs.term: Software CEF on Hardware Routers
pairs.definition: On hardware-based platforms, software CEF is not used for packet switching; it is used to program the hardware CEF.

pairs.term: CPU Rate Limiter
pairs.definition: Packets processed by the CPU are typically subject to a rate limiter when an invalid or incomplete adjacency exists, to prevent starving CPU cycles from other essential processes.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Process Switching
pairs.definition: Also called software switching or slow path, the general-purpose CPU performs packet switching. The ip_input process runs on the CPU to process incoming IP packets.

pairs.term: Packets Needing Software Handling
pairs.definition: Packets sourced or destined to the router (control traffic/routing protocols), packets too complex for hardware (IP options), and packets needing extra info (unresolved ARP) are punted to the CPU.

pairs.term: ip_input Process
pairs.definition: The ip_input process runs on the general-purpose CPU to process incoming IP packets. It consults the routing and ARP tables, rewrites MAC addresses, decrements TTL, and recomputes the checksum.

pairs.term: Software Switching Speed
pairs.definition: Software switching is significantly slower than hardware switching. The ip_input process is designed to handle a very small percentage of traffic; packets are hardware switched whenever possible.

pairs.term: Process Switching as Fallback
pairs.definition: Process switching is the fallback for CEF, dedicated to processing punted IP packets that cannot be switched by CEF.

pairs.term: sdm prefer {vlan | advanced}

pairs.term: SDM Boot Allocation
pairs.definition: The memory used for TCAM tables is limited and statically allocated during the bootup sequence of the switch. A reload is required after changing the SDM template.

pairs.term: SDM Template Resources
pairs.definition: The Advanced (high scale) template on a Catalyst switch supports 4094 VLANs, 32,768 unicast MAC addresses, 16,384 directly connected routes, and 7168 indirect routes.

pairs.term: SDM Templates
pairs.definition: SDM (Switching Database Manager) templates set allocation ratios between TCAM tables. On Catalyst 9300 switches they are configured with sdm prefer and require a reload.

pairs.term: TCAM Overflow
pairs.definition: TCAM memory is limited and statically allocated during bootup. When a hardware resource section is full, overflow processing is sent to the CPU, seriously impacting switch performance.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: TCAM Multi-Field Matching
pairs.definition: TCAM is an extension of CAM enhanced to allow upper-layer processing such as identifying Layer 2/3 source and destination addresses, protocol, and QoS markings.

pairs.term: TCAM Allocation
pairs.definition: Most switches implement multiple TCAM entries so inbound/outbound security, QoS, and Layer 2 and Layer 3 forwarding decisions occur at once. TCAM is not infinite, and balancing allocations has trade-offs.

pairs.term: Ternary Content Addressable Memory (TCAM)
pairs.definition: TCAM allows matching and evaluating a packet on more than one field. It provides three results: 0 for true, 1 for false, and X for do not care (ternary).

pairs.term: TCAM VMR Format
pairs.definition: TCAM entries are stored in Value, Mask, and Result (VMR) format. Value lists fields to search, mask indicates fields of interest, and result is the action taken on a match.

pairs.term: TCAM Advantages
pairs.definition: TCAM operates in hardware, providing faster processing and scalability than process switching. ACLs process at the same speed whether there are 10 or 500 entries. TCAM is not infinite, and allocations have trade-offs.

pairs.definition: A popular SaaS offering for reviewing and displaying source code (enterprise edition also available for a cost).

pairs.term: What is GitLab as a code review platform?
pairs.definition: The community edition is open source and free to download and run behind your firewall; there is also a tiered SaaS offering, as well as a closed-source enterprise edition.

pairs.term: What is Gerrit as a code review platform?
pairs.definition: Open source, complicated, but with lots of integrations available, and a popular choice for some very large open source projects.

pairs.term: What is Bitbucket?
pairs.definition: Atlassian's code review and CI/CD platform; useful if your organization already uses other Atlassian products like Jira or Confluence.

pairs.term: What do GitHub, GitLab, Gerrit, and Bitbucket have in common?
pairs.definition: All of them leverage Git for the actual version control portion (and Git is the way you interface with them when submitting code), but on top of Git they all have subtle differences when it comes to their workflow.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Why is copying a Git repository with a tool like cp able to produce an intact repository?
pairs.definition: Because Git uses SHA-1 hashes to identify all content, identical content produces identical hashes, and the contents of the Git repository are immutable. The combination of these attributes means a simple copy preserves all data and metadata intact.

pairs.term: git remote
pairs.definition: Lists any existing remotes for the repository.

pairs.term: git remote add first ~/net-auto
pairs.definition: Adds a remote with a symbolic name ('first') and a location (~/net-auto, here a filesystem path). The name is purely symbolic; the location can be a filesystem path or a network URL.

pairs.term: git remote add -f name location
pairs.definition: Adds a remote and fetches information from the remote repository in a single step, instead of the two-step git remote add followed by git remote update.

pairs.term: git remote update first
pairs.definition: Updates (fetches) information from the specified remote repository only. Without a remote name it updates all remotes for the repository.

pairs.term: git remote -v
pairs.definition: Shows remotes with more verbose output, including the full location of each remote repository for both fetch and push.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: git config --global user.email "john.smith@example.com"
pairs.definition: Sets the user email address as a user-specific (--global) configuration value stored in the home directory's .gitconfig file.

pairs.term: git config --global init.defaultBranch <name>
pairs.definition: Configures the name Git uses for the initial branch in all new repositories (commonly set to main instead of master), which suppresses the initial branch-name hint.

pairs.term: git config --global core.excludesfile /path/to/.gitignore_global
pairs.definition: Configures Git to use a global excludes file (such as ~/.gitignore_global) for excluding files from all repositories on the computer.

pairs.term: git config pull.rebase false
pairs.definition: Sets the Git configuration so that git pull uses merge (the default strategy) rather than rebase when reconciling divergent branches; it also silences the pull hint about divergent branches.

pairs.term: git config --global user.name "John Smith" (without --global)
pairs.definition: Sets the user name as a repository-specific value stored in the current repository's .git/config file. You must be in the working directory of an active repository first, or Git reports an error.

pairs.term: git init
pairs.definition: Initializes, or creates, a new Git repository. It creates the .git directory and all its subdirectories and contents, and sets up the initial branch.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: sudo apt-get install -y git
pairs.definition: Installs Git via the apt package-management tool on Ubuntu.

pairs.term: git --version
pairs.definition: Verifies the Git installation, printing output like `git version 2.7.4`.

pairs.term: git config --global user.name "Your Name"
pairs.definition: Configures the global Git user name so commit messages contain the correct author information.

pairs.term: git config --global user.email "email@domain.com"
pairs.definition: Configures the global Git user email so commit messages contain the correct author email.

pairs.term: git config --global core.editor "vim"
pairs.definition: Sets VIM as the default text editor for typing commit messages instead of the default Emacs (optional setting).

pairs.term: git config --list
pairs.definition: Lists the configured Git settings, e.g. user.name=Your Name, user.email=email@domain.com.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is stashing in Git?
pairs.definition: Stashing places uncommitted changes into a temporary storage area so you can recall them later. It's useful for switching branches or moving uncommitted changes from one branch to another.

pairs.term: git stash push -m "Updated changes for sw5"
pairs.definition: Pushes uncommitted changes onto the stash (the -m adds a stash-specific message), restoring the working directory to match HEAD. Without -m, the last commit message is used as the description.

pairs.term: git stash list
pairs.definition: Lists the stashed changes, showing the syntax Git uses to refer to each stash (such as stash@{0}).

pairs.term: git stash show stash@{0}
pairs.definition: Shows the changes in a specific stash as a diff (similar to git diff), between the stashed contents and the commit when the stash entry was first created.

pairs.term: git stash pop stash@{0}
pairs.definition: Takes the changes from a specified stash, applies them to the checked-out branch, and then drops the stash (assuming no conflicts were encountered).

pairs.term: git stash apply
pairs.definition: Takes changes from a stash and applies them against the working directory of the checked-out branch, but does not drop the stash afterward; you must use git stash drop manually.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: git add sw1.txt
pairs.definition: Stages (adds) the specified file from the working directory into the index, putting the index in sync with the working directory and marking the file as ready to commit.

pairs.term: git add sw*.txt
pairs.definition: Uses shell globbing to stage multiple files at the same time—in this example, all files beginning with 'sw' and ending with '.txt'.

pairs.term: git add sw{1,2,3}.txt
pairs.definition: Uses bash brace expansion to stage multiple files with a single command—in this case sw1.txt, sw2.txt, and sw3.txt.

pairs.term: git add .
pairs.definition: Stages everything in the current directory, such as staging and committing a newly added .gitignore file into the repository.

pairs.term: git rm --cached <file>
pairs.definition: Removes a file from the index to unstage it (as suggested in git status output), leaving the file in the working directory untracked.

pairs.term: git restore <file>
pairs.definition: Discards changes in the working directory, restoring the file to the content referenced by HEAD.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is a lightweight tag in Git?
pairs.definition: A tag that is only a pointer to a commit. Lightweight tags are primarily intended for temporary object labels and don't require a tag message.

pairs.term: What is an annotated tag in Git?
pairs.definition: A tag that is a full object in the repository with its own metadata (such as a tag message and the tagger). Annotated tags should be used for any long-term purposes, such as version/release management, and can even be cryptographically signed using GnuPG.

pairs.term: git tag golive d40fe74
pairs.definition: Creates a lightweight tag named 'golive' pointing to the specified commit. If the commit hash is omitted, the tag is added to the latest commit (HEAD).

pairs.term: git tag -a v1.0 d268c37 -m "Version 1.0 release"
pairs.definition: Creates an annotated tag (full object with its own metadata) named v1.0 on the specified commit, with a tag message supplied via -m.

pairs.term: git tag
pairs.definition: Lists all the tags found in a Git repository (git tag --list works the same way). Any tag listed can be used in place of a commit hash in commands like git diff.

pairs.term: git tag -d <tag-name>
pairs.definition: Deletes a tag from the repository.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Who created Git and when?
pairs.definition: Linus Torvalds, the creator of the Linux kernel, in April 2005. He created it after a disagreement between the Linux kernel developer community and BitKeeper, the proprietary system they were using.

pairs.term: What is a Git pull?
pairs.definition: Fetching and merging a repository (getting the code and merging it locally).

pairs.term: Where does the name Git come from?
pairs.definition: In British English slang, a git is an insult for an unpleasant, annoying person. Linus named his projects after himself, though some suggest the name is short for 'Global Information Tracker' (GIT).

pairs.term: What is a Git tag?
pairs.definition: A mark in a point in time in a repository that is significant. In the Ansible chapter, tags were used to specify release points such as v2.5.0a1.

pairs.term: How quickly did the Linux kernel move to Git?
pairs.definition: About ten days after its creation Linus felt the basic ideas for Git were right and started committing the first Linux kernel code with Git.

pairs.term: Why is Git described as 'free, as in freedom'?
pairs.definition: Git was born out of the disagreement between the free (as in beer) version of the Linux kernel with the BitKeeper VCS, and it makes sense that the tool has a very liberal usage license.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does the range keyword provide when iterating over a slice?
pairs.definition: The range keyword can provide just the index, or both the index and the value at each index (e.g., for i, val := range vlanSliceIter), and can be combined with break or continue.

pairs.term: Why might a key-value data structure (map) be a better choice than a slice?
pairs.definition: In a map a value can be looked up simply using its key regardless of where that value is stored in memory, and unlike iterating a slice, this operation is extremely fast because it doesn't require iteration.

pairs.term: What happens if you write to a map that was declared but not initialized?
pairs.definition: Trying to write to a nil map will cause a runtime panic; it's much safer to declare and initialize the map at the same time, such as with make() or the literal syntax.

pairs.term: What happens when you read a key that doesn't exist in a Go map?
pairs.definition: It does not produce an error (as it would in Python); instead you get back the zero value for the type used as that map's value (for example, 0 for an int).

pairs.term: Why can't you rely solely on the retrieved value to determine whether a key exists in a Go map?
pairs.definition: Because reading a missing key returns the zero value, and a stored value could legitimately be that type's zero value too, so you'd get the zero value back either way.

pairs.term: What is the comma-ok idiom for testing whether a key exists in a Go map?
pairs.definition: Reading a key from a map can optionally return a second boolean value (found); you can test it on the same line by adding a semicolon and the found variable, e.g., if val, found := vlanMap["VLAN_999"]; found { ... }.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: go mod tidy
pairs.definition: Makes sure the go.mod file matches what your program needs: it downloads/adds any missing modules, but also removes any unused modules.

pairs.term: go mod vendor
pairs.definition: Vendors the modules you depend on so their source is stored alongside your code in a vendor/ subdirectory within your module's directory, rather than only in the system's module cache.

pairs.term: go get
pairs.definition: Finds and downloads the source for a module; using a Git repository location as the module path makes it easier for go get to locate and download the source.

pairs.term: go test
pairs.definition: Runs the tests for the Go packages in the current module (e.g., unit tests).

pairs.term: mkdir myfirstmodule && cd myfirstmodule
pairs.definition: Creates the new directory myfirstmodule and then enters into it, as the first step before initializing a Go module.

pairs.term: go run 1-first-program.go
pairs.definition: Quickly compiles and executes a Go program with a single command, giving the same 'scripting' experience as Python but with Go's benefits.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What happens if multiple goroutines try to write to the same map at the same time?
pairs.definition: If Go detects multiple goroutines trying to write to a map at the same time, it will trigger a panic and your program will crash; you must ensure only one goroutine accesses a shared resource at a time.

pairs.term: What is a mutex?
pairs.definition: A mutex is a synchronization tool used to ensure only one goroutine accesses a shared resource at a time: you Lock the mutex before accessing the resource (like checking a book out of the library) and Unlock it when finished (checking the book back in).

pairs.term: How are mutexes in Go related to the shared resource itself?
pairs.definition: Mutexes are not tied directly to the shared resource; it's up to you to ensure you access the resource only after acquiring a lock. Sometimes defer is used to call Unlock() automatically at the end of the function.

pairs.term: What caution is given about introducing concurrency into a program?
pairs.definition: Be careful not to introduce concurrency for the wrong reasons; it is not a panacea that will automatically make your program faster, and it opens you up to a new class of problems (like shared-resource access) that require their own solutions.

pairs.term: What is concurrency?
pairs.definition: Concurrency is a program's capability to handle multiple tasks at the same time; for example, executing tasks A and B simultaneously, waiting for them to finish, and only then executing task C, versus executing tasks serially (A, then B, then C).

pairs.term: Why is concurrency frequently brought up when discussing Go's strengths?
pairs.definition: First, Go includes native support for concurrency (built into the language itself, as opposed to only third-party libraries); second, the way Go exposes concurrency primitives is remarkably simple compared to other languages.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How does an if statement work in Go?
pairs.definition: An if statement tests whether an expression evaluates to a boolean true or false; the expression can be a simple expression (even a single boolean variable) or a complex one with chained logical or arithmetic operators.

pairs.term: How many types of loops does Go have?
pairs.definition: Go has only a single type of loop, the for loop, which can iterate over a set of values or simply execute instructions until a specified condition (the exit condition) is met.

pairs.term: What does the continue keyword do in Go?
pairs.definition: The continue keyword allows you to effectively skip over any remaining instructions in the loop and cause the loop to repeat earlier than it normally would.

pairs.term: What does the break keyword do in Go?
pairs.definition: The break keyword is used to exit from a loop entirely, even if the exit condition hasn't yet been reached; a loop with no exit condition will loop indefinitely unless a break or return statement is used.

pairs.term: How do continue and break behave in nested loops by default?
pairs.definition: By default they apply only to the loop in which they appear; in nested loops the compiler assumes you're referring to the innermost loop. Labels allow you to refer to a loop scope other than the immediately local scope.

pairs.term: What is a label in Go and when is it useful?
pairs.definition: A label lets you refer to a loop scope other than the immediately local scope, so with deeply nested loops you can break out of a loop scope of your choosing (e.g., a break deviceloop statement in the innermost loop stops all three loops).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Why is a function named main in a package named main special?
pairs.definition: Because of its special name and location within a package also called main, it will be automatically called when the resulting binary is executed.

pairs.term: How do you calculate an exponent in Go?
pairs.definition: Go doesn't have an exponent operator, so you use the Pow() function in the math package, e.g., math.Pow(2.0, float64(x)); both parameters and the return value of math.Pow are float64.

pairs.term: How do you declare a function with multiple parameters and multiple return types?
pairs.definition: Input parameters are separated by commas (e.g., x, y int), and return types are separated by commas and wrapped in parentheses, e.g., func sumAndProduct(x, y int) (int, int).

pairs.term: What benefits do functions provide?
pairs.definition: Reusable code (chunks of code that can be reused by you or other programmers) and improved readability and maintainability (focusing on a specific task makes it easier to reason about).

pairs.term: similar structure
pairs.definition: a main package and a main() function. You

pairs.term: How does Go declare variables?
pairs.definition: Two ways: (1) 'var name type = value' (explicit) or 'var name type' (zero-value). (2) Short declaration: 'name := value' — type inference, can only be used inside functions. Multiple: 'var x, y int = 1, 2' or 'x, y := 1, 2'.

pairs.term: package
pairs.definition: strconv. This contains functions for parsing and converting between strings

pairs.term: Len
pairs.definition: parameter of type int

pairs.term: What is Go benchmarking?
pairs.definition: Performance testing built into the testing package. 'func BenchmarkXxx(b *testing.B) { for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { myFunc() } }'. Run: 'go test -bench=.'. b.N adjusted by framework for stable timing. Use -benchmem for memory allocation stats.

pairs.definition: a uint8 is an 8-bit unsigned integer (also called a byte), and a float64 is a

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does the built-in len command do in a Go template pipeline?
pairs.definition: It prints the length of the value passed to it, rather than the value itself.

pairs.term: What other built-in commands are available in Go templates besides len?
pairs.definition: slice (for subslicing an argument), and and or (for comparing two arguments for emptiness), and call (for calling a function).

pairs.term: How do you make custom functions available to a Go template?
pairs.definition: Create a mapping between the function and a name using template.FuncMap, then pass it in with the Funcs() method of the template object.

pairs.term: What does the with statement do in Go templates?
pairs.definition: It creates a new variable within the template context, e.g., {{with $loc := $interface | ifparse}} creates $loc from the pipelined result.

pairs.term: What can be passed as the first parameter to Execute() in Go templates?
pairs.definition: Anything that satisfies io.Writer, including os.Stdout or a file opened via os.Create().

pairs.term: How do you iterate over a slice in Go templates?
pairs.definition: Using {{range $i, $switch := .}}, where $i is the index value of each element and $switch is a copy of the element itself.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does the basicAuth(username, password string) string helper function in the Go example do?
pairs.definition: It constructs the expected format of the basic authentication string by concatenating username:password and encoding it with base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString. The result is placed in the Authorization header as "Basic " + basicAuth(...).

pairs.term: What does http.NewRequest do in the Go RESTCONF example?
pairs.definition: It creates a new HTTP request with a method, URL, and optional body (nil for GET). Headers are then set via request.Header.Set (e.g., Accept: application/yang-data+json and the Authorization header).

pairs.term: What do the client.Do(request), ioutil.ReadAll(result.Body), and result.Body.Close() calls do in the Go HTTP example?
pairs.definition: client.Do() performs the HTTP request; ioutil.ReadAll() reads the body content from the response; result.Body.Close() closes the response body.

pairs.term: How do you narrow a RESTCONF GET in Go to a specific interface?
pairs.definition: Use URI-encoded path expressions, e.g., restconf/data/ietf-interfaces:interfaces/interface=GigabitEthernet1. The expression matches the identifier field (name) of the interface in the YANG model and returns only that interface's configuration.

pairs.term: What does the TLSClientConfig: &tls.Config{InsecureSkipVerify: true} transport configuration do in the Go example?
pairs.definition: It creates an http.Transport that ignores expired/self-signed SSL certificates so the HTTP client can connect to devices that don't have valid certificates.

pairs.term: Why does the chapter recommend starting with PATCH and gradually migrating to PUT for RESTCONF configuration management?
pairs.definition: Because PUT declaratively replaces the entire targeted section, so a small change sent via PUT can have catastrophic consequences (e.g., eliminating all other routing protocol configs). PATCH makes small additions safely.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are packages used for in Go?
pairs.definition: Packages allow you to create logical groupings to organize your code better; for example, you might have packages named devices, generator, and ssot for interacting with network devices, generating config files, and retrieving intended state.

pairs.term: Why must the main() function exist within a package called main?
pairs.definition: When you execute a Go program, the main() function is invoked automatically, and this function must exist within a package called main (declared with the package keyword).

pairs.term: What are Go modules used for?
pairs.definition: Modules describe a collection of packages: they unify a set of related packages into one easily distributable repository (commonly at the root of a Git repository) and are the mechanism by which Go manages dependencies on third-party libraries.

pairs.term: What is the go.mod file?
pairs.definition: The file created by go mod init in your directory, showing the module path and the version of Go it was initialized with; a newly initialized go.mod file contains lines like 'module github.com/oreilly-npa-book/myfirstmodule' and 'go 1.18'.

pairs.term: What does '// indirect' mean next to a module in go.mod?
pairs.definition: Modules followed by // indirect are not directly referenced in your code but are modules that your dependencies rely on; the Go tooling navigates the full tree of dependencies and makes sure they're all available so your program can compile.

pairs.term: What is pkg.go.dev?
pairs.definition: A great starting point for locating a new module; it offers a search engine for Go packages and modules, where you can view a module's README and follow links to the code repository (e.g., GitHub) to vet the module.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are encoding/binary and text/template used for?
pairs.definition: encoding/binary is used for encoding to/from binary formats (covered more in Chapter 8); text/template is used for Go's templating functionality, which is powerful and covered in Chapter 9.

pairs.term: What does strings.Join() do?
pairs.definition: It performs the reverse of strings.Split(): it creates a single string from a []string, joined with a delimiter of your choice.

pairs.term: What does the regexp package provide?
pairs.definition: Robust regular expression support for advanced string-search and replacement tasks; a common step is regexp.Compile() to obtain a *regexp.Regexp before using methods like MatchString(), FindString(), and ReplaceAllString().

pairs.term: What do the encoding/json and encoding/xml packages do?
pairs.definition: They perform serialization and deserialization of data structures to and from JSON and XML formats, which is often necessary to send/receive data between disparate systems like the HTTP API on a network device.

pairs.term: With what kinds of types will serialization/deserialization packages work?
pairs.definition: They will work with only exported types and fields (which start with a capital letter).

pairs.term: How do you send custom HTTP headers with a request in net/http?
pairs.definition: You need more control than high-level functions offer, so you create your own Client and Request (the method and URL are parameters to http.NewRequest), add headers to the request object, then pass the request to client.Do().

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How is the size of a type like int determined when no size suffix is given?
pairs.definition: The target system determines the size; for example, int is 32 bits long on 32-bit systems and 64 bits long on 64-bit systems. It is a Go best practice to use these more flexible types when possible.

pairs.term: What is the zero value for a string, bool, and int in Go?
pairs.definition: A string defaults to a zero-length string (""), a bool defaults to false, and an int defaults to 0.

pairs.term: What happens in Go if a program has unused variables?
pairs.definition: The program will fail to compile with the message 'variable name declared but not used'; Go won't compile a program successfully if unused variables are present, whereas Python has no problem running it.

pairs.term: What are constants in Go, and how do they differ from variables?
pairs.definition: Constants always retain the value they were initialized with and cannot be reassigned (using the const keyword); unlike variables, unused constants are permitted at compile time, and the compiler can make optimizations since they never change.

pairs.term: What is an advantage of using constants for potentially larger values?
pairs.definition: A floating-point number defined as a constant can have much higher precision than even the float64 type, and since constants are unchanging by design the compiler can safely make optimizations not always possible with variables.

pairs.term: What is a dynamic type system?
pairs.definition: In a dynamic type system like Python's, the types used within a program are not checked for validity until runtime; the program runs fine until it encounters the line of code that makes the mistake.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Who designed Go and when?
pairs.definition: Go was initially designed by Google in 2007 and is used today by thousands of companies around the world.

pairs.term: According to the 2021 Go Developer Survey, what percentage of respondents use Go at work?
pairs.definition: 76% of respondents use Go at work, and nearly 40% said they use Go for automation or scripting use cases.

pairs.term: What is one of Go's strengths when it comes to speed of development?
pairs.definition: Go was built for simplicity from the beginning; it typically provides only one or two ways to do something, so once you understand Go code generally, reading others' code is not too difficult.

pairs.term: What is a major operational advantage of Go programs being compiled to a single, statically linked binary?
pairs.definition: Once a Go program is compiled, you don't need to install Go on every machine that will run the program, nor any third-party libraries, resulting in a lower operational burden.

pairs.term: Is Go faster than Python, and how important is raw speed for network automation?
pairs.definition: In any objective test Go will be many times faster than Python, but for most network automation use cases seeking Go solely for performance is likely a red herring, since most use cases involve a lot of waiting for I/O.

pairs.term: Why is Go sometimes perceived as harder than Python?
pairs.definition: Go is statically typed whereas Python is dynamically typed, Go is a compiled language requiring an extra step before a working program is produced, and Go often complains about invalid types and unused variables, preventing compilation until resolved.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the OpenConfig gNMIc Go package?
pairs.definition: The inner Go package (github.com/openconfig/gnmic/api) used to build Go scripts that interact with the gNMI interface programmatically, emulating the same operations done with the gNMIc CLI.

pairs.term: go get github.com/openconfig/gnmic/api
pairs.definition: Gets and installs the OpenConfig gNMIc package to use it in Go applications (e.g., adding gnmic v0.27.1).

pairs.term: In the gNMIc Get example, how is the value extracted from the gNMI response?
pairs.definition: descriptionGnmiValue := getResp.GetNotification()[0].GetUpdate()[0].GetVal(), then value.ToScalar() converts the value into a scalar, and a type assertion casts it into a string.

pairs.term: In the gNMIc subscribe example, what are the subscription modes and list modes?
pairs.definition: SubscriptionMode can be sample, on_change, or target_defined. SubscriptionListMode selects stream instead of poll. sample mode uses a SampleInterval; on-change only sends data when there is a change in the data source.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How does a server demand authentication via HTTP?
pairs.definition: Rejects the request while specifying an authentication type and a prompt string.

pairs.term: In which header line is user login data sent back to the server?
pairs.definition: Authorization.

pairs.term: HTTP basic authentication credentials are encoded how?
pairs.definition: Base-64, which leaves them as cleartext to tools like dsniff.

pairs.term: What did the authors note is missing from the Authorization header data?
pairs.definition: It is not encrypted.

pairs.term: What shows when the browser pops up a login/password dialog?
pairs.definition: The server's request for authentication with type and prompt.

pairs.term: User can be tricked by server-chosen __ over 'never click a URL'.
pairs.definition: Redirect (Location).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Which HTTP methods can upload data to a server?
pairs.definition: POST and PUT.

pairs.term: The HTTP method that is 'charming' but rarely used?
pairs.definition: DELETE.

pairs.term: GET uploads data how, if used?
pairs.definition: Data is appended onto the URL.

pairs.term: GET is mainly for ___; POST/PUT for ___.
pairs.definition: retrieving; uploading

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Is HTTP stateless?
pairs.definition: Yes, HTTP is stateless; each request involves a separate TCP connection.

pairs.term: What is the most important HTTP method for retrieving documents?
pairs.definition: GET.

pairs.term: What header carries the protocol version the client speaks?
pairs.definition: None; HTTP relies on the request line version (HTTP/1.0).

pairs.term: What does 'stateless' mean concretely for HTTP?
pairs.definition: Each request opens a separate TCP connection that is torn down after the document.

pairs.term: What is the blank line significance in an HTTP message?
pairs.definition: Data above it are headers; the body follows below it.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does the User-Agent header inform the server of?
pairs.definition: The browser and operating system you are running, and hence what bugs your system has.

pairs.term: What does the Referer header contain?
pairs.definition: The URL that has a link to this page (the page you came from).

pairs.definition: Tells the compiler to enable all instruction subsets supported by the local machine, needed for the cache timing/measurement code to work correctly.

pairs.definition: Reads the CPU's timestamp (TSC) counter. Reading it before and after a memory access and taking the difference gives the access time in CPU cycles.

pairs.definition: Flushes the given memory address from the CPU cache, so the next access will be a cache miss (useful to flush the probing array before the attack).

pairs.term: In the CacheTime.c experiment, why are accesses to array[3*4096] and array[7*4096] consistently faster?
pairs.definition: Because those two elements were explicitly accessed before the timing loop, so they are already in the CPU cache (cache hit), while the other elements were flushed (cache miss).

pairs.definition: Compiles the cache-timing program, enabling all instruction subsets supported by the local machine (-march=native).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the FLUSH+RELOAD technique?
pairs.definition: A well-known cache side-channel attack technique (Yarom and Falkner 2014) used to infer which memory locations a victim program accessed, by flushing an array, letting the victim access one element, then timing reloads of all elements.

pairs.term: What is a cache hit?
pairs.definition: When data the CPU needs is already present in the CPU cache; the data is fetched directly from the cache, so the access is much faster.

pairs.term: What is a cache miss?
pairs.definition: When the data the CPU needs is NOT in the cache; the CPU must go to the main memory (RAM) to fetch it, which takes significantly longer.

pairs.term: What is the typical CPU cache block size?
pairs.definition: 64 bytes. Caching is done at the cache block level, not at the byte level.

pairs.term: Why does the side-channel code use array[k*4096] instead of array[k]?
pairs.definition: Because caching is done at block level (64 bytes); adjacent elements of array[k] would fall into the same cache block and also get cached, making it hard to infer the secret. With stride 4096 (larger than 64), no two probed elements share a cache block.

pairs.term: What is the purpose of the DELTA constant (1024) in the side-channel code?
pairs.definition: To offset all probed elements to array[k*4096+DELTA] so that index 0 is avoided, because array[0*4096] may accidentally be cached by adjacent program variables.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How does the OS normally prevent user programs from accessing kernel memory?
pairs.definition: Through the supervisor bit of the processor, which defines whether a memory page of the kernel can be accessed. The bit is set when the CPU enters kernel space and cleared when it exits to user space.

pairs.term: What happens when a user-space program directly reads a kernel memory address?
pairs.definition: The access fails and raises a SIGSEGV fault; if the program does not handle the signal, the OS kills the process and the program crashes (Segmentation fault).

pairs.term: How can a C program survive a catastrophic memory-access exception?
pairs.definition: By registering a SIGSEGV signal handler and using sigsetjmp()/siglongjmp() to emulate a try/catch clause, so the program can roll back to a checkpoint and continue.

pairs.term: What does sigsetjmp(jbuf, 1) do?
pairs.definition: Saves the stack context/environment in jbuf for later use by siglongjmp(). It returns 0 when the checkpoint is set up, so the program takes the true branch; after a rollback it returns the value passed to siglongjmp (e.g., 1).

pairs.term: What does siglongjmp(jbuf, 1) do?
pairs.definition: Inside the exception handler, restores the state saved by sigsetjmp() and starts execution from the sigsetjmp() return point, making sigsetjmp() return 1 (the second argument), so the program continues from the else branch.

pairs.term: What does insmod MeltdownKernel.ko do?

pairs.definition: Builds the kernel module using the running kernel's build tree, producing MeltdownKernel.ko.

pairs.definition: Installs the kernel module into the running kernel as root, creating /proc/secret_data and caching-related setup.

pairs.definition: Searches the kernel message buffer for the secret address printed by the module, e.g., secret data address: 0xfb61b000.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Where is the secret data stored in this lab, and what is its content?
pairs.definition: Inside a kernel module (MeltdownKernel.c) as the array secret[8] = 'SEEDLabs'.

pairs.term: What is the /proc/secret_data entry used for in the lab?
pairs.definition: A proc virtual file created by the kernel module via proc_create_data(). When a user program reads it, read_proc() loads the secret variable into memory (caching it) but does NOT return the secret to user space; it does not leak the secret by itself.

pairs.term: What two conditions must hold for the Meltdown attack to succeed easily?
pairs.definition: 1) The address of the secret data must be known (in the lab it is printed by the module via printk and read with dmesg; real attackers must guess or find it). 2) The secret data must be cached in the CPU.

pairs.term: How is the secret data address obtained in the lab?
pairs.definition: The kernel module prints it with printk('secret data address:%p\n', &secret) into the kernel message buffer; the user runs 'dmesg | grep secret data address' to read it.

pairs.term: Why does accessing a proc entry cache the secret data?
pairs.definition: The read_proc() function in the kernel module executes memcpy(secret_buffer, &secret, 8), loading the secret into the CPU cache as a side effect, even though the secret bytes are not returned to the user program.

pairs.term: How do you steal the remaining 7 bytes of the 8-byte secret?
pairs.definition: Replace the target address with the successive addresses (0xfb61b001, 0xfb61b002, ...) and run the attack again for each byte.

pairs.term: On which CPUs does the Meltdown attack work?
pairs.definition: Intel CPUs (the flaw exists in Intel CPUs; some ARM CPUs are also affected). It will NOT work on AMD machines.

pairs.term: $ gcc -march=native MeltdownAttack.c
pairs.definition: Compiles the statistical Meltdown attack program that retries 1000 times and prints the most likely secret byte.

pairs.term: Why may the Meltdown attack fail even on an Intel machine?
pairs.definition: Intel is working to fix the problem in newer CPUs, so the attack may not work on new Intel CPUs. It also fails on OSes that have been patched (KPTI).

pairs.term: Why should the pre-built VM's operating system NOT be updated before the Meltdown lab?
pairs.definition: The pre-built Ubuntu 16.04 VM is unpatched, so the attack works there. Updating the VM's OS installs the kernel workaround and the attack may no longer work.

pairs.term: Why must the secret kernel data be in the CPU cache for the Meltdown attack to succeed?
pairs.definition: If the secret is cached, loading it into a register is fast, so the CPU can reach the critical instruction that loads the probing array before the failed access check aborts the out-of-order execution. Uncached secrets make the attack very difficult.

pairs.term: Why did the naive Meltdown approach (array[kernel_data*4096+DELTA]) fail?
pairs.definition: The out-of-order execution could not reach the array-accessing instruction fast enough before the access check failed and aborted execution; the attack needed the secret cached and a delay to keep ALUs busy.
