pairs.definition: IPv6-address/prefix-length, where IPv6-address is any valid address and prefix-length is the number of contiguous bits comprising the prefix, e.g., 200F::AB00:0:0:0:0/56. As with host addresses, the double colon is used only once.

pairs.term: How is an IPv6 address written in text?
pairs.definition: As eight 16-bit pieces separated by colons, each piece represented by four hexadecimal digits, e.g., FEDC:BA98:7654:3210:FEDC:BA98:7654:3210.

pairs.term: What is the rule for removing leading zeros in an IPv6 address?
pairs.definition: In any 16-bit field, you can remove leading zeros, but at least one digit must be present in every field. Multiple contiguous fields of all zeros can be replaced with a double colon (::), which can be used only once per address.

pairs.term: Why can the :: notation be used only once in an IPv6 address?
pairs.definition: Because multiple ::s would make the address ambiguous - the number of zero fields it represents would be unclear. For example, 1080::3245::200c:417A does not provide sufficient information about the correct position of 3245.

pairs.term: The mixed IPv6/IPv4 text representation
pairs.definition: X:X:X:X:X:X:d.d.d.d, where X represents the hexadecimal IPv6 fields and d.d.d.d denotes the last 32 bits of the address in dotted-decimal notation, e.g., ::13.1.68.3. It provides a method for IPv6 and IPv4 nodes to coexist on the same network.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Reserved field (RES) in the aggregatable global address
pairs.definition: Not currently used (all bits set to zero), except in the case of TLA 0x0001. Future use could include growth of the TLA ID and NLA ID.

pairs.term: Site-Level Aggregation Identifier (SLA ID)
pairs.definition: Used by a site to create as many levels of hierarchy as appropriate within its 16-bit SLA field, from a flat numbering scheme to further subdivision into subnets.

pairs.term: Interface Identifier in IPv6 addresses
pairs.definition: The 64-bit interface identifier, unique to the link, used to identify interfaces on a specific link. All addresses with high-order bits between 001 and 111 (excluding multicast) must have interface IDs in EUI-64 format.

pairs.term: How is an EUI-64 interface ID derived from a MAC address?
pairs.definition: FFFE is inserted between the company ID (OUI) and the node ID of the 48-bit MAC address, and the universal/local (U/L) bit is set to 1 to indicate global value. For example, MAC 0000:0C0A:2C51 becomes EUI-64 0200:0CFF:FE0A:2C51.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What command enables IPv6 routing on a Cisco router?
pairs.definition: ipv6 unicast-routing (global configuration)

pairs.term: What command assigns an IPv6 address to an interface?
pairs.definition: ipv6 address <ipv6-address>/<prefix-length> (interface configuration). It can also be used with the keyword eui-64 to derive the interface identifier from the MAC address.

pairs.term: What command assigns a link-local address to an interface?
pairs.definition: ipv6 enable (interface configuration). It enables IPv6 processing and assigns the link-local address derived from the EUI-64 interface identifier.

pairs.term: What command enables the IPv6 RIP routing process?
pairs.definition: ipv6 router rip <process-name> (global configuration), and then ipv6 rip <process-name> enable on the interfaces that should participate.

pairs.term: What command enables OSPFv3 on an interface?
pairs.definition: ipv6 ospf <process-id> area <area-id> (interface configuration). The OSPFv3 process is created with router ospfv3 <process-id> or ipv6 router ospf <process-id>.

pairs.term: What command displays the IPv6 neighbor cache?
pairs.definition: show ipv6 neighbors

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How are ICMPv6 informational and error messages distinguished?
pairs.definition: By the high-order bit in the ICMP Type field: an error message has a zero in the high-order bit. An ICMP error message includes as much of the offending packet as possible without exceeding the minimum IPv6 MTU of 1280 bytes.

pairs.term: The four ICMPv6 error messages
pairs.definition: Destination Unreachable, Packet Too Big, Time Exceeded, and Parameter Problem.

pairs.term: Destination Unreachable ICMPv6 codes
pairs.definition: 0 - no route to the destination, 1 - access is administratively prohibited, 3 - address unreachable, 4 - port unreachable. Sent when a node cannot forward a packet for some reason other than congestion.

pairs.term: The Time Exceeded ICMPv6 message
pairs.definition: Sent when the IPv6 hop limit reaches zero. A zero hop limit usually indicates a routing loop.

pairs.term: What is the IPv6 Next-Header value that identifies ICMPv6?
pairs.definition: 58. ICMPv6 follows the IPv6 header or an extension header and is a modified version of ICMP for IPv4. Every node that implements IPv6 must fully implement ICMPv6.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Tulip#traceroute ipv6 fec0:0:0:2:210:7bff:fe3a:ce8a
pairs.definition: IPv6 configuration command

pairs.term: MLD (Multicast Listener Discovery)
pairs.definition: IPv6 equivalent of IGMP. MLDv1 (RFC 2710) ≈ IGMPv2. MLDv2 (RFC 3810) ≈ IGMPv3 (source-specific reporting). Messages carried in ICMPv6.

pairs.term: interface fastethernet 0
pairs.definition: interface fastethernet

pairs.term: What address do global unicast addresses resemble?
pairs.definition: IPv4 addresses.

pairs.term: network management application on the network.
pairs.definition: network management

pairs.term: IPv6 over MPLS (6PE)
pairs.definition: IPv6 provider edge — MPLS backbone carries IPv6 across IPv4 MPLS network. CE routers run IPv6. PE routers run MP-BGP with IPv6 address family, label-switch IPv6 packets.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are the parts of a global unicast IPv6 address?
pairs.definition: Global routing prefix (typically /48, assigned by RIR/ISP) + subnet ID (typically 16 bits → /64) + interface ID (64 bits, e.g., EUI-64 or random).

pairs.term: What is a Unique Local Address (ULA) and its prefix?
pairs.definition: ULA (fc00::/7, commonly fd00::/8) is IPv6's equivalent of private IPv4: not routable on the public Internet, but globally unique within an organization. Format: FD + 40-bit global ID + 16-bit subnet + interface ID.

pairs.term: How do you subnet an IPv6 global unicast prefix?
pairs.definition: Borrow bits from the subnet ID field: e.g., a /48 with a /56 mask gives 2^8 = 256 subnets; the subnet ID is the 4th group incremented (0x0000, 0x0100, ...). The interface ID (last 64 bits) is always separate.

pairs.term: How many subnets does a /48 with /64 mask give?
pairs.definition: 16 subnet bits → 65,536 /64 subnets. A /64 per LAN is the standard — each has 2^64 addresses, so subnet sizing (like IPv4 VLSM math) is rarely needed.

pairs.term: What is the IPv6 address range for global unicast?
pairs.definition: 2000::/3 (2000:: to 3FFF:FFFF:...). All public unicast IPv6 addresses (except ULA fc00::/7 and link-local fe80::/10) fall in this range.

pairs.term: How are addresses assigned to hosts in an IPv6 subnet?
pairs.definition: Manually, via SLAAC (host builds its own interface ID from RA-learned prefix), via stateful DHCPv6 (server assigns addresses), or stateless DHCPv6 (RA gives prefix, DHCP gives DNS etc.).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How many hexadecimal digits is a full IPv6 address and how are groups separated?
pairs.definition: 128 bits = 32 hex digits, written as 8 groups of 4 hex digits separated by colons, e.g., 2001:0DB8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001.

pairs.term: What are the two rules for abbreviating IPv6 addresses?
pairs.definition: 1) Leading zeros within a group can be dropped (0001 → 1). 2) One (and only one) longest run of all-zero groups can be replaced by '::'. E.g., 2001:0DB8:0:0:0:0:0:1 → 2001:DB8::1.

pairs.term: How do you represent the prefix length of an IPv6 address?
pairs.definition: CIDR notation after the address: 2001:DB8:1:1::1/64 — the prefix (network part) is the first 64 bits, the interface ID is the remaining 64.

pairs.term: How do you find the IPv6 subnet prefix (subnet ID) of an address?
pairs.definition: Keep the bits up to the prefix length, set all remaining bits to 0. For a /64: the subnet ID is the first 4 groups (first 64 bits); e.g., 2001:DB8:1:1:1234::/64 → subnet ID 2001:DB8:1:1::/64.

pairs.term: What IPv6 routing protocols exist?
pairs.definition: OSPFv3 (OSPF for IPv6), EIGRP for IPv6, and RIPng (legacy). Static IPv6 routes also work. BGP carries IPv6 routes (MP-BGP) for the Internet.

pairs.term: Why was IPv6 created?
pairs.definition: IPv4's 32-bit address space (~4.3 billion) is exhausted — IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses (3.4×10^38), plus built-in features: simpler header, no NAT required, integrated security (IPsec), auto-configuration (SLAAC), and better multicast support.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are connected and local IPv6 routes?
pairs.definition: Connected (C): routes for each subnet configured on interfaces. Local (L): one route per specific interface address (the /128 itself) — used for forwarding packets addressed to the router and for next-hop resolution.

pairs.term: How do you configure a static IPv6 route?
pairs.definition: ipv6 route <prefix>/<len> <next-hop> — e.g., 'ipv6 route 2001:DB8:2::/64 2001:DB8:1:2::2'. The next hop can be a global address, a link-local address (must specify outgoing interface), or an outgoing interface on point-to-point links.

pairs.term: Why must a link-local next-hop static route include the outgoing interface?
pairs.definition: Because link-local addresses are ambiguous — the same fe80:: address exists on every link. 'ipv6 route 2001:DB8:2::/64 Gi0/0 fe80::1' identifies both the link and the neighbor.

pairs.term: How do you configure an IPv6 default route?
pairs.definition: ipv6 route ::/0 <next-hop> — equivalent of IPv4's 0.0.0.0/0, sending all unmatched traffic to the next hop.

pairs.term: What is a floating static IPv6 route?
pairs.definition: A static IPv6 route with a higher AD (e.g., 'ipv6 route ... 200') than the dynamic protocol's, providing backup if the dynamic route disappears.

pairs.term: Why might a static IPv6 route not appear in the routing table?
pairs.definition: If the next-hop address is unreachable (no connected or local route for it). Verify with 'show ipv6 route' and check the next-hop network — same logic as IPv4 static routes.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: 6to4 encapsulates v6 in IPv4 using which IP protocol number?
What port does Teredo use?
pairs.definition: UDP port 3544.

pairs.term: What does Teredo allow tunneling through?
pairs.definition: Network Address Translation (NAT) boxes.

pairs.term: What should you block if you don't want IPv6 tunneled over IPv4?
pairs.definition: Tunneled IPv6 traffic (protocol 41, 6to4/6in4, and UDP 3544 Teredo).

pairs.term: What circuit-relay approach converts IPv6 TCP to IPv4 TCP?
pairs.definition: Router-based relay agents mapping IPv6 TCP connections to IPv4 TCP.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What command shows the IPv6 neighbor cache (NDP table) on a router?
pairs.definition: show ipv6 neighbors

pairs.term: What command shows the IPv6 routing table?
pairs.definition: show ipv6 route

pairs.term: What command traces the IPv6 path to a destination?
pairs.definition: traceroute 2001:DB8:1:1::2

pairs.term: What is Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP) and what does it replace from IPv4?
pairs.definition: NDP is IPv6's ICMPv6-based replacement for ARP and more: NS/NA messages replace ARP (address resolution), RS/RA let hosts discover routers and prefixes, and it also does Duplicate Address Detection (DAD).

pairs.term: How does IPv6 address resolution work (NS/NA)?
pairs.definition: A host sends a Neighbor Solicitation to the solicited-node multicast address of the target; the owner replies with a Neighbor Advertisement containing its link-layer (MAC) address — filling the neighbor cache (IPv6's ARP table).

pairs.term: What are Router Solicitation and Router Advertisement used for?
pairs.definition: Hosts send RS to the all-routers multicast (FF02::2); routers reply with RA (to all-nodes FF02::1) containing the link-local router address, on-link prefixes, and flags (whether to use SLAAC/DHCPv6). RAs are also sent periodically.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How do you statically configure a global unicast IPv6 address on an interface?
pairs.definition:
interface Gi0/0
ipv6 address 2001:DB8:1:1::1/64 — this is the 'ip address' equivalent for IPv6. Note: the link-local address is created automatically.

pairs.term: What is Modified EUI-64 and how does it generate an interface ID?
pairs.definition: It derives the 64-bit interface ID from the MAC address: splits the 48-bit MAC, inserts FFFE in the middle, and flips the U/L bit. E.g., MAC 0200.0000.1234 → interface ID 0200:00FF:FE00:1234 (with bit 7 inverted).

pairs.term: What is a link-local IPv6 address and its prefix?
pairs.definition: Link-local addresses (fe80::/10) are only valid on the local link — routers use them for neighbor discovery and next-hop addressing on point-to-point links. They are auto-generated (EUI-64 or random) on every interface.

pairs.term: Can you route IPv6 with only link-local addresses on an interface?
pairs.definition: Yes — for next-hop addressing over a point-to-point link, a link-local address suffices (e.g., static route 'via fe80::1'). For hosts to use the subnet, a global prefix must be configured/advertised.

pairs.term: What are the well-known IPv6 multicast addresses?
pairs.definition: FF02::1 = all nodes on the link, FF02::2 = all routers on the link, FF02::5 = all OSPFv3 routers, FF02::9 = all RIPng routers, FF02::1:FFxx:xxxx = solicited-node multicast (for NDP).

pairs.term: What are the IPv6 unspecified and loopback addresses?
pairs.definition: Unspecified: :: (used as source when a host has no address yet, e.g., during DAD). Loopback: ::1 (equivalent of 127.0.0.1, used on the router for testing — 'ping ::1').

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: In IPv6, what replaces ARP?
pairs.definition: Neighbor Discovery (ND) protocol.

pairs.term: What does ND do beyond address resolution?
pairs.definition: Sets many parameters on end systems.

pairs.term: What security requirement helps ND against off-link attackers?
pairs.definition: ND packets must have hop limit set to 255.

pairs.term: How do routers advertise prefixes/ routers to hosts?
pairs.definition: Multicat Router Advertisement (RA) messages.

pairs.term: What is dangerous about false RA messages?
pairs.definition: They can divert traffic.

pairs.term: What timers do RA messages carry?
pairs.definition: Prefix lifetime, default route lifetime, Neighbor Solicitation retransmission intervals.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: The INCOMPLETE neighbor cache state
pairs.definition: Address resolution is in progress; an NS has been sent but no reply has yet been received.

pairs.term: The REACHABLE neighbor cache state
pairs.definition: Forward-direction communication has been verified within the past 30 seconds. The state remains REACHABLE as long as forward-direction communication continues to be verified.

pairs.term: The STALE neighbor cache state
pairs.definition: An entry in the neighbor cache has not been verified as reachable within the past 30 seconds. An unsolicited NA (or RA) adds an entry to the cache with state STALE. No action is required until traffic is sent to the STALE entry.

pairs.term: The PROBE neighbor cache state
pairs.definition: An NS has been sent to verify reachability, but no NA has yet been received. Solicitations continue every second in the absence of a response; if no response is received for 1 second after three solicitations, the entry is deleted from the cache.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the IPv6 next-header value for OSPF?
pairs.definition: 89. IPv6 OSPF operates directly over IPv6 and is known as OSPFv3 (version number changed from 2 to 3). The fundamental mechanisms - flooding, DR election, area support, SPF - have remained unchanged.

pairs.term: How do multiple OSPFv3 instances run on a single link?
pairs.definition: The instance ID in OSPFv3 packet headers enables multiple OSPFv3 protocol processes to run on a single link, useful when multiple areas need to share a single link or when multiple companies running OSPF share a link. This is not possible with OSPFv2.

pairs.term: The OSPFv3 LSA types and their function codes
pairs.definition: 1 - 0x2001 Router-LSA, 2 - 0x2002 Network-LSA, 3 - 0x2003 Inter-Area-Prefix-LSA, 4 - 0x2004 Inter-Area-Router-LSA, 5 - 0x4005 AS-External-LSA, 6 - 0x2006 Group-Membership-LSA, 7 - 0x2007 Type-7-LSA, 8 - 0x0008 Link-LSA, 9 - 0x2009 Intra-Area-Prefix-LSA.

pairs.term: Which OSPFv2 LSAs were renamed in OSPFv3?
pairs.definition: Type-3 Network Summary-LSAs were renamed Inter-Area-Prefix-LSAs (advertised by an ABR for networks external to an area). Type-4 ASBR Summary-LSAs were renamed Inter-Area-Router-LSAs (advertise ASBRs external to an area).

pairs.term: The new OSPFv3 Intra-Area-Prefix-LSA
pairs.definition: Carries IPv6 prefix information that in OSPFv2 was carried in Router-LSAs and Network-LSAs. It is used by a router to advertise address prefixes assigned to the router itself, such as attached stub networks and attached transit networks.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are the three methods that an RA message can use?
pairs.definition: Method 1: SLAAC only; Method 2: SLAAC with a stateless DHCPv6 server; Method 3: stateful DHCPv6 (no SLAAC).

pairs.term: With SLAAC, what two parts of the address are created?
pairs.definition: The prefix (advertised in the RA message) and the interface ID (created using the EUI-64 process or a randomly generated 64-bit number).

pairs.term: What does a stateless DHCPv6 server provide?
pairs.definition: Other information such as DNS server addresses and a domain name. It does not allocate GUAs.

pairs.term: What does a stateful DHCPv6 server provide?
pairs.definition: An IPv6 GUA, prefix length, DNS server addresses, domain name, and other addressing information. It allocates and maintains a list of which device receives which address.

pairs.term: Which method does a stateful DHCPv6 server use to allocate addresses?
pairs.definition: Stateful, similar to DHCP for IPv4: the server allocates and keeps track of addresses and which devices received them.

pairs.term: How can the default gateway be obtained in dynamic IPv6 configurations?
pairs.definition: Only from the RA message (the router LLA). The stateless or stateful DHCPv6 server does not provide the default gateway address.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What 16-bit value is inserted in the middle of the MAC address during EUI-64?
pairs.definition: fffe (in hexadecimal), which in binary is 1111 1111 1111 1110.

pairs.term: What happens to the 7th bit (U/L bit) during the EUI-64 process?
pairs.definition: It is reversed (flipped): if it is a 0 it becomes a 1, and vice versa. The first 2 hexadecimal values of the OUI are converted to binary and the U/L bit is flipped.

pairs.term: How can you quickly identify that an interface ID was created using EUI-64?
pairs.definition: The presence of fffe in the middle of the interface ID.

pairs.term: Why might a device use a randomly generated interface ID instead of EUI-64?
pairs.definition: Privacy concerns: EUI-64 embeds the MAC address, allowing packets to be traced to a physical computer. Beginning with Windows Vista, Windows uses randomly generated interface IDs.

pairs.term: What is the EUI-64 process?
pairs.definition: The Extended Unique Identifier (modified EUI-64) process defined by IEEE that uses the 48-bit Ethernet MAC address and inserts another 16 bits in the middle to create a 64-bit interface ID.

pairs.term: What is the organizationally unique identifier (OUI)?
pairs.definition: A 24-bit (6 hexadecimal digits) vendor code assigned by the IEEE, forming the first part of an Ethernet MAC address.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the Cisco IOS command to configure an IPv6 GUA on an interface?
pairs.definition: ipv6 address ipv6-address/prefix-length (with no space between the address and prefix length), e.g., ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:1::1/64.

pairs.term: What is the Cisco IOS command to configure an IPv6 LLA statically on an interface?
pairs.definition: ipv6 address ipv6-link-local-address link-local. When an address begins with a hextet in the range fe80 to febf, the link-local parameter must follow the address.

pairs.term: What address is used as the default gateway when configuring IPv6 on a Windows host?
pairs.definition: The GUA of the router interface on the same network (e.g., 2001:db8:acad:1::1) or the LLA of the interface. Using the LLA is considered best practice.

pairs.term: Why is static configuration of IPv6 addresses on clients discouraged?
pairs.definition: Statically configuring addresses on clients does not scale to larger environments; most administrators enable dynamic assignment of IPv6 addresses.

pairs.term: What are the two ways a device can obtain an IPv6 GUA automatically?
pairs.definition: Stateless address autoconfiguration (SLAAC) and stateful DHCPv6.

pairs.term: Why statically configure LLAs on routers?
pairs.definition: To create addresses that are recognizable and easier to remember; router LLAs are used as default gateway addresses and in routing advertisement messages.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is NAT64?
pairs.definition: Network Address Translation 64 allows IPv6-enabled devices to communicate with IPv4-enabled devices by translating an IPv6 packet to an IPv4 packet and vice versa.

pairs.term: Why was IPv6 developed and what is its address size?
pairs.definition: IPv6 is the successor to IPv4, designed to fix IPv4 limitations including address depletion. It has a larger 128-bit address space, providing 340 undecillion (340 followed by 36 zeros) possible addresses.

pairs.term: What is the theoretical maximum number of IPv4 addresses?
pairs.definition: 4.3 billion addresses.

pairs.term: What enhancements does ICMPv6 include compared to ICMPv4?
pairs.definition: ICMPv6 includes address resolution and address autoconfiguration not found in ICMP for IPv4.

pairs.term: What are the problems with NAT that motivate IPv6 migration?
pairs.definition: NAT is problematic for many applications, creates latency, and has limitations that severely impede peer-to-peer communications.

pairs.term: What are the three categories of IPv4-to-IPv6 migration techniques?
pairs.definition: Dual stack, tunneling, and translation.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is Rule 1 for reducing IPv6 address digits?
pairs.definition: Omit any leading 0s (zeros) in any hextet. For example, 01ab becomes 1ab and 00ab becomes ab. Trailing 0s cannot be omitted.

pairs.term: What is Rule 2 for reducing IPv6 address digits?
pairs.definition: A double colon (::) can replace any single, contiguous string of one or more 16-bit hextets consisting of all 0s. The double colon can be used only once in an address.

pairs.term: When an address has more than one string of all-0 hextets, where should the double colon be used?
pairs.definition: On the longest string; if the strings are equal in length, use the double colon on the first string.

pairs.term: What is compressed format?
pairs.definition: An IPv6 address written by both omitting leading 0s and using the double colon rule, greatly reducing the number of characters.

pairs.term: What is the compressed form of the unspecified address 0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000?
What is the compressed form of the IPv6 loopback address 0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001?

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the recommended IPv6 prefix length for LANs?
pairs.definition: /64, because SLAAC uses 64 bits for the interface ID and it makes subnetting easier to create and manage.

pairs.term: What is a global unicast address (GUA)?
pairs.definition: An IPv6 address similar to a public IPv4 address: globally unique and internet-routable. GUAs can be configured statically or assigned dynamically.

pairs.term: What is a link-local address (LLA)?
pairs.definition: An IPv6 address required for every IPv6-enabled device, used to communicate with other devices on the same local link (subnet). LLAs are not routable beyond the link.

pairs.term: What is the IPv6 unique local address range and its purpose?
pairs.definition: fc00::/7 to fdff::/7. Unique local addresses are used for local addressing within a site or between a limited number of sites; they are not globally routed or translated.

pairs.term: Which IPv6 addresses can be assigned to a device in the all-0s and all-1s host address positions?
pairs.definition: Unlike IPv4, in IPv6 the all-0s and all-1s host addresses can be assigned. The all-1s can be used because broadcast addresses do not exist in IPv6; the all-0s is reserved as a subnet-router anycast address and should be assigned only to routers.

pairs.term: What are the three broad categories of IPv6 addresses?
pairs.definition: Unicast, multicast, and anycast.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are the three parts of an IPv6 global unicast address?
pairs.definition: Global routing prefix, subnet ID, and interface ID.

pairs.term: What is the global routing prefix?
pairs.definition: The prefix (network) portion of a GUA assigned by a provider such as an ISP to a customer or site; it is commonly a /48.

pairs.term: What is the subnet ID?
pairs.definition: The field between the global routing prefix and the interface ID, used to identify subnets within a site. The larger the subnet ID, the more subnets available.

pairs.term: What is the interface ID?
pairs.definition: The IPv6 equivalent of the host portion of an IPv4 address; it identifies a specific interface. A 64-bit interface ID allows for 18 quintillion devices or hosts per subnet.

pairs.term: What range of first hextet values is currently assigned for GUAs?
pairs.definition: Only GUAs that start with 001, or 2000::/3, are currently being assigned. The first hexadecimal digit begins with a 2 or 3.

pairs.term: What is the 2001:db8::/32 address reserved for?
pairs.definition: Documentation purposes, including use in examples.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are the two ways a device can obtain an IPv6 LLA?
pairs.definition: Statically (manually configured) or dynamically (device creates its own interface ID using random values or the EUI-64 method).

pairs.term: What is the IPv6 link-local address range?
pairs.definition: fe80::/10. The first hextet ranges from fe80 (1111 1110 1000 0000) to febf (1111 1110 1011 1111).

pairs.term: How does a device obtain an IPv6 LLA automatically?
pairs.definition: The device creates its own LLA without communicating with a DHCP server, even if it has no GUA. The interface ID is either randomly generated or created with EUI-64.

pairs.term: Which IPv6 address is typically used as the default gateway on a link?
pairs.definition: The LLA of the router, not the GUA. Hosts use the router LLA as the default gateway, and routers use neighbor LLAs for routing updates.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the ff02::1 all-nodes multicast group?
pairs.definition: A multicast group that all IPv6-enabled devices join; a packet sent to it is processed by all IPv6 interfaces on the link. It has the same effect as a broadcast in IPv4.

pairs.term: What is the ff02::2 all-routers multicast group?
pairs.definition: A multicast group that all IPv6 routers join when enabled as IPv6 routers with the ipv6 unicast-routing command. IPv6 devices send RS messages to this address.

pairs.term: What does the scope digit in an IPv6 multicast address indicate?
pairs.definition: The fourth digit indicates scope; a 2 indicates link-local scope, meaning packets are not routed off the link or network.

pairs.term: What is a solicited-node multicast address?
pairs.definition: A multicast address similar to all-nodes, but mapped to a special Ethernet multicast address so the NIC can filter the frame without sending it to the IPv6 process.

pairs.term: What prefix do IPv6 multicast addresses have?
pairs.definition: ff00::/8. Multicast addresses can only be destination addresses, never source addresses.

pairs.term: What are the two types of IPv6 multicast addresses?
pairs.definition: Well-known multicast addresses (assigned) and solicited-node multicast addresses.

pairs.definition: Configures a GUA on a different subnet, e.g., the GigabitEthernet 0/0/1 interface on subnet 2001:db8:acad:2::/64.

pairs.term: How is an IPv6 network subnetted?
pairs.definition: Using the separate subnet ID field in the GUA, between the global routing prefix and the interface ID. IPv6 was designed with subnetting in mind.

pairs.term: With a /48 global routing prefix and /64 interface ID, what subnet ID size results?
pairs.definition: A 16-bit subnet ID, which creates up to 65,536 subnets; the 64-bit interface ID supports up to 18 quintillion host IPv6 addresses per subnet.

pairs.term: How do you determine the next available IPv6 subnet?
pairs.definition: Just count up in hexadecimal in the subnet ID hextet; no conversion to binary is required.

pairs.term: In IPv6, is the serial link subnet prefix length different from the LAN subnets?
pairs.definition: No. Unlike IPv4, the serial link subnet has the same /64 prefix length as the LANs. Address conservation is not a concern in IPv6.

pairs.definition: Verifies Layer 3 IPv6 connectivity to a destination. When pinging an LLA, Cisco IOS prompts for the exit interface.

pairs.definition: Displays interface statistics, including the MAC address used to dynamically create the LLA with EUI-64.

pairs.definition: Windows command that displays IPv6 addressing information on a host, including the GUA, LLA, and default gateway.

pairs.term: ping ::1
pairs.definition: Pings the IPv6 loopback address; a successful reply indicates IP is properly installed on the host.

pairs.term: In show ipv6 interface brief output, what does [up/up] indicate?
pairs.definition: The Layer 1/Layer 2 interface state, the same as the Status and Protocol columns in the equivalent IPv4 command.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is a Type 0 password?
pairs.definition: The most insecure password type; it is not encrypted or hashed and is visible in plaintext in the device configuration.

pairs.term: What is a Type 7 password?
pairs.definition: A password encrypted with a Cisco proprietary Vigenere cypher, which is a very weak encryption algorithm that can be decrypted in less than a second.

pairs.term: What is a Type 5 password?
pairs.definition: A password that uses the MD5 hashing algorithm with password salting; much stronger than types 0/7 but still very easy to crack.

pairs.term: What is a Type 8 password?
pairs.definition: A password that uses PBKDF2 with a SHA-256 hashed secret and password salting; considered uncrackable and recommended to be used.

pairs.term: What is a Type 9 password?
pairs.definition: A password that uses the scrypt hashing algorithm and password salting; considered uncrackable and recommended by Cisco.

pairs.term: Why should Type 4 passwords never be used?
pairs.definition: They contain a security flaw in the implementation; they were deprecated and type 8 and 9 password hashing was introduced instead.

pairs.term: Switch Virtual Interface (SVI)
pairs.definition: A virtual interface on a multilayer switch (interface vlan X) used to route between VLANs, avoiding an external router.

pairs.term: Requirements for an SVI to be up/up
pairs.definition: The VLAN for the SVI must be created, an IP address must be assigned, and at least one interface must support it. It then goes up/up and is added to the routing table.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Describe the behavior pattern of hackers (traditional intruders).
pairs.definition: They hack for the thrill or for status, the community is a meritocracy based on competence, they look for targets of opportunity, and they share information with others.

pairs.term: Describe the behavior pattern of criminal intruders.
pairs.definition: Organized gangs of hackers (often young, Eastern European, Russian, or southeast Asian) who usually have specific targets or classes of targets; once a site is penetrated, they act quickly, scooping up as much valuable information as possible and exiting.

pairs.term: Why are insider attacks among the most difficult to detect and prevent?
pairs.definition: Employees already have access and knowledge about the structure and content of corporate databases; insider attacks can be motivated by revenge or a feeling of entitlement.

pairs.term: What are CERTs and what do they do?
pairs.definition: Computer Emergency Response Teams are cooperative ventures that collect information about system vulnerabilities and disseminate it to systems managers.

pairs.term: How can IDSs/IPSs be supplemented against the hacker threat?
pairs.definition: Organizations can restrict remote logons to specific IP addresses and/or use virtual private network (VPN) technology.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is a masquerader?
pairs.definition: An individual who is not authorized to use the computer and who penetrates a system's access controls to exploit a legitimate user's account.

pairs.term: What is a misfeasor?
pairs.definition: A legitimate user who accesses data, programs, or resources for which such access is not authorized, or who is authorized for such access but misuses his or her privileges.

pairs.term: What is a clandestine user?
pairs.definition: An individual who seizes supervisory control of the system and uses this control to evade auditing and access controls or to suppress audit collection.

pairs.term: What three classes of intruders did Anderson identify?
pairs.definition: Masquerader, misfeasor, and clandestine user.

pairs.term: How do the three intruder classes map to insider/outsider status?
pairs.definition: The masquerader is likely to be an outsider, the misfeasor generally is an insider, and the clandestine user can be either an outsider or an insider.

pairs.term: What is an intruder?
pairs.definition: An individual (often called a hacker or cracker) who gains unauthorized access to a system; with viruses, it is one of the two most publicized threats to security.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How can intruders gain access without learning a password?
pairs.definition: By exploiting attacks such as buffer overflows on a program that runs with certain privileges; privilege escalation can be done this way as well.

pairs.term: Why is intrusion prevention an uphill battle?
pairs.definition: The defender must attempt to thwart all possible attacks, whereas the attacker is free to find the weakest link in the defense chain and attack at that point.

pairs.term: What is the objective of the intruder?
pairs.definition: To gain access to a system or to increase the range of privileges accessible on a system.

pairs.term: How can the password file be protected using a one-way function?
pairs.definition: The system stores only the value of a one-way (non-reversible) function based on the user's password; when the user presents a password, the system transforms it and compares it with the stored value, producing a fixed-length output.

pairs.term: How can the password file be protected using access control?
pairs.definition: Access to the password file is limited to one or a very few accounts.

pairs.term: Why are login-verification guessing attacks easily countered?
pairs.definition: If the intruder must verify each guess by attempting to log in, the attack is tedious; for example, a system can simply reject any login after three password attempts, so it is not practical to try more than a handful of passwords that way.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What fields does the Denning detection-specific audit record contain?
pairs.definition: Subject, Action, Object, Exception-Condition, Resource-Usage, and Time-Stamp.

pairs.term: What is the Subject field of an audit record?
pairs.definition: A subject initiates actions; it could be a user or a process acting on behalf of users or groups of users, and subjects may be grouped into overlapping access classes.

pairs.term: What is the Action field of an audit record?
pairs.definition: An action initiated by a subject refers to some object; examples include login, read, perform I/O, and execute.

pairs.term: What is the Object field of an audit record?
pairs.definition: Objects are the entities on which actions are performed, such as files, programs, messages, records, terminals, and printers; when a subject is the recipient of an action (e.g., e-mail), that subject is considered an object.

pairs.term: What is the Exception-Condition field of an audit record?
pairs.definition: If an exception condition occurs, this field contains identifying information.

pairs.term: What is the Resource-Usage field of an audit record?
pairs.definition: A list in which each item gives the amount used of some resource, e.g., number of lines printed or displayed, records read or written, processor time, I/O units used, and session elapsed time.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: In practice, which detection approach combination is used and why?
pairs.definition: A system may exhibit a combination of both statistical anomaly detection and rule-based approaches to be effective against a broad range of attacks, since each approach alone is best against only certain intruder types.

pairs.term: What is statistical anomaly detection?
pairs.definition: It involves collecting data relating to the behavior of legitimate users over a period of time, then applying statistical tests to observed behavior to determine with high confidence whether that behavior is not legitimate user behavior.

pairs.term: What is threshold detection?
pairs.definition: An approach to statistical anomaly detection that defines thresholds, independent of user, for the frequency of occurrence of various events; if a count surpasses a reasonable number, intrusion is assumed.

pairs.term: What is profile-based anomaly detection?
pairs.definition: An approach to statistical anomaly detection that develops a profile of the activity of each user and uses it to detect changes in the behavior of individual accounts.

pairs.term: What is rule-based intrusion detection?
pairs.definition: It involves defining a set of rules or attack patterns that can be used to decide that a given behavior is that of an intruder; often referred to as signature detection.

pairs.term: How do anomaly approaches differ from signature-based approaches?
pairs.definition: Anomaly approaches attempt to define normal, or expected, behavior, whereas signature-based approaches attempt to define proper behavior.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is distributed intrusion detection?
pairs.definition: Coordination and cooperation among intrusion detection systems across the network to defend a distributed collection of hosts, which is more effective than stand-alone IDS on each host.

pairs.term: Compare centralized and decentralized distributed IDS architectures.
pairs.definition: Centralized has a single point of collection and analysis, easing correlation but creating a potential bottleneck and single point of failure; decentralized has more than one analysis center that must coordinate activities and exchange information.

pairs.term: What is the host agent module in a distributed IDS?
pairs.definition: An audit collection module operating as a background process on a monitored system whose purpose is to collect data on security-related events on the host and transmit them to the central manager.

pairs.term: What is the LAN monitor agent module in a distributed IDS?
pairs.definition: It operates like a host agent module but analyzes LAN traffic and reports the results to the central manager; it audits host-host connections, services used, and volume of traffic, searching for significant events such as sudden changes in network load.

pairs.term: What is the central manager module in a distributed IDS?
pairs.definition: It receives reports from LAN monitor and host agents and processes and correlates these reports to detect intrusion; it includes an expert system that draws inferences from received data and may query individual systems for copies of host audit records.

pairs.term: What is a host audit record (HAR)?
pairs.definition: A standardized format to which native audit records of security interest are filtered and reformatted by the agent before analysis.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the sensor in an IDS?
pairs.definition: The component that collects data from the data source and forwards events to the analyzer.

pairs.term: What is the analyzer in an IDS?
pairs.definition: The ID component or process that analyzes the data collected by the sensor for signs of unauthorized or undesired activity; in many existing IDSs the sensor and analyzer are part of the same component.

pairs.term: What is the manager in an IDS?
pairs.definition: The ID component from which the operator manages the various components; management functions include sensor configuration, analyzer configuration, event notification management, data consolidation, and reporting.

pairs.term: What are the roles of the administrator and operator in an IDS?
pairs.definition: The administrator sets the security policy and makes decisions about deploying and configuring the IDS; the operator is the primary user of the IDS manager, often monitoring output and initiating or recommending further action.

pairs.term: Give examples of IDS responses.
pairs.definition: Logging the activity, recording the raw data that characterized the event, terminating a network/user/application session, or altering network or system access controls.

pairs.term: What are the functional components of the intrusion detection message exchange model?
pairs.definition: Data source, sensor, analyzer, manager, administrator, and operator.

pairs.term: What is the purpose of the IETF Intrusion Detection Working Group's standards?
pairs.definition: To define data formats and exchange procedures for sharing information of interest to intrusion detection and response systems and to management systems that need to interact with them, facilitating interoperability across platforms.

pairs.term: What does RFC 4766 define?
pairs.definition: Intrusion Detection Message Exchange Requirements: requirements for the Intrusion Detection Message Exchange Format (IDMEF) and requirements for a communication protocol for communicating IDMEF.

pairs.term: What does RFC 4765 describe?
pairs.definition: The Intrusion Detection Message Exchange Format (IDMEF): a data model to represent information exported by intrusion detection systems, with an XML implementation, an XML Document Type Definition, and examples.

pairs.term: What does RFC 4767 describe?
pairs.definition: The Intrusion Detection Exchange Protocol (IDXP), an application-level protocol for exchanging data between intrusion detection entities that supports mutual authentication, integrity, and confidentiality over a connection-oriented protocol.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the second line of defense after intrusion prevention?
pairs.definition: Intrusion detection; the best intrusion prevention system will inevitably fail.

pairs.term: What assumption is intrusion detection based on?
pairs.definition: That the behavior of the intruder differs from that of a legitimate user in ways that can be quantified.

pairs.term: What is a false positive in intrusion detection?
pairs.definition: An authorized user identified as an intruder; a loose interpretation of intruder behavior that catches more intruders also leads to more false positives.

pairs.term: What is a false negative in intrusion detection?
pairs.definition: An intruder not identified as an intruder; a tight interpretation of intruder behavior limits false positives but increases false negatives.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are IDES and Emerald?
pairs.definition: The SRI Intrusion Detection Expert System (IDES) and its follow-on program Emerald, which used various statistical measures/models for intrusion detection.

pairs.term: What is the main advantage of statistical profiles?
pairs.definition: No prior knowledge of security flaws is required; the detector learns what is normal and looks for deviations, and because it is not based on system-dependent characteristics it is readily portable among systems.

pairs.term: Why is threshold analysis by itself a crude detector?
pairs.definition: Both the threshold and the time interval must be determined, and because of variability across users, such thresholds generate either a lot of false positives or a lot of false negatives.

pairs.term: What is a counter metric for profile-based detection?
pairs.definition: A nonnegative integer that may be incremented but not decremented until reset by management action; examples include the number of logins by a user during an hour and the number of password failures during a minute.

pairs.term: What is a gauge metric for profile-based detection?
pairs.definition: A nonnegative integer that may be incremented or decremented, typically used to measure the current value of some entity; examples include the number of logical connections assigned to a user application.

pairs.term: What is an interval timer metric for profile-based detection?
pairs.definition: The length of time between two related events; an example is the length of time between successive logins to an account.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are the layers of the three-layer IoT architecture?
pairs.definition: The perception layer, the network layer, and the application layer.

pairs.term: What is the perception layer?
pairs.definition: The physical layer where the collection, transfer, and sending of data about the physical environment is accomplished, using sensors, network sensors, actuators, tags, near field communication (NFC), and radio-frequency identification.

pairs.term: What is the application layer?
pairs.definition: The layer where the data is delivered to the IoT user.

pairs.term: What three additional layers expand the three-layer architecture into five layers?
pairs.definition: The transport layer, the processing layer (or middleware layer), and the business layer.

pairs.term: What is the transport layer in the five-layer IoT architecture?
pairs.definition: It resembles the network layer and is responsible for transmitting the data from the sensors of the perception layer to the processing layer across the network.

pairs.term: What is the processing layer or middleware layer?
pairs.definition: It is responsible for aggregating data, data storage (cloud computing and databases), processing data received from the transport layer, and protecting against security attacks.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How is IoT used in the automotive sector?
pairs.definition: Sensors collect enormous amounts of data that are processed, visualized, and streamed to the cloud; a fleet operator can monitor driver behavior, vehicle maintenance, on-board diagnostics, fuel monitoring, and delivery delays.

pairs.term: What is a Vehicular ad hoc Network (VANET)?
pairs.definition: A network that helps vehicles communicate with each other and their surrounding environment via wireless connectivity.

pairs.term: What are the VANET communication paths?
pairs.definition: Vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V), vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I), vehicle-to-sensor on-board (V2S), and vehicle-to-Internet (V2I).

pairs.term: What is the autonomous vehicle and what is the greatest challenge in developing it?
pairs.definition: The car that drives itself; since a range of sensors and algorithms is needed to ensure the motorist's safety, developing these applications is currently the greatest challenge to the auto industry.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Where can data processing and storage be performed in an IoT system?
pairs.definition: On the edge of the network, in the cloud servers, or on the device itself. Cloud computing provides centralization, easy access, and cost savings, but is limited by resources, size, energy, power, and computational capability.

pairs.term: What is edge computing?
pairs.definition: A paradigm that eliminates the centralized cloud servers and brings processing closer to the IoT device or data source, making devices more flexible, minimizing delays, and theoretically providing more security since all data are not in the same place.

pairs.term: What is fog computing and who introduced the standard?
pairs.definition: A standard introduced by Cisco that defines how edge computing should work; it brings intelligence down to the Local Area Network (LAN) architecture and processes the data in a fog node.

pairs.term: What can be a fog node?
pairs.definition: Any computing device with storage and network connectivity, implemented anywhere within a network connection - controllers, switches, routers, servers, video surveillance cameras, and more.

pairs.term: What is the IoT gateway?
pairs.definition: The fog/edge node within the network where IoT data are collected, processed, and stored, and through which the fog interacts with the cloud.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What basic hardware do IoT devices consist of?
pairs.definition: A sensor, an actuator, a transceiver, and a power supply.

pairs.term: What does a sensor do?
pairs.definition: It captures physical characteristics, processes them into electrical signals, and then interprets them to provide readable information. Example: the microphone converts air vibrations (sound waves) into electrical energy (audio signals).

pairs.term: What does an actuator do?
pairs.definition: It converts electrical signals into action - for example, turning a furnace on or off.

pairs.term: What does the processor do in an IoT device?
pairs.definition: It processes and stores data within an application, on a server, or in the cloud.

pairs.term: What does a wireless communication transceiver provide?
pairs.definition: Communication through wireless links, allowing people to monitor or configure IoT devices and enabling interaction between the owner and the device.

pairs.term: What are the requirements for an IoT power supply?
pairs.definition: It may be alternating current (AC) or direct current (DC); it must be reliable, affordable, efficient, and space-saving.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is IPv4?
pairs.definition: Internet Protocol version 4 uses a 32-bit address and can handle 4,294,967,296 (2^32) unique addresses; because IPv4 is running out of addresses, the protocol is switching to IPv6.

pairs.term: What is IPv6?
pairs.definition: Internet Protocol version 6 uses a 128-bit address, theoretically delivering 2^128 unique addresses.

pairs.term: What is RPL?
pairs.definition: Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks - a simple, interoperable, resource-constrained networking protocol for wireless networks and IoT devices with low power consumption; standardized by IETF as RFC 6550.

pairs.term: What is 6LoWPAN?
pairs.definition: Low Power Wireless Personal Area Networks standard that makes it possible for IoT devices to transmit IPv6 packets over wireless networks; standardized by IETF as RFC 6282 and used with wireless sensors for smart home automation.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How does the textbook define the Internet of Things (IoT)?
pairs.definition: Intelligent network-connected devices or systems, embedded in the physical environment, to improve the lives of people with minimal or no human intervention. IoTs connect the physical world and the digital or virtual world.

pairs.term: Who coined the phrase 'Internet of Things' and in what year?
pairs.definition: Kevin Ashton in 1999. He was assigned to help launch a cosmetics line and came up with the idea of using RFID to tag each tube of lipstick to track where it was.

pairs.term: What technology did Kevin Ashton propose to track lipstick inventory?
pairs.definition: Radio-frequency identification (RFID) - tagging each tube of lipstick and communicating with a radio receiver to keep track of exactly where it was.

pairs.term: Which book by Neil Gershenfeld jumpstarted the development and use of IoTs?
pairs.definition: 'When Things Start to Think'.

pairs.term: What characterized the second stage of modern computing adoption?
pairs.definition: The introduction of microcomputers and development of the personal computer (PC) in the early 1980s, when computer costs fell and became affordable for consumers.

pairs.term: What is the fourth stage of modern computing adoption?
pairs.definition: The gradual evolution of IoTs and the steady trend toward Internet-connected devices, including the computerization of everything in our lives, enabled by 5G mobile broadband and cloud computing.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is Industry 4.0 (the Fourth Industrial Revolution)?
pairs.definition: The developing trend toward automation, smart factories, real-time data analysis, and network connectivity enabled by industrial IoT devices and 5G mobile broadband, improving productivity and product quality.

pairs.term: What characterized the First Industrial Revolution?
pairs.definition: The steam engine, powered by coal, near the end of the 18th century.

pairs.term: What characterized the Second Industrial Revolution?
pairs.definition: The discovery of oil in the late 19th century and early manufacturing innovations such as Henry Ford's assembly line and Frederick Winslow Taylor, the father of scientific management.

pairs.term: What characterized the Third Industrial Revolution?
pairs.definition: When manufacturing data moved from analog and mechanical to digital in the 1970s, bringing automation changes comparable in scale to steam engine technology.

pairs.term: What examples does the chapter give of Industry 4.0 technologies?
pairs.definition: 3D printers that can print just about anything, smart home devices, autonomous vehicles, logistics management, automation, and robotics machinery.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is Bluetooth as an IoT protocol?
pairs.definition: A low-energy, short-range wireless communication protocol central for resource-constrained devices like battery-operated sensors and actuators; uses the 2.4 GHz ISM spectrum band (2,400 to 2,483.5 MHz) and has a range of 100 meters.

pairs.term: What is LPWAN?
pairs.definition: Low Power Wide Area Network - uses existing cellular technology for broad utilization of low-power IoT devices like wireless sensors and actuators; LTE-Advanced (LTE-A) is designed specifically for IoT communication in cellular networks.

pairs.term: What is Dash7?
pairs.definition: A wireless communication protocol for wireless sensors, actuators, and messaging applications; developed by the DASH7 Alliance and based on ISO/IEC 18000-7; uses active RFID to support encryption for secure IoT communication.

pairs.term: What is Ethernet IEEE 802.3?
pairs.definition: An entire family of standards and protocols defining wired connectivity in Local Area Networks (LAN), including wiring, signaling, connectors, and protocol rules; defines the physical layer and the MAC (hardware) addresses of the data link layer.

pairs.term: What is NFC?
pairs.definition: A collection of short-range wireless communication protocols using electromagnetic fields that enable communication with other devices and wireless transfer of data; standardization is provided by the NFC Forum.

pairs.term: What is Wi-Fi IEEE 802.11 and the 802.11ah (Wi-Fi Halo) standard?
pairs.definition: Wi-Fi is a wireless networking protocol based on IEEE 802.11. The IEEE 802.11ah standard (Wi-Fi Halo) is designed for low-energy consumption with data rates from 150 kb/s to 347 Mb/s and supports outdoor applications up to 1 km at 150 kb/s.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is a LAN (Local Area Network)?
pairs.definition: A medium-range network that spans a small area inside a single room, building, factory, or school; examples include smart home products such as smart thermostats and surveillance equipment.

pairs.term: What is a MAN (Metropolitan Area Network)?
pairs.definition: A long-range network providing communications over a larger area than a LAN; examples include citywide networks where IoT sensors tell the sanitation department when trash reaches a certain level.

pairs.term: What is a WAN (Wide Area Network)?
pairs.definition: The widest communications network, spanning a large geographic area and connecting multiple networks across a country or the world; the best-known example is the Internet.

pairs.term: What is a PAN (Personal Area Network)?
pairs.definition: A short-range network, found for example when using an app on a mobile device over a Bluetooth device such as wrist fitness trackers, heart rate monitors, and pedometers.

pairs.term: What is a protocol in the IoT context?
pairs.definition: A procedure or set of rules used by systems to communicate with one another; well-known examples include Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS).

pairs.term: What is a standard in the IoT context?
pairs.definition: A set of rules followed by systems manufacturers that define how devices communicate in different settings; for example, Ethernet is defined by IEEE 802.3 and Bluetooth devices by Bluetooth Low Energy 5.1.

pairs.term: Which organizations develop IoT standards and protocols?
pairs.definition: The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), OASIS, the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), and NIST (NISTIR 8259).

pairs.term: What is the TCP/IP model and its history?
pairs.definition: A simplified four-layer version of the OSI model (application, transport, Internet, network access); developed in the 1970s and adopted as the protocol standard for the ARPANET (predecessor to the Internet) in 1983.

pairs.term: How do the OSI and TCP/IP models map to each other?
pairs.definition: OSI's seven layers condense into TCP/IP's four: application (OSI 5-7), transport (OSI 4), Internet (OSI 3), and network access (OSI 1-2). IoT networking protocols map more closely to TCP/IP levels than to OSI levels.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What was the Mirai botnet attack of 2016?
pairs.definition: IoT botnet malware that took advantage of unprotected IoT devices by using default usernames and passwords to log in and infect them with malware, then used the devices to issue massive distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks.

pairs.term: What are device limitations as an IoT security challenge?
pairs.definition: IoT devices generally have short battery lifetimes and limitations in memory and processing power, so they cannot handle the requirements of advanced cryptography algorithms that would protect them from security threats.

pairs.term: What is a physical attack on an IoT device?
pairs.definition: An attack performed in the proximity of the IoT device where the attacker is close enough to analyze electrical signals such as electromagnetic waves emitted, and can gather sensitive information.

pairs.term: What are network attacks on IoT?
pairs.definition: Attacks where an attacker accesses, manipulates, or intercepts an IoT network system remotely and causes damage - including DoS attacks, malware, breaches, man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks, routing information or traffic attacks, and RFID spoofing.

pairs.term: What are software attacks on IoT?
pairs.definition: Attacks including phishing attacks, malware, virus, worms, Trojan horse, spyware, and adware.

pairs.term: What are encryption attacks on IoT?
pairs.definition: Attacks where an attacker tries to break the encryption scheme and obtain the private key to the device; they include cryptanalysis attacks, side channel attacks, MITM attacks, sleep deprivation attacks, eavesdropping, and interference.

pairs.term: IoT (Internet of Things)
pairs.definition: Network of physical objects embedded with sensors, software, and connectivity enabling data exchange over internet. Three layers: Perception (sensors), Network (connectivity), Application (processing). IoT devices constrained in power, memory, and processing.

pairs.term: IoT Perception Layer
pairs.definition: Lowest IoT layer — sensors, actuators, RFID tags, cameras. Collects physical data. Security challenges: physical capture, sensor spoofing, side-channel attacks. Constrained resources (battery, CPU, memory).

pairs.term: IoT Network Layer
pairs.definition: Middle IoT layer — connectivity between perception and application layers. Protocols: IPv6, 6LoWPAN, RPL, MQTT, CoAP. Security challenges: DoS, MITM, routing attacks, rogue gateways. Must bridge heterogeneous networks.

pairs.term: IoT Application Layer
pairs.definition: Top IoT layer — data processing, storage, user interface. Smart home, healthcare, smart city applications. Security challenges: data privacy, authentication, access control, insecure APIs. Cloud integration introduces added attack surface.

pairs.term: MQTT (Message Queue Telemetry Transport)
pairs.definition: Lightweight publish/subscribe messaging protocol for IoT (ISO 20922). Uses broker architecture, TCP port 1883. QoS levels: 0 (at most once), 1 (at least once), 2 (exactly once). Minimal packet overhead (2-byte header). Ideal for constrained devices.

pairs.term: 6LoWPAN (IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks)
pairs.definition: Adaptation layer enabling IPv6 over IEEE 802.15.4 (RFC 4944). Fragmentation: 1280-byte IPv6 packet over 127-byte MAC frames. Header compression (HC1, IPHC) reduces IPv6/UDP headers from 48 to ~7 bytes. Supports mesh networking.

pairs.term: RPL (IPv6 Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks)
pairs.definition: Distance-vector routing protocol for LLNs (RFC 6550). Builds DODAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) using objective functions. Supports multipoint-to-point, point-to-multipoint, point-to-point traffic. Uses trickle timer for control message suppression.

Standard for low-rate wireless personal area networks (LR-WPANs). Defines PHY/MAC layers. Data rates: 20-250 kbps. Range: 10-100m. 16-bit/64-bit addressing. Superframe structure with beacon mode. Used by ZigBee, 6LoWPAN, Thread, Zigbee IP.

pairs.term: What does the upper filter do?
pairs.definition: It capitalizes the text piped to it, e.g., {{ interface.desc|upper }} turns 'uplink port' into 'UPLINK PORT'.

pairs.term: Can Jinja filters be chained?
pairs.definition: Yes, in much the same way you might pipe commands together in Linux, e.g., {{ interface.desc|upper|reverse }} capitalizes first, then reverses.

pairs.term: How do you register a custom filter in Jinja2?
pairs.definition: Define a function, then add it to the ENV object: ENV.filters['filter_name'] = function.

pairs.term: When registering a custom Jinja filter, do you pass the function or run it?
pairs.definition: You pass the function reference and do not run it; the template engine will execute the function when template.render() is called.

pairs.term: Do you always have to create your own function to use as a Jinja filter?
pairs.definition: No. Plenty of libraries provide helpful functions that you can import and simply pass right into the Jinja2 environment.

pairs.term: What are Jinja filters?
pairs.definition: Little modular functions you can call upon at any point in templates; they take data or text as input, perform a specialized task, and output the result.

pairs.term: Why is it bad form to embed data directly in Python applications for templates?
pairs.definition: Because keeping data in external files (like YAML) is better; it allows someone with no Python experience to edit the network configuration by changing the data file.

pairs.term: What does the .items() notation do in a Jinja for loop over a dictionary?
pairs.definition: It properly unpacks the key/value pairs, so at each iteration name is a key and desc is the corresponding value (e.g., for name, desc in interface_dict.items()).

pairs.term: What does the range() function do in a Jinja loop?
pairs.definition: It returns a list of integers to iterate over. Because range() starts at 0, switchports typically use n+1 so the interface numbering starts at 1.

pairs.term: How has Python 3.7 changed dictionary iteration order?
pairs.definition: As of Python 3.7, dictionaries preserve insertion order for literals like these, so interface order in rendered output is guaranteed.

pairs.term: What is the difference between dict['key'] and dict.key in Jinja?
pairs.definition: They are identical—both access the dictionary key. A key error will be raised if the key does not exist.

pairs.term: How do you access an optional dictionary key in Jinja without a key error?
pairs.definition: Use the get() method, e.g., dict.get(key, 'UNKNOWN'), which returns the provided default value if the key does not exist.

pairs.term: Is Jinja2 part of the Python standard library?
pairs.definition: No. The Jinja2 rendering engine is not part of the standard library and must be installed with pip3, using the command pip3 install jinja2.

pairs.term: What function renders a Jinja template in Python?
pairs.definition: The render() function of the template object, which passes data into the template engine.

pairs.term: How does the keyword argument to render() correspond to the template?
pairs.definition: The keyword argument name corresponds to the references in the Jinja template (e.g., interface=interface_dict satisfies references to interface and its keys).

pairs.term: What data structures can be passed to a Jinja template from Python?
pairs.definition: A Python dictionary or a Python class (object). The renderer automatically places the corresponding values/keys or class properties.

pairs.term: What does the include statement do in Jinja?
pairs.definition: It renders another template file and inserts the resulting text into the rendered output of the template that includes it.

pairs.term: What does the block statement do in Jinja?
pairs.definition: It specifies portions of a template that may be overridden by a child template; if a child template does not override it, default text is still rendered.

pairs.term: What does the extends statement do in Jinja?
pairs.definition: It makes the current template a child of a parent template, so the parent's blocks can be overridden by the child's blocks when the child is rendered.

pairs.term: How does inheritance help organize network configuration templates?
pairs.definition: Templates can be broken into smaller, specialized pieces (VLAN config, interfaces, routing protocols) and composed together, keeping multiple template files organized.

pairs.term: Kubernetes control plane
pairs.definition: Runs on one or more nodes and provides the management functions for the cluster. It has three pieces: the API server, the controller manager, and the scheduler.

pairs.term: Kubernetes scheduler
pairs.definition: The control plane component responsible for placing workloads on worker nodes.

pairs.term: Kubernetes API server
pairs.definition: The control plane component that exposes the control plane to users and other systems. It implements a RESTful declarative API.

pairs.term: etcd
pairs.definition: The distributed key-value store that backs the Kubernetes control plane. It needs an odd number of instances to establish and maintain quorum; typically you see three etcd instances along with three control plane instances in a highly available cluster.

pairs.term: Reconciliation loop
pairs.definition: Kubernetes constantly reconciles the desired state (what you told the cluster) against the actual state (what is actually running). Reconciling desired state against actual state sits at the heart of everything Kubernetes does.

pairs.term: Custom resource definition (CRD)
pairs.definition: A way to create new types of API objects in Kubernetes. The new object types will also require a controller that understands their lifecycle: how they are created, updated, and deleted.

pairs.definition: The nodes in the cluster with their status, roles, age, and version (for Minikube, a single control-plane node named minikube).

pairs.definition: The part of the cluster where deployed containers actually run; the number of nodes depends on your workload, with nodes brought up as needed and decommissioned when not.

pairs.term: What is the kubelet?
pairs.definition: The service at the heart of each data plane node; it registers its node with the API server and runs containers requested through a PodSpec, keeping them in a healthy state.

pairs.term: What is a PodSpec?
pairs.definition: The specification that directs the kubelet to run a container requested from the API server and make sure it continues to run in a healthy state.

pairs.term: What is the container runtime?
pairs.definition: The container engine that runs on each node to launch, manage, and delete containers as required by the PodSpec.

pairs.term: Why was Docker deprecated in Kubernetes?
pairs.definition: In Kubernetes v1.23 the use of Docker in Kubernetes was deprecated, and Docker was replaced by containerd as the default container runtime.

pairs.term: What is containerd?
pairs.definition: The default container runtime for Kubernetes after Docker was deprecated in Kubernetes v1.23.

pairs.term: What is scalability in enterprise Kubernetes?
pairs.definition: Kubernetes adds more pods if applications are overloaded and more nodes if capacity is reached, and shuts them down as demand reduces.

pairs.term: What is self-healing in Kubernetes?
pairs.definition: Kubernetes performs health checks of containers, pods, nodes, services, and other objects and replaces them if they have failed or are degraded.

pairs.term: What is high availability in Kubernetes?
pairs.definition: Using scalability and self-healing to keep applications available; clusters can be spread across multiple locations so an outage diverts work to systems in other locations.

pairs.term: What are three things Kubernetes lets you do with containers?
pairs.definition: Group sets of containers into a larger application, scale each component individually as demand requires, and set the state of an application (for example, run three copies and replace any that go down).

pairs.definition: If the host running a container fails or becomes overloaded, the container recovers quickly and starts up on another host computer.

pairs.definition: Kubernetes routes requests for a service by name, so applications do not need to know the hostnames, IP addresses, or port numbers of those services.

pairs.term: What other container orchestration platforms were Kubernetes competitors?
pairs.definition: Mesos and Docker Swarm; Kubernetes has become the undisputed leader in orchestrating, deploying, and managing containerized applications.

pairs.definition: 802.1Q adds 32 bits to the header: TPID (16-bit), PCP (3-bit), DEI (1-bit), and VLAN ID (12-bit).

pairs.term: Collision Domain Definition
pairs.definition: A network segment where one device can detect if another device is transmitting, regardless of the destination device. Simultaneous transmissions become garbled due to data collisions.

pairs.term: Hub Versus Switch
pairs.definition: Hubs have no intelligence and repeat traffic out of every port, enlarging the collision domain. Switches use a MAC address table to forward only to the destination port, shrinking the collision domain and enabling full duplex.

pairs.term: Switch Collision Domains
pairs.definition: On a switch each port is its own collision domain. The switch connects collision domains using the MAC address table, letting devices transmit and receive simultaneously (full duplex).

pairs.term: Early Ethernet Media
pairs.definition: IEEE 802.3 CSMA/CD first used Thinnet (10BASE-2) and Thicknet (10BASE-5) coaxial cable with T connectors. Changing to Category 3/4 cable with hubs increased the collision domain size.

pairs.term: Half Duplex on Hubs
pairs.definition: On a hub, all devices are in one collision domain and must wait for the cable to be quiet, so devices can only transmit or receive at a time (half duplex).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: OSI Model
pairs.definition: TCP/IP is based on the conceptual OSI model of seven layers. Each layer describes a specific function and can be modified without requiring changes to layers above or below it, providing a structured approach for vendor compatibility.

pairs.term: Layer 2 Forwarding Information
pairs.definition: Forwarding from a Layer 2 perspective uses the destination MAC address. The data link layer handles addressing beneath the IP stack so communication is directed between hosts.

pairs.term: Multilayer Switch (MLS)
pairs.definition: Multilayer switches forward Layer 2 traffic in hardware like switches but can also route packets from a Layer 3 perspective using ASICs.

pairs.term: Layer 2 Addressing Examples
pairs.definition: Ethernet commonly uses MAC addresses for Layer 2 addressing. Other data link layer protocols such as Frame Relay use an entirely different method of Layer 2 addressing.

pairs.term: OSI Data Flow
pairs.definition: Applications generate data at Layer 7, and the host sends data down the OSI model. Data moves up the stack on the receiving side from Layer 1 to Layer 7.

pairs.term: Layer 3 OSI Function
pairs.definition: Layer 3 (Network) handles logical addressing and routing of packets. Layer 2 (Data Link) handles hardware addressing.

pairs.term: Auto-Negotiation Indicators
pairs.definition: In show interfaces status, duplex and speed that were auto-negotiated are prefixed by a- (for example, a-full and a-1000).

pairs.term: Routed VLAN Field
pairs.definition: In show interfaces status, trunk links appear as trunk in the VLAN column, and ports configured as Layer 3 interfaces display routed.
