pairs.definition: The MAC address table identifies the switch ports and VLANs associated with devices. Switches build it by examining the source MAC of received traffic.

pairs.term: Multiple MACs on a Port
pairs.definition: Multiple MAC addresses on one port indicate a switch, hub, or server with a virtual switch is connected. Downstream switches may need to be checked to locate a device.

pairs.term: mac address-table static mac-address vlan vlan-id {drop | interface interface-id}
pairs.definition: Global command adding a manual MAC entry associated with a specific port or to drop traffic upon receipt.

pairs.term: clear mac address-table dynamic [{address mac-address | interface interface-id | vlan vlan-id}]
pairs.definition: Flushes the MAC address table for the whole switch, or for a specific MAC, port, or VLAN.

pairs.term: Static MAC Drop
pairs.definition: A static MAC address table entry can be configured to associate with a specific switch port or to drop traffic upon receipt.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Trunk Port
pairs.definition: A trunk port carries multiple VLANs and is typically used between a switch and another switch, router, or firewall over a single port.

pairs.term: switchport mode trunk
pairs.definition: Interface command that statically defines a Catalyst switch port as a trunk port.

pairs.term: Hypervisor Virtual Switches
pairs.definition: Thanks to virtualization, some servers run a hypervisor containing a virtualized switch with different VLANs. These servers provide connectivity via a trunk port.

pairs.term: Trunk Load Balancing Use Case
pairs.definition: Select VLANs can be allowed on one trunk link while a different set of VLANs are allowed on another trunk port as a form of load balancing between links.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: VLAN 0
pairs.definition: VLAN 0 is reserved for 802.1p traffic and cannot be modified or deleted.

pairs.term: VLAN 1
pairs.definition: VLAN 1 is the default VLAN and cannot be modified or deleted.

pairs.term: Normal VLAN Range
pairs.definition: VLANs 2 to 1001 are in the normal range and can be added, deleted, or modified.

pairs.term: Reserved VLANs 1002-1005
pairs.definition: VLANs 1002 to 1005 are reserved and cannot be deleted.

pairs.term: Extended VLAN Range
pairs.definition: VLANs 1006 to 4094 are in the extended range and can be added, deleted, or modified.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Virtual LAN (VLAN)
pairs.definition: VLANs provide logical segmentation by creating multiple broadcast domains on the same switch. Devices in different VLANs cannot communicate without a router interconnecting the VLAN segments.

pairs.term: When VLAN Headers Are Added
pairs.definition: VLAN headers are not added to packets forwarded locally in the switch. They are added to packets sent across trunk ports.

pairs.term: VLAN Name
pairs.definition: A friendly name of up to 32 characters is associated with a VLAN through the VLAN submode name command. The VLAN is not created until the CLI returns to global config or a different VLAN ID.

pairs.term: show vlan Output Sections
pairs.definition: The output of show vlan is split into four main sections: VLAN-to-port assignments, system MTU, SPAN sessions, and private VLANs.

pairs.term: show vlan summary
pairs.definition: Displays a count of VLANs, VLANs participating in VTP, and VLANs in the extended VLAN range.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: show interfaces trunk
pairs.definition: Shows trunk interfaces, encapsulation, native VLAN, allowed VLANs, and VLANs in the STP forwarding state.

pairs.term: show mac address-table [address mac-address | dynamic | vlan vlan-id]
pairs.definition: Displays the MAC address table. Filters show an explicit MAC, only dynamic entries, or entries for a VLAN.

pairs.term: show interfaces status
pairs.definition: Displays condensed port status including port, name, status, VLAN, duplex, speed, and type. Status values include connected, notconnect, err-disabled.

pairs.term: show interfaces interface-id switchport
pairs.definition: Displays all relevant operational info for a switch port including administrative mode, operational mode, and access mode VLAN.

pairs.term: show vlan [{brief | id vlan-id | name vlan-name | summary}]
pairs.definition: Displays VLANs and their port assignments. brief shows port-to-VLAN mappings, summary shows VLAN counts, id/name filter by VLAN number or name.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Connected Routes
pairs.definition: A configured, up interface injects its network into the RIB as a connected route with administrative distance zero. No routing protocol or static route can preempt it.

pairs.term: Routed Subinterfaces
pairs.definition: A subinterface is created by appending a period and numeric value to an interface. The VLAN is associated using encapsulation dot1q vlan-id. The subinterface number need not match the VLAN ID.

pairs.term: Switched Virtual Interface (SVI)
pairs.definition: An SVI, or VLAN interface, lets a multilayer switch route between VLANs without an external router. The switch needs an interface in the VLAN in the up state for the SVI to be up.

pairs.term: Routed Switch Port
pairs.definition: A multilayer switch port can be converted from Layer 2 to a routed port with the no switchport command, then assigned an IP address, avoiding a transit VLAN.

pairs.term: ip address ip-address subnet-mask
pairs.definition: Interface command assigning an IPv4 address and subnet mask to a routed interface.

pairs.term: ip address ip-address subnet-mask secondary
pairs.definition: Interface command attaching a secondary IPv4 network to an interface already carrying a primary address.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: show ip arp [mac-address | ip-address | vlan vlan-id | interface-id]
pairs.definition: Displays the ARP table, with optional filters for MAC, IP, VLAN, or interface.

pairs.term: show ip interface [brief | interface-id | vlan vlan-id]
pairs.definition: Displays IP interface information such as MTU, DHCP relay, ACLs, and primary IP. The brief keyword condenses output.

pairs.term: show ipv6 interface [brief | interface-id | vlan vlan-id]
pairs.definition: Displays IPv6 interface information, including link-local and global addresses.

pairs.term: show ip interface brief | exclude unassigned
pairs.definition: Uses the CLI parser to filter out interfaces without IP addresses for a streamlined view of configured interfaces.

pairs.term: show ipv6 interface brief | exclude unassigned|GigabitEthernet
pairs.definition: Uses the CLI parser to filter out unassigned and physical interfaces, showing only the VLAN SVIs with IPv6 addresses.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does the | (pipe) character do in bash?
pairs.definition: It tells bash to use the output of one command as the input of the next command. For example, ip --brief addr list eth0 | awk '{print $3}' takes the output of the ip command and pipes it to awk.

pairs.term: How do you store the output of a command in a variable in bash?
pairs.definition: Use the $(command) syntax. For example, IP_ADDR=$(ip --brief addr list eth0 | awk '{print $3}') stores the output of the command in the variable IP_ADDR, which is then referenced later with a leading $ sign (as $IP_ADDR).

pairs.term: What is the difference between imperative and declarative automation?
pairs.definition: Bash scripts are imperative: they execute a command whether it needs to be executed or not (for example, attempting to add an interface regardless of whether it already exists). Declarative systems make changes only if necessary.

pairs.term: What are some practical use cases for bash scripting in Linux networking?
pairs.definition: Distribution of network interface files (using scp to copy files from a central location and mv to place them, for example in /etc/network/interfaces.d), mass updates of routes, and complex network configuration changes that involve multiple steps.

pairs.term: IP_ADDR=$(ip --brief addr list eth0 | awk '{print $3}')
pairs.definition: Stores the first IP address from the eth0 interface in the variable IP_ADDR by piping the ip command output to awk, which returns only the IP address. Later references use $IP_ADDR.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: ss -lnu
pairs.definition: Shows listening UDP sockets, to check that a daemon's networking configuration is working properly. Replaces the now-deprecated netstat command.

pairs.term: ps
pairs.definition: Presents information on the currently running processes.

pairs.term: systemctl start service-name
pairs.definition: Starts a daemon (background service) using systemd, where service-name is the name of a systemd unit.

pairs.term: systemctl stop service-name
pairs.definition: Stops a daemon (background service) using systemd.

pairs.term: systemctl restart service-name
pairs.definition: Stops and then starts a daemon using systemd. This is almost always disruptive to the daemon.

pairs.term: systemctl reload service-name
pairs.definition: Causes a daemon to reload its configuration, which may be less disruptive than restarting the daemon. Not all daemons apply new configuration automatically.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Docker bridge networking (default)
pairs.definition: The default Docker networking type. It uses veth interfaces, a Linux bridge, and IP masquerading to connect containers to physical networks. Containers attached to the same Linux bridge have immediate container-to-container connectivity on the same host.

pairs.term: Docker host networking
pairs.definition: When using host mode, the container is not isolated in its own network namespace; it uses the host (default) network namespace. Exposed ports from the container are available on the host's IP address. It can be launched with the --network=host flag.

pairs.term: Docker overlay networking
pairs.definition: Creates a distributed network spanning multiple Docker hosts. Overlay networks are built using VXLAN, defined in RFC 7348. This mode is directly tied to Docker's container orchestration mechanism, called Swarm.

pairs.term: Default Docker bridge network subnet
pairs.definition: 172.17.0.0/16. Docker automatically creates the necessary IP masquerading rules for this network, and the bridge name is docker0.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: chmod 755 bin
pairs.definition: Sets the permissions of the bin directory to mode 755: owner has read/write/execute, all others have read/execute (rwxr-xr-x).

pairs.term: chmod u+rw config.txt
pairs.definition: Uses symbolic notation to add read/write permissions for the user who owns config.txt while leaving all other permissions intact.

pairs.term: chmod u+rw,g-w /opt/share/config.txt
pairs.definition: Adds read/write permissions for the file owner but removes write permission for the file group.

pairs.term: chmod -R 755 directory
pairs.definition: Applies permission changes recursively, propagating them to files and subdirectories (works only when used against a directory).

pairs.term: chown
pairs.definition: Changes the ownership of a file or directory. Supports the -R option to act recursively.

pairs.term: chgrp
pairs.definition: Changes the file group of a file or directory. Supports the -R option to act recursively.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: cp -r source-dir destination-dir
pairs.definition: Copies a directory recursively, including both files and subdirectories.

pairs.term: man cp
pairs.definition: Displays the manual page for the cp command, providing a more detailed explanation of how to use the various commands and their options.

pairs.term: ls -l
pairs.definition: Lists the contents of a directory and shows the permissions assigned to the files (along with ownership and group information).

pairs.term: touch config.txt
pairs.definition: Creates a new file named config.txt with no content in the current working directory.

pairs.term: mkdir bin
pairs.definition: Creates a directory named bin in the current working directory.

pairs.term: mkdir -p sw/network
pairs.definition: Creates the directory sw/network without reporting an error if a directory already exists, creating parent directories along the path as needed.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: cd bin
pairs.definition: Change directory - moves into the bin subdirectory of the current working directory (relative path, no leading slash).

pairs.term: cd ..
pairs.definition: Changes to the parent directory of the current working directory, moving up one level in the filesystem.

pairs.term: cd ../share
pairs.definition: Moves laterally to a sibling directory whose path is up one level (..) and named share; for example from /usr/local to /usr/share.

pairs.term: cd (with no parameters)
pairs.definition: Changes to your home directory.

pairs.term: pwd
pairs.definition: Print working directory - returns the directory where you're currently located in the filesystem.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: ip -d link list
pairs.definition: Shows more detailed interface information. The extra output includes a line with the word veth to denote a member of a veth pair, and clearly indicates bridge interfaces (shows bridge) and bridge members (bridge_slave).

pairs.term: ethtool -S <veth-interface>
pairs.definition: Shows interface statistics; when the @ifX suffix is absent, the output includes a peer_ifindex value that refers to the interface index of the other member of the veth pair.

pairs.term: ip addr list <interface>
pairs.definition: Shows the IP addresses assigned to an interface. Example: sudo nsenter --net=/run/docker/netns/b87b15b217e8 ip addr list eth0 verifies the container is using an address from the 172.17.0.0/16 network (172.17.0.2/16).

pairs.term: ip -br link list
pairs.definition: Shows abbreviated (brief) output of interfaces with name, state, and MAC address. For example, it confirms the bridge created by Docker is named docker0 and shows the veth interface veth68bba38@if4.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is brctl?
pairs.definition: Legacy Linux command-line tool for managing Ethernet bridges. Modern replacement: 'bridge' command from iproute2. Used to create/delete bridges and add/remove interfaces.

pairs.definition: Using bin (no leading slash) tells bash to change into the bin subdirectory of the

pairs.term: tions
pairs.definition: the Red Hat/CentOS branch and the Debian and Debian-derivative branch.

pairs.term: Following concept
pairs.definition: Following the colon is the current directory, noted in this case as ~, meaning that

pairs.term: What is Open vSwitch (OVS)?
pairs.definition: Production-quality open-source virtual switch designed for virtualization and network automation, supporting OpenFlow, VXLAN, GRE, and advanced features like QoS, bonding, and STP.

pairs.term: Linux permissions are built around a couple of key ideas — bullet
pairs.definition: Permissions are assigned based on the user (the user who owns the file), group

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How are Debian GNU/Linux release code names chosen?
pairs.definition: All releases since version 1.1 use a code name taken from a character in one of the Toy Story movies. For example, Debian GNU/Linux 1.1 was code-named Buzz and the most recent stable version, 11.0, was code-named Bullseye.

pairs.term: What is Ubuntu Linux?
pairs.definition: A Debian derivative started in April 2004 and funded in large part by Canonical, a company founded by Mark Shuttleworth. All Ubuntu releases are based on packages taken from Debian's unstable branch.

pairs.term: How does Ubuntu handle release scheduling and support?
pairs.definition: Ubuntu uses time-based releases, releasing a new version every six months and a long-term support (LTS) release every two years. LTS releases are supported by Canonical and the Ubuntu community for a total of five years after release.

pairs.term: What is a Linux distribution (distro)?
pairs.definition: The combination of the Linux kernel plus a selection of open source utilities, applications, and software packages that are bundled together and distributed together.

pairs.term: How are Ubuntu code names constructed?
pairs.definition: All Ubuntu codenames are composed of an adjective and an animal with the same first letter, such as Warty Warthog, Hoary Hedgehog, and Breezy Badger.

pairs.term: What are the two major branches of Linux distributions?
pairs.definition: The Red Hat/CentOS branch and the Debian and Debian-derivative branch.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does the execute permission mean for a directory?
pairs.definition: It means the ability to look into and list the contents of the directory. For a file it means the ability to execute the file as a program.

pairs.term: What do the symbols r, w, and x represent?
pairs.definition: Read (r), write (w), and execute (x) permissions. For example, 755 is written symbolically as rwxr-xr-x, indicating read/write/execute for user and read/execute for group and others.

pairs.term: What are the three entities to which Linux permissions are assigned?
pairs.definition: Permissions are assigned based on the user (the user who owns the file), group (other users in the file's group), and others (other users not in the file's group).

pairs.term: What numeric values are assigned to read, write, and execute permissions?
pairs.definition: Read is set to 4, write is set to 2, and execute is set to 1. To allow multiple actions, add the values for each underlying action (for example, read + write = 6).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What was the GNU Project?
pairs.definition: An effort launched by Richard Stallman in the early 1980s to provide a free Unix-like operating system. It produced free versions of a wide collection of Unix utilities and applications, and the GNU General Public License (GPL).

pairs.term: What does GNU stand for?
pairs.definition: GNU's Not Unix, a recursive acronym created by Richard Stallman to describe the free Unix-like OS he was attempting to create.

pairs.term: What is the GNU Hurd?
pairs.definition: The kernel for the GNU Project's OS, which never gained momentum, leaving the GNU Project without a working kernel.

pairs.term: How did the Linux kernel begin?
pairs.definition: Linus Torvalds created a MINIX clone in 1991 as the start of Linux, driven by the lack of a free OS kernel. In 1992 the kernel was licensed under the GNU GPL with the release of version 0.99.

pairs.term: Why do some organizations refer to the full OS as GNU/Linux?
pairs.definition: Because Linux originally referred only to the OS kernel and needed the GNU Project's software collection to form a full operating system. Debian, for example, still uses that designation today.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are the most common types of Linux network interfaces?
pairs.definition: Physical interfaces, VLAN interfaces, and bridge interfaces. Linux treats many things as interfaces, including bridges and VLANs.

pairs.term: What can iptables and its successor nftables be used for on a Linux router?
pairs.definition: They add functionality like network address translation (NAT) and access control lists (ACLs).

pairs.term: What is the difference between an interface being down and administratively down?
pairs.definition: If an interface is down because there is no link, you'll see NO_CARRIER in the brackets after the interface name. If the interface is administratively down (disabled), you won't see UP, LOWER_UP, or NO_CARRIER, and the state will be listed as DOWN.

pairs.term: What is brctl and what supersedes it?
pairs.definition: brctl is an older command for working with Linux bridges. In much the same way that ip superseded ifconfig, the ip command also supersedes brctl, though brctl is still available on most modern Linux distributions.

pairs.term: Are ip command changes persistent across a reboot?
pairs.definition: No. The ip commands change the current (running) configuration but are immediate and not persistent. To make changes persistent you must edit the interface configuration files.

pairs.term: How do you assign an IP address to a bridge interface?
pairs.definition: Change inet manual to inet dhcp (for DHCP) or inet static (for static address assignment) in the bridge's configuration stanza. When using static assignment you also need the address, netmask, and optionally the gateway directives.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does the .. shortcut refer to?
pairs.definition: Every directory contains a special entry named .. (two periods) that is a shortcut for that directory's parent directory - the directory one level above it. It can be used to move up one or more levels in the filesystem.

pairs.term: What does the single period (.) refer to?
pairs.definition: Every directory has an entry noted by a single period (.) that refers to the current directory. Thus touch config.txt and touch ./config.txt both create a file named config.txt in the current working directory.

pairs.term: What is the PATH environment variable?
pairs.definition: The environment variable (conventionally specified in uppercase) that controls the search path and search order that bash uses to locate programs. Modifying this variable modifies the search order.

pairs.term: What is bash?
pairs.definition: The Bourne Again Shell - the most common Linux shell, a play on the name of one of the original Unix shells, the Bourne Shell. In the vast majority of cases you are using bash when interacting with Linux.

pairs.term: What is a single-root filesystem?
pairs.definition: A filesystem in which all the drives, directories, and files in a Linux installation fall into a single namespace, referred to as /. This contrasts with Windows, where each drive typically has its own root (a drive letter like C: or D:).

pairs.term: Why is the single-root filesystem important?
pairs.definition: Because Linux treats everything like a file - including storage devices (treated as block devices), serial ports, and I/O devices - so the single-root filesystem encompasses devices as well as storage.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: lsns -t net
pairs.definition: Lists the network namespaces on the system. Unlike ip netns, lsns shows network namespaces created by Docker and other container runtimes, even with sudo.

pairs.term: lsns -t net -J
pairs.definition: Lists the network namespaces serialized as JSON, showing the nsfs path for each namespace.

pairs.term: nsenter --net=/run/docker/netns/<ns-id> <command>
pairs.definition: Runs a command within another process's network namespace. The -n (or --net) flag specifies the network namespace. Example: sudo nsenter --net=/run/docker/netns/b87b15b217e8 ip link list.

pairs.term: ip netns
pairs.definition: The iproute2 subcommand that allows a user to create, manipulate, and delete network namespaces. However, network namespaces created by Docker and other container runtimes generally aren't visible to it, even with sudo.

pairs.term: Use cases for Linux network namespaces
pairs.definition: Per-process routing, enabling VRF-like configurations, supporting overlapping IP address spaces (often combined with overlay networking and/or NAT), and container networking.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: ip link list ens5
pairs.definition: Lists only the specified interface (for example ens5), filtering the output of ip link list to a specific interface.

pairs.term: ip link delete ens3.150
pairs.definition: Deletes (removes) the VLAN interface. The recommended procedure is to first disable the interface with ip link set ens3.150 down, then delete it.

pairs.term: ip link del br0
pairs.definition: Removes a bridge named br0. You don't need to remove interfaces from a bridge before removing the bridge itself.

pairs.term: ip link set eth0 down
pairs.definition: Disables the eth0 interface (sets its status to administratively down). The state will show DOWN with no UP, LOWER_UP, or NO_CARRIER flags.

pairs.term: ip route list
pairs.definition: Views the current routing table of the Linux host, including the default gateway and directly connected networks.

pairs.term: ip link set eth0 up
pairs.definition: Enables (or re-enables) the eth0 interface, setting its status to UP.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: cat /proc/cpuinfo | grep -i avx
pairs.definition: Checks whether your CPUs support AVX or AVX-512 features needed for parallel processing of large amounts of data.

pairs.term: Why are CPU features like AVX or AVX-512 recommended for Ollama, and how do you check for them?
pairs.definition: AVX/AVX-512 let the CPU do parallel processing of data in large amounts, improving performance. Check support with cat /proc/cpuinfo | grep -i avx; the flags field lists avx/avx2 features when supported.

pairs.term: What CPU core counts are recommended (and minimum) for running Ollama models?
pairs.definition: Eight cores are recommended, but you can get by with four cores for smaller SLMs. The author ran several models successfully with six cores.

pairs.term: How much GPU VRAM is recommended for Ollama models?
pairs.definition: About 4 GB of VRAM is recommended for 7B models (with 4-bit quantization); for a 13B model, 8 GB minimum of VRAM is recommended. Models with larger parameter counts require more VRAM.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is Mistral and what makes it distinctive?
pairs.definition: A language model developed by the French start-up Mistral AI, trained in English, French, Spanish, German, and Italian, so it can handle multilingual queries (e.g., translation).

pairs.term: Why is llama3.1:8b considered an LLM despite being as small as some SLMs?
pairs.definition: Because its architecture is shared with the large Llama 3.1 LLMs; smaller models based on models architected as LLMs are still referred to as LLMs even when reduced in size.

pairs.term: What is the largest size that Llama 3.1 can reach in parameters?
pairs.definition: Llama 3.1 has versions with up to 405 billion parameters, although the llama3.1:8b version used in the chapter has just 8 billion parameters.

pairs.term: What tasks did Llama 3.1 say it was good at?
pairs.definition: Conversational dialogue, generating text for articles, stories, and entire documents, creative writing, dialogue role-playing, and language semantics and structure (while admitting it can make mistakes and be biased).

pairs.term: What was the author's overall experience with answer accuracy versus code-writing across the models?
pairs.definition: Results were mixed regarding the accuracy of the answers, but the models did well when it came to writing code (e.g., Phi 3 produced a bash script to copy PNG files).

pairs.term: Why might a reduced-size model still be called an LLM rather than an SLM?
pairs.definition: Because some smaller models are architected as LLMs and simply reduced in size; they retain the name LLM based on their original architecture even when they have few parameters (like llama3.1:8b).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is Ollama?
pairs.definition: A tool designed to run AI language models on your local computer. After installation it runs as a systemd service and exposes an API at 127.0.0.1:11434.

pairs.term: ollama run phi3:mini
pairs.definition: Runs the Phi 3 mini model (Microsoft), which can write code such as shell scripts but tends to give long-winded answers.

pairs.term: /show license
pairs.definition: Reads the license for the current model, which is a good idea to address privacy concerns and explain any constraints on commercial use.

pairs.term: What memory (RAM) is needed to run different model sizes in Ollama?
pairs.definition: 13B models need at least 32 GB of RAM, 7B models need at least 16 GB, and 3B models need at least 8 GB.

pairs.term: ollama list
pairs.definition: Lists downloaded/run language models with NAME, ID, SIZE, and last-modified time.

pairs.term: /show info
pairs.definition: Displays information about the current model, such as architecture, parameters, context length, embedding length, and quantization.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How does a process's user and group account affect it?
pairs.definition: Each process is associated with a particular user and group account, which helps determine what system resources the process can access. A process run as root has much more access than one run by a regular user.

pairs.term: Where do commands that display process information get their raw data, and how is it organized?
pairs.definition: They get most of their data from raw data stored in the /proc filesystem. Each process stores its information in a subdirectory of /proc named after that process's PID.

pairs.term: What is a process in Linux?
pairs.definition: A process is a running instance of a command. For example, one vi command on the system can be represented by many different processes if 15 users run it at the same time.

pairs.term: What is a PID, and what guarantees does it provide?
pairs.definition: A PID (process ID) is the unique identifier of a process on the current system. No other process can use that number while the process is running, but after the process ends, another process can reuse that number.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What can you see under Properties for a process in System Monitor?
pairs.definition: Other settings associated with the process, such as security context, memory usage, and CPU use percentages.

pairs.term: gnome-system-monitor
pairs.definition: The System Monitor tool on the GNOME desktop for graphically displaying processes. You can sort by clicking columns and right-click processes to stop, kill, or renice them. To start it, press the Windows key, type System Monitor, and select Processes.

pairs.term: What do Stop, Continue, Terminate, and Kill do in System Monitor?
pairs.definition: Stop pauses the process (same as Ctrl+Z); Continue resumes a paused process; Terminate sends signal 15 (SIGTERM) to terminate cleanly; Kill sends signal 9 (SIGKILL) to kill immediately regardless of whether it could be done cleanly.

pairs.term: In System Monitor, what is Set Affinity and what does it do?
pairs.definition: Set Affinity lets you choose which processor(s) can be used to run a particular process by selecting a process and choosing which processors it can run on.

pairs.term: What do Memory Maps and Open Files show in System Monitor?
pairs.definition: Memory Maps lets you view the system memory map to see which libraries and components are held in memory for the process. Open Files lets you view which files are currently held open by the process.

pairs.term: How do you start System Monitor, and what does it show by default?
pairs.definition: Press the Windows key, type System Monitor, and press Enter, then select the Processes tab. By default only running processes associated with your user account are displayed, listed alphabetically; you can sort by clicking field headings like %CPU or Memory.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are cgroups used for?
pairs.definition: Cgroups (control groups) identify a process as a task belonging to a particular control group, letting you limit and contain the resources (CPU, memory, IO) a group of processes can consume. Child processes inherit the limitations set for the parent.

pairs.term: Why does the chapter caution against new administrators creating and managing cgroups?
pairs.definition: Setting up cgroups can be tricky and, if done improperly, can make your system unstable or even unbootable. Creating and managing cgroups is generally not a job for new Linux system administrators.

pairs.term: How do child processes relate to cgroup limitations?
pairs.definition: As a task launches a process, other processes that the initial process launches (child processes) inherit the limitations set for the parent process, such as access to particular processors or up to 30 percent of total processing power.

pairs.term: What is the Cpuset controller in cgroups v2?
pairs.definition: It lets you confine a set of processes so that they run on a particular group of memory and CPU hardware. This is useful for separating important tasks from other parts of your Linux system.

pairs.term: What is the PID controller in cgroups v2?
pairs.definition: It lets cgroups prevent new tasks from being created (forked or cloned) after a set limit has been reached.

pairs.term: What is the RDMA controller in cgroups v2?
pairs.definition: The Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) controller allows a computer to directly access memory on another computer, which can speed the transfer of data from one system to another.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: jobs
pairs.definition: Lists the commands you have running in the background, showing job number and status. For example, [2] Running ... and [5]+ Stopped ... . A + marks the most recently backgrounded job; a - marks the one before it.

pairs.term: jobs -l
pairs.definition: Adds the -l (lowercase L) option to jobs to show the process ID for each background job, so you can use ps to identify the command for a particular background job.

pairs.term: What do the + and - symbols mean in jobs output?
pairs.definition: The plus sign (+) next to a job number shows it was most recently placed in the background. The minus sign (-) shows it was placed in the background just before the most recent background job.

pairs.term: Why does a background job sometimes remain Stopped?
pairs.definition: A job that requires terminal input (like vi) cannot run in the background, so it is Stopped until it is brought to the foreground again (with fg).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: kill 10432 / kill -15 10432 / kill -SIGKILL 10432
pairs.definition: Sends a signal to PID 10432. The first two are equivalent because 15 (SIGTERM) is the default. The third sends SIGKILL (also -9) to force-kill the process.

pairs.term: kill -1 1833 / killall -HUP gnome-shell
pairs.definition: Two ways to send SIGTERM (SIGHUP) to gnome-shell (PID 1833): kill with the PID, or killall by name (HUP), causing it to reread config files and restart the desktop.

pairs.term: Besides ending a process, what can kill and killall be used for?
pairs.definition: They can send any valid signal to a running process, such as telling it to reread configuration files, pause (stop), or continue after being paused.
Sends signal 15 (SIGTERM) to PID 10432, terminating the process cleanly. This is identical to running 'kill 10432' because 15 is the default signal.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: killall -9 testme
pairs.definition: Sends SIGKILL (9) to all processes named testme by name rather than by PID. Useful for killing many commands of the same name, but be careful because you can kill more than you mean to.

pairs.term: killall bash
pairs.definition: Signals all processes named bash by name. This risks killing many shells you did not intend to kill, since killall matches by process name.

pairs.term: killall (general)
pairs.definition: Signals processes by name instead of by process ID. Like kill it defaults to SIGTERM (15) if no signal is given, and it can be useful to kill a bunch of commands of the same name (e.g., killall -9 testme).

pairs.term: killall -HUP gnome-shell
pairs.definition: Sends a SIGHUP signal to gnome-shell by name, causing it to reread its configuration files and restart the desktop (useful if something on the GNOME desktop was corrupted).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are the restrictions on regular users setting nice values?
pairs.definition: A regular user can set nice values only from 0 to 19 (no negatives), can raise but not lower the value (e.g., 10 back to 5 fails), and can set values only on their own processes. Root can set any value on any process, up or down.

pairs.term: nice -n +5 updatedb &
pairs.definition: Runs the updatedb command with a nice value of +5 in the background, giving it less CPU attention so it doesn't interrupt other work. The top output shows the nice value under the NI column.

pairs.term: renice -n -5 20284
pairs.definition: Changes the nice value of process 20284 (the updatedb command) to -5. As root the nice value can be reduced, giving the process more CPU priority.

pairs.term: NI column (top)
pairs.definition: Shows the nice value of each process. For example, after 'nice -n +5 updatedb &', the updatedb process shows NI=5; after renice to -5, it shows NI=-5 and moves up the CPU list.

pairs.term: What is the nice value, its range, and its default?
pairs.definition: Every process has a nice value between -20 and 19, defaulting to 0. The lower the nice value, the more CPU access a process gets. A -20 nice value gets more attention than a 19 value: the nicer a process, the less CPU attention.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: procs --insert TcpPort --insert Processor nginx
pairs.definition: Lists nginx processes with added TcpPort and Processor fields inserted into the default output, letting you see which ports (e.g., [80]) are associated with each process. Run as root because ports are not exposed to all users.

pairs.term: procs -w
pairs.definition: Runs procs with a built-in watch process that refreshes the output over time (every 1000 ms by default). Keys: Next: n, Prev: p, Ascending: a, Descending: d, Quit: q or Ctrl-C.

pairs.term: What unique field can procs show that ps cannot?
pairs.definition: The TcpPort field, which reveals the ports associated with a process (e.g., showing an nginx server listening on port 80). Ports are not exposed to all users, so you typically run this as root.

pairs.term: procs (default output)
pairs.definition: Displays fields in color with eight columns of information for all running processes: PID, User, TTY, CPU %, MEM %, CPU Time, and Command. You can add fields with --insert.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: procs
pairs.definition: A more modern replacement for ps for listing processes. It is easy to install: with snap on Ubuntu and with dnf on Fedora. Its default output displays fields in color and shows eight columns.

pairs.term: ps u
pairs.definition: Displays process information for the current user with columns USER, PID, %CPU, %MEM, VSZ, RSS, TTY, STAT, START, TIME, and COMMAND. The u option is equivalent to -u.

pairs.term: ps ux | less
pairs.definition: Pipes the list of processes for the current user to the less command so you can page through them using the spacebar and quit with q.

pairs.term: ps aux | less
pairs.definition: Pipes the list of all processes running for all users to less so you can page through the entire process list.

pairs.term: ps -eo pid,user,uid,group,gid,vsz,rss,comm | less
pairs.definition: Lists every running process (-e) and displays selected columns via -o using keywords: pid, user, uid, group, gid, vsz, rss, and comm (the full command line). By default output is sorted by PID.

pairs.term: ps -eo pid,user,group,gid,vsz,rss,comm --sort=-vsz | head
pairs.definition: Lists running processes sorted by the vsz field. The hyphen before vsz sorts from highest to lowest (descending), letting you see which processes use the most memory first.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Which signals cannot be blocked by a process?
pairs.definition: Processes cannot block SIGKILL and SIGSTOP signals. SIGKILL kills a process outright and SIGSTOP pauses it.

pairs.term: What does the note about multiple numbers for SIGCONT and SIGSTOP mean?
pairs.definition: Different architectures use different numbers for SIGCONT and SIGSTOP. For most x86 and Power architectures, use the middle value; the first value works for Alpha and SPARC, and the last is for MIPS.

pairs.term: kill
pairs.definition: Sends a signal to a process (usually to end it), assuming you have permission. It can also send different signals to change a process's behavior. The default signal sent is 15 (SIGTERM).

pairs.term: SIGKILL (9)
pairs.definition: The kill signal. It kills a process immediately and cannot be blocked. Used when a SIGTERM fails to terminate a process.

pairs.term: SIGTERM (15)
pairs.definition: The termination signal, the default sent by kill; it tries to terminate a process cleanly.

pairs.term: SIGHUP (1)
pairs.definition: Hang-up signal; depending on the program it can tell a process to reread its configuration files (e.g., restarting the GNOME desktop).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: R and u (top keys)
pairs.definition: R reverses the sort order of the output. u lets you enter a username to display processes only for a particular user.

pairs.term: h (top key)
pairs.definition: Shows help options. Press any key to return to the top display.

pairs.term: What do the top interactive keys h, M, P, 1, R, and u do?
pairs.definition: h shows help; M sorts by memory usage; P returns to sorting by CPU; 1 toggles showing CPU usage for all CPUs; R reverses the sort order; u lets you filter to show only a particular user's processes.

pairs.term: 1 (top key)
pairs.definition: Toggles showing CPU usage of all your CPUs if you have more than one CPU on your system.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: gpg2 --gen-key
pairs.definition: Generates a public/private key pair and a key ring for the current user, prompting for User ID, email, and passphrase.

pairs.term: gpg --list-secret-keys --keyid-format=long
pairs.definition: Lists secret keys and their User IDs, showing the key ring contents.

pairs.term: gpg2 --armor --export 8432C5004E6ACF5388F7F206F1CBFDAF4DD13075 > JohnDoe.pub
pairs.definition: Exports the public key to a file (as a PGP public key block) so it can be shared.

pairs.term: gpg2 --import JohnDoe.pub
pairs.definition: Imports another user's public key into your key ring so you can encrypt to them and verify their signatures.

pairs.term: What is asymmetric (private/public key) cryptography?
pairs.definition: Cryptography that uses two keys called a key pair: a public key (no need to keep it secret) and a private key (must be kept secret). A file encrypted with the public key can be decrypted only with its matching private key.

pairs.term: gpg2 --out MessageForJohn --recipient 'John Doe' --encrypt MessageForJohn.txt
pairs.definition: Encrypts a message file using the recipient's public key, writing the encrypted output to the --out file.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is a compliance review?
pairs.definition: An audit of the overall computer system environment to ensure the policies and procedures you have set are being carried out correctly.

pairs.term: What is a security review?
pairs.definition: An audit of current policies and procedures to ensure they follow accepted best security practices.

pairs.term: What is penetration testing (pen testing / ethical hacking)?
pairs.definition: An evaluation method that tests a computer system's security by simulating malicious attacks. Kali Linux is a distribution created specifically for penetration testing, usable from a live DVD or flash drive.

pairs.term: Name organizations that help you stay informed about best security practices.
pairs.definition: NIST (Computer Security Resource Center, offers Security Content Automation Protocol), CISA (National Cyber Alert System), the SANS Institute (Computer Security Research newsletters), and Gibson Research Corporation (Security Now! netcast).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: authselect create-profile myprofile -b sssd
pairs.definition: Creates a custom authselect profile named myprofile based on the sssd profile (-b sssd).

pairs.term: What does the sssd authselect profile provide?
pairs.definition: System authentication both locally (including passwd and group files) and remotely (allowing authentication against remote servers such as LDAP and Kerberos).

pairs.term: What optional authselect features did the chapter highlight for the sssd profile?
pairs.definition: with-faillock (account locking after too many consecutive authentication failures), with-mkhomedir (automatic creation of home directories on first login), with-silent-lastlog, with-fingerprint, and with-mdns4.

pairs.term: How do you add an optional feature to the current authselect profile and back up the setup?
pairs.definition: authselect select sssd -b with-mkhomedir with-silent-lastlog with-fingerprint with-mdns4. The -b option backs up the current setup (to /var/lib/authselect/backups) and the new features are enabled.

pairs.term: How do you restore an authselect backup?
pairs.definition: List available backups with authselect backup-list, then restore with authselect backup-restore <backupname> (e.g., authselect backup-restore 2025-07-06-11-16-49.drbcIq).

pairs.term: How do you create and use a custom authselect profile?
pairs.definition: Create it with authselect create-profile myprofile -b sssd, select it with authselect select custom/myprofile/ -b, add features as desired, and edit files in /etc/authselect/custom/myprofile/. This gives you copies of the whole set of authselect-managed files.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is AES (Advanced Encryption Standard), also called Rijndael?
pairs.definition: A symmetric cryptography block cipher that encrypts data in 128-, 192-, or 256-bit blocks using a 128-, 192-, or 256-bit key for encrypting/decrypting.

pairs.term: What are Blowfish and CAST5?
pairs.definition: Blowfish is a symmetric block cipher encrypting 64-bit blocks using a 32-bit to 448-bit key; CAST5 is a symmetric block cipher encrypting 64-bit blocks using an up to 128-bit key.

pairs.term: Why are DES and 3DES no longer considered secure?
pairs.definition: DES (Data Encryption Standard) is no longer considered secure because of its small 56-bit key size. 3DES improves on DES by encrypting data up to 48 times with three different 56-bit keys, but it is the improved (still dated) DES cipher.

pairs.term: What is the general relationship between cipher key size and security?
pairs.definition: The key size is directly related to how easily the cipher is cracked. The bigger the key size, the less the chance of cracking the cipher; a cipher with a 256-bit or 512-bit key is considered secure because it would take trillions of years to brute-force.

pairs.term: What are RC4/ArcFour, RC5, and RC6?
pairs.definition: RC4 (also called ArcFour or ARC4) is a stream cipher encrypting data using a variable key size; RC5 is a symmetric block cipher encrypting 32-, 64-, or 128-bit blocks using up to 2,048-bit keys; RC6 is the same as RC5 but slightly faster.

pairs.term: What is the Caesar Cipher and why is it insecure?
pairs.definition: One of the original ciphers, created and used by Julius Caesar, that was terribly easy to crack. It illustrates that the strength of the cipher you choose should relate to the security needs of your data.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are encryption and decryption?
pairs.definition: Encryption is the process of converting plain text into ciphertext using an algorithm; decryption is the process of converting ciphertext back into plain text using an algorithm.

pairs.term: What is a cipher, a block cipher, and a stream cipher?
pairs.definition: A cipher is the algorithm used to encrypt plain text into ciphertext and decrypt ciphertext back. A block cipher breaks data into blocks before encrypting; a stream cipher encrypts data without breaking it up.

pairs.term: What is a key in cryptography?
pairs.definition: A piece of data required by the cipher to encrypt or decrypt data successfully. The key can be either a single key or a pair of keys.

pairs.term: What is plain text versus ciphertext?
pairs.definition: Plain text is text that a human or machine can read and comprehend; ciphertext is text that a human or machine cannot read and comprehend.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How does the sender create a digital signature for a file?
pairs.definition: Using gpg2, create a hash (message digest) of the file, then encrypt the hash and the file using an asymmetric cipher—the private key of the key pair is used for this encryption. The result is a digitally signed encrypted file.

pairs.term: How does the receiver verify a digital signature?
pairs.definition: The receiver re-creates the hash of the received encrypted file, then uses gpg2 with the public key to decrypt the received digital signature and obtain the original hash, and compares the two hashes. If they match, the signature is good.

pairs.term: Which ciphers are used specifically for creating digital signatures?
pairs.definition: RSA can be used for both encryption and creating signatures; DSA (Digital Signature Algorithm) can be used only for creating digital signatures. Today Ed25519 is considered more secure and faster than RSA, and ECDSA provides better protection than DSA.

pairs.term: How do you sign and encrypt a file with gpg2 in one step?
pairs.definition: gpg2 --output JohnDoe.DS --sign MessageForJill.txt, which creates a message digest, encrypts it (the digital signature), encrypts the message file, and places the encrypted contents in the --output file.

pairs.term: How do you decrypt and verify a signed file in one step?
pairs.definition: gpg2 --decrypt JohnDoe.DS, which decrypts the message and checks the digital signature in one step, reporting a good signature from the sender (unless the sender's public key is missing from the key ring, in which case decryption fails).

pairs.term: How do you keep a signed document truly private?
pairs.definition: Use the public key of the recipient to encrypt, combining the gpg2 options --sign and --encrypt; the recipient can then decrypt with their private key.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What should a disaster recovery plan specify?
pairs.definition: What data is included in backups, where backups are stored, how long backups are maintained, and how backup media is rotated through storage. Backup data, media, and software should be in the Access Control Matrix checklist.

pairs.term: What backup utilities are available on a Linux system?
pairs.definition: amanda (Advanced Maryland Automatic Network Disk Archiver), cpio, dump/restore, tar, and rsync. cpio, dump/restore, and tar are typically pre-installed; dump/restore and amanda are not normally installed by default.

pairs.term: What is amanda and why is it popular?
pairs.definition: The Advanced Maryland Automatic Network Disk Archiver, a backup utility popular for its flexibility; it can even back up a Windows system. It is not typically installed by default.

pairs.term: What is the rsync utility used for in backups?
pairs.definition: A simple but effective tool for backing up data over networks; you can set up a cron job to keep copies of all data in selected directories or mirror exact copies of directories on remote machines.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the SGID (set GID) permission?
pairs.definition: A permission in the Group category requiring execute in the Other category that lets anyone temporarily become a group member of the file's group while executed in memory. Set on a directory, SGID makes new files inherit the directory's group ID.

pairs.term: Why must /usr/bin/passwd and /usr/bin/sudo keep their SUID permissions?
pairs.definition: passwd needs SUID so a regular user becomes root temporarily to write to /etc/shadow (only to change their own password), and sudo needs SUID so users can escalate to root only when granted permission. Both are designed to be SUID programs.

pairs.term: How can you find hidden or inappropriate SUID and SGID commands on your system?
pairs.definition: Use the find command with the permission mask, e.g., find / -perm /6000 -ls, which lists files with SUID and/or SGID set, revealing things like a hidden copy of vi (myvi) that can change root-owned files.

pairs.term: What should the /etc/passwd file permissions be?
pairs.definition: Owner root, Group root, permissions 644 (Owner rw-, Group r--, Other r--). Users need read access to see usernames associated with UID/GID, but must not be able to modify the file (which would allow adding accounts).

pairs.term: What should the /etc/shadow file permissions be?
pairs.definition: Owner root, Group root, permissions 000 (no access for owner, group, or other). Only root can read it; regular users change their passwords via the SUID /usr/bin/passwd command.

pairs.term: What permissions should /etc/group and /etc/gshadow have?
pairs.definition: /etc/group should match /etc/passwd (root:root, 644); /etc/gshadow (the group password file) should match /etc/shadow (root:root, 000).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How do you view more information about an encrypted volume with cryptsetup?
pairs.definition: cryptsetup status <luks-device-name> shows whether it is active and in use, along with the type (e.g., LUKS1), cipher (e.g., aes-xts-plain64), keysize (e.g., 512 bits), device, offset, size, and mode.

pairs.term: Why does Ubuntu need the lvm2 package for the lvs command?
pairs.definition: Ubuntu does not have the lvs command installed by default; install it with sudo apt-get install lvm2.

pairs.term: lvs -o devices
pairs.definition: Lists all logical volumes and their underlying device names (starting with luks for LUKS-encrypted volumes).

pairs.term: cryptsetup status luks-b099fbbe-0e56-425f-91a6-44f129db9f4b
pairs.definition: Shows whether the encrypted volume is active and in use, along with its type, cipher, keysize, device, offset, size, and mode.

pairs.term: What is LUKS (Linux Unified Key Setup)?
pairs.definition: A Free and Open Source Software third-party standard for hard disk encryption (from cryptsetup). Encrypted volumes' device names commonly start with luks-.

pairs.term: How can you encrypt the root partition during Linux installation?
pairs.definition: Many Linux distributions include an encryption option during installation; after selecting it you are asked for a password (symmetric key cryptography) that must be at least eight characters, and you are prompted for the key password at every boot.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: sha256sum --ignore-missing -c Fedora-Workstation-42-1.1-x86_64-CHECKSUM
pairs.definition: Verifies ISO file integrity by comparing hashes in the CHECKSUM file against the downloaded ISO; an OK result confirms the file matches.

pairs.term: What is hashing and how does it differ from encryption?
pairs.definition: Hashing is a one-way mathematical process used to create ciphertext; however, unlike encryption, after you create a hash you cannot de-hash it back to its original plain text. It is a form of cryptography but not encryption.

pairs.term: What does it mean for a hashing algorithm to be collision-free?
pairs.definition: The hashing algorithm does not output the same hash for two totally different inputs; each input must have a unique hashed output. Thus cryptographic hashing is a one-way mathematical process that is collision-free.

pairs.term: What is hashing used for on Linux systems?
pairs.definition: Passwords (stored as hashes in /etc/shadow), verifying files, digital signatures, and virus signatures.

pairs.term: What are the other names for a hash, and which utility produces them?
pairs.definition: A hash is also called a message digest, checksum, fingerprint, or signature. The sha256sum utility produces message digests.

pairs.term: How do you verify the integrity of a downloaded ISO using a CHECKSUM file?
pairs.definition: Place the ISO and the CHECKSUM file in the same directory and run sha256sum --ignore-missing -c <CHECKSUM file>; an 'OK' next to a file confirms it matches (e.g., Fedora-Workstation-Live-42-1.1.x86_64.iso: OK).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: cp /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new.gz /var/lib/aide/aide.db.gz
pairs.definition: Moves the initial aide database to its permanent name/location so it is not overwritten and comparisons can be made.

pairs.term: aide -C
pairs.definition: Creates a new aide database ('second picture') and compares it to the original database, reporting added, removed, and changed entries.

pairs.term: What are popular Linux intrusion detection systems?
pairs.definition: aide (Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment), Snort, and tripwire. aide is installed with dnf install aide or apt-get install aide; the open source tripwire is no longer actively maintained.

pairs.term: How does the aide IDS detect intrusions?
pairs.definition: It uses a comparison method: a 'first picture' database is created (best right after a fresh install), later a 'second picture' database is created, and aide compares the two and reports differences.

pairs.term: How do you initialize the aide database and run a comparison check?
pairs.definition: Create the initial database with aide -i (written to /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new.gz), move it with cp /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new.gz /var/lib/aide/aide.db.gz, then check with aide -C which creates a new database and compares it to the original.

pairs.term: What is configured in /etc/aide.conf?
pairs.definition: Where aide databases are created, what comparisons are made, and other settings, including the database directory (DBDIR, e.g., /var/lib/aide) and log directory (LOGDIR).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is a false positive in malware detection?
pairs.definition: An indication of a virus, rootkit, or other malicious activity that does not really exist. Antivirus and rootkit-detecting software often produce false positives (e.g., chkrootkit reporting a Suckit infection from a known bug).

pairs.term: What is Rootkit Hunter (rkhunter)?
pairs.definition: Another rootkit detector. Configure it in /etc/rkhunter.conf and run rkhunter -c to check the filesystem for a variety of rootkits and vulnerabilities; install the rkhunter package.

pairs.term: dnf install clamav
pairs.definition: Installs the ClamAV antivirus software on Fedora or RHEL systems.

pairs.term: chkrootkit | grep INFECTED
pairs.definition: Runs the chkrootkit rootkit detector and searches the output for infected files.

pairs.term: rkhunter -c
pairs.definition: Runs the Rootkit Hunter check on the filesystem for a variety of rootkits and vulnerabilities.

pairs.term: Why scan for Windows viruses on a Linux system used as a mail server?
pairs.definition: Linux systems often handle services, such as mail servers, for Windows desktop systems, so they need to be scanned for Windows viruses as well. It is a misconception that there are no Linux viruses.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How do you see the full list of installed cryptography tools on a distribution?
pairs.definition: Type man -k crypt at the command line to see a list of installed cryptography tools.

pairs.term: What are duplicity and zipcloak used for?
pairs.definition: duplicity encrypts backups (install with dnf install duplicity on Fedora or sudo apt install duplicity on Ubuntu); zipcloak encrypts entries in a Zip file and is installed by default.

pairs.term: What do openssl and ssh provide in terms of cryptography?
pairs.definition: openssl is a toolkit that implements SSL and TLS protocols (which require encryption), installed by default; ssh encrypts remote access across a network, also installed by default.

pairs.term: What is seahorse?
pairs.definition: A GNU Privacy Guard encryption key manager installed by default on Ubuntu; install with dnf install seahorse on Fedora/RHEL or sudo apt install seahorse on Ubuntu.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: stat /sbin/tricks
pairs.definition: Shows detailed file information including access, modify, change, and birth times, used to investigate a suspect binary.

pairs.term: find /home -name .rhosts
pairs.definition: Finds .rhosts files in /home directories, which allow one system to trust another completely and should not be present.

pairs.term: find / -nouser
pairs.definition: Finds files not associated with any username (ownerless files), a common scan for malicious activity.

pairs.term: What does rpm -V package_name do?
pairs.definition: Verifies an installed software package by comparing the installed package files against package metadata in the rpm database. If no problems are found, it returns nothing; discrepancies produce a coded listing.

pairs.term: find / -nogroup
pairs.definition: Finds files not associated with any group name (groupless files).

pairs.term: How do you verify packages on Ubuntu (where rpm -V is not used)?
pairs.definition: Use the debsums utility (install with sudo apt-get install debsums). Check all installed packages with debsums -a, or a single package with debsums packagename.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Where are Linux system log files primarily located?
pairs.definition: In the /var/log directory. Some log files have dates appended (e.g., error_log-20250329). Many /var/log files are directed there from the systemd journal through the rsyslogd service.

pairs.term: What do the /var/log boot.log and btmp files record?
pairs.definition: boot.log contains messages indicating which services started/shut down successfully and which failed (most recent at the end). btmp logs bad login attempts.

pairs.term: Which /var/log files require special viewing commands rather than cat/tail/less?
pairs.definition: btmp (use dump-utmp btmp), dmesg (use dmesg), lastlog (use lastlog), and wtmp (use dump-utmp wtmp).

pairs.term: What are the /var/log wtmp, lastlog, and secure files?
pairs.definition: wtmp contains a history of logins and logouts; lastlog records the last time an account logged in; secure records the date, time, and duration of login attempts and sessions.

pairs.term: How do you view kernel messages from the systemd journal and follow them live?
pairs.definition: Run journalctl -k; add -f (journalctl -k -f) to follow messages as they come in; press Ctrl+C to stop.

pairs.term: How do you view journal messages for a specific service and follow them?
pairs.definition: Use journalctl -u <servicename> for a service and add -f to follow live, e.g., journalctl -f -u NetworkManager.service.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How do you know which /etc/pam.d files are managed directly by authselect?
pairs.definition: List those that are symbolic links to /etc/authselect: ls -l /etc/pam.d/ | grep lrw shows links such as fingerprint-auth, password-auth, postlogin, smartcard-auth, and system-auth.

pairs.term: What do the pam_cracklib options minlen, minclass, and maxrepeat do?
pairs.definition: minlen=N sets the minimum acceptable password size (default 9); minclass=N requires N out of four character classes (digits, uppercase, lowercase, other) (default 0); maxrepeat=N rejects passwords with more than N same consecutive characters (default 0).

pairs.term: What is a PAM-aware application?
pairs.definition: An application written to use PAM. A PAM-aware application does not need to be rewritten or recompiled to change its authentication settings; changes are made in a PAM configuration file, so authentication management is centralized and simplified.

pairs.term: How can you quickly find which PAM configuration files authselect may rewrite?
pairs.definition: Use grep 'Generated by authselect' /etc/pam.d/*; files containing this comment (fingerprint-auth, password-auth, postlogin, smartcard-auth, system-auth) are directly managed by authselect and may be rewritten, removing local changes.

pairs.term: How do you enforce passwords of at least 10 characters containing two digits with pam_cracklib?
pairs.definition: Add to /etc/pam.d/system-auth: password required pam_cracklib.so minlen=10 dcredit=-2 (minlen=10 forces at least 10 characters; dcredit=-2 requires two digits).

pairs.term: How can you check whether an application is PAM-aware?
pairs.definition: Check whether it is compiled with the PAM library, libpam.so, using the ldd command: ldd /usr/bin/crontab | grep pam shows libpam.so.0 if the application is PAM-aware.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is a hashed password?
pairs.definition: A password transformed by a one-way mathematical process. You cannot re-create the original characters from the hash; on login the system rehashes the entered password and compares it to the stored hash.

pairs.term: What is salting a hash?
pairs.definition: Adding a randomly generated value to the original password before it is hashed, making it harder for the hashed password to be matched to its original. In Linux the salt is stored with the hashed password.

pairs.term: Why were hashed passwords moved from /etc/passwd to /etc/shadow?
pairs.definition: /etc/passwd is readable by everyone (-rw-r--r--, 644), exposing hashes (and salts) to rainbow table attacks. /etc/shadow has no permission set (000) and can be read only by root, protecting the hashed passwords.

pairs.term: What is pwconv and when would you use it?
pairs.definition: A command that creates the /etc/shadow file and moves hashed passwords from /etc/passwd into it. Use it if you inherit a system still storing hashed passwords in /etc/passwd.

pairs.term: Besides the account name and hashed password, what is stored in /etc/shadow?
pairs.definition: Days (since Jan 1 1970) since the password changed, days before it can change, days before it must change, days to warn before change, days after expiry the account is disabled, and days (since 1970) the account has been disabled.

pairs.term: pwconv
pairs.definition: Creates the /etc/shadow file and moves hashed passwords from /etc/passwd into it, for systems still using the old storage method.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: passwd <username>
pairs.definition: As root, sets a new password for the named user (prompts twice for the new password, no old password needed). Without a username, a user changes their own password.

pairs.term: Which user is the only one permitted to assign a 'bad' password that cracklib rejects?
pairs.definition: The root user. Non-root users are required to try a different password if the one they choose is not judged good by cracklib.

pairs.term: What does the passwd command do when run as root with a username argument?
pairs.definition: passwd joe prompts twice to enter a new password for the user joe; it does not prompt for the old password in this case.

pairs.term: What are the two primary requirements for a strong password?
pairs.definition: It should be at least 8 characters (complexity is more important than length) and contain lowercase letters, uppercase letters, numbers, and special characters such as : ! $ % * ( ) - + = , < > '.

pairs.term: Why should PASS_MIN_DAYS be set to a number larger than zero?
pairs.definition: To keep users from changing their password to a new one and then immediately changing it right back to the previous password; it sets the soonest a password can be changed again.

pairs.term: What should you avoid when choosing a password?
pairs.definition: Avoid any variation of your login or full name, dictionary words, proper names, phone numbers/address/family/pet names, website names, contiguous keyboard lines (qwerty, asdfg), and any of these with added numbers/punctuation or typed backward.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: gpg2 -d --force-mdc /tmp/backup.tar.gz.gpg > /tmp/backup.tar.gz
pairs.definition: Decrypts the .gpg file back to the original tar archive, requiring the secret passphrase.

pairs.term: What is symmetric key (secret key/private key) cryptography?
pairs.definition: Cryptography that encrypts plain text using a single-keyed cipher; the same key is needed to decrypt the data. Its advantage is speed; its disadvantage is the need to share the single key if another person must decrypt the data.

pairs.term: What is gpg (GNU Privacy Guard) and which package provides it?
pairs.definition: The OpenPGP utility GNU Privacy Guard, an example of symmetric (and asymmetric) encryption. The gnupg2 package is installed by default in Fedora and RHEL; on Ubuntu install the gnupg package to get the gpg command.

pairs.term: How do you encrypt a file with gpg2 using a symmetric key?
pairs.definition: gpg2 -c --force-mdc -o /tmp/backup.tar.gz.gpg /tmp/backup.tar.gz. The -c option encrypts with a symmetric key, keeping the original and creating a new encrypted file with a .gpg extension (e.g., PGP symmetric key encrypted data - AES with 256-bit key).

pairs.term: How do you decrypt a symmetrically encrypted file with gpg2?
pairs.definition: gpg2 -d --force-mdc /tmp/backup.tar.gz.gpg > /tmp/backup.tar.gz, providing the passphrase for the secret key when prompted; the original tar file is decrypted and copied to the target.

pairs.term: What is the passphrase used to protect a symmetric key, and what are the recommendations for it?
pairs.definition: A password or phrase chosen by the user at the time of encryption. It should be at least eight characters long and have at least one digit or special character.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: passwd joe
pairs.definition: As root, prompts twice to set a new password for the user joe, without requiring the old password.

pairs.term: What are the correct steps to remove an unused user account along with its data?
pairs.definition: 1. Find files owned by the account (find / -user username); 2. Expire or disable the account; 3. Back up the files; 4. Remove the files or reassign them to a new owner; 5. Delete the account from the system.

pairs.term: What risk exists if you forget to delete an expired/disabled account?
pairs.definition: A malicious user who gains access could renew the account and then masquerade as a legitimate user, so expired accounts should be removed, not merely disabled.

pairs.term: How is an account expiration date stored in the /etc/shadow file?
pairs.definition: In the eighth field of each record, expressed as the number of days since January 1, 1970 (a large integer, not a readable date).

pairs.term: How do you set a shell variable with the current date in days since January 1, 1970?
pairs.definition: Use the date command to get seconds since 1970 and divide by 86400 (seconds per day): TODAY=$(( $(date --utc +%s) / 86400 )).

pairs.term: usermod -e 2027-01-01 tim
pairs.definition: Sets an expiration date (January 1, 2027) on the tim user account so it cannot be used after that date.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: dnf install selinux-policy-doc
pairs.definition: Installs the selinux-policy-doc package, which provides man pages such as httpd_selinux that show proper file contexts and available Booleans for httpd.

pairs.term: setsebool -P httpd_enable_homedirs true
pairs.definition: Sets the SELinux Boolean permanently (-P) to allow users to share HTML content from their home directories with httpd.

pairs.term: chcon -R --reference=/var/www/html/ /home/*/public_html
pairs.definition: Sets the proper SELinux file context (referenced from /var/www/html) recursively on each user's public_html directory so SELinux allows httpd access. Normally /home/*/www, /home/*/web, and /home/*/public_html already have the httpd_user_content_t context set.

pairs.term: setenforce 0
pairs.definition: Temporarily sets SELinux to permissive mode, logging violations but not preventing them. Useful to test whether SELinux is causing a problem.

pairs.term: setenforce 1
pairs.definition: Temporarily sets SELinux back to enforcing mode after testing in permissive mode.

pairs.term: How do you set SELinux to permissive mode permanently?
pairs.definition: Edit the /etc/sysconfig/selinux file so the SELINUX value is set to SELINUX=permissive. On the next reboot the system is in permissive mode: broken SELinux policies are logged but not prevented (as they would be in enforcing mode).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: dnf install mod_ssl
pairs.definition: Installs the module needed to implement SSL on the web server (mod_ssl.so) and the configuration file for SSL hosts (/etc/httpd/conf.d/ssl.conf). A self-signed certificate and private key are created when the package is installed.

pairs.term: dnf install openssl
pairs.definition: Installs the openssl package used to generate public and private keys for SSL certificates.

pairs.term: openssl genrsa -out server.key 2048
pairs.definition: Generates a 2048-bit RSA private key and saves it to the file server.key. Run in /etc/pki/tls/private.

pairs.term: chmod 600 server.key
pairs.definition: Sets restrictive permissions (read/write for owner only) on the private key file.

pairs.term: openssl genrsa -des3 -out server.key 1024
pairs.definition: Generates an RSA key that is itself encrypted with DES3, prompting for a passphrase. This is a good idea in higher-security environments.

pairs.term: openssl req -new -x509 -nodes -sha1 -days 365 -key /etc/pki/tls/private/server.key -out server.crt
pairs.definition: Generates a self-signed certificate (server.crt) valid for 365 days using server.key, prompting for country, state, locality, organization, common name, and email.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: rpm -qpc httpd-core*rpm
pairs.definition: Lists the configuration files in the httpd-core package, including /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf, /etc/httpd/conf.d/welcome.conf, /etc/httpd/conf/magic, /etc/logrotate.d/httpd, and others.

pairs.term: dnf groupinstall "Web Server"
pairs.definition: Installs the entire Web Server group in Fedora (Basic Web Server group in RHEL), including httpd-core, httpd-manual, mod_ssl, crypto-utils, mod_perl, php, squid, webalizer, and others.

pairs.term: yumdownloader httpd-core
pairs.definition: Downloads the latest version of the httpd-core package to the current directory. The command comes from the dnf-utils package.

pairs.term: rpm -qpi httpd-core*rpm
pairs.definition: Queries the httpd-core RPM package just downloaded for information (Name, Version, Release, Architecture, License, Vendor, etc.).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does the httpd-core package contain?
pairs.definition: The essential httpd binaries needed to run a simple Apache web server, including the Apache daemon (/usr/sbin/httpd) and its related files. On Fedora and RHEL the Apache web server comes in the httpd package.

pairs.term: What is the main Apache configuration file on Fedora/RHEL?
pairs.definition: /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf. In Ubuntu the main configuration file is /etc/apache2/apache2.conf. Configuration is read from start to finish, with most directives processed in the order they are read.

pairs.term: What is the purpose of the /etc/httpd/conf.modules.d directory?
pairs.definition: Apache modules drop configuration files (*.conf) into it. Any file in that directory that ends in .conf is pulled into the main httpd.conf file and used to configure Apache.

pairs.term: What do the welcome.conf and magic files do in the httpd-core package?
pairs.definition: welcome.conf defines the default home page for your website until you add content. The magic file defines rules the server can use to figure out a file's type when the server tries to open it.

pairs.term: What does the /etc/logrotate.d/httpd file do?
pairs.definition: It defines how log files produced by Apache are rotated over time. The /usr/lib/tmpfiles.d/httpd.conf file defines a directory that contains temporary runtime files (no need to change it).

pairs.term: What does the httpd-manual package provide?
pairs.definition: It fills the /var/www/manual directory with Apache documentation manuals. After starting httpd you can access them from a browser on the local machine at http://localhost/manual.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: systemctl enable httpd.service
pairs.definition: Enables the httpd service to start on every reboot.

pairs.term: systemctl start httpd.service
pairs.definition: Starts the httpd service immediately.

pairs.term: systemctl status httpd.service
pairs.definition: Shows the status of the httpd service, including whether it is active (running), the main PID, and the command line (e.g., /usr/sbin/httpd -D FOREGROUND).

pairs.term: chkconfig httpd on
pairs.definition: Older (RHEL 6 and earlier Fedora) way to enable the httpd service to start at boot.

pairs.term: service httpd start
pairs.definition: Older (RHEL 6 and earlier Fedora) way to start the httpd service, which in the newest systems is replaced by systemctl start httpd.service.

pairs.term: ps -ef | grep httpd
pairs.definition: Shows running httpd processes. Output shows root as the parent httpd process and apache as the child worker processes (e.g., /usr/sbin/httpd -e debug -DFOREGROUND).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the gFTP client?
pairs.definition: A graphical FTP client that shows both the local (left) and remote (right) sides of an FTP session. To start it, launch it from the applications menu or run gftp & from the shell. It supports bookmarks of FTP site addresses.

pairs.term: dnf install lftp
pairs.definition: Installs the lftp command-line FTP client.

pairs.term: lftp -u chris localhost
pairs.definition: Connects to the FTP server as user chris using lftp, prompting for the Linux user password and opening an lftp prompt for interactive commands.

pairs.term: dnf install gftp
pairs.definition: Installs the gFTP graphical FTP client.

pairs.term: gftp &
pairs.definition: Starts the gFTP graphical FTP client from the shell in the background.

pairs.term: What does putting an exclamation mark (!) in front of an lftp command do?
pairs.definition: It causes the command to be interpreted by the client system instead of the server. Examples: !pwd shows the current directory on the initiating system (where downloaded files go), !cd changes directories locally, and !ls lists local files.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: setsebool -P samba_enable_home_dirs on
pairs.definition: Turns on the SELinux Boolean that allows Samba to share users' home directories (off by default).

pairs.term: semanage fcontext -l | grep -i samba
pairs.definition: Lists files and directories associated with the Samba service and smbd daemon that have file contexts preset, including samba_etc_t, samba_log_t, and samba_var_t.

pairs.term: semanage fcontext -l | grep -i smb
pairs.definition: Lists preset file context rules related to smb (the smbd daemon).

pairs.term: mkdir /var/mystuff; ls -Zd /var/mystuff
