pairs.term: firewall-cmd --permanent --info-zone=public
pairs.definition: Shows detailed information about the public zone including its allowed services and ports.
UDP port scan of the local loopback address.

pairs.term: firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=nfs
pairs.definition: Permanently adds the NFS service to the default zone.

pairs.term: firewall-cmd --add-service=http
pairs.definition: Temporarily (runtime) opens the http service in the default zone.
TCP Connect scan without ping probes (used when host blocks pings).

pairs.term: systemctl start ufw
pairs.definition: Starts the Uncomplicated Firewall service on Ubuntu.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: auto secure
pairs.definition: Privileged EXEC command that invokes the Cisco AutoSecure feature to assist in securing a Cisco router. AutoSecure enhances router security but does not make the router absolutely secure from all attacks.

pairs.term: show ip ports all
pairs.definition: Privileged EXEC command that displays the open ports on IOS XE devices. Output typically shows only HTTPS (port 443) and DHCP (port 67) listening.

pairs.term: show control-plane host open-ports
pairs.definition: Command used on IOS versions prior to IOS XE to display open ports. Output may show insecure services such as Telnet (port 23) and HTTP (port 80) that should be disabled.

pairs.term: no ip http server
pairs.definition: Global configuration command that disables the insecure HTTP server on a device.

pairs.term: Cisco AutoSecure
pairs.definition: A Cisco IOS feature that can be used to assist in securing Cisco routers. It enhances the security of the router but does not make it absolutely secure from all security attacks. It is invoked with the auto secure command in privileged EXEC mode.

pairs.term: Additional password security steps for routers and switches
pairs.definition: Encrypt all plaintext passwords, set a minimum acceptable password length, deter brute-force password guessing attacks, and disable an inactive privileged EXEC mode access after a specified amount of time.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is endianness?
pairs.definition: The order in which a multi-byte data item (e.g. a short int or int) is stored in memory: most-significant byte first (big-endian) or least-significant byte first (little-endian).

pairs.term: Which architectures are big-endian and which are little-endian?
pairs.definition: Big-endian: Atmel AVR32 and IBM z/Architecture; little-endian: x86.

pairs.term: What is network byte order?
pairs.definition: The common order defined by IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) that computers must use for multi-byte data inside packets, regardless of their own endianness; it is the same as big-endian order.

pairs.term: Why are htons()/htonl()/ntohs()/ntohl() needed in network programs?
pairs.definition: They convert multi-byte data between host byte order and network byte order so that machines with different endianness can interpret packet fields correctly; using them makes code portable.

pairs.term: What does htons() do?
pairs.definition: Converts an unsigned short integer (2 bytes, the 's' in the name) from host byte order to network byte order.

pairs.term: What does ntohl() do?
pairs.definition: Converts an unsigned 4-byte integer (the 'l' in the name means long) from network byte order to host byte order.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is static port forwarding?
pairs.definition: SSH port forwarding where the final destination is fixed when the tunnel is set up, e.g. ssh -L 8000:work:23 seed@apollo.

pairs.term: What is dynamic port forwarding?
pairs.definition: SSH port forwarding where the final destination is not specified at setup; the client supplies it at connect time via a SOCKS handshake. Example: ssh -D 9000 -C seed@home, with the browser configured to use localhost:9000 as a SOCKS proxy.

pairs.term: Why does simply typing localhost:9000 not work with dynamic port forwarding (ssh -D 9000)?
pairs.definition: Because no final destination was provided at setup; the browser must be configured to treat localhost:9000 as a SOCKS proxy, and then you type the real destination in the address bar.

pairs.term: What does 'ssh -R 8000:web-server:80 seed@home' do?
pairs.definition: Creates a reverse SSH tunnel from an inside machine: requests sent to port 8000 on 'home' are forwarded through the tunnel to port 80 of the internal 'web-server', allowing outside users to access an internal website even when incoming SSH is blocked.

pairs.term: When is reverse SSH tunneling needed?
pairs.definition: When an internal website uses a private IP or the firewall blocks all access from outside, and incoming SSH traffic is also blocked, but outgoing SSH is allowed — the inside machine creates the tunnel to the outside (ssh -R).

pairs.term: How does a VPN evade firewalls?
pairs.definition: A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel between a computer inside the network and one outside at the IP layer; since the tunnel traffic is encrypted, firewalls cannot see what is inside and therefore cannot filter it.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is a firewall policy?
pairs.definition: The rules enforced by a firewall, normally defined to provide user control, service control, and direction control over the network traffic.

pairs.term: What is user control in a firewall policy?
pairs.definition: Controls access to data based on the role of the user attempting to access it; typically applied to users inside the firewall perimeter.

pairs.term: What is service control in a firewall policy?
pairs.definition: Access is controlled by the type of service offered by the protected host, enforced on the basis of network address, port number, protocol, etc.

pairs.term: What is direction control in a firewall policy?
pairs.definition: Determines the direction in which requests may be initiated and are allowed to flow — inbound (from the network into the firewall) or outbound (from the firewall to the network).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is a packet filter firewall?
pairs.definition: Makes a decision on each packet based only on the header information without looking at payload or connection state; because it keeps no state it is also called a stateless firewall, and its main advantage is speed.

pairs.term: What is a stateful firewall?
pairs.definition: Tracks the state of traffic by monitoring all connection interactions until the connection closes, maintaining a connection state table to understand the context of packets; some also inspect application data for well-known protocols.

pairs.term: What advantage does a stateful firewall have over a packet filter for a server with many public ports?
pairs.definition: The stateful firewall only allows packets belonging to existing connections, drastically reducing the port range that must be opened and reducing the chances of spoofing.

pairs.term: What are the limitations of an application proxy firewall?
pairs.definition: New proxies must be implemented for new protocols, and because it must read the entire packet it is significantly slower, making it poorly suited for real-time or high-bandwidth applications.

pairs.term: What advantage does an application proxy firewall have regarding IP spoofing?
pairs.definition: It can authenticate users directly rather than depending on network addresses, which reduces the risk of IP spoofing attacks that are easy to launch against a network.

pairs.term: Which layers do packet filters and stateful firewalls inspect up to, versus application firewalls?
pairs.definition: Packet filters and stateful firewalls inspect up to the transport layer; application firewalls inspect up to the application layer.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does MASQUERADE do in the firewall bypass experiment?
pairs.definition: MASQUERADE on VPN Server enp0s3 rewrites the source IP of packets leaving that interface (from 10.4.2.99 to VPN Server IP 10.0.2.69), so the NAT on the path can return reply packets to VPN Server.

pairs.term: Why is the iptables OUTPUT block placed on the user machine itself in the experiment?
pairs.definition: To emulate the egress firewall without a dedicated firewall VM; the user machine plays the role of the firewall blocking its own direct Facebook traffic on the Internet interface.

pairs.term: dig www.facebook.com (run several times)
pairs.definition: Resolves Facebook IP addresses (e.g., 31.13.71.36, 31.13.74.36) so the experiment can block the 31.13.0.0/16 prefix; the addresses are stable over short periods, especially their prefixes.

pairs.term: In the firewall bypass experiment, which IP prefixes are blocked and how were they found?
pairs.definition: 31.13.0.0/16 (Facebook IP prefix). The IPs 31.13.71.36 and 31.13.74.36 were obtained by running dig www.facebook.com several times. A full block would require all Facebook prefixes (AS32934).

pairs.term: Why must the iptables blocking rule be limited to the enp0s3 interface?
pairs.definition: Without specifying an interface, the rule applies to all interfaces including the TUN interface, which would prevent the VPN tunnel application from even getting the packet. Limiting to enp0s3 (the Internet interface) only blocks direct traffic.

pairs.term: How is the NAT problem solved in the firewall bypass experiment?
pairs.definition: Set up a NAT server on VPN Server so packets from 10.4.2.99 always have their source IP replaced by VPN Server IP (10.0.2.69). The command: sudo iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -j MASQUERADE -o enp0s3.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are the extra firewall rule capabilities beyond allow/block?
pairs.definition: Block outbound packets, forward packets between interfaces (routing), port forward, mangle packet headers, and IP masquerading for private networks over a single public IP.

pairs.term: Packet filtering (firewall technique)
pairs.definition: Prevents or allows access based on IP addresses or MAC addresses.

pairs.term: Why should firewall audits consider network components beyond the host?
pairs.definition: Security settings on network components like the server's firewall and the company's routers should all be considered when conducting audit scans.

pairs.term: What are firewalld zones?
pairs.definition: A set of firewall rules selections based on the services you want to share and protection level (e.g., block, dmz, drop, external, public, trusted, work, home, internal).

pairs.term: What is port forwarding?
pairs.definition: Rerouting a packet intended for a selected port to another port on the local system or to a remote system so other locations can handle the request.

pairs.term: Application filtering (firewall technique)
pairs.definition: Prevents or allows access by specific application types based on port numbers.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does 'the response packet should carry the same payload data as that in the request' mean for the echo design?
pairs.definition: The heartbeat receiver must copy the payload bytes back unchanged; it is this echo-construction step (memcpy) that the Heartbleed attack abuses.

pairs.term: What is the record length 0x0029 in the TLS record header?
pairs.definition: The size of the TLS record payload (excluding the record header): 3 bytes heartbeat header + 22 bytes payload + 16 bytes padding = 41 (0x29) bytes.

pairs.term: What is the Heartbleed bug?
pairs.definition: An implementation flaw in OpenSSL's TLS/SSL heartbeat extension that allows an attacker to read (over-read) data beyond a heartbeat request's payload from the server's memory. It is CVE-2014-0160, discovered/fixed in 2014.

pairs.term: What is a TLS record?
pairs.definition: The framing unit of the TLS protocol. A Heartbeat message is a special type of TLS record, so it starts with a TLS record header.

pairs.term: Why may repeated Heartbleed attacks return different data?
pairs.definition: Each request packet may be stored at a different memory address, so the bytes adjacent to (beyond) the payload differ between runs.

pairs.term: Why does the attack 'deviate from the protocol' succeed against the vulnerable implementation?
pairs.definition: The implementation assumed declared payload size equals actual size and never validated it; deviation (lying about the length) exploits that unchecked trust.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: $ sudo apt-get upgrade
pairs.definition: Installs the updated packages (including the fixed OpenSSL library), closing the Heartbleed vulnerability.

pairs.term: What is the recommended fix for the Heartbleed bug?
pairs.definition: Update the system's OpenSSL library: run 'sudo apt-get update' followed by 'sudo apt-get upgrade' (Ubuntu).

pairs.term: What check does the patched OpenSSL code add before copying the payload?
pairs.definition: It compares the declared payload length plus overhead (1 + 2 + payload + 16) against the actual request length s->s3->rrec.length; if it is larger, the function returns 0 and silently discards the packet per RFC 6520 section 4.

pairs.term: What does RFC 6520 section 4 specify for malformed heartbeat messages?
pairs.definition: They should be silently discarded (the patched code returns 0 with no reply).

pairs.term: Why are there still many vulnerable systems after Heartbleed was fixed?
pairs.definition: Either they have not been patched, or they have no mechanism to get patched.

pairs.term: Which exact check in the fixed OpenSSL code rejects oversized declared lengths?
pairs.definition: if (1 + 2 + payload + 16 > s->s3->rrec.length) return 0; - the 1 is the type field size, 2 the length field size, 16 the minimum padding.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How much faster is C than Scapy for sending packets?
pairs.definition: In the chapter's informal test, sending 1000 UDP packets took 0.25 s with C (~4000 pkts/s) vs 9.4 s with Scapy (~106 pkts/s) — C is about 37 times faster.

pairs.term: Why must the UDP checksum be set to 0 in the Scapy-generated template?
pairs.definition: A zero UDP checksum is treated by receivers as a missing checksum and the packet is accepted; a nonzero checksum that is incorrect causes the packet to be discarded. TCP and ICMP checksums are strictly verified, so they must be recalculated if modified.

pairs.term: In the C hybrid send program, what fields are modified and at which byte offsets?
pairs.definition: The source IP is written at offset 12 (memcpy(ip+12, &src_ip, 4)) and the source port at offset 20 (memcpy(ip+20, &src_port, 2)).

pairs.term: Why is the hybrid approach needed for the Kaminsky (DNS) attack?
pairs.definition: The attack must send many spoofed packets in a very short time window, and Scapy is too slow; the hybrid approach cuts the time needed while keeping packet construction easy.

pairs.term: What is the hybrid approach to fast packet spoofing?
pairs.definition: Use Scapy to construct a packet template (with checksums set to 0) and save it to a file, then load the template into a C program that modifies only a few fields (e.g. source IP and source port) and sends many packets via a raw socket.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What must be present to build loadable kernel modules?
pairs.definition: A pre-built kernel with its configuration and header files, typically under /usr/src; the makefile uses make -C /lib/modules/$(shell uname -r)/build M=$(PWD) modules.

pairs.term: sudo insmod telnetFilter.ko
pairs.definition: Loads the telnet-filter kernel module into the running kernel.

pairs.term: sudo rmmod telnetFilter
pairs.definition: Removes the telnet-filter module, restoring normal telnet functionality.

pairs.term: lsmod | grep kMod
pairs.definition: Lists loaded kernel modules and filters for kMod to verify the module is inserted.

pairs.term: dmesg
pairs.definition: Shows the kernel log buffer, e.g. 'Registering a Telnet filter' and 'Dropping telnet packet to 10.0.2.5'.

pairs.term: What are loadable kernel modules?
pairs.definition: Pieces of code that can be loaded and unloaded on-demand at runtime into the kernel; they do not run as processes but are executed in the kernel on behalf of the current process.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Which netfilter hooks are on the packet-outgoing path?
pairs.definition: NF_IP_LOCAL_OUT (first hook for locally generated packets) and NF_IP_POST_ROUTING (before leaving the host).

pairs.term: What are the five IPv4 netfilter hooks?
pairs.definition: NF_IP_PRE_ROUTING (before routing), NF_IP_LOCAL_IN (packets destined for the host), NF_IP_FORWARD (packets forwarded to other hosts), NF_IP_LOCAL_OUT (packets generated locally), and NF_IP_POST_ROUTING (before packets leave the host).

pairs.term: Which netfilter hook is hit by all incoming packets before any routing decision?
pairs.definition: NF_IP_PRE_ROUTING — all incoming packets, except those caused by promiscuous mode, hit this hook first.

pairs.term: Which netfilter hook is very useful for implementing a firewall?
pairs.definition: NF_IP_FORWARD — packets that are forwarded to other hosts reach this hook.

pairs.term: Where is Source Network Address Translation (SNAT) implemented in the netfilter hooks?
pairs.definition: At the NF_IP_POST_ROUTING hook, when a packet (forwarded or generated) is going out of the host.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Reconnaissance attack
pairs.definition: An attack that involves discovery and mapping of systems, services, or vulnerabilities. Its objective is to discover and map systems.

pairs.term: Three types of reconnaissance attacks
pairs.definition: Internet queries, ping sweeps, and port scans.

pairs.term: Ping sweeps (reconnaissance)
pairs.definition: The threat actor initiates a ping sweep to determine which IP addresses are active. A ping sweep tool such as fping or gping is used to systematically ping all network addresses in a given range or subnet.

pairs.term: Port scans (reconnaissance)
pairs.definition: The threat actor performs a port scan on the discovered active IP addresses, the third step after internet queries and ping sweeps.

pairs.term: Four types of access attacks
pairs.definition: Password attacks, trust exploitation, port redirection, and man-in-the-middle attacks.

pairs.term: Methods threat actors can use for password attacks
pairs.definition: Brute-force attacks, Trojan horse attacks, and packet sniffers.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Why is UDP scanning slow compared to TCP?
pairs.definition: UDP is connectionless and sends packets to every port; the scan must wait, often with reduced timeouts, because services respond slowly or not at all.

pairs.term: What does 'closed' and 'unfiltered' mean in nmap?
pairs.definition: closed means accessible but no service waiting (still indicates a server exists); unfiltered means nmap cannot decide open or closed.

pairs.term: Why should a TCP Connect scan be paired with a UDP scan for audits?
pairs.definition: Some services (like rpcbind on port 111) communicate over both TCP and UDP, so both scans are needed to build a complete service list.

pairs.term: What is the default nmap scan and its command?
pairs.definition: The TCP SYN scan is the default and slots scan style; its explicit command is nmap -sS ip_address.

pairs.term: What does the rpcbind service do?
pairs.definition: The Remote Procedure Call (RPC) service, listening on port 111 over both TCP and UDP; it maps RPC services to ports.

pairs.term: Why should you scan from multiple locations during an audit?
pairs.definition: To compare what the server looks like from inside vs outside, since malicious activity often originates from internal employees or those who already penetrated defenses; scans from the server, another same-network server, and from outside.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the BSD Packet Filter (BPF)?
pairs.definition: A Unix facility that lets a user-space program attach a filter to a socket, telling the kernel to discard unwanted packets as early as possible instead of delivering them to the sniffer application.

pairs.term: Why is kernel-level BPF filtering more efficient than filtering in the application?
pairs.definition: Without it, the system must process and deliver every unwanted packet from the kernel to the sniffer application; BPF discards unwanted packets early, saving significant time when there are many unwanted packets.

pairs.term: How is a compiled BPF filter attached to a socket?
pairs.definition: Using setsockopt(sock, SOL_SOCKET, SO_ATTACH_FILTER, &bpf, sizeof(bpf)).

pairs.term: What is the BPF Pseudo-Machine?
pairs.definition: A kernel-level state machine specially designed for packet filtering; it interprets the compiled BPF filter pseudo-code attached to a socket.

pairs.term: What is a Network Interface Card (NIC)?
pairs.definition: The physical or logical link between a machine and a network; each NIC has a hardware address called the MAC address.

pairs.term: What is the MAC address?
pairs.definition: The hardware address of a NIC, used to identify the card on a local network (Ethernet/WiFi).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How do you compute the actual IP header length of a captured packet?
pairs.definition: int ip_header_len = ip->iph_ihl * 4; the IHL (iph_ihl) field stores the header length in 32-bit words, and must be used instead of sizeof(struct ipheader) because some headers contain an extra IP options field.

pairs.term: What is a raw socket (for sniffing)?
pairs.definition: A special socket type through which the kernel passes a copy of a packet, including the link-layer header, to the application first, before passing it further up the protocol stack. The raw socket does not intercept the packet; it simply gets a copy.

pairs.term: What fields does the ethheader struct contain?
pairs.definition: Destination MAC (ether_dhost, 6 bytes), source MAC (ether_shost, 6 bytes), and protocol type (ether_type, e.g. IP, ARP, RARP).

pairs.term: What does the protocol argument htons(ETH_P_ALL) do when creating a raw socket?
pairs.definition: It indicates that packets of all protocols should be passed to the raw socket; setting htons(ETH_P_IP) would pass only IP packets.

pairs.term: What does inet_ntoa() do?
pairs.definition: Converts an IP address in network byte order to a dotted-quad string, used to print ip->iph_sourceip and ip->iph_destip.

pairs.term: How is promiscuous mode enabled on a raw socket?
pairs.definition: With setsockopt(sock, SOL_PACKET, PACKET_ADD_MEMBERSHIP, &mr, sizeof(mr)) where mr.mr_type = PACKET_MR_PROMISC.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What fields must an attacker set in a TCP session hijacking attack?
pairs.definition: Another user's IP address in the IP header plus the correct sequence numbers and port numbers in the TCP header.

pairs.term: What does the IP length field (iph_len) contain?
pairs.definition: The total IP packet length (header plus data), e.g. sizeof(struct ipheader) + sizeof(struct udpheader) + data_len.

pairs.term: What must a DNS cache poisoning spoofed reply look like?
pairs.definition: It must carry the legitimate DNS server's IP address in the source IP field, and the DNS information in the DNS header and payload must be constructed correctly.

pairs.term: What is Scapy?
pairs.definition: A powerful Python packet manipulation tool that can forge or decode packets of many protocols, send them on the wire, capture them, and match requests and replies.

pairs.term: What does socket(AF_INET, SOCK_RAW, IPPROTO_RAW) create?
pairs.definition: A raw socket for sending packets in which the application supplies the entire IP header; IPPROTO_RAW implies that IP_HDRINCL is enabled (the system will not construct an IP header).

pairs.term: What does IP_HDRINCL tell the kernel?
pairs.definition: That the IP header is included in the packet provided by the application, so the OS should keep the header information as-is instead of filling it in.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Examples of strong passwords and why they are strong
pairs.definition: b67n42d39c combines alphanumeric characters; 12^h u4@1p7 combines alphanumeric characters and symbols and includes a space.

pairs.term: security passwords min-length length
pairs.definition: Global configuration command that ensures all configured passwords are a minimum specified length. For example, security passwords min-length 8 requires any new password to be at least eight characters.

pairs.term: exec-timeout minutes seconds
pairs.definition: Line configuration command (applied on console, auxiliary, and vty lines) that automatically disconnects an inactive user after a specified idle time. For example, exec-timeout 5 30 disconnects an idle vty user after 5 minutes and 30 seconds.

pairs.term: Examples of weak passwords and why they are weak
pairs.definition: secret (simple dictionary password), smith (maiden name of mother), toyota (make of a car), bob1967 (name and birthday of the user), Blueleaf23 (simple words and numbers).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Hardware threats (physical security class)
pairs.definition: Physical damage to servers, routers, switches, the cabling plant, and workstations.

pairs.term: Environmental threats (physical security class)
pairs.definition: Temperature extremes (too hot or too cold) or humidity extremes (too damp or too dry).

pairs.term: Electrical threats (physical security class)
pairs.definition: Voltage spikes, insufficient supply voltage (brownouts), unconditioned power (noise), and total power loss.

pairs.term: Maintenance threats (physical security class)
pairs.definition: Poor handling of key electrical components (electrostatic discharge), lack of critical spare parts, poor cabling, and poor labeling.

pairs.term: Four classes of physical threats
pairs.definition: Hardware threats, environmental threats, electrical threats, and maintenance threats.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Why SSH is recommended over Telnet
pairs.definition: Telnet simplifies remote device access, but it is not secure because data contained in a Telnet packet is transmitted unencrypted. Secure Shell (SSH) provides encryption for secure remote access, so it is highly recommended to enable SSH on devices.

pairs.term: transport input ssh
pairs.definition: Line configuration command for vty lines that enables only SSH inbound sessions (by default, no input session is allowed on vty lines). Multiple protocols can be specified, e.g., transport input ssh telnet.

pairs.term: ip domain name name
pairs.definition: Global configuration command that configures the IP domain name of the network, required before generating RSA keys for SSH. For example, ip domain name span.com.

pairs.term: username name secret password
pairs.definition: Global configuration command that creates or verifies a local database entry. The secret parameter encrypts the password using MD5. For example, username Bob secret cisco.

pairs.term: login local
pairs.definition: Line configuration command that authenticates the vty lines against the local database created with the username command.

pairs.term: ssh -D 9000 -C seed@home
pairs.definition: Creates a dynamic SOCKS proxy tunnel on local port 9000 to 'home' with compression (-C); the browser is configured to use localhost:9000 as a SOCKS proxy.

pairs.term: ssh -R 8000:web-server:80 seed@home
pairs.definition: Creates a reverse SSH tunnel from an inside machine: requests to port 8000 on 'home' are forwarded to port 80 of the internal 'web-server', letting outsiders reach the internal website.

pairs.term: telnet localhost 8000
pairs.definition: Connects to the local SSH tunnel endpoint (port 8000) so the telnet traffic travels through the tunnel to the real destination.

pairs.term: ssh -L 8000:work:23 seed@apollo
pairs.definition: Establishes a static SSH tunnel: forwards local port 8000 to port 23 (telnet) on machine 'work' through apollo, evading the ingress firewall.

pairs.term: ssh -L 8000:www.facebook.com:80 seed@home
pairs.definition: Establishes an SSH tunnel from inside the company to 'home', forwarding local port 8000 to Facebook's port 80 to evade egress filtering.

pairs.term: How do you install Scapy for Python 3?
pairs.definition: sudo pip3 install scapy; if pip3 is missing, install it with sudo apt-get install python3-pip or via curl -O https://bootstrap.pypa.io/get-pip.py followed by sudo python3 get-pip.py.

pairs.term: curl -O https://bootstrap.pypa.io/get-pip.py; sudo python3 get-pip.py
pairs.definition: Alternative way to install pip3 by downloading and running the get-pip bootstrap script.

pairs.term: What is the first line of every Scapy program?
pairs.definition: from scapy.all import * — it imports all of Scapy's modules.

pairs.term: sudo python3
pairs.definition: Starts Python 3 interactive mode as root so Scapy commands can be run one line at a time (root is required for spoofing).

pairs.term: What does sniff(filter='icmp', prn=print_pkt) do?
pairs.definition: Starts capturing packets matching the BPF filter 'icmp' and invokes the callback print_pkt for each captured packet.

pairs.term: sudo ./mycode.py
pairs.definition: Runs a Scapy program directly as root after making it executable.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: TLS (Transport Layer Security)
pairs.definition: Successor to SSL. Provides encrypted, authenticated communications over TCP. Handshake protocol negotiates cipher suite, exchanges keys, authenticates peers. Record protocol provides encryption. TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) removes weak algorithms.

pairs.term: IPsec (IP Security)
pairs.definition: Suite of protocols for secure IP communications. Two modes: Transport (protects payload) and Tunnel (protects entire packet). ESP provides encryption+authentication. AH provides authentication only. Uses IKE for key exchange.

pairs.term: IKE (Internet Key Exchange)
pairs.definition: Protocol for establishing security associations (SAs) in IPsec. IKEv1: two phases (main/aggressive mode + quick mode). IKEv2: simpler, single exchange, more resilient. Uses Diffie-Hellman for key agreement.

pairs.term: Kerberos
pairs.definition: Network authentication protocol (MIT, 1980s). Uses ticket-based system with Key Distribution Center (KDC). Provides SSO. Three components: Authentication Server (AS), Ticket Granting Server (TGS), Client. Uses symmetric encryption.

pairs.term: RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service)
pairs.definition: AAA protocol for network access. Uses UDP ports 1812/1813. Client-server: Network Access Server (NAS) forwards credentials to RADIUS server. Supports PAP, CHAP, EAP authentication.

pairs.term: EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol)
pairs.definition: Authentication framework used in network access. Supports multiple methods: EAP-TLS (certificate-based), EAP-TTLS (tunneled), EAP-PEAP (protected), EAP-MD5. Defined in RFC 3748.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Identity theft (as a network threat)
pairs.definition: A form of information theft in which personal information is stolen for the purpose of taking over someone's identity. Using this information, a threat actor can obtain legal documents, apply for credit, and make unauthorized online purchases.

pairs.term: Disruption of service (as a network threat)
pairs.definition: A threat that involves preventing legitimate users from accessing services to which they are entitled. Examples include denial-of-service (DoS) attacks on servers, network devices, or network communications links.

pairs.term: Four types of threats that may arise after a threat actor gains access to a network
pairs.definition: Information theft, data loss and manipulation, identity theft, and disruption of service.

pairs.term: Threat actor
pairs.definition: An intruder who gains access to a network by modifying software or exploiting software vulnerabilities.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does the simple iptables firewall allow?
pairs.definition: Incoming TCP to ports 22 (ssh) and 80 (http), all outgoing TCP, loopback traffic, and DNS (UDP port 53) queries/replies; the default policy is set to DROP for INPUT, OUTPUT, and FORWARD.

pairs.term: Why does the simple firewall need a loopback rule?
pairs.definition: Programs on the same system communicate using the loopback pseudo-interface (127.0.0.1); without -I INPUT 1 -i lo -j ACCEPT, local inter-process communication would be blocked.

pairs.term: Why are four DNS rules needed when the local DNS server runs on 127.0.1.1?
pairs.definition: Because the DNS server is on the local host, the firewall must allow both directions on both chains: OUTPUT dport 53, INPUT sport 53, OUTPUT sport 53, and INPUT dport 53.

pairs.term: What does sudo iptables -L do?
pairs.definition: Lists the current firewall rules for each chain (INPUT, FORWARD, OUTPUT) with their targets, protocols, sources, destinations, and policies.

pairs.term: What is the effect of 'sudo iptables -P INPUT DROP'?
pairs.definition: Sets the default policy of the INPUT chain to DROP, so packets not matching an explicit allow rule are dropped.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the conntrack connection state RELATED?
pairs.definition: A special state that establishes relationships among different connections; e.g. in FTP the control traffic (port 21) is ESTABLISHED while the data-transfer traffic (high port) is RELATED.

pairs.term: What is the conntrack connection state INVALID?
pairs.definition: Used for packets that do not follow the expected behavior of a connection.

pairs.term: Why is allowing all outgoing TCP traffic dangerous on a network of systems?
pairs.definition: An attacker who compromises an internal host can exfiltrate data over TCP: even though incoming TCP is blocked except to ssh/http, outgoing TCP packets are permitted, which is sufficient for data exfiltration.

pairs.term: How do you restrict outgoing TCP to established connections only?
pairs.definition: Replace the allow-all outgoing TCP rule with: sudo iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT.

pairs.term: Why does telnet out of a machine fail with the stateful OUTPUT rule above?
pairs.definition: New outgoing telnet packets are in the NEW state, but the rule only allows ESTABLISHED,RELATED, so the initial telnet connection packets are all blocked.

pairs.term: What is a connection state in the context of a firewall?
pairs.definition: It signifies whether a given packet is part of an existing flow or not; it differs from TCP connection states and applies to connection-oriented (TCP) and connection-less (UDP, ICMP) protocols alike.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Creating a TCP socket in C
pairs.definition: int sockfd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, IPPROTO_TCP) creates a TCP socket.

pairs.term: The sockaddr_in fields used to fill destination information
pairs.definition: server.sin_family = AF_INET, server.sin_addr.s_addr = inet_addr("10.0.2.5"), and server.sin_port = htons(8080) specify the address family, IP address, and port number.

pairs.term: connect() system call
pairs.definition: connect(sockfd, (struct sockaddr*) &server, sizeof(struct sockaddr_in)) establishes the TCP connection to the destination server.

pairs.term: How to send data through a TCP connection normally
pairs.definition: Use the write() system call, e.g., write(sockfd, data, strlen(data)); the reverse shell instead redirects with dup2() so printf()/scanf() use the socket.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Is a TUN interface persistent?
pairs.definition: No. The interface is transient: it is destroyed when the process that created it terminates. (Persistent TUN devices exist but are out of scope.)

pairs.term: Why does the output of reading from the TUN interface start with the byte 0x45?
pairs.definition: 0x45 is the first octet of most IPv4 packets (version 4, header length 5), confirming that the TUN interface delivers entire IP packets including the header.

pairs.term: Why is a physical NIC connected to physical media while a TUN/TAP interface connects to a user-space program?
pairs.definition: A physical NIC connects a computer to a physical network. TUN/TAP interfaces connect a computer to a user-space program; they act as a simple point-to-point device where one endpoint is a program that pretends to be a computer.

pairs.term: How do you get a packet from a hexdump back into the kernel via the TUN interface?
pairs.definition: Convert the hexdump to binary with xxd -r (saving to packetfile), then write it to the TUN file descriptor with cat packetfile >& 3. The kernel treats it as an incoming packet.

pairs.term: Why was the loopback device given as an example of a virtual network interface?
pairs.definition: Traffic sent to the loopback device is passed back to the kernel as if the packet comes from a network; it is entirely virtual, illustrating what a virtual network interface is.

pairs.term: ifconfig -a
pairs.definition: Lists all network interfaces including inactive ones (the -a option is needed because a newly created TUN interface is not yet active).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: telnet 10.0.2.5
pairs.definition: Attempts a telnet connection to 10.0.2.5; fails when the telnet-filter module or firewall blocks port 23, succeeds after it is removed.

pairs.term: telnet 10.0.2.6
pairs.definition: Tests the simple firewall: blocked because the firewall only allows ports 22 and 80.
Downloads the default page over HTTP (port 80), succeeding because the firewall allows port 80.

pairs.term: su bob
pairs.definition: Switches to user bob, used to verify the owner-module rule only affects user seed.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are the three steps of a UDP server program?
pairs.definition: 1) Create a socket with socket(AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM, IPPROTO_UDP); 2) bind the socket to a port and IP address using bind(); 3) receive packets in a loop with recvfrom().

pairs.term: What does INADDR_ANY mean when binding a socket?
pairs.definition: It binds the socket to all available IP addresses on the machine (a computer may have one IP per network interface card).

pairs.term: What are the three steps of a UDP client program?
pairs.definition: 1) Create a socket; 2) provide destination information (IP address, port) in a sockaddr_in struct; 3) send data with sendto().

pairs.term: What is netcat (nc) and what does nc -luv 9090 do?
pairs.definition: netcat is a network utility; nc -luv 9090 starts a UDP server (-u) on port 9090 with verbose (-v) output, listening on 0.0.0.0.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is a private network?
pairs.definition: A communication channel established between a group of computers owned by an organization or home to share information among themselves. It uses private IP addresses (10.0.0.0/8, 192.168.0.0/16) or firewall rules to block unauthorized outside access.

pairs.term: What three protection guarantees does being private provide?
pairs.definition: (1) User authenticated - users of a private network are authorized and their identities verified; (2) Content protected - communication cannot be seen from outside; (3) Integrity preserved - nobody outside can insert fake data or modify existing data.

pairs.term: What is the transparency criterion for VPN?
pairs.definition: Regardless of whether an application supports secure communication, its communication with private-network hosts is always secured. The best way to achieve transparency is to do it at the IP packet level.

pairs.term: What is IPSec Tunneling Mode?
pairs.definition: An IPSec mode where the entire original IP packet is encapsulated into a new IP packet with a new header, done inside the IP layer. It is designed to implement IP tunneling and has been used to build VPNs.

pairs.term: Why is TLS/SSL tunneling becoming more popular than IPSec tunneling?
pairs.definition: It is implemented inside an application rather than inside the IP layer in the kernel. Application-level solutions take complexity out of the kernel and are much easier to update than updating operating systems.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Why can a VPN packet not travel directly with its original IP header over the Internet?
pairs.definition: Routers cannot read or modify an encrypted IP header, but they do need to change the time-to-live field and the checksum. Encapsulating the protected packet inside a new IP packet (tunneling) lets routers process the outer header normally.

pairs.term: What are the three main tasks of the VPN client and server?
pairs.definition: (1) Establish a secure tunnel between them; (2) forward IP packets that need to go to the other private network through this tunnel; (3) after receiving an IP packet from the other end, release it into the private network so it reaches its final destination.

pairs.term: What mutual authentication is needed before establishing a TLS/SSL VPN tunnel?
pairs.definition: The server authenticates the client (password or other credentials) to ensure the client may join; the client authenticates the server (usually via public-key certificate) so it does not send passwords or traffic to a wrong server.

pairs.term: How does a packet from U to V get to the VPN client first?
pairs.definition: Via routing. Both private networks are configured as different subnets (e.g., client side 10.0.7.0/24, server side 10.0.8.0/24); routers are set up so all 10.0.8.0/24-bound traffic arrives at VPN Client and all 10.0.7.0/24-bound traffic arrives at VPN Server.

pairs.term: Why is a TLS/SSL channel alone not yet an IP tunnel?
pairs.definition: The TLS/SSL channel is a secure channel between the client and server applications, but it is what goes inside the channel that makes it an IP tunnel: whole IP packets placed as the payload, creating an IP-packet-inside-an-IP-packet structure.

pairs.term: What properties does the TLS/SSL channel provide for tunnel traffic?
pairs.definition: Encryption (data is encrypted) and integrity protection using a Message Authentication Code (MAC) to prevent adversaries from tampering with the data.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What port and protocol does the book simplified VPN tunnel use?
pairs.definition: A UDP-based tunnel on port 55555 (PORT_NUMBER). The server binds a UDP socket and accepts whoever sends the first UDP request (peerAddr). The book omits TLS/SSL encryption, authentication, and error checking for simplicity.

pairs.term: What does tunSelected() do?
pairs.definition: When the TUN interface has data, it reads an IP packet from tunfd with read() and sends it (after encryption, omitted here) as the payload of a UDP packet to peerAddr via sendto() - from TUN to tunnel.

pairs.term: What does socketSelected() do?
pairs.definition: When the socket has data, it receives a UDP packet with recvfrom(), extracts the encapsulated IP packet (decryption omitted), and injects it into the kernel via write(tunfd, ...) - from tunnel to TUN.

pairs.term: In the book UDP server, how is the tunnel partner established?
pairs.definition: The server binds its UDP socket to port 55555 and blocks on recvfrom(); the first UDP request (a hello message from the client) is stored in peerAddr, so the server only supports one tunnel with whoever connects first.

pairs.term: What is the purpose of the hello message in connectToUDPServer()?
pairs.definition: The client sends a hello message via sendto() to the server to establish the tunnel; the server's recvfrom() returns once this hello arrives, letting the server learn the client's peerAddr.

pairs.term: Why does the VPN program use select() instead of polling?
pairs.definition: Polling wastes CPU because the process keeps running in an idle loop when there is no data. select() blocks the process until data are available on one of the monitored file descriptors, so it does not waste CPU when idle.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Why must packets from Host U to Host V use the TUN interface IP as source?
pairs.definition: Because the source IP of a packet is decided by which network interface sends it out. Packets to Host V go out via tun0, so the source IP is 10.4.2.99 (the address assigned to tun0).

pairs.term: sudo route add -net 10.4.2.0/24 gw 192.168.60.5 enp0s3 (on Host V)
pairs.definition: Routes all 10.4.2.0/24 traffic from Host V toward VPN Server (192.168.60.5) via enp0s3, so reply packets return through the VPN tunnel.

pairs.term: What routing must be added on Host V so replies return through the tunnel?
pairs.definition: Host V must route all 10.4.2.0/24 traffic toward the tunnel (VPN Server), since reply packets are destined to 10.4.2.99. Command: sudo route add -net 10.4.2.0/24 gw 192.168.60.5 enp0s3. Replies must go back through the same tunnel or they are not protected.

pairs.term: Which interface on VPN Server is connected to the emulated Internet, and which to the private network?
pairs.definition: The NAT Network adapter (already has an IP) connects to the emulated Internet; enp0s8 is attached to the Internal Network and gets the static IP 192.168.60.1. Host V connects to the Internal Network via enp0s3 with IP 192.168.60.6.

pairs.term: Why does VPN Server need two network interfaces in the experiment?
pairs.definition: One interface (NAT Network) connects to the emulated Internet; the other (enp0s8, Internal Network, 192.168.60.1) connects to the private network where Host V lives. VPN Server bridges the two.

pairs.term: Which IP prefix is used for the tunnel network and what addresses are assigned at each end?
pairs.definition: 10.4.2.0/24. VPN Server tun0 gets 10.4.2.5 and VPN Client tun0 gets 10.4.2.99. Packets through the tunnel carry the source IP of the interface they leave by (10.4.2.99 on the client).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are the two SEED labs for this chapter?
pairs.definition: Bypassing Firewall using VPN, and the comprehensive VPN Lab (covering VPN, PKI, and TLS programming; Tasks 1 and 2 focus on building a non-encrypted VPN tunnel).

pairs.term: What two parts does a real VPN implementation consist of?
pairs.definition: Building a tunnel and securing the tunnel. The book code only covers building the (plaintext) tunnel; real-world VPNs implement the tunnel on top of TLS. Readers combine the VPN code with Chapter 25 TLS code to get a protected tunnel.

pairs.term: What are the two representative VPN tunneling techniques and which is preferred?
pairs.definition: IPSec Tunneling and TLS/SSL Tunneling. TLS/SSL (application-level) is becoming more popular and is technically better, largely because it is easier to update than kernel-level IPSec.

pairs.term: What is the enabling technology of TLS/SSL VPN?
pairs.definition: TUN/TAP, which allows building an IP tunnel at the transport layer: a user-space tunnel application exchanges whole IP packets with the kernel through a virtual TUN interface, while TLS/SSL secures the tunnel between the two ends.

pairs.term: What is the security guarantee of the book VPN code alone?
pairs.definition: None for confidentiality: the book code only builds the (unencrypted) tunnel and explicitly omits encryption and authentication. Real VPNs build the tunnel on top of TLS/SSL to protect the data.

pairs.term: Why is OpenVPN mentioned but not used in the lab?
pairs.definition: OpenVPN is an existing sophisticated VPN product that hides technical details; the book builds its own simple VPN so readers can see what is actually going on under the hood.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: When the ICMP echo reply returns and is written to the client tun0, why does the ping program receive it?
pairs.definition: The kernel sees the destination IP 10.4.2.99, which is the client's own tun0 address, so it passes the ICMP echo reply up to the ping program.

pairs.term: Why does telnet echo each typed character back to the client?
pairs.definition: Telnet echoes characters: when the server receives a character it echoes it back to the client, which prints it. If a character cannot reach the server, it is not printed, which is why telnet appears frozen when the tunnel breaks.

pairs.term: Why do characters typed blindly into telnet show up after the tunnel is reconnected?
pairs.definition: The typed characters are not lost; they are buffered and TCP retransmits them. Once the tunnel is restored, the retransmitted characters reach the telnet server, which echoes them back, and they suddenly appear on the client.

pairs.term: What two commands are used to test the VPN after setup?
pairs.definition: ping 192.168.60.6 (ICMP over the tunnel) and telnet 192.168.60.6 (TCP over the tunnel), both from Host U to Host V. Before the VPN is up, Host V is unreachable.

pairs.term: Why must reply packets go back through the same VPN tunnel?
pairs.definition: If reply packets take an arbitrary route, they will not be protected by the tunnel. The return trip mirrors the forward trip: replies are routed toward VPN Server and into its TUN interface, then tunneled back to the client.
From Host U, tests ICMP connectivity to Host V over the VPN tunnel; replies are received only after the VPN is set up.

pairs.definition: Many products have default settings that create or enable holes in security.

pairs.term: Configuration vulnerability: misconfigured network equipment
pairs.definition: Misconfigurations of equipment can cause significant security problems. For example, misconfigured access lists, routing protocols, or SNMP community strings can create or enable holes in security.

pairs.term: Policy vulnerability: lack of written security policy
pairs.definition: A security policy cannot be consistently applied or enforced if it is not written down.

pairs.term: Policy vulnerability: politics
pairs.definition: Political battles and turf wars can make it difficult to implement a consistent security policy.

pairs.term: Policy vulnerability: lack of authentication continuity
pairs.definition: Poorly chosen, easily cracked, or default passwords can allow unauthorized access to a network.

pairs.term: Vulnerability
pairs.definition: The degree of weakness in a network or device. Some degree of vulnerability is inherent in routers, switches, desktops, servers, and even security devices. Typically, the network devices under attack are the endpoints, such as servers and desktop computers.

pairs.term: What is the mangle table and which chains does it contain?
pairs.definition: The table for packet content modification; it contains chains in all five positions (PREROUTING, INPUT, FORWARD, OUTPUT, POSTROUTING).

pairs.term: sudo iptables -I INPUT 1 -i lo -j ACCEPT
pairs.definition: Inserts a rule at the first position of the INPUT chain accepting all packets bound for the loopback (lo) interface.

pairs.term: How do iptables chains map to netfilter hooks?
pairs.definition: The FORWARD chain is enforced at the NF_IP_FORWARD hook, INPUT at NF_IP_LOCAL_IN, OUTPUT at NF_IP_LOCAL_OUT, PREROUTING at NF_IP_PRE_ROUTING, and POSTROUTING at NF_IP_POST_ROUTING.

pairs.term: sudo iptables -A OUTPUT -p udp --dport 53 -j ACCEPT
pairs.definition: Allows outgoing UDP DNS queries (destination port 53).

pairs.term: What happens if no rule in a chain matches a packet?
pairs.definition: The chain's default policy is enforced (ACCEPT or DROP).

pairs.term: sudo iptables -A INPUT -p udp --sport 53 -j ACCEPT
pairs.definition: Allows incoming UDP packets whose source port is 53 (DNS replies from a local or remote DNS server).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are iptables extensions/modules?
pairs.definition: Optional modules that extend iptables functionality; many are not in the standard kernel and must be installed. Examples are conntrack (connection-based rules) and owner (user/group-based rules).

pairs.term: What does the conntrack module do?
pairs.definition: Provides connection tracking, letting iptables specify rules based on connections (a set of packets) instead of individual packets; it is used to build stateful firewalls.

pairs.term: What does the owner module do and on which chain does it mainly work?
pairs.definition: It matches packets based on the user/group ID of the process that created them; it mainly works on the OUTPUT chain because for incoming packets (and kernel-generated packets like ICMP responses) there is no owner information.

pairs.term: Give an example of an owner-module rule.
pairs.definition: sudo iptables -A OUTPUT -m owner --uid-owner 1000 -j DROP drops any packet generated by a program run by user with UID 1000.

pairs.term: tcpdump -i eth0 -nn 'tcp port 80'
pairs.definition: Capture HTTP traffic on eth0 without name resolution (-nn). Display packets in real-time. Filter expression: TCP port 80. Useful for troubleshooting firewall rules.

pairs.term: tcpdump -i eth0 -w capture.pcap -s 0
pairs.definition: Capture full packets (-s 0 = snaplen unlimited) to file for offline analysis. Capture file can be opened in Wireshark for deep protocol inspection.

pairs.term: tcpdump -i eth0 'icmp[icmptype]=8'
pairs.definition: Capture only ICMP echo requests (ping). Can detect Smurf attacks or ICMP tunneling. ICMP type 8 = echo request, type 0 = echo reply.

pairs.term: tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn|tcp-rst) != 0'
pairs.definition: Capture only TCP SYN and RST packets — useful for detecting port scans (SYN flood) and connection resets (RST attacks).

pairs.term: How does an added address alias appear in ip addr output?
pairs.definition: Each alias IP appears on the interface, with the original address marked scope global and the added one marked scope global secondary noprefixroute, both with valid_lft forever.

pairs.term: How do you add address aliases in the GNOME Settings IPv4 screen?
pairs.definition: In the same screen used to configure a manual wired interface, simply fill in a subsequent Addresses box and add the new IP address information; multiple aliases can be attached to one interface.

pairs.term: What are alias network interfaces and when are they useful?
pairs.definition: Attaching multiple IP addresses to a single network interface card, useful for example when a web server serves HTTPS content for multiple domains, each requiring a separate IP address. Add address1, address2, address3 entries to the connection file.

pairs.term: When would you set up network address aliases on one NIC?
pairs.definition: When a web server serves HTTPS content for multiple domains, each domain requires a separate IP address (associated with a separate certificate). Instead of adding multiple NICs, you create multiple aliases on a single NIC.

pairs.term: How are address aliases stored on a Fedora NetworkManager connection?
pairs.definition: In the /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections file, add address1, address2, and address3 entries under [ipv4], e.g. address1=192.168.1.195/24, address2=192.168.1.196/24, address3=192.168.1.197/24.

pairs.term: How do you add multiple addresses for an Ubuntu netplan connection?
pairs.definition: Edit the netplan YAML file so that multiple IPv4 addresses appear under the addresses line (for example, three addresses like 192.168.1.195/24, 192.168.1.196/24, and 192.168.1.197/24), then restart NetworkManager.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How many areas must an Autonomous System define?
pairs.definition: At least one area; each area in a network running OSPF or IS-IS is identified by a uniquely assigned area number.

pairs.term: What is an area border router (ABR)?
pairs.definition: In OSPF, a router that interconnects the various areas, supporting OSPF interfaces that connect to multiple areas and maintaining a copy of the LSDB for each attached area; the IS-IS equivalent is a Level 2 router.

pairs.term: What is an area in link-state routing?
pairs.definition: A partition of the network that contains a subset of the routers that make up the entire network; routers within an area flood LSAs only within that area and maintain an LSDB only for that area.

pairs.term: What are the benefits of partitioning a large network into areas?
pairs.definition: Smaller LSDBs require less memory, SPF runs with fewer CPU cycles on the smaller LSDB, LSA flooding and bandwidth use are reduced, routing instabilities (e.g., route flaps) are confined to the area, and areas introduce hierarchy to the network architecture.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is an Autonomous System Number (ASN)?
pairs.definition: A unique number assigned to an Autonomous System that connects to other systems or the public Internet using BGP, uniquely identifying it globally.

pairs.term: When is a public ASN used?
pairs.definition: When an Autonomous System must exchange routing information with other Autonomous Systems on the public Internet; the routes exchanged are visible on the Internet along with their public ASNs.

pairs.term: When is a private ASN used?
pairs.definition: When an Autonomous System only needs to communicate with a single provider or peer system via BGP without being visible on the public Internet; the routes exchanged with private ASNs are not visible on the Internet.

pairs.term: Who allocates ASNs and how?
pairs.definition: IANA allocates ASNs in blocks to Regional Internet Registries (RIRs), and each RIR assigns the blocks to entities (e.g., ISPs) within its designated area.

pairs.term: What does the balance-rr bonding mode do?
pairs.definition: It is a round-robin policy that enables fault tolerance and load balancing between the interfaces added to the bond. The bond interface (bond0) uses this mode in the examples.

pairs.term: What must be in /etc/modprobe.d/bonding.conf for the bond to work?
pairs.definition: The entry alias bond0 bonding, which makes the bonding module available to the bond0 interface created in NetworkManager.

pairs.term: What is Ethernet channel bonding?
pairs.definition: Having more than one network interface card on a computer associated with a single IP address, providing high availability (if one NIC breaks, the address is still reachable) and performance (traffic spread across multiple NICs).

pairs.term: What does the balance-rr bonding mode provide?
pairs.definition: A round-robin policy that enables fault tolerance and load balancing between the interfaces added to the bond.

pairs.term: sudo nmcli con add type bond con-name bond0 ifname bond0 mode balance-rr
pairs.definition: Adds a new bonding connection named bond0 using the balance-rr (round-robin) mode, enabling fault tolerance and load balancing.

pairs.term: nmcli con mod bond0 ipv4.method manual ipv4.addr 192.168.100.10/24
pairs.definition: Sets the IPv4 address on the bond0 connection to 192.168.100.10/24 using manual (static) configuration.

pairs.definition: A power-on self test (POST) that runs diagnostics from ROM on all hardware modules verifying CPU, memory, and network interface ports.

pairs.definition: Use a single search entry followed by one or more domain names separated by spaces or tabs, for example search example.com example.org example.net.

pairs.term: What entries typically appear at the top of an /etc/hosts file?
pairs.definition: The first lines set addresses for the local system: 127.0.0.1 localhost localhost.localdomain (IPv4) and ::1 localhost localhost.localdomain (IPv6), followed by entries mapping other hosts' IP addresses to their hostnames and aliases.

pairs.definition: As of Fedora 36 the /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts directory is no longer used by default. NetworkManager stores interfaces in keystore files in either the /etc/netplan or /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections directory.

pairs.term: What is the format of a NetworkManager connection file?
pairs.definition: Connection information is stored in key/value pairs in files in /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections (Fedora, ini-style with [connection], [wifi], [wifi-security], [ipv4], [ipv6], [proxy] sections) or /etc/netplan (Ubuntu, YAML-style).

pairs.term: What fields must be provided to set an IP address manually?

pairs.term: What is a network address alias?

pairs.term: What is the default port for an HTTP proxy?

pairs.term: What are Search Domains used for in network configuration?
pairs.definition: They are used when you request a host without using a fully qualified domain name. For example, with an example.com search path, typing ping host1 tries to ping host1.example.com.
