pairs.term: Switch(config)# spanning-tree vlan 1,10,20 priority 61440
pairs.definition: Sets the switch priority of VLANs 1, 10, and 20 to 61440, ensuring this switch does not become the root switch for those VLANs.

pairs.term: Best practice for access ports with BPDU Guard
pairs.definition: Best practice is to enable PortFast at the same time as BPDU Guard on access ports, and to set spanning-tree vlan <list> priority 61440 on switches that must never become root.

pairs.term: Switch(config)# interface range fastethernet 0/6 - 12
pairs.definition: Moves to interface range configuration mode for ports 6 to 12.

pairs.term: How to ensure a switch never becomes the root
pairs.definition: Set the switch priority very high, e.g. spanning-tree vlan 1,10,20 priority 61440, and consider Root Guard on uplink ports. In the example, Access2 uses priority 61440 so it never becomes root.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Indirect Failure Detection
pairs.definition: In an indirect failure, data is impaired or corrupted but the link stays up. SW3 stops receiving config BPDUs on its RP, waits for Max Age to expire, and flushes the RP cached entry before transitioning the blocking port to listening.

pairs.term: Direct Link Failure
pairs.definition: When layer-1 signaling places a port into a down state (power loss, reboot, cable removal), STP treats it as a direct link failure and can react without waiting for the Max Age timer.

pairs.term: Direct Link Failure to Blocked Port
pairs.definition: If a link between two non-root switches fails and one port was already blocking, there is no impact to traffic between them, but both advertise a TCN toward the root, flushing the MAC table.

pairs.term: Root-to-Switch Link Failure Timing
pairs.definition: With a direct link failure between the root and a switch, the switch restarts listening and learning without waiting for Max Age. Total convergence is 30 seconds: 15 seconds listening plus 15 seconds learning.

pairs.term: Indirect Failure Timing
pairs.definition: For an indirect link failure, SW3 waits for the Max Age timer (20 seconds) before moving a port to listening. Total reconvergence is 50 seconds: 20 seconds Max Age plus 15 listening plus 15 learning.

pairs.term: Indirect Link Failure
pairs.definition: A scenario where STP communication is impaired or filtered while the network link stays up. Timers are required to detect and remediate the topology.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Switch(config)# spanning-tree vlan 5
pairs.definition: Enables STP on VLAN 5.

pairs.term: Switch(config)# no spanning-tree vlan 5
pairs.definition: Disables STP on VLAN 5.

pairs.term: Is STP enabled by default?
pairs.definition: Yes. Spanning tree is enabled by default on VLAN 1 and on all newly created VLANs up to the spanning-tree limit. Disable it only if you are sure there are no loops.

pairs.term: Maximum spanning-tree instances
pairs.definition: Access switches such as the Catalyst 2960, 3550, 3560, 3750, 9200, and 9300 support a maximum of 128 spanning trees using PVST+ or Rapid PVST+. The 2950 supports only 64.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Switch# show spanning-tree bridge
pairs.definition: Displays the extended system ID as part of the bridge ID.

pairs.term: Extended system ID
pairs.definition: Also known as MAC address reduction. The 12-bit extended system ID is the VLAN number for PVST+/PVRST+ instances; in MST these 12 bits carry the instance number.

pairs.term: Switch(config)# spanning-tree extend system-id
pairs.definition: Enables the extended system ID, also known as MAC address reduction.

pairs.term: Switch# show spanning-tree summary
pairs.definition: Verifies that the extended system ID is enabled.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: PVST+ (Per VLAN Spanning Tree Plus)
pairs.definition: Based on IEEE 802.1D with Cisco proprietary extensions. It runs on each VLAN, ensuring each has a loop-free path, and provides Layer 2 load balancing. Each instance on a VLAN has a single root device.

pairs.term: Rapid PVST+
pairs.definition: Same as PVST+ but uses rapid convergence based on IEEE 802.1w. Beginning from IOS Release 15.2(4)E it is the default STP mode. It immediately deletes dynamically learned MAC entries per-port on topology change.

pairs.term: Multiple Spanning Tree Protocol (MSTP)
pairs.definition: Based on IEEE 802.1s. It maps multiple VLANs to the same spanning-tree instance, reducing the number of instances. MSTP runs on top of RSTP (802.1w) for rapid convergence.

pairs.term: Default STP mode
pairs.definition: The default implementation on Catalyst 2950, 2960, 3550, 3560, and 3750 switches is PVST+. Beginning from IOS Release 15.2(4)E the default is Rapid PVST+ on all switch platforms.

pairs.term: How does PVST+ provide load balancing?
pairs.definition: PVST+ provides Layer 2 load balancing by running a separate instance per VLAN. You can create different logical topologies so all links are used and no single link is oversubscribed, with a different root per VLAN.

pairs.term: Rapid PVST+ MAC address aging
pairs.definition: Rapid PVST+ immediately deletes dynamically learned MAC address entries on a per-port basis upon receiving a topology change. PVST+ instead uses a short aging time for those entries.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Switch(config)# no spanning-tree uplinkfast
pairs.definition: Removes the UplinkFast programming line when migrating to Rapid PVST+.

pairs.term: Switch(config)# no spanning-tree backbonefast
pairs.definition: Removes the BackboneFast programming line when migrating to Rapid PVST+.

pairs.term: UplinkFast/BackboneFast in Rapid PVST+
pairs.definition: The UplinkFast and BackboneFast features in 802.1D-based PVST+ are already incorporated in 802.1w-based Rapid PVST+ and are disabled when you enable Rapid PVST+.

pairs.term: Rapid PVST+ BPDU interoperability
pairs.definition: Rapid PVST+ uses the same BPDU format as 802.1D, which enables a longer conversion time in large networks without disrupting services. PortFast, BPDU Guard, BPDU filter, root guard, and loop guard still apply in Rapid PVST+.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Path Cost Advertisement Example
pairs.definition: SW1 advertises a root path cost of 0. SW3 adds its port cost (4) for a root path cost of 4 and advertises it. SW5 then adds its port cost (4) for a root path cost of 8.

pairs.term: Interface STP Cost
pairs.definition: The interface STP cost is used for root path calculation. The cumulative interface cost to reach the root bridge determines the root path.

pairs.term: Short Mode Cost
pairs.definition: The original method, using a 16-bit value with a reference speed of 20 Gbps. Short mode has been the default for most switches.

pairs.term: Long Mode Cost
pairs.definition: Uses a 32-bit value with a reference speed of 20 Tbps. It has been transitioning to be the default on specific platforms and OS versions.

pairs.term: Short-Mode Costs
pairs.definition: Short-mode STP costs: 10 Mbps=100, 100 Mbps=19, 1 Gbps=4, 10 Gbps=2, 20 Gbps=1, 100 Gbps=1, 1 Tbps=1, 10 Tbps=1.

pairs.term: Long-Mode Costs
pairs.definition: Long-mode STP costs: 10 Mbps=2,000,000, 100 Mbps=200,000, 1 Gbps=20,000, 10 Gbps=2000, 20 Gbps=1000, 100 Gbps=200, 1 Tbps=20, 10 Tbps=2.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Switch(config-if)# spanning-tree cost 100000
pairs.definition: Configures the cost for the interface that is an access port. Range is 1 to 200000000; default derives from media speed.

pairs.term: Switch(config-if)# spanning-tree vlan 5 cost 1500000
pairs.definition: Configures the VLAN cost for an interface that is a trunk port. The VLAN can be a single ID, range (hyphen), or series (comma); cost range is 1 to 200000000.

pairs.term: Path cost default
pairs.definition: The default path cost is derived from the media speed of the interface. The configurable range is 1 to 200000000. A higher path cost means a lower-speed transmission.

pairs.term: VLAN specification in the cost command
pairs.definition: The VLAN number can be specified as a single VLAN ID, a range separated by a hyphen, or a series separated by a comma; the VLAN range is 1 to 4094.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Switch(config-if)# spanning-tree port-priority 64
pairs.definition: Configures the port priority for the interface that is an access port.

pairs.term: Switch(config-if)# spanning-tree vlan 5 port-priority 64
pairs.definition: Configures the VLAN port priority for an interface that is a trunk port.

pairs.term: Switch(config)# interface gigabitethernet 0/1
pairs.definition: Moves to interface configuration mode for Gigabit Ethernet port 0/1.

pairs.term: Port priority range and default
pairs.definition: The port priority number can be between 0 and 240 in increments of 16. The default port priority is 128.

pairs.term: How is port priority used?
pairs.definition: If a loop occurs, spanning tree uses the port priority when selecting an interface to put into the forwarding state. A higher priority value (lower number) is selected first. Port priority supersedes the physical port number.

pairs.term: Port priority increments
pairs.definition: The port priority number can be between 0 and 240 in increments of 16. The default port priority is 128.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Switch(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast disable
pairs.definition: Overrides the global spanning-tree portfast default command on this interface.

pairs.term: Switch# show spanning-tree interface fastethernet 0/10 portfast
pairs.definition: Displays PortFast information on interface fastethernet 0/10.

pairs.term: PortFast purpose
pairs.definition: Places a port directly into forwarding mode, bypassing the listening and learning states. It should be used only when connecting a single end station to an access or trunk port.

pairs.term: PortFast caution
pairs.definition: Use PortFast only when connecting a single end station to an access or trunk port. Using it on a port connected to a switch or hub might prevent spanning tree from detecting loops.

pairs.term: PortFast and the voice VLAN feature
pairs.definition: If you enable the voice VLAN feature, PortFast is enabled automatically. If you disable voice VLAN, PortFast is still enabled.

pairs.term: Overriding the global PortFast default
pairs.definition: You can override spanning-tree portfast default with the spanning-tree portfast disable interface configuration command.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: RSTP Synchronization Purpose
pairs.definition: RSTP uses a synchronization process to add a switch to the topology without introducing a forwarding loop, moving non-edge ports to discarding during the process.

pairs.term: RSTP Agreement
pairs.definition: The inferior switch sends an agreement (configuration BPDU) to the root bridge signifying that synchronization is occurring on that switch, then moves its RP to forwarding.

pairs.term: RSTP Origin
pairs.definition: Cisco created PVST and PVST+ for flexibility, allowing different STP topologies per VLAN and load balancing. These concepts were incorporated with enhancements into the IEEE 802.1W RSTP for faster convergence.

pairs.term: RSTP Convergence Requirement
pairs.definition: In a large Layer 2 topology running RSTP, the infrastructure does not need to fully converge before any packets can be forwarded, unlike traditional STP.

pairs.term: RSTP Backward Compatibility
pairs.definition: RSTP (802.1W) is backward compatible with 802.1D. A switch defaults a port to 802.1D behavior when it cannot establish an RSTP handshake with the neighbor.

pairs.term: RSTP Discarding Combines
pairs.definition: RSTP discarding state combines the traditional STP states of disabled, blocking, and listening.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: RSTP Discarding State
pairs.definition: The port is enabled but not forwarding traffic to avoid a loop. This state combines the traditional STP disabled, blocking, and listening states.

pairs.term: RSTP Learning State
pairs.definition: The port modifies the MAC address table with received traffic but does not forward other network traffic besides BPDUs.

pairs.term: RSTP Forwarding State
pairs.definition: The port forwards all network traffic and updates the MAC address table as expected. This is the final state.

pairs.term: RSTP Number of Port States
pairs.definition: RSTP reduces the number of port states to three: discarding, learning, and forwarding.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Point-to-Point Port
pairs.definition: Any port that connects to another RSTP switch with full duplex. Full-duplex links do not permit more than two devices on a segment.

pairs.term: Half Duplex and RSTP
pairs.definition: Multi-access Layer 2 devices such as hubs connect only at half duplex. If a port can only connect at half duplex, it must operate under traditional 802.1D forwarding states.

pairs.term: RSTP Edge Port and Portfast
pairs.definition: RSTP edge ports directly correlate to ports with the STP portfast feature enabled. They connect hosts and cannot form a loop.

pairs.term: Full Duplex as RSTP Check
pairs.definition: Determining whether a link is full duplex is the fastest way to check the feasibility of being connected to an RSTP switch, because full-duplex links do not permit more than two devices on a segment.

pairs.term: Edge Port
pairs.definition: A port at the edge of the network where hosts connect with one interface and cannot form a loop. These ports directly correlate to ports with STP portfast enabled.

pairs.term: Non-Edge Port
pairs.definition: A port that has received a BPDU.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Priority With Sys-ID-Ext
pairs.definition: In configuration BPDUs, the priority shown is the priority plus the sys-id-ext (VLAN number). VLAN 1 priority is 32,769 (32,768 + 1); VLAN 10 is 32,778.

pairs.term: Root Path Cost Propagation
pairs.definition: The advertised root path cost in a BPDU does not include the cost of the port the BPDU is advertised out of. The receiving switch adds its port cost. Root path cost is always zero on the root bridge.

pairs.term: Older Switch Preference
pairs.definition: Generally, older switches have a lower MAC address and are considered more preferable for root bridge election. Configuration changes can optimize root placement to prevent an older switch from becoming root.

pairs.term: Inferior BPDU Handling
pairs.definition: If a neighbor's configuration BPDU is inferior to a switch's own BPDU, the switch ignores that BPDU. If preferred, the switch updates its BPDUs with the new root bridge identifier and new root path cost.

pairs.term: Root Bridge Election
pairs.definition: A switch assumes it is the root bridge on initialization, then listens to neighbor configuration BPDUs. It ignores inferior BPDUs and updates to preferred BPDUs (lower priority, then lower system MAC) until all switches agree on the root.

pairs.term: Bridge Preference Logic
pairs.definition: A switch prefers a configuration BPDU with a lower priority. If priorities are equal, it prefers the BPDU with the lower system MAC address.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Switch(config)# spanning-tree vlan 5 root primary
pairs.definition: Configures the switch to become the root switch for VLAN 5 by lowering the switch priority to 24576.

pairs.term: Switch(config)# spanning-tree vlan 5 root primary diameter 7
pairs.definition: Configures the switch as root for VLAN 5 and sets the network diameter to 7 switches.

pairs.term: Switch(config)# spanning-tree vlan 5 root secondary
pairs.definition: Configures the switch to become the root for VLAN 5 should the primary root fail. It resets priority to 28672.

pairs.term: Switch(config)# spanning-tree vlan 5 root secondary diameter 7
pairs.definition: Configures the switch as secondary root for VLAN 5 and sets the network diameter to 7.

pairs.term: Priority set by spanning-tree vlan X root primary
pairs.definition: The switch sets its priority to 24576. If any other switch has priority below 24576, it sets its own priority to 4096 less than the lowest switch priority; if that would be less than 1, the command fails.

pairs.term: Priority set by spanning-tree vlan X root secondary
pairs.definition: The switch resets its priority to 28672. If the root fails and all other switches are at the default priority 32768, this switch becomes the new root.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Purpose of STP
pairs.definition: STP enables switches to become aware of other switches through the advertisement and receipt of BPDUs. It builds a Layer 2 loop-free topology by temporarily blocking traffic on redundant ports.

pairs.term: Layer 2 Loop Problem
pairs.definition: Broadcasts and unknown unicast floods loop continuously in a redundant topology with no TTL mechanism for Layer 2. This increases CPU and memory use and can crash the switch, while the MAC table constantly changes ports.

pairs.term: 802.1D STP
pairs.definition: The original version of STP, which provides a loop-free topology for one VLAN. It is the foundation for RSTP and MST.

pairs.term: STP Iterations
pairs.definition: STP has multiple iterations: 802.1D, Per-VLAN Spanning Tree (PVST), Per-VLAN Spanning Tree Plus (PVST+), 802.1W RSTP, and 802.1S MST. Catalyst switches operate in PVST+, RSTP, and MST modes, all backward compatible with 802.1D.

pairs.term: PVST and PVST+
pairs.definition: Per-VLAN Spanning Tree and Per-VLAN Spanning Tree Plus were Cisco proprietary protocols that maintained a separate STP topology for each VLAN, enabling load balancing and traffic steering. Their concepts were incorporated into RSTP.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: BPDU Destination MAC
pairs.definition: BPDUs use the destination MAC address 01:80:c2:00:00:00.

pairs.term: Root Bridge
pairs.definition: The most important switch in the Layer 2 topology, considered the top of the spanning tree. All ports are in a forwarding state and are categorized as designated ports.

pairs.term: Bridge Protocol Data Unit (BPDU)
pairs.definition: A network packet used by switches to identify a hierarchy and notify of topology changes. A BPDU uses the destination MAC 01:80:c2:00:00:00. There are two types: configuration BPDU and TCN BPDU.

pairs.term: Configuration BPDU
pairs.definition: Used to identify the root bridge, root ports, designated ports, and blocking ports. Fields include STP type, root path cost, root bridge identifier, local bridge identifier, max age, hello time, and forward delay.

pairs.term: Topology Change Notification (TCN) BPDU
pairs.definition: Used to communicate changes in the Layer 2 topology to other switches.

pairs.term: Root Path Cost
pairs.definition: The combined cost for a specific path toward the root switch.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Max Age
pairs.definition: The maximum time a bridge port stores its BPDU information. Default is 20 seconds. If the source is lost, the switch assumes the info is valid for the Max Age duration.

pairs.term: Hello Time
pairs.definition: The interval at which a BPDU is advertised out of a port. Default is 2 seconds, configurable from 1 to 10 seconds.

pairs.term: Forward Delay
pairs.definition: The amount of time a port stays in the listening and learning states. Default is 15 seconds, configurable from 4 to 30 seconds.

pairs.term: Default STP Timers
pairs.definition: Default timers: Max Age 20 seconds, Hello Time 2 seconds, Forward Delay 15 seconds.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Switch(config)# spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
pairs.definition: Enables Rapid PVST+ (IEEE 802.1w based).

pairs.term: Switch# clear spanning-tree detected-protocols
pairs.definition: If any port is connected to a legacy IEEE 802.1D device, this restarts the protocol migration process on the entire device. Optional if the designated device detects Rapid PVST+.

pairs.term: Switch(config)# spanning-tree mode pvst
pairs.definition: Enables PVST+ (Per VLAN Spanning Tree Plus). This is the default setting.

pairs.term: Switch(config)# spanning-tree mode mst
pairs.definition: Enters MST (Multiple Spanning Tree) mode.

pairs.term: Switch(config)# spanning-tree mst configuration
pairs.definition: Enters MST configuration submode. Use no spanning-tree mst configuration to clear the MST configuration.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Switch(config)# spanning-tree vlan 5 hello-time 4
pairs.definition: Changes the hello-delay timer to 4 seconds on VLAN 5. Range is 1 to 10 seconds; default is 2.

pairs.term: Switch(config)# spanning-tree vlan 5 forward-time 20
pairs.definition: Changes the forward-delay timer to 20 seconds on VLAN 5. Range is 4 to 30 seconds; default is 15.

pairs.term: Switch(config)# spanning-tree vlan 5 max-age 25
pairs.definition: Changes the maximum-aging timer to 25 seconds on VLAN 5. Range is 6 to 40 seconds; default is 20.

pairs.term: STP timer defaults and ranges
pairs.definition: hello-time: 1 to 10 seconds, default 2. forward-time: 4 to 30 seconds, default 15. max-age: 6 to 40 seconds, default 20.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Switch(config)# spanning-tree vlan 5 priority 12288
pairs.definition: Configures the switch priority of VLAN 5 to 12288. Range is 0 to 61440 in increments of 4096; default is 32768.

pairs.term: Switch priority range and default
pairs.definition: With the priority keyword the range is 0 to 61440 in increments of 4096. The default is 32768. The lower the priority, the more likely the switch will be chosen as root.

pairs.term: Cisco recommendation for changing switch priority
pairs.definition: Cisco recommends using spanning-tree vlan x root primary or spanning-tree vlan x root secondary instead of the priority keyword to modify the switch priority.

pairs.term: Valid switch priority values

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Topology Change Notification Process
pairs.definition: A switch that detects a link status change sends a TCN BPDU toward the root bridge out its RP. Upstream switches acknowledge and forward the TCN. The root bridge then sends a config BPDU with the Topology Change flag set, which is flooded to all switches.

pairs.term: TCN Effect on MAC Aging
pairs.definition: Upon receiving a config BPDU with the Topology Change flag set, switches change the MAC address learning timer to the forwarding delay (default 15 seconds). This flushes MACs of devices not communicating in that window while keeping active ones.

pairs.term: Flushing MAC Table Side Effect
pairs.definition: Flushing the MAC address table prevents sending to an unreachable host but temporarily increases unknown unicast flooding while it rebuilds, which can impact hosts due to CSMA/CD. The MAC timer resets to normal (300 seconds) after the second config BPDU.

pairs.term: TCN VLAN Basis
pairs.definition: TCNs are generated on a VLAN basis. The impact correlates to the number of hosts in a VLAN; more hosts mean more TCN generation and more hosts impacted by broadcasts.

pairs.term: TCN on Link Between Non-Root Switches
pairs.definition: If a link between two non-root switches fails and one port was already blocking, both switches advertise a TCN toward the root, which results in the Layer 2 topology flushing its MAC address table.

pairs.term: TCN Acknowledgment
pairs.definition: If an upstream switch receives a TCN, it sends out an acknowledgment and forwards the TCN out its RP toward the root bridge.

pairs.definition: Displays spanning-tree port state changes.

pairs.term: spanning-tree vlan vlan-id max-age maxage
pairs.definition: Changes the STP Max Age timer for a VLAN. Default is 20 seconds.

pairs.term: spanning-tree vlan vlan-id hello-time hello-time
pairs.definition: Changes the STP hello interval for a VLAN. Default is 2 seconds, configurable 1 to 10 seconds.

pairs.term: spanning-tree vlan vlan-id forward-time forward-time
pairs.definition: Changes the STP forward delay for a VLAN. Default is 15 seconds, configurable 4 to 30 seconds.

pairs.definition: Changes the interface STP cost method to long mode (32-bit, reference 20 Tbps).

pairs.term: show spanning-tree interface detail Fields
pairs.definition: The detail keyword provides port cost, port priority, port identifier, number of transitions to forwarding, link type, and count of BPDUs sent and received for every VLAN on the interface.

pairs.term: Switch# show spanning-tree
pairs.definition: Displays STP information.

pairs.term: show spanning-tree Output Sections
pairs.definition: The output shows root bridge information (priority, address, cost, port), followed by local bridge information (priority, address, timers, aging time), and the interface table with role, state, cost, priority, and port type.

pairs.term: Switch# show spanning-tree active
pairs.definition: Displays STP information on active interfaces only.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the syntax for configuring a default static route in Cisco routers?
pairs.definition: ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 [outgoing_interface] [next_hop] [admin_distance]. Configuring a static route to network 0.0.0.0/0 is a way of adding a gateway of last resort on a router.

pairs.term: What precedence do specific Routing Table entries have over a default static route?
pairs.definition: Entries in the Routing Table that identify a specific destination with a larger network mask (or network prefix) for a packet's destination address take precedence over the default static route.

pairs.term: What is a gateway of last resort?
pairs.definition: The default static route (0.0.0.0/0) identifies the gateway (next-hop router) to which packets with destination addresses that do not match any specific dynamically learned or static route are forwarded; this is the gateway of last resort on a router.

pairs.term: ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 [outgoing_interface] [next_hop] [admin_distance]
pairs.definition: Configures a default static route (0.0.0.0/0), adding a gateway of last resort used when no specific route matches a packet's destination address.

pairs.term: What is the minimum configuration information required to configure a default static route?
pairs.definition: At a minimum: the outgoing interface, the destination IP address (0.0.0.0), the network mask (0.0.0.0), the IP address of the next-hop router (gateway), and an optional Administrative Distance value.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the primary benefit of dynamic routing protocols?
pairs.definition: They allow routers to exchange routing information automatically when changes in the network topology or state occur, enabling routers to discover new remote networks and determine alternate paths when existing paths become unavailable.

pairs.term: Why are dynamic routing protocols generally implemented in all of today's networks?
pairs.definition: They reduce significantly the burden of configuring and maintaining routes in a dynamic network, allowing greater network design flexibility and scalability, and the best discovered routes are installed in the Routing Tables automatically.

pairs.term: What are the drawbacks of dynamic routing protocols compared to static routing?
pairs.definition: They consume more computing and memory resources for protocol operation, use more network bandwidth for protocol messaging, and are relatively less secure when used natively due to the broadcast and/or multicast mechanisms used to propagate routing updates.

pairs.term: Why do dynamic routing protocol interfaces require additional security mechanisms?
pairs.definition: Because dynamic routing protocols use broadcast and/or multicast mechanisms to propagate updates, the interfaces used to send updates require additional mechanisms for the authentication of routing protocol exchanges.

pairs.term: Which dynamic routing protocols are generally considered capable of operating independent of network size?
pairs.definition: Most of today's dynamic routing protocols like EIGRP, OSPF, IS-IS, and BGP can operate independent of network size, allowing a network to automatically reconfigure routing to reroute traffic and adapt to changes in topology and state.

pairs.term: Why is static routing appealing and widely used?
pairs.definition: Because it does not require the same amount of processing and memory resources, nor the routing information messaging overhead, as in dynamic routing protocols.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.definition: Configures a static route to 10.22.22.0/24 via 10.12.1.2 with an administrative distance of 10, used as a floating (backup) static route.

pairs.term: When is a floating static route actually used to forward traffic?
pairs.definition: Only when the preferred primary route (static or dynamic) with a better Administrative Distance becomes unavailable. The floating static route is configured and enabled but is not used to forward traffic while the primary route is active.

pairs.term: Is the use of a floating static route dependent on the encapsulation type of an interface?
pairs.definition: No. The use of a floating static route is independent of the type of encapsulation used on an interface, so it can be created on any interface to forward traffic irrespective of its encapsulation type, and can serve as a backup route to multiple interfaces.

pairs.term: How does route flapping affect a floating static route?
pairs.definition: A primary route that experiences flapping (being continuously dropped and re-established) can cause the floating static route and its backup interface to be unnecessarily activated and deactivated.

pairs.term: What Routing Table contents do routers maintain in networks that employ both dynamic and static routing?

pairs.term: How long do static routes remain in the Routing and Forwarding Tables?

pairs.term: How are the steps for configuring a summary static route different from those for a standard static route?
pairs.definition: They are similar to those of a standard static route. A single static summary route can be configured to replace a set of static routes with contiguous IP addresses, reducing Routing Table entries and advertised routes.

pairs.term: Why does route summarization reduce the overall end-to-end latency in a network?
pairs.definition: Because the smaller Routing Tables result in faster Forwarding Table lookups and processing latencies in routers, which reduces overall end-to-end latency, especially when a path consists of many routers.

pairs.term: What are LACP Fast, minimum-links, and max-bundle features?

pairs.term: What does a switch do with a frame whose destination MAC is unknown?
pairs.definition: It floods the frame out all ports except the port it arrived on (unknown unicast flooding). The recipient will reply, and the switch then learns the MAC-to-port mapping from that reply.

pairs.term: Why does a switch forward broadcast frames out all ports?
pairs.definition: Broadcast frames (destination FFFF.FFFF.FFFF) are addressed to every device on the LAN — the switch's only way to deliver them is to flood them out all ports. This is also why large broadcast domains hurt performance.

pairs.term: What is the MAC address table (CAM table) and how is it managed?
pairs.definition: It maps MAC addresses to switch ports. Entries are learned dynamically and age out (default 300 s on Cisco). You can view it with 'show mac address-table' and clear it with 'clear mac address-table dynamic'.

pairs.term: Why does a redundant LAN topology require Spanning Tree Protocol?
pairs.definition: Without STP, redundant links create physical loops — broadcast frames circulate forever (broadcast storm), and switches get confused by multiple copies of frames (multiple frames, MAC flap). STP blocks redundant paths to create a loop-free tree topology.

pairs.definition: Same speed/duplex, same switchport mode (access or trunk), same VLANs (allowed list, native VLAN), same STP settings. Mismatches prevent the bundle from forming and the switch may report errors.

pairs.term: How does EtherChannel load distribution work?
pairs.definition: The switch hashes frame fields (e.g., source/destination MAC or IP) to pick a member link — all frames of a given conversation (flow) use the same link to preserve ordering. Hash inputs are configurable ('port-channel load-balance').

pairs.term: How does a switch choose its root port?
pairs.definition: The root port is the switch's port with the lowest cost path to the root switch (lowest root cost). Ties broken by: lowest neighbor Bridge ID, then lowest neighbor port priority, then lowest neighbor port number.

pairs.term: What is the Spanning Tree election process?
pairs.definition: 1) Root Bridge election (lowest Bridge ID = priority + MAC), 2) Root Port selection on non-root switches (lowest path cost to root), 3) Designated Port selection on each segment (lowest path cost to root), 4) Non-designated ports are blocked.

pairs.term: How is the designated port chosen on each LAN segment?
pairs.definition: On each segment, the switch with the lowest root cost (and tie-breakers) becomes the designated port owner; the other side's port becomes non-designated (blocked). The root switch's ports are always designated.

pairs.term: What are common Spanning Tree problems?
pairs.definition: 1) Duplex mismatch — causes TCNs and topology changes, 2) Unidirectional links — one-way traffic causes BPDU loss, leading to loops, 3) CPU overload — BPDUs may not be processed in time.

pairs.term: What are the STP port states and the listening/learning delays?
pairs.definition: Blocking (no forwarding, BPDUs only) → Listening (15s, no user data) → Learning (15s, builds MAC table) → Forwarding (data flows). Disabled is a special state. Classic STP takes ~30-50s to converge (forward delay default 15s each).

pairs.term: What is SPAN (Switched Port Analyzer)?
pairs.definition: Port mirroring — copies traffic from one or more source ports to a destination port where a monitoring device (e.g., Wireshark or IPS) can capture and analyze the traffic. RSPAN and ERSPAN extend this across switches.

pairs.term: What is a Voice VLAN?
pairs.definition: A dedicated VLAN for IP phone traffic. The switch can use CDP/LLDP to inform the phone which VLAN to use for voice. Data traffic from the PC behind the phone goes on the native (data) VLAN. Enables QoS marking on the voice VLAN.

pairs.term: What is Flex Links?
pairs.definition: A Layer 2 redundancy feature for access switches. A pair of interfaces (active/backup) provide fast failover. Unlike STP, one link is always in standby. Typically used with dual-homed servers or uplinks to different distribution switches.

pairs.term: What is Storm Control on switches?
pairs.definition: A feature that monitors broadcast, multicast, or unicast traffic levels and drops traffic exceeding a configured threshold. Prevents storm events from overwhelming the switch.

pairs.term: How does IEEE autonegotiation work for speed and duplex on Ethernet links?
pairs.definition: Both devices exchange capability information using Fast Link Pulses (FLPs) and agree on the fastest common speed and best duplex (full duplex preferred). Works when both sides have it enabled.

pairs.term: What happens when one side uses autonegotiation and the other is set manually?
pairs.definition: Speed is usually detected automatically (via signal encoding), but duplex often defaults to half duplex on the auto side — creating a duplex mismatch that causes collisions and errors on the link.

pairs.term: What are the symptoms of a duplex mismatch?
pairs.definition: The link appears up/up but suffers many FCS/alignment errors, late collisions, and slow throughput — one side sends full duplex while the other only half duplex, so frames collide on the half-duplex side.

pairs.term: What do the interface status codes 'up/up', 'up/down', 'down/down', and 'admin down' mean?
pairs.definition: 'up/up' — operational. 'up/down' — physical layer ok but Layer 2 problem (e.g., no VLAN, err-disabled). 'down/down' — physical problem (cable, other end down). 'administratively down' — the port was shut with 'shutdown'.

pairs.term: What is the 'interface range' command used for?
pairs.definition: It lets you configure multiple interfaces at once, e.g., 'interface range GigabitEthernet0/1-10' then apply common settings — reducing repetitive configuration.

pairs.definition: When multiple processes map the same file using MAP_SHARED, writes to the mapped memory update the shared physical memory, so the update is immediately visible to other processes and is carried through to the underlying file.

pairs.term: What is Copy On Write (COW)?
pairs.definition: An optimization technique that allows virtual pages of memory in different processes to map to the same physical memory pages if they have identical contents; the memory copy is delayed until a write actually occurs.

pairs.term: What is a 'dirty page' in COW terminology?
pairs.definition: The page that is written and therefore needs a private copy; only the affected (dirty) page gets a new physical memory block allocated and copied.

pairs.definition: Arguments, Return Address, Previous Frame Pointer, and Local Variables.

pairs.term: What is stored in the Arguments region of a stack frame?
pairs.definition: The values of the arguments passed to the function, e.g. func(5, 8) pushes 5 and 8 onto the stack. They are pushed in reverse order.

pairs.term: What is the Return Address region of a stack frame?
pairs.definition: Before jumping to the function entrance, the computer pushes the address of the next instruction (the instruction right after the function-invocation instruction) onto the top of the stack. When the function returns, it jumps to this address.

pairs.term: What is the Previous Frame Pointer region of a stack frame?

pairs.definition: It must be random and it cannot be stored on the stack. The random value is initialized using /dev/urandom, and the copy is kept in %gs:20, which is physically isolated from the stack/heap.

pairs.definition: 0 = standard input, 1 = standard output, and 2 = standard error. Each Unix process has these three standard streams.

pairs.definition: File descriptors 0, 1, and 2 (standard input, output, and error) have already been created for every process, so the next available entry in the file descriptor table is 3.

pairs.term: How a process inherits standard file descriptors
pairs.definition: A process usually inherits file descriptors 0, 1, and 2 from its parent process. Most programs are started from a shell running in a terminal; the shell sets the standard input, output, and error to the terminal, and these are passed down to child processes.

pairs.term: How scanf() and printf() are implemented
pairs.definition: scanf() reads from the standard input device; printf() writes to the standard output device. Reading/writing these standard devices is what implements these functions.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: SIEM (Security Information and Event Management)
pairs.definition: Combines SIM (log management) and SEM (real-time monitoring). Collects, correlates, analyzes security events. Provides alerting, reporting, compliance management, incident response.

pairs.term: NAC (Network Access Control)
pairs.definition: Security solution enforcing policy compliance on devices before granting network access. Controls: authentication, device posture check (antivirus, patches), quarantine non-compliant devices.

pairs.term: DLP (Data Loss Prevention)
pairs.definition: Systems and processes to prevent unauthorized access or transmission of sensitive data. Types: network DLP (monitors traffic), endpoint DLP (monitors devices), storage DLP (scans data at rest).

pairs.term: Intrusion Detection System (IDS)
pairs.definition: Monitors network traffic or system activity for malicious activity. Types: NIDS (network-based), HIDS (host-based). Detection methods: signature-based, anomaly-based, stateful protocol analysis.

pairs.term: Intrusion Prevention System (IPS)
pairs.definition: Inline IDS that can actively block detected threats. Sits in-line with traffic. Capable of dropping packets, resetting connections, blocking IPs. Can introduce latency and false positives.

pairs.term: Firewall
pairs.definition: Network security system that monitors and controls traffic based on predetermined rules. Types: packet filter, stateful inspection, application-level gateway (proxy), next-generation firewall (NGFW).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What key do you press at the GRUB screen to edit the anaconda kernel command line and initrd line?
pairs.definition: With the bootable entry highlighted, press 'e' to edit the anaconda kernel command line and initial RAM disk line. Press Tab to pause the boot process on the GRUB screen first.

pairs.term: In a /boot/loader/entries file, what does the 'linux' line identify?
pairs.definition: The location of the kernel (for example, /root/boot/vmlinuz-6.15.6-100.fc41.x86_64), followed by the location of the initrd (initial RAM disk).

pairs.term: What is the major function of the GRUB 2 boot loader?
pairs.definition: To find and start the operating system you want, but with much more power and flexibility built into the tools and configuration files, including scripting syntax with functions, loops, and variables.

pairs.term: What is SYSLINUX?
pairs.definition: A set of boot loaders not typically used for installed Linux systems, but commonly used for bootable Linux CDs and DVDs. It was particularly good for booting ISO9660 CD images (isolinux), USB sticks (syslinux), and PXE booting over the network (pxelinux).

pairs.term: Where are the GRUB 2 configuration files located?
pairs.definition: /boot/grub/grub.cfg, /etc/grub2/grub.cfg, or /etc/grub2-efi.cfg (for systems booted with EFI).

pairs.term: How is grub.cfg generated and how should you configure GRUB 2?
pairs.definition: grub.cfg is generated automatically from the /etc/default/grub file and the /etc/grub.d/ directory. You should modify or add to those files to configure GRUB 2 yourself rather than editing grub.cfg by hand.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How does a VNC installation work?
pairs.definition: You start the installation on one computer with the 'vnc' boot option, then open a vnc viewer on another system and give it the address of the installation machine (such as 192.168.0.99:1) to answer installation questions remotely.

pairs.term: What does the 'numa-off' boot option tell the installer?
pairs.definition: To disable Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) for the AMD64 architecture.

pairs.term: What does the 'askmethod' boot option do?
pairs.definition: It forces the installer to prompt for the repository location (CD/DVD, hard drive, NFS, FTP, or HTTP) when booting from an installation medium that contains little more than the kernel and initial RAM disk.

pairs.term: What do the 'nompath', 'noparport', and 'nopcmcia' boot options tell the installer?
pairs.definition: nompath: don't enable support for multipath devices; noparport: don't load support for parallel ports; nopcmcia: don't load support for PCMCIA controllers.

pairs.term: What do the 'rescue' and 'mediacheck' boot options do?
pairs.definition: 'rescue' runs the kernel to open Linux rescue mode instead of installing; 'mediacheck' checks the installation medium for checksum errors.

pairs.term: What does the 'nofb' boot option do for video problems?
pairs.definition: It tells the system not to use the VGA 16 framebuffer driver during installation.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What command updates installed packages if an upgrade is ready?
pairs.definition: sudo apt-get upgrade

pairs.term: What file format is a Debian software package?
pairs.definition: An ar archive file that holds multiple files (executables, configuration files, documentation) and metadata (dependencies, licensing, package sizes, descriptions).

pairs.term: Name three Debian package management tools.
pairs.definition: Ubuntu App Center (graphical), aptitude (screen-oriented menu tool), and the apt* set of commands (apt-get, apt, apt-config, apt-cache). dpkg is also used for managing DEB packages.

pairs.term: What command updates the apt package list with the latest package versions?
pairs.definition: sudo apt-get update

pairs.term: What command searches apt for a package by keyword such as vsftpd?
pairs.definition: sudo apt-cache search vsftpd

pairs.term: What command displays information about the vsftpd package with apt?
pairs.definition: sudo apt-cache show vsftpd
