pairs.term: Which dnf subcommand shows detailed information about a package (version, release, architecture, size, repository, summary, license)?
pairs.definition: dnf info, for example 'dnf info emacs'.

pairs.term: What command finds which package provides the dvdrecord command?
pairs.definition: dnf provides dvdrecord

pairs.term: What command undoes dnf transaction number 5?
pairs.definition: dnf history undo 5

pairs.term: If you know the command, configuration file, or library name but not the package, which dnf subcommand finds the containing package?
pairs.definition: dnf provides, for example 'dnf provides dvdrecord' shows it is in the wodim package.

pairs.term: What command lists all available packages?
pairs.definition: dnf list --available

pairs.term: What command downloads the firefox RPM to the current directory without installing it?
pairs.definition: dnf download firefox

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is a kickstart file?
pairs.definition: A file containing all the questions you answer during a manual install and all the packages you select. When you start a Fedora or RHEL installer, you can provide a kickstart file at the boot prompt and the entire installation completes on its own.

pairs.term: How does PXE boot enable automated enterprise installation?
pairs.definition: A PXE server lets client computers boot an anaconda (installer) kernel and a selected kickstart file. A blank computer with a PXE-booting NIC can boot from its NIC to launch a fresh installation without intervention.

pairs.term: What is Red Hat Satellite Server (Spacewalk) used for?
pairs.definition: Deploying RHEL systems. It has the same features as Red Hat CDN to manage and deploy new systems and updates, can schedule automatic software updates, and can quickly deploy sets of packages called Errata that fix specific problems.

pairs.term: What is a container image compared with an RPM?
pairs.definition: Instead of installing individual RPMs, you package up a few or a few hundred RPMs into a container image. It holds a set of software like an RPM, but is more easily added to a system, run directly, and deleted from a system.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How does a PXE server help enterprise installations?
pairs.definition: If you set your computer's BIOS to boot from a PXE-enabled NIC and a PXE server is on the network, that server presents a menu to the computer containing entries to launch an installation process.

pairs.term: What is the anaconda kernel and what does the bootloader point to?
pairs.definition: The bootloader points to the special anaconda kernel (and possibly an initial RAM disk) that starts the Linux installer called anaconda. Any bootable medium needs to point to the location of the kernel and initial RAM disk to start the installation.

pairs.term: Where is the kickstart file saved after a RHEL installation?
pairs.definition: In the /root/anaconda-ks.cfg file. It contains answers to all installation questions for the installation you just did and can be presented to the next installation to repeat the configuration or used as a model.

pairs.term: What is an install server?
pairs.definition: A server where you copy all software packages from the RHEL installation medium to a web (http), FTP (ftp), or NFS (nfs) server, then point the booted installer to that location. This avoids carrying software packages to each machine.

pairs.term: What locations can hold the software repository for a kickstart/network installation?
pairs.definition: A local CD (cdrom), website (http), FTP site (ftp), NFS share (nfs), NFS ISO (nfsiso), or local disk (hd).

pairs.term: sudo dnf upgrade
pairs.definition: The command to get software updates for a newly installed, registered RHEL system.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the minimum processor for a GUI Linux installation and what is needed for virtualization?
pairs.definition: A 1GHz Pentium processor is the minimum for a GUI installation; an old 32-bit (x86) processor works for most applications. To set up virtualization you need a 64-bit processor (x86_64); an ARM processor (aarch64) is also an option.

pairs.term: How much RAM does Fedora recommend for a good workstation experience?
pairs.definition: At least 4GB of RAM. A browser, word processor, and a couple of terminal windows can consume more than 3GB of RAM.

pairs.term: What special hardware feature is required to use Fedora or RHEL as a KVM virtualization host?
pairs.definition: A processor that supports virtualization, including AMD-V or Intel-VT chips. Most recent computers have this feature.

pairs.term: What lightweight Ubuntu distributions are mentioned for less powerful computers?
pairs.definition: Peppermint OS (peppermintos.com) and Lubuntu (lubuntu.net). For a lightweight Fedora-based distribution, try the LXDE desktop spin, and Tiny Core Linux requires a minuscule amount of resources.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the Fedora Media Writer?
pairs.definition: Software used to burn a Fedora ISO image to a USB drive. On Windows 11, it may require the Microsoft Visual C++ Redistributable package to provide the MSVCP140.dll file for it to work.

pairs.term: What minimum USB drive capacity is needed to create Fedora installation media?
pairs.definition: At least 3GB capacity for a USB drive that can be completely erased to hold the Fedora installation ISO.

pairs.term: What is a single-boot computer installation?
pairs.definition: The easiest way to install Linux: Linux replaces everything on the computer, and when done, the computer boots directly to the distribution (such as Fedora) with no other operating system present.

pairs.term: What is a multi-boot computer installation?
pairs.definition: Installing Linux alongside an existing operating system (such as Windows) on the same computer. At boot time you choose which operating system to start. It requires extra disk space outside the Windows partition or shrinking Windows to make room.

pairs.term: What risk exists with dual-boot (Windows/Linux) systems and what should you always do first?
pairs.definition: Different operating systems often have different views of partition tables and master boot records, which can make the machine unbootable or lose data permanently. Always back up your data before resizing a Windows filesystem to make space for Linux.

pairs.term: What is the main advantage of an installation DVD over a Live media ISO?
pairs.definition: Instead of just copying the whole Live media contents to disk, with an installation DVD you can choose exactly which software packages you want, allowing anything from a minimal system to a fully featured desktop to a full-blown server.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What filesystem type do filesystems on CD-ROM typically use?
pairs.definition: The iso9660 filesystem type. Different filesystem types must be on their own partitions.

pairs.term: What are two reasons to have separate /home and /var partitions within one operating system?
pairs.definition: Protection from denial-of-service attacks (a full partition doesn't shut down the whole computer) and protection from corrupted filesystems (corruption of a smaller partition is easier to fix and often lets the computer stay in service).

pairs.term: gparted
pairs.definition: Launches the GParted graphical partitioning tool; it must be run as root. Use it to create or resize disk partitions, including resizing Windows NTFS partitions.

pairs.term: What is partitioning?
pairs.definition: The act of dividing a disk into logical areas that can be worked with separately. Linux systems partition disks to support multiple operating systems, multiple filesystem types, and to protect the OS from running out of disk space.

pairs.term: What are the limits of MBR vs GPT partition tables?
pairs.definition: An MBR partition table can contain four primary partitions, one of which can be marked to contain 184 logical drives. On a GPT partition table you can have a maximum of 128 primary partitions on most operating systems, including Linux.

pairs.term: Why should you install Windows first when setting up a dual-boot system?
pairs.definition: If you partition the disk first and install Windows afterward, the Windows installation may make the Linux partitions inaccessible.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What command installs snapd on Fedora?
pairs.definition: sudo dnf install snapd

pairs.term: What command installs the kolourpaint Snap?
pairs.definition: snap install kolourpaint

pairs.term: What command lists installed Snaps?
pairs.definition: snap list

pairs.term: What command searches Homebrew formulae for 'top'?
pairs.definition: brew search top

pairs.term: What command shows information about the htop Homebrew package?
pairs.definition: brew info htop

pairs.term: What command installs htop with Homebrew?
pairs.definition: brew install htop

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What Software Selection options are available in a RHEL installation?
pairs.definition: Server With GUI (GNOME 3 desktop on top of a basic server), Server (no GUI), Minimal Install (basic package set), Workstation (geared for end users), Custom Operating System (basic RHEL system), and Virtualization Host (set up to run virtual machines).

pairs.term: What is kdump and how much RAM does it reserve by default?
pairs.definition: kdump sets aside RAM to capture a kernel dump in the event of a kernel crash. By default it sets aside 160MB plus 2 bits for every 4KB of RAM for saving kernel crashes.

pairs.term: What is the purpose of the wheel group during RHEL installation?
pairs.definition: Adding a user to the wheel group provides sudo access, allowing the account to act as the root user as needed. The user created during installation has sudo privileges.

pairs.term: What is the first thing you should do after logging into a newly installed, registered RHEL system?
pairs.definition: Get software updates by running 'sudo dnf upgrade' from a Terminal window.

pairs.term: What can you do on the RHEL Installation Source screen?
pairs.definition: The installation medium you booted from is used by default. You can select On the network and choose a web URL (http, https, or ftp) for the RHEL repository, or select Red Hat CDN to use the Red Hat Content Delivery Network for packages.

pairs.term: What is the Connect to Red Hat step during RHEL installation?
pairs.definition: It registers the system with Red Hat Network using your username/password or activation key, allowing updates and Red Hat Insights. Options let you choose a proxy, satellite server, or custom base URL instead of directly connecting to Red Hat Network.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does it indicate if a binary (such as one in /bin) has changed since package installation?
pairs.definition: It is probably an indication that your system has been cracked, since it is not normal for binaries to change after installation (configuration files changing is normal though).

pairs.term: What command shows the change log of the httpd package?
pairs.definition: rpm -q --changelog httpd

pairs.term: What command installs an RPM file from the current directory?
pairs.definition: rpm -i zsh-5.9-16.fc42.x86_64.rpm

pairs.term: What command verifies that files in the installed zsh package have not been tampered with?
pairs.definition: rpm -V zsh

pairs.term: What command upgrades/installs an RPM with hash marks and verbose output?
pairs.definition: rpm -Uhv zsh-5.9-16.fc42.x86_64.rpm

pairs.term: What command reinstalls the zsh package to restore original file state?
pairs.definition: rpm -i --replacepkgs zsh-5.9-16.fc42.x86_64.rpm

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does the package name firefox-141.0-2.fc42.x86_64 tell you?
pairs.definition: Base name firefox, version 141.0 (assigned by the upstream Mozilla Project), release 2 (assigned by the packager Fedora each time it is rebuilt), built for Fedora 42 (fc42), compiled for x86_64 architecture.

pairs.term: Where is information about installed packages stored after an RPM is installed?
pairs.definition: In the local RPM database (files stored in /var/lib/dnf or /var/lib/rpm, depending on the RHEL or Fedora release).

pairs.term: Which rpm query option shows information (who built it, when built, when installed, license, size) about a package?
pairs.definition: rpm -qi (query information), for example 'rpm -qi firefox'.

pairs.term: What are upstream software providers?
pairs.definition: The thousands of open source projects all over the world from which the software included with Linux distributions comes. They usually make the software available to anyone under certain licensing conditions.

pairs.term: After a distribution builds a package, what two things happen before it is used?
pairs.definition: The RPM package is signed (so users can test the package for validity) and is placed in a repository of RPMs for the specific distribution and architecture. The repository is put on install media or a directory available via FTP, web, or NFS server.

pairs.term: What are two major drawbacks of installing RPM packages with just the rpm command?
pairs.definition: (1) Dependencies: installing fails if a dependent package isn't installed, leading to dependency hell. (2) Location: rpm expects the exact location of the RPM file when installing it (a filename in the current directory or a full URL).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are the two main Linux software packaging formats?
pairs.definition: DEB (.deb) used by Debian and derivatives (Ubuntu, Linux Mint, MX Linux), and RPM (.rpm) used by SUSE, Red Hat distributions (RHEL and Fedora), and those based on Red Hat (Amazon Linux, CentOS, Oracle Linux).

pairs.term: What is a tarball?
pairs.definition: A single file in which multiple files are gathered together for convenient storage or distribution, often containing executable files (commands), documentation, configuration files, and libraries.

pairs.term: Why does installing software from a tarball make dependency management, removal, and updating difficult?
pairs.definition: You would have to know dependencies yourself, wouldn't know where all the files went for later removal, and tarballs don't hold metadata about their contents so you can't tell what version you are using.

pairs.term: What does the 'rpm' acronym originally stand for, and what is it now?
pairs.definition: Originally Red Hat Package Manager; later recursively renamed RPM Package Manager. The rpm command was the first tool to manage RPMs.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does the RPM Fusion Nonfree repository contain?
pairs.definition: Such things as codecs needed to play many popular multimedia formats.

pairs.term: What command enables the RPM Fusion Nonfree repository in Fedora?
pairs.definition: rpm -Uhv http://download1.rpmfusion.org/nonfree/fedora/rpmfusion-nonfree-release-stable.noarch.rpm

pairs.term: What command installs snapd on Fedora to enable Snap support?
pairs.definition: sudo dnf install snapd

pairs.term: What is the recommended third-party repository for Fedora and for RHEL?
pairs.definition: The RPM Fusion repository (http://rpmfusion.org) for Fedora and the EPEL repository for Red Hat Enterprise Linux. RPM Fusion is a fusion of Freshrpms, Livna.org, and Dribble repositories.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: dnf system-upgrade download --refresh --releasever=42
pairs.definition: Downloads the packages needed for a new release (here Fedora 42) before performing a system upgrade, refreshing metadata.

pairs.term: What does the --allowerasing option do during a Fedora release upgrade?
pairs.definition: It allows the upgrade to delete some packages in order to fix conflicts between existing packages and new versions of those packages.

pairs.term: Why is installing Linux from scratch recommended over upgrading?
pairs.definition: A fresh installation goes faster than an upgrade, results in a cleaner Linux system, and is recommended if you don't need the data on the system (or have a backup), after which you can restore your data.

pairs.term: What does 'dnf system-upgrade reboot' do?
pairs.definition: It starts the Fedora upgrade process after packages for the new version have been downloaded and conflicts fixed. You should not interrupt this process once started, or it could result in a broken system. The system reboots when it is done.

pairs.term: Which Linux distribution uses a continuous 'rolling release' model?
pairs.definition: Gentoo. Instead of taking a new release every few months, you continuously grab updated packages as they become available and install them.

pairs.term: dnf upgrade --refresh
pairs.definition: Refreshes package metadata and updates all packages to the latest versions for the current release, done before upgrading to a new release.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are low-numbered server ports called?
pairs.definition: Privileged ports (on UNIX, only root can create ports < 1024).

pairs.term: Why should one not safely rely on the privileged-port convention?
pairs.definition: It is a convention only, not required by the spec, meaningless on non-UNIX systems, and only trustable if the originating system enforces it properly.

pairs.term: What is a listening port described as?
pairs.definition: A half-open connection where only the local host and port number are known.

pairs.term: Who selects the local (client) port?
pairs.definition: Almost always selected at random by the OS; clients may select their own.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What enables TCP to detect stale packets from prior incarnations of a circuit?
pairs.definition: The ISN for new connections changes constantly.

pairs.term: What is the modest security benefit of ISN changes?
pairs.definition: A connection can't be fully established until both sides acknowledge the other's ISN.

pairs.term: What is a sequence number attack?
pairs.definition: An attacker predicts the target's starting points to trick it into believing it talks to a trusted machine, exploiting protocols that depend on IP source address for authentication.

pairs.term: Who showed that predicting starting points is possible?
pairs.definition: Morris (1985) and Bellovin (1989).

pairs.term: How can a firewall block Morris's sequence-number attack?
pairs.definition: By blocking legitimate connections to the target machine.

pairs.term: Why might a gateway machine be vulnerable despite firewalls?
pairs.definition: It may extend too much trust to inside machines depending on configuration.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are the three steps of TCP open?
pairs.definition: 1) Client sends SYN+ISN, 2) Server replies SYN+ACK (ISN+1), goes half-open, 3) Client sends ACK.

pairs.term: What state is the connection in after the server receives the initial SYN?
pairs.definition: Half-opened state.

pairs.term: How do attackers game the half-open state?
pairs.definition: SYN attacks flood the server with the first packet only, swamping it with half-open connections.

pairs.term: What can the first part of the three-step handshake detect?
pairs.definition: Active TCP services without alerting applications (which aren't informed until the handshake completes).

pairs.term: What three flags/numbers are exchanged in the TCP handshake?
pairs.definition: SYN (client), SYN+ACK (server), ACK (client).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: sudo netwox 76 -i 10.0.2.69 -p 23 -s raw
pairs.definition: Launches the Synflood tool (netwox 76) against destination IP 10.0.2.69 port 23 (telnet); -s raw means IP spoofing at the IP4/IP6 level instead of the link level; requires root privilege.

pairs.term: What two things must an attacker do to fill the half-open connection queue?
pairs.definition: (1) Continuously send a lot of SYN packets to the server; (2) never finish the third step of the three-way handshake (never send the final ACK).

pairs.term: netwox 76 -i ip -p port [-s spoofip]
pairs.definition: The usage of the Synflood netwox tool: -i/--dst-ip = destination IP address, -p/--dst-port = destination port number, -s/--spoofip = IP spoof initialization type.

pairs.term: What three events can cause a TCB record to be dequeued from the half-open connection queue?
pairs.definition: (1) The client finishes the three-way handshake; (2) the record times out after staying too long (timeout can be ~40 seconds); (3) the server receives an RST packet for the half-open connection.

pairs.term: telnet 10.0.2.69
pairs.definition: Attempts a telnet connection from the User machine to Server; during a successful SYN flooding attack it hangs and eventually fails with 'Connection timed out'.

pairs.term: Why do SYN flooding attackers use random source IP addresses?
pairs.definition: Otherwise their attacks can be easily blocked by firewalls; with spoofed addresses the server's SYN+ACK replies are often dropped, so the half-open connections stay in the queue until they time out.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What buffers does the OS allocate for each end of a TCP connection?
pairs.definition: Two buffers per end: one for sending data (send buffer) and one for receiving data (receive buffer). TCP is duplex, so both ends can send and receive.

pairs.term: Why does TCP delay sending small amounts of data?
pairs.definition: To avoid sending packets with small data and wasting network bandwidth; TCP usually waits a little bit (e.g., 200 ms) or until the data is enough to fill one packet without causing IP fragmentation.

pairs.term: What socket type does TCP use and what does UDP use?
pairs.definition: TCP uses SOCK_STREAM; UDP uses SOCK_DGRAM.

pairs.term: How does TCP ensure out-of-order packets are arranged correctly?
pairs.definition: Each octet in the send buffer has a sequence number; the TCP header's sequence number field indicates the first octet in the payload, and the receiver uses these to place data in the correct position in the receive buffer.

pairs.term: What two pieces of information are needed to identify a TCP server?
pairs.definition: The IP address and the port number.

pairs.term: How does a TCP receiver acknowledge received data?
pairs.definition: It does not acknowledge each packet; it tells the sender the next sequence number it expects to receive. If it received 100 contiguous octets after x, its next expected sequence number is x+100, which it puts in the acknowledgment packet.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does the Window field (16 bits) in the TCP header do?
pairs.definition: It is the window advertisement specifying how many octets the sender is willing to accept, usually based on available receive-buffer space; its purpose is flow control. A smaller value tells the sender to slow down.

pairs.term: What is included in the TCP checksum calculation?
pairs.definition: Part of the IP header, the TCP header, and the TCP data.

pairs.term: What are urgent data in TCP and how do they behave?
pairs.definition: When the URG bit is set, the first part of the data is urgent, out-of-band data that does not consume sequence numbers. TCP delivers urgent data immediately via a different mechanism (such as an exception); they do not wait in line.

pairs.term: What is the purpose of the TCP Options field?
pairs.definition: TCP segments can carry a variable length of options (0-320 bits, divisible by 32) that provide a way to deal with limitations of the original header.

pairs.term: What does the Sequence number field (32 bits) in the TCP header contain?
pairs.definition: The sequence number of the first octet in the payload of this TCP segment; if the SYN bit is set, it is the initial sequence number.

pairs.term: What does the Acknowledgment number field (32 bits) in the TCP header contain and when is it valid?
pairs.definition: It contains the value of the next sequence number expected by the sender of the segment; it is only valid if the ACK bit is set.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Why is resetting video-streaming connections (e.g., YouTube) harder than telnet?
pairs.definition: The sequence number increases very fast between the client and server, so manual sniff-and-type does not keep up; the attack must be automated using a sniff-and-spoof program.

pairs.term: Why might a Python/Scapy sniff-and-spoof RST attack be too slow for video streaming?
pairs.definition: The attack must use the correct, current sequence number; with lots of traffic, by the time the slow program sends the reset, the sequence number has already been consumed by other packets, so the RST is discarded.

pairs.term: sudo netwox 78 --filter "src host 10.0.2.68"
pairs.definition: Runs netwox tool 78 (reset every TCP packets): sends an RST packet for each packet coming from 10.0.2.68, automatically breaking all of that host's TCP connections.

pairs.term: What is the TCP FIN protocol (civilized close)?
pairs.definition: One end A sends a FIN packet; B replies with ACK, closing the A-to-B direction while B-to-A stays open. B then sends a FIN and A replies with ACK, closing the whole connection.

pairs.term: What does a TCP RST packet do?
pairs.definition: A single RST packet immediately breaks a TCP connection. It is used in emergency situations when there is no time for the FIN protocol, and is also sent when errors are detected (e.g., a machine receiving an unexpected SYN+ACK replies with RST).

pairs.term: What is the TCP Reset attack?
pairs.definition: An attack that breaks an existing TCP connection between two victims: the attacker spoofs a TCP RST packet from A to B or from B to A with the correct connection signature and sequence number, causing the connection to be closed immediately.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is TCP session hijacking?
pairs.definition: An attack where the attacker injects spoofed TCP packets whose signature matches an existing session and whose sequence number is correct, causing the receiver to accept the data as if from the legitimate sender, effectively taking control of the session.

pairs.term: What is /dev/tcp/host/port in Bash?
pairs.definition: A built-in virtual file keyword in the Bash shell (not a real device). Redirecting input/output to /dev/tcp/host/port makes Bash first establish a TCP connection to that host's port and then redirects the command's I/O to the TCP connection.

pairs.term: Why does the session hijacking payload need to start with a newline (\r)?
pairs.definition: Otherwise the injected command may be concatenated with strings typed by the victim, changing the meaning of the command. E.g., if the victim typed 'ls' at sequence x+98 and the attack uses N+100, the server would run 'lscat', which is not a valid command.

pairs.term: What is a reverse shell?
pairs.definition: A shell process running on a remote (compromised) machine that connects back to the attacker's machine, using a TCP connection for its input/output so the attacker can control it. It is a very common hacking technique.

pairs.term: What are Unix file descriptors 0, 1, and 2?
pairs.definition: 0 = standard input, 1 = standard output, 2 = standard error.

pairs.term: What does '2>&1' mean in a shell command?
pairs.definition: It redirects the standard error device (file descriptor 2) to file descriptor 1 (standard output), so the program also uses the standard output device for printing error messages.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Which of the three classical TCP attacks are DoS and which allows injection?
pairs.definition: TCP SYN flooding and TCP Reset attacks are Denial-of-Service (DoS) attacks; TCP session hijacking allows attackers to inject spoofed data into an existing TCP connection between two target peers.

pairs.term: Which TCP attacks can be mitigated by encryption?
pairs.definition: TCP session hijacking can be mitigated using encryption; the SYN flooding and TCP Reset attacks cannot benefit from encryption.

pairs.term: What protocol improvements make TCP attacks more difficult?
pairs.definition: Randomizing the source port number, randomizing the sequence number, and adoption of the SYN cookies mechanism; however, completely solving TCP's security problems without changing the protocol is hard.

pairs.term: What is the key lesson about protocol design from the TCP attacks chapter?
pairs.definition: When designing a network protocol, security needs to be built in to mitigate potential attacks; otherwise the protocol will likely be attacked. TCP was not designed with built-in security, making it subject to many attacks.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: First step of router discovery?
pairs.definition: Host sends multicast router-solicitation to all routers.

pairs.term: Why do ICMP errors not generate their own ICMP messages?
pairs.definition: To avoid error reports generating more error reports and increasing congestion.

pairs.term: Router(config-if)# no ip redirects
pairs.definition: Disables ICMP redirects on a specific interface.

pairs.term: What condition causes a datagram to travel in a circle?
pairs.definition: Two routers routing a datagram back and forth because each thinks the other is the next hop.

pairs.term: Timestamp units?
pairs.definition: Milliseconds elapsed since midnight Universal Time (UT).

pairs.term: When is a router-solicitation generated?
pairs.definition: In response to a missing default gateway.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does connection-oriented mean in TCP?
pairs.definition: End stations are aware of each other and constantly communicate about the connection.

pairs.term: What is a classic non-technical example of connection-oriented communication?
pairs.definition: A telephone conversation between two people.

pairs.term: What is an example of connectionless communication?
pairs.definition: The U.S. postal service.

pairs.term: TCP is a peer-to-peer communication. What does this mean?
pairs.definition: Either side can begin communicating and either side can break the communication.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is a DoS attack?
pairs.definition: A type of attack designed to halt system response by flooding it with useless traffic, denying services to legitimate hosts.

pairs.term: What is SYN flooding?
pairs.definition: A DoS attack occurring during the TCP three-way handshake synchronization process.

pairs.term: In a SYN flood attack, what does the hacker falsify?
pairs.definition: The source IP address in the SYN packet.

pairs.term: Where is a waiting synchronization request placed?
pairs.definition: In a connection queue or a holding area in memory.

pairs.term: What resources are consumed by SYN flood waiting requests?
pairs.definition: System resources such as memory, committed until the connection timer times out.

pairs.term: How do administrators defend against DoS synchronization attacks?
pairs.definition: Decrease the connection timeout period, increase the connection queue size, and use attack-detection software.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What field follows the sequence number in a TCP segment?
pairs.definition: The Acknowledgement field (also referred to as the Code field).

pairs.term: Where are ACKs and SYNs indicated?
pairs.definition: In the Acknowledgement/Code field of the TCP segment.

pairs.term: What does positive acknowledgement and retransmission mean?
pairs.definition: The source sends a packet, starts a timer, waits for an ACK, and retransmits if the timer expires before an ACK is received.

pairs.term: What does an expected acknowledgment number refer to?
pairs.definition: The next octet that is expected.

pairs.term: What problem does IP have that TCP addresses with positive ACK?
pairs.definition: No verification method exists in IP to determine that data segments reached their destination.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Why does TCP apply sequence numbers to data segments?
pairs.definition: So the receiver can reassemble the bytes in their original order.

pairs.term: What do sequencing numbers do?
pairs.definition: They indicate to the destination device the correct order to put the bytes when received.

pairs.term: What should a host do if a sequence number is missing?
pairs.definition: Retransmit the missing segment.

pairs.term: What is the efficiency benefit of sequencing numbers?
pairs.definition: The sender retransmits only missing segments instead of the entire set of data.

pairs.term: What is the sequence number assigned to?
pairs.definition: The first octet in the user data field.

pairs.term: How does a receiving station reassemble segments?
pairs.definition: It uses the sequence numbers to reassemble the segments into a complete message.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the header length field of a TCP segment?
pairs.definition: The number of 32-bit words in the header.

pairs.term: What is the TCP reserved field set to?
pairs.definition: Set to 0.

pairs.term: What do the TCP code bits indicate?
pairs.definition: Control functions such as setup and termination of a session.

pairs.term: What is the TCP window field?
pairs.definition: The number of octets that the sender is willing to accept.

pairs.term: What is the TCP checksum field?
pairs.definition: The calculated checksum of the header and data fields.

pairs.term: What does the TCP urgent field indicate?
pairs.definition: An indicator of the end of the urgent data.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does NBSTAT troubleshoot?
pairs.definition: NetBIOS name resolution and viewing/removing entries from the name cache.

pairs.term: What does ARP stand for?
pairs.definition: Address Resolution Protocol.

pairs.term: What is WINS?
pairs.definition: A Microsoft-developed standard for Windows NT that automatically associates NT workstations with Internet domain names.

pairs.term: What does NETSTAT provide?
pairs.definition: Information about TCP/IP statistics, the status of TCP/IP connections, and summaries of ICMP, TCP, and UDP.

pairs.term: What does RARP stand for?
pairs.definition: Reverse Address Resolution Protocol.

pairs.term: What is the HOSTS file?
pairs.definition: A file created by network administrators on servers providing static mappings between IP addresses and computer names.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What layers does the TCP/IP 4-layer model contain?
pairs.definition: Application, Transport, Internet, and Network Interface (physical/data link).

pairs.term: What does the TCP/IP application layer combine from the OSI model?
pairs.definition: The functionality found in the OSI session, presentation, and application layers.

pairs.term: What three elements identify a particular network connection?
pairs.definition: Source address, source port, and destination address, destination port (four-part sequence).

pairs.term: What is formed when a port number and a network address combine?
pairs.definition: A socket. A pair of sockets (one on each host) forms a unique connection.

pairs.term: What organization developed the TCP/IP protocol suite?
pairs.definition: The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA).

pairs.term: For what original purpose was TCP/IP developed?
pairs.definition: It was originally developed to provide communication within DARPA.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the Layer 4 data stream also called?
pairs.definition: An end-to-end service, a logical connection between the endpoints of a network.

pairs.term: What is the advantage of TCP?
pairs.definition: It provides guaranteed delivery of segments.

pairs.term: What does TCP provide between end-user applications?
pairs.definition: A virtual circuit.

pairs.term: What is the advantage of UDP?
pairs.definition: Speed, because it provides no acknowledgments and less control traffic across the network.

pairs.term: When must TCP be used?
pairs.definition: When applications need to guarantee that a packet arrives intact, in sequence, and unduplicated.

pairs.term: What do application layer protocols using UDP provide for reliability?
pairs.definition: They must provide error detection and retransmission because UDP uses no windowing or acknowledgments.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: In step 2 of the handshake, what does the receiving host send?
pairs.definition: An acknowledgment of x + 1 and its own ISN y.

pairs.term: What does an acknowledgment of x + 1 mean?
pairs.definition: All octets up to and including x have been received, expecting x + 1 next.

pairs.term: In step 3 of the handshake, what is sent?
pairs.definition: A simple acknowledgement (ACK) of y + 1 from the initiating host.

pairs.term: Why is the three-way handshake necessary?
pairs.definition: TCPs may use different mechanisms for picking the ISN; the receiver cannot know if a segment was an old delayed one unless it remembers the last sequence number used.

pairs.term: Why do sequence numbers matter during initiation?
pairs.definition: They act as reference starting numbers; the receiver knows the sender is responding to the proper connection request by ACKing the SYN.

pairs.term: What figure illustrates the three-way handshake?
pairs.definition: Figure 19-7 Three-Way Handshake.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does a DNS request to a DNS server have in the UDP header?
pairs.definition: A Destination Port field of 53 (the UDP port number for DNS).

pairs.term: When must a destination host use ports after a UDP segment arrives?
pairs.definition: To determine the destination application of the segment.

pairs.term: What does UDP provide for applications that TCP does not?
pairs.definition: Connectionless, non-guaranteed transmission of packets.

pairs.term: Where is TFTP commonly used on a router?
pairs.definition: To transfer configuration files and IOS images.

pairs.term: Why does TFTP use UDP over TCP?
pairs.definition: Because the quality of physical connections is usually very good and TCP acknowledgments/retransmission are not necessary.

pairs.term: What is UDP designed for?
pairs.definition: Applications that do not need to put sequences of segments together.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Is the UDP source port field required?
pairs.definition: No, the source port is optional, used only if information needs to return to the sending host.

pairs.term: What does the UDP destination port field specify?
pairs.definition: The application to which UDP must pass the protocol.

pairs.term: What does the UDP length field identify?
pairs.definition: The number of octets in the UDP segment.

pairs.term: Is the UDP checksum required?
pairs.definition: It is optional but should be used to ensure data has not been damaged during transmission.

pairs.term: How is UDP encapsulated for transport across a network?
pairs.definition: UDP is encapsulated within the IP packet.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does the sender do after receiving the window size?
pairs.definition: It sends that many octets to the receiving host.

pairs.term: What does TCP utilize for determining transmission size?
pairs.definition: A sliding window that enables devices to negotiate a window size.

pairs.term: What can the destination device do with a sliding window?
pairs.definition: It can indicate a need to decrease the amount of data sent, or instruct the source to increase data if it can process more.

pairs.term: With a window size of 1, what must happen?
pairs.definition: Each individual segment must be acknowledged before the next segment can be sent.

pairs.term: What is the number of messages or bytes that can be transmitted while awaiting an acknowledgment called?
pairs.definition: Window size.

pairs.term: What figure shows a window size of 1?
pairs.definition: Figure 19-9 Window Size of 1.

pairs.definition: The MAC addresses and IP addresses of devices connected to the same LAN.

pairs.definition: The corresponding (physical) MAC addresses.

pairs.definition: An ARP request.

pairs.definition: The IP address, a router (default gateway) address, a server address, and vendor-specific information.

pairs.term: BOOTP uses what transport protocol to carry messages?
pairs.definition: UDP (encapsulated in an IP packet).

pairs.term: A computer uses BOOTP to send a broadcast IP packet using what destination IP address?

pairs.term: One problem with BOOTP is that it was not designed to provide dynamic address assignment; instead, what does it require?

Class E addresses are reserved by whom and for what?
pairs.definition: Reserved by the IANA for research; not released for use on the Internet.

pairs.term: The first 4 bits of a Class D address are always what?
A network address has binary 0s in all host bit positions. What does this mean?
pairs.definition: It identifies the network itself and is never used as a host address.

pairs.term: Class E addresses range from which first-octet decimal value to which?
An IP address that uses all 1s in the entire host part is used for what?
pairs.definition: A broadcast address.

pairs.term: IPv4 uses how many bits for addresses?

pairs.term: IPv6 uses how many bits for addresses?

pairs.term: IPv6 uses hexadecimal numbers to represent its 128 bits. How many 16-bit groups are there?
pairs.definition: Eight 16-bit groups shown as four hexadecimal digits, separated by colons.

pairs.term: The shorthand representation of IPv6 allows leading 0s in hex groups to be what?
pairs.definition: Omitted.

pairs.term: IPv6 provides approximately how many addresses?
pairs.definition: 16 billion IP addresses (3.4 x 10^38 addresses).

pairs.definition: Uses ICMP (or UDP) to discover the path and intermediate hops a packet takes toward a destination, leveraging ICMP control messaging.

pairs.term: ICMP provides what kind of capabilities at the Internet layer?
pairs.definition: Control and messaging capabilities.

pairs.definition: Three blocks (one Class A, a range of Class B, and a range of Class C).

pairs.definition: It determines IP addresses when data link layer (MAC) addresses are known.

pairs.definition: Smaller pieces (subnets) to conserve IP addresses and prevent exhaustion.

pairs.definition: Which part of an address is the network number (including the subnet) and which part is the host.

pairs.term: Are web browsers, e-mail programs, FTP clients client/server apps?

pairs.definition: By copying and moving files from server to client and vice versa

pairs.definition: The pair of destination and source port numbers

pairs.term: What happens when a fatal alert is sent in TLS?
pairs.definition: TLS immediately terminates the connection. Other connections on the same session may continue, but no new connections on this session may be established.

pairs.definition: unexpected_message, bad_record_mac, decompression_failure, handshake_failure, illegal_parameter, decryption_failed, record_overflow, unknown_ca, access_denied, decode_error, export_restriction, protocol_version, insufficient_security, and internal_error.

pairs.term: What is the close_notify alert?
pairs.definition: Notifies the recipient that the sender will not send any more messages on this connection. Each party is required to send a close_notify alert before closing the write side of a connection.

pairs.term: Which TLS alerts are not always fatal?

pairs.term: How is the TLS key block material generated?
pairs.definition: key_block = PRF(SecurityParameters.master_secret, 'key expansion', SecurityParameters.server_random || SecurityParameters.client_random), iterated until enough output is generated for the MAC secret keys, session encryption keys, and IVs.

pairs.term: In what order are cryptographic parameters generated from the TLS master secret?
pairs.definition: Client write MAC secret, server write MAC secret, client write key, server write key, client write IV, and server write IV.

pairs.term: What is the TLS pseudorandom function (PRF)?
pairs.definition: A function that expands secrets into blocks of data for key generation or validation. It takes a secret, a label, and a seed and produces an output of arbitrary length, using two hash algorithms in a way that should guarantee security if either remains secure.

pairs.term: What is P_hash(secret, seed) in TLS?
pairs.definition: The data expansion function: P_hash(secret, seed) = HMAC_hash(secret, A(1) || seed) || HMAC_hash(secret, A(2) || seed) || HMAC_hash(secret, A(3) || seed) || ... , iterated as needed to produce the required quantity of data.

pairs.term: How is the A() sequence defined in P_hash?
pairs.definition: A(0) = seed; A(i) = HMAC_hash(secret, A(i-1)).

pairs.term: How many iterations are needed to generate 80 bytes with P_SHA256 and P_MD5?
pairs.definition: P_SHA256 must be iterated three times (through A(3)), producing 96 bytes of which the last 16 are discarded; P_MD5 must be iterated four times, producing exactly 64 bytes.

pairs.term: What is the server_done message?
pairs.definition: The final message in Phase 2, always required, sent by the server to indicate the end of the server hello and associated messages; it has no parameters and the server then waits for a client response.

pairs.term: What is the purpose of the TLS Handshake Protocol?
pairs.definition: It allows the server and client to authenticate each other and to negotiate an encryption and MAC algorithm and cryptographic keys to be used to protect data sent in a TLS record. It is used before any application data is transmitted.

pairs.term: What does the client_key_exchange message contain for RSA key exchange?
pairs.definition: The client generates a 48-byte pre-master secret and encrypts it with the public key from the server's certificate (or the temporary RSA key from a server_key_exchange message).

pairs.term: What is the format of a TLS Handshake Protocol message?
pairs.definition: Three fields: Type (1 byte, indicating one of 10 messages), Length (3 bytes, length of the message), and Content (0 or more bytes, the parameters associated with the message).

pairs.term: What does the client_key_exchange message contain for Diffie-Hellman?
pairs.definition: For ephemeral or anonymous DH, the client's public DH parameters are sent. For fixed DH, the client's public DH parameters were already sent in a certificate message, so the content is null.

pairs.term: What are the ten TLS Handshake Protocol message types?
pairs.definition: hello_request, client_hello, server_hello, certificate, server_key_exchange, certificate_request, server_done, certificate_verify, client_key_exchange, and finished.

pairs.term: What is the TLS Heartbeat Protocol?
pairs.definition: Defined in 2012, it runs on top of the TLS Record Protocol and consists of two message types: heartbeat_request and heartbeat_response. Support for heartbeats is established during Phase 1 of the Handshake Protocol.

pairs.term: What fields does a heartbeat_request message include?
pairs.definition: Payload length, payload (a random content between 16 bytes and 64 Kbytes), and padding (random content). The heartbeat_response must include an exact copy of the received payload.

pairs.term: What two purposes does the TLS Heartbeat Protocol serve?
pairs.definition: (1) It assures the sender that the recipient is still alive even when there has been no activity over the underlying TCP connection; (2) it generates activity during idle periods, avoiding closure by firewalls that do not tolerate idle connections.

pairs.term: What is DTLS?
pairs.definition: Datagram Transport Layer Security, a connectionless version of TLS. Because it is subject to packet loss, the heartbeat payload enables matching of responses to requests.

pairs.term: How does the heartbeat padding support path MTU discovery?
pairs.definition: The sender performs path MTU (maximum transfer unit) discovery by sending requests with increasing padding until there is no answer anymore, because one of the hosts on the path cannot handle the message.

pairs.term: Maximum length of a TLS record payload
pairs.definition: The Length field of the TLS record header is not to exceed 2^14 bytes (16384 bytes).

pairs.term: TLS versions supported as of July 2017 (per the chapter)
pairs.definition: SSL 3.0, TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, TLS 1.2, and TLS 1.3. The Version field in the TLS record header identifies the major and minor version.

pairs.term: What TLS (Transport Layer Security) provides
pairs.definition: A protocol that provides a secure channel between two communicating applications so that data transmission in the channel is private and its integrity is preserved.

pairs.term: Three properties of the TLS secure channel
pairs.definition: 1. Confidentiality: only the two ends can see the data content. 2. Integrity: tampering during transmission is detected. 3. Authentication: at least one end (usually the server) is authenticated so the client knows it talks to the intended host.

pairs.term: Where TLS sits in the network stack
pairs.definition: TLS sits between the Application Layer and the Transport Layer. Applications give unprotected data to the TLS layer, which handles encryption, decryption, and integrity checking, then passes the protected data to TCP.

pairs.term: TLS Record Layer and the five TLS protocols
pairs.definition: TLS is a layered protocol. The bottom layer, the Record Protocol, defines the format of TLS records. On top of it run five message protocols: Handshake, Alert, Change Cipher Spec, Heartbeat, and Application.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What two services does the TLS Record Protocol provide?
pairs.definition: Confidentiality (the Handshake Protocol defines a shared secret key used for conventional encryption of TLS payloads) and message integrity (a shared secret key is used to form a MAC).

pairs.term: What steps are involved in the TLS Record Protocol transmission?
pairs.definition: Fragment the application data into blocks of 2^14 bytes or less, optionally compress, compute a MAC over the compressed data, encrypt the compressed message plus MAC, and prepend a TLS record header; the resulting unit is transmitted in a TCP segment.

pairs.term: What is the maximum fragment size in the TLS Record Protocol?
pairs.definition: Each upper-layer message is fragmented into blocks of 2^14 bytes (16,384 bytes) or less.

pairs.term: What constraints apply to TLS compression?
pairs.definition: Compression must be lossless and may not increase the content length by more than 1024 bytes. In TLSv1.2 no compression algorithm is specified, so the default compression algorithm is null.

pairs.term: What MAC algorithm does TLS use?
pairs.definition: TLS makes use of the HMAC algorithm defined in RFC 2104, with either MD5 or SHA-1 as the embedded hash function.

pairs.term: What fields does the TLS MAC calculation cover?
pairs.definition: HMAC_hash(MAC_write_secret, seq_num || TLSCompressed.type || TLSCompressed.version || TLSCompressed.length || TLSCompressed.fragment).

pairs.term: What is a TLS connection?
pairs.definition: A connection is a transport that provides a suitable type of service; for TLS, connections are peer-to-peer relationships that are transient, and every connection is associated with one session.

pairs.term: What parameters define a TLS connection state?
pairs.definition: Server and client random, server write MAC secret, client write MAC secret, server write key, client write key, initialization vectors (for CBC block ciphers), and sequence numbers for transmitted and received messages.

pairs.term: How are sequence numbers handled in a TLS connection?
pairs.definition: Each party maintains separate sequence numbers for transmitted and received messages for each connection. When a change cipher spec message is sent or received, the appropriate sequence number is set to zero; sequence numbers may not exceed 2^64 - 1.

pairs.term: How are initialization vectors maintained in TLS when a CBC block cipher is used?
pairs.definition: An IV is maintained for each key, first initialized by the TLS Handshake Protocol. Thereafter, the final ciphertext block from each record is preserved for use as the IV with the following record.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Why a sequence number is included in the TLS MAC calculation
pairs.definition: Each record has a sequence number included in the MAC calculation, so records cannot be replayed or reordered without detection.

pairs.term: Where the IV is placed in a TLS block-cipher record
pairs.definition: A random IV is used for block ciphers and placed at the beginning of the payload field; the IV itself is not encrypted.

pairs.term: How SSL_read() behaves when the TLS buffer is empty
pairs.definition: One TLS record is retrieved from the TCP buffer and processed; if that is not enough for the request, more records are retrieved and processed until the request is satisfied or no more data is available. Leftover data is stored in the TLS buffer.

pairs.term: How SSL_read() behaves when the TLS buffer is not empty
pairs.definition: TLS tries to get the requested amount from the TLS buffer. If it has enough, it delivers the requested amount; if not, it returns all buffered data to the application, and the next call restarts with an empty buffer and follows the record-reading procedure.

pairs.term: What the Length field of a TLS record contains
pairs.definition: The Length field contains the length of the payload, not to exceed 2^14 bytes, excluding the protocol header but including the MAC and padding trailers.

pairs.term: The three fields in a TLS record header
pairs.definition: 1. Content Type: which protocol (Alert, Handshake, Application, Heartbeat, ChangeCipherSpec) carries the data. 2. Version: TLS major and minor version. 3. Length: the length of the payload, not exceeding 2^14 bytes.

pairs.term: What TLS certificate validation does NOT check
pairs.definition: Whether the identity information in the certificate matches the identity of the intended server. That check is the responsibility of applications; without it a client could be talking to attacker32.com impersonating facebook.com.

pairs.term: Client write keys vs server write keys
pairs.definition: client_write keys (MAC and encryption) secure data from the client to the server; server_write keys secure data from the server to the client. The communication is bidirectional and each direction uses its own keys.

pairs.term: What the client random and server random are used for
pairs.definition: They are nonces exchanged during the handshake; together with the pre-master secret they are used to generate the master secret and then the session keys.

pairs.term: Pre-master secret length dependence
pairs.definition: The length of the pre-master secret depends on the key exchange algorithm. The client generates it as a random number and sends it to the server encrypted with the server's public key.

pairs.term: Master secret size
pairs.definition: The master secret is 48 bytes long, generated from the pre-master secret plus client_random and server_random. It is then used to generate the session keys (two MAC keys and two encryption keys).

pairs.term: Primary purpose of the TLS Handshake Protocol
pairs.definition: To let the client and server agree on cryptographic parameters: the encryption algorithm and keys, the MAC algorithm, the key exchange algorithm, and other parameters.

pairs.definition: If no callback is specified, TLS uses its default callback, which aborts the TLS connection if the hostname check or other checks fail. The safest custom behavior is to return 0 (abort/exit) on any failed check.

pairs.term: What Firefox's warning listed when it detected the MITM (example.org impersonating facebook.com)
pairs.definition: 'www.facebook.com uses an invalid security certificate. The certificate is only valid for the following names: www.example.org, example.com, example.edu, ...' with error code SSL_ERROR_BAD_CERT_DOMAIN. The site also uses HSTS, so no exception can be added.

pairs.term: HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) effect in the warning
pairs.definition: HSTS specifies that Firefox may only connect to the site securely, so it is not possible to add a certificate exception for that site - the MITM is blocked.

pairs.term: Certificate alternative names (SAN) in the hostname check
pairs.definition: Certificates may contain a list of alternative names in their extension field (e.g., example.com, www.example.com, example.edu, etc. in addition to the common name). Hostname checking must consider these names, which is why OpenSSL automates it since 1.0.2.

pairs.term: What happens if the verify callback returns 0 on a failed hostname check
pairs.definition: The TLS handshake is immediately terminated; the client exits with 'certificate verify failed' (ssl3_get_server_certificate error). This is the safe behavior.

pairs.term: Why failing to check the server's hostname is dangerous
pairs.definition: It is a very common security flaw (Georgiev et al. 2012). Without checking whether the server's hostname matches the certificate's subject, a client can be susceptible to MITM attacks: it will securely communicate with the wrong server.

pairs.term: What is intelligent code analysis?

pairs.term: What is integrated error checking?
pairs.definition: An intelligent code analysis feature that tells you right away if there's a problem with your code, instead of finding out only after compiling or running the code, especially important before reaching production.

pairs.term: What is autocompletion?
pairs.definition: A feature that detects when you are beginning to type a recognized variable, function, method, or type, and provides a drop-down list from which you can quickly locate and choose the correct option instead of typing the rest.

pairs.term: What is linting in a text editor?
pairs.definition: Bringing stylistic problems to your attention early - code that might run or compile properly but otherwise violates established idioms of the language (e.g., PEP 8 for Python). In some cases violations can even be automatically corrected.

pairs.term: What is the complete range of TCP and UDP port numbers?
pairs.definition: 0 through 65535, based on the 16 bits used to identify source and destination port numbers.

pairs.term: What are well-known ports?
pairs.definition: Port numbers 0 to 1023, reserved for common or popular services and applications such as web browsers, email clients, and remote access clients.

pairs.term: What are registered ports?
pairs.definition: Port numbers 1024 to 49,151, assigned by IANA to a requesting entity for use with specific processes or applications, primarily individual applications a user chooses to install.

pairs.term: What are private and/or dynamic (ephemeral) ports?
pairs.definition: Port numbers 49,152 to 65,535, usually assigned dynamically by the client OS when a connection to a service is initiated, to identify the client application during communication.

pairs.term: Which standards organization assigns 16-bit port numbers?
pairs.definition: The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA).

pairs.term: Which port number did Cisco register for its RADIUS server authentication process?
pairs.definition: Port 1812 (a registered port).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the destination port number?
pairs.definition: The port number associated with the destination application on the remote host, which identifies the type of service being requested.

pairs.term: How does a server manage multiple services simultaneously?
pairs.definition: A server can offer more than one service simultaneously, such as web services on port 80 and FTP connection establishment on port 21.

pairs.term: What are port numbers used for at the transport layer?
pairs.definition: Both TCP and UDP use port numbers to manage multiple simultaneous conversations and to identify the proper application layer process.

pairs.term: What is the source port number?
pairs.definition: The port number associated with the originating application on the local host, dynamically generated by the host to uniquely identify the conversation.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is a conversation at the transport layer?
pairs.definition: Each set of data flowing between a source application and a destination application. The transport layer is responsible for maintaining and tracking all conversations separately.

pairs.term: What are the transport layer blocks called when data is divided?
pairs.definition: Segments (when TCP is used) or datagrams (when UDP is used). They are also commonly referred to generically as segments.

pairs.term: Why does the transport layer divide application data into blocks?
pairs.definition: Because most networks have a limitation on the amount of data that can be included in a single packet; dividing data into manageable pieces allows it to be transported and reassembled.

pairs.term: How does the transport layer identify the target application for a data stream?
pairs.definition: By using an identifier called a port number. Each software process that needs to access the network is assigned a port number unique to that host.

pairs.term: What is segmentation and multiplexing in the transport layer?
pairs.definition: The process of dividing data and interleaving different communication conversations on the same network, enabling multiple conversations to occur at the same time.

pairs.term: What does IP alone not specify about delivery?
pairs.definition: IP is concerned only with the structure, addressing, and routing of packets. It does not specify how the delivery or transportation of the packets takes place.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is a socket?
pairs.definition: The combination of the source IP address and source port number, or the destination IP address and destination port number.

pairs.term: What is a socket pair?
pairs.definition: The combination of two sockets that form the endpoints of a conversation, such as 192.168.1.5:1099, 192.168.1.7:80.

pairs.term: What purpose do sockets serve?
pairs.definition: Sockets enable multiple processes running on a client to distinguish themselves from each other and make it possible for multiple connections to a server process to be distinguished from each other.

pairs.term: How does the source port number act during communication?
pairs.definition: The source port number acts as a return address for the requesting application. The transport layer keeps track of this port and the application that initiated the request so responses can be forwarded to the correct application.

pairs.term: What are the six control bits (flags) in the TCP header Control Bits field?
pairs.definition: URG, ACK, PSH, RST, SYN, and FIN. A flag is a bit that is set to either on or off.

pairs.term: What does the URG flag do?
pairs.definition: Allows an application to process the data immediately.

pairs.term: What does the ACK flag do?
pairs.definition: Acknowledgment flag used in connection establishment and session termination.

pairs.term: What does the PSH flag do?
pairs.definition: Performs the push function.

pairs.term: What does the RST flag do?
pairs.definition: Used to reset the connection when an error or timeout occurs.

pairs.term: What does the SYN flag do?
pairs.definition: Used to synchronize sequence numbers used in connection establishment.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the purpose of the TCP Header Length field (data offset)?
pairs.definition: A 4-bit field that indicates the length of the TCP segment header.

pairs.term: What is the purpose of the TCP Control Bits field?
pairs.definition: A 6-bit field that includes bit codes, or flags, which indicate the purpose and function of the TCP segment.

pairs.term: What is the purpose of the TCP Window Size field?
pairs.definition: A 16-bit field used to indicate the number of bytes that can be accepted at one time.

pairs.term: What is the purpose of the TCP Checksum field?
pairs.definition: A 16-bit field used for error checking of the segment header and data.

pairs.term: What is the purpose of the TCP Urgent field?
pairs.definition: A 16-bit field used to indicate whether the contained data is urgent.

pairs.term: How many bytes of overhead does a TCP segment add when encapsulating application layer data?
pairs.definition: 20 bytes (160 bits).

pairs.term: Why is UDP known as a stateless protocol?
pairs.definition: Because UDP does not track information sent or received between the client and server.

pairs.term: Why is UDP known as a best-effort delivery protocol?
pairs.definition: Because it provides no acknowledgment that the data is received at the destination, and there are no transport layer processes that inform the sender of a successful delivery.

pairs.term: Which applications are good candidates for UDP?
pairs.definition: Delay-sensitive applications such as VoIP, and simple request-and-reply applications such as DNS and DHCP, where retransmission can be done quickly.

pairs.term: Why is UDP preferable for VoIP?
pairs.definition: Because acknowledgments and retransmissions would slow down delivery and make a voice conversation unacceptable.

pairs.term: Which applications require TCP?
pairs.definition: Applications such as databases, web browsers, and email clients that require all data sent to arrive at the destination in its original condition.

pairs.term: Which transport protocol do applications that stream stored audio and video typically use?
pairs.definition: TCP, because the application can use TCP to perform buffering, bandwidth probing, and congestion control for a better user experience.

pairs.definition: Establish a theory of probable causes. This step often yields more than a few probable causes to the problem.

pairs.definition: Test the theory to determine the cause. A technician often applies a quick procedure to see if it solves the problem. If it does not, research the problem further to establish the exact cause.

pairs.term: What is IP subnet zero?

pairs.term: What command re-enables the use of the all-0s and all-1s subnets?

pairs.definition: A simple Ethernet link (10 Mbps) is faster than a serial link (1.544 Mbps).

pairs.term: What links are used almost exclusively between routers in today's modern networks?
pairs.definition: Ethernet links; serial links are rapidly becoming obsolete but remain cost-effective for testing labs.

pairs.term: What is the speed of a serial link and of a simple Ethernet link?
pairs.definition: A serial link is 1.544 Mbps; a simple Ethernet link is 10 Mbps (faster).

pairs.definition: Network E = .0/30, Network F = .4/30, Network G = .8/30, and Network H = .12/30.

pairs.definition: 00 is the original pattern of subnetting, NNNN are the extra bits you have (creating 16 /30 subnets), and 00 is the 2 H bits needed for the serial links.

pairs.term: What is the global VRF?
pairs.definition: The VRF to which all router interfaces belong until they are specifically assigned to a user-defined VRF; it is synonymous with the regular routing table of non-VRF routers.

pairs.term: Why can overlapping IP address ranges be used with VRF?
pairs.definition: Because every router's VRF maintains a separate routing table, so the same IP range can exist in different VRFs without conflict.

pairs.term: What segmentation does VRF create on a router?
pairs.definition: VRF creates segmentation between network interfaces, network subinterfaces, IP addresses, and routing tables, ensuring path isolation and increased security; encryption is not needed to maintain privacy between VRF instances.

pairs.term: How does VRF allow overlapping addresses without conflict?
pairs.definition: Each VRF maintains a separate routing table, so the same IP address (for example, 10.0.3.1) can be used in the global table and in a VRF without conflict.

pairs.term: What is the VTP Server role?
pairs.definition: The server switch is responsible for the creation, modification, and deletion of VLANs within the VTP domain.

pairs.term: What is the VTP Client role?
pairs.definition: The client switch receives VTP advertisements and modifies the VLANs on that switch; VLANs cannot be configured locally on a VTP client.

pairs.term: What is the VTP Transparent role?
pairs.definition: VTP transparent switches receive and forward VTP advertisements but do not modify the local VLAN database; VLANs are configured only locally.

pairs.term: What is the VTP Off role?
pairs.definition: A switch in Off mode does not participate in VTP advertisements and does not forward them out of any ports; VLANs are configured only locally.

pairs.term: What are the advantages of virtual devices?
pairs.definition: They are easier to set up, relatively cheap, and allow quick changes to the topology; time-to-build is quicker because they are usually just software programs.

pairs.term: What are the disadvantages of virtual devices?
pairs.definition: They are usually a scaled-down version of their physical counterpart and sometimes there are feature gaps between the virtual and the physical device.

pairs.term: What are the advantages of a physical lab?
pairs.definition: It is an easy transition from lab to production, easier to understand by managers and engineers who can see and touch the devices, and the comfort level is extremely high because of familiarity.

pairs.term: What are the disadvantages of a physical lab?
pairs.definition: It is relatively expensive to pay for a device used only in the lab, requires engineering hours to rack and stack, and is not very flexible once constructed.

pairs.definition: The special format in which Vagrant images are distributed. Boxes are similar to the virtual images you might download to run in VirtualBox natively, but also include the necessary modifications to use that virtual image in Vagrant.

pairs.term: What is Vagrant Cloud?
pairs.definition: Vagrant's official image repository where Vagrant boxes are hosted (e.g., vyos/current). Vagrant can automatically download and use an image from it without modifications.

pairs.term: What are Vagrant provisioners?
pairs.definition: A feature that allows you to perform additional configuration steps after the VMs have been provisioned and booted up. One relevant provisioner is ansible, which runs an Ansible playbook on your VMs to bootstrap the topology with real-world configuration.

pairs.term: What are two shortcomings of using VirtualBox directly (without Vagrant) for a network dev environment?
pairs.definition: Collaborating over VM changes is difficult because even small VM images can be multiple gigabytes and impractical to share, and even simple config changes through the VirtualBox GUI can be tedious, making complex topologies time-consuming and error prone.

pairs.definition: A hypervisor virtualizes hardware to run multiple VMs: Type 1 (bare-metal, runs directly on hardware — VMware ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM; used in data centers) and Type 2 (hosted, runs as an application on an OS — VirtualBox, Workstation).

pairs.term: What is a virtual machine (VM)?
pairs.definition: A software emulation of a computer running a guest OS, isolated from other VMs on the same host; the hypervisor allocates vCPUs, memory, virtual NICs, and virtual disks. Snapshots capture VM state; migration (vMotion) moves running VMs between hosts.

pairs.term: What is device virtualization in Cisco networking?
pairs.definition: Virtualizing network devices: IOS-XE on a hypervisor (vIOS, CSR1000v), virtual switches (VMware vSwitch), and containerized network functions — enabling network functions in software on commodity hardware, a foundation of SDN/NFV.

pairs.definition: D4/Superframe (SF) — 12 frames, less overhead, no CRC. Extended Superframe (ESF) — 24 frames, includes CRC6 and facility data link for diagnostics. ESF is the modern standard.

pairs.term: What are the two T1 line encoding methods?
pairs.definition: AMI (Alternate Mark Inversion) — transmits 1s as alternating voltage pulses. Requires 1s density for timing. B8ZS (Bipolar 8-Zero Substitution) — substitutes 8 consecutive zeros with a special pattern to maintain timing. B8ZS is preferred.

pairs.term: What do T1 alarms (Red, Yellow, Blue) mean?
pairs.definition: Red Alarm — local device has lost signal/packet from remote (LOS, LOF, AIS). Yellow Alarm — remote device is reporting a red alarm condition to us. Blue Alarm (AIS) — upstream device is sending an alarm indication signal (no traffic).

pairs.term: What is LEC?
pairs.definition: LEC (pronounced leck) is short for local exchange carrier. A LEC is a phone com- pany that provides local service, as opposed to an IXC, which interconnects LECs to provide long-distance service. Most of the largest LECs are RBOCs.

pairs.term: What is Local loop?
pairs.definition: The local loop (also referred to as the last mile) is the copper handoff for a circuit from the telecom facility to your facility. While a T1 may be converted and multi- plexed into a larger circuit like a DS3 or SONET circuit, the last mile is usually copper.

pairs.term: SMDS
pairs.definition: Switched Multimegabit Data Service (SMDS) is closely related to ATM and typically used in MANs; max bandwidth 44.736 Mbps; typical media are twisted-pair and fiber; not very widespread; relatively high cost.

pairs.term: Cell-switched services
pairs.definition: Cell-switched services provide a dedicated-connection switching technology that organizes digital data into cell units and transmits them over a physical medium using digital signal technology.

pairs.term: ATM
pairs.definition: Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) is closely related to broadband ISDN, uses small fixed 53-byte length cells, has max bandwidth 622 Mbps (with higher speeds in development), uses twisted-pair and fiber, widespread and increasing, high cost.

pairs.term: ATM cell size
pairs.definition: ATM uses small, fixed 53-byte length cells to carry data.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Circuit switching
pairs.definition: Circuit switching is a WAN switching method in which a dedicated physical circuit through a carrier network is established, maintained, and terminated for each communication session; ISDN is an example.

pairs.term: POTS
pairs.definition: Plain old telephone service (POTS) is not a computer data service but is included because its technologies are part of the growing data infrastructure; the typical medium is twisted-pair copper wire.

pairs.term: Narrowband ISDN
pairs.definition: Narrowband ISDN is a versatile, historically important, all-digital dialup service with moderate cost; BRI max bandwidth is 128 kbps and PRI is about 3 Mbps; typical medium is twisted-pair copper wire.

pairs.term: TDM and STM
pairs.definition: POTS and ISDN are dialup services: when the call is made an end-to-end physical path is set up and bandwidth is reserved; both use time-division multiplexing (TDM), also called synchronous transfer mode (STM).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Dedicated digital services characteristic
pairs.definition: Dedicated digital services provide circuit-switched services but the connection is 'always-up'.

pairs.term: T/E series TDM
pairs.definition: The T series (US) and E series (Europe) use TDM to slice up and assign time slots for data transmission; media are twisted-pair copper wire and optical fiber; extremely widespread; moderate cost.

pairs.term: T1 bandwidth
pairs.definition: 1.544 Mbps.

pairs.term: T3 bandwidth
E1 bandwidth
