pairs.term: E3 bandwidth

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Dialup modem
pairs.definition: Dialup modems (switched analog) are limited in speed but versatile; work with the existing phone network, max bandwidth approximately 56 kbps, low cost, very widespread; typical medium is the twisted-pair phone line.

pairs.term: Wireless
pairs.definition: Wireless requires no medium since signals are electromagnetic waves transmitted through the air; a variety of wireless WAN links exist.

pairs.term: Terrestrial wireless
pairs.definition: Terrestrial wireless has bandwidths typically in the 11 Mbps range (e.g., microwave), relatively low cost, usually requires line of sight (LOS), and has moderate usage.

pairs.term: Satellite wireless
pairs.definition: Satellite wireless can serve mobile users (cellular) and remote users too far from wires/cables; usage is widespread and cost is high.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: IOS command-line interface
pairs.definition: Network administrators mostly use a command-line interface to develop a logical configuration; the configuration is a profile of the system: numbers, locations, and types of each I/O port plus addressing and bandwidth details.

pairs.term: Configuration modes
pairs.definition: A router's configuration can include security information such as which users are permitted access to specific I/O ports and configuration modes.

pairs.term: IOS help feature
pairs.definition: The help feature in the command-line interface assists administrators in entering correct commands and abbreviations.

pairs.term: show controllers
pairs.definition: Displays information about the physical controllers and the state of the interfaces, including clocking information.

pairs.term: show interfaces serial 0/0
pairs.definition: Displays detailed status, encapsulation, bandwidth, and error counters for the serial 0/0 interface.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Single point of interconnection risk
pairs.definition: Using a single interconnection point between adjacent networks is easy to control but introduces a single point of failure.

pairs.term: Multiple interconnection risk
pairs.definition: Introducing a second or more interconnection points between adjacent networks solves the single point of failure problem but can create the opportunity for infinite routing loops.

pairs.term: Routing between nonadjacent networks
pairs.definition: Two nonadjacent networks can use a third network as an intermediary; the boundary router must overcome different routing protocols, routed protocols, and address architectures while guarding the border.

pairs.term: Border router ACL role
pairs.definition: For nonadjacent networks, the border router implements a set of criteria in an access control list to allow specific external users into the private network while disallowing access to everyone else.

pairs.term: Route summarization benefit
pairs.definition: Route summarization aggregates routes to multiple networks into one or two routing entries, reducing routing table size.

pairs.term: Three internetworking scenarios
pairs.definition: Routing within a network, routing between adjacent networks, and routing between nonadjacent networks.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Remote configuration via modem
pairs.definition: The router can also be configured from a remote location by dialing into a modem connected to the console or auxiliary port.

pairs.term: Management port purpose
pairs.definition: The management port provides a text-based connection for the configuration and troubleshooting of the router, unlike LAN/WAN ports that pass frame packets.

pairs.term: Console and AUX ports
pairs.definition: The console and auxiliary (AUX) ports are management ports; they are EIA-232 asynchronous serial ports connected to a communications port on a computer running terminal emulation.

pairs.term: Initial configuration port
pairs.definition: One of the console or auxiliary ports is required for the initial configuration; the console port is recommended for this initial configuration.

pairs.term: Aux port availability
pairs.definition: Not all routers have an auxiliary port.

pairs.term: No network parameters at startup
pairs.definition: When the router is first put into service, no networking parameters are configured; therefore, the router cannot communicate with any network until configured.

pairs.definition: X.25 is an older, widely used packet-switched technology with extensive error-checking capabilities from when WAN links were error-prone; bandwidth can be as high as 2 Mbps; typical medium is twisted-pair copper wire.

pairs.term: Frame Relay bandwidth
pairs.definition: Frame Relay is a packet-switched version of narrowband ISDN; more efficient than X.25 with similar services; maximum bandwidth is 44.736 Mbps; 56 kbps and 384 kbps are extremely popular in the US.

pairs.term: X.25 vs Frame Relay reliability
pairs.definition: X.25 is connection-oriented and reliable at both Layers 2 and 3, which is a large part of why it is slower than Frame Relay; Frame Relay has no defined Layer 3 protocol and is not reliable, but it is connection-oriented.

pairs.term: Statistical TDM
pairs.definition: Packet-switched services use statistical TDM and are sometimes said to be asynchronous (similar to ATM), unlike circuit-switched services that use TDM/STM (synchronous).

pairs.term: Packet-switched services
pairs.definition: Packet-switched services route small units of data called packets through a network based on the destination address contained within each packet.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Router need for IOS
pairs.definition: Just as computers need operating systems, routers need Cisco IOS Software to run configuration files.

pairs.term: Configuration file purpose
pairs.definition: Configuration files contain the instructions and parameters that control the flow of traffic in and out of routers.

pairs.term: Routing table function
pairs.definition: By using routing protocols to direct routed protocols and routing tables, routers make decisions about the best path for packets.

pairs.term: NVRAM function
pairs.definition: Nonvolatile random-access memory (NVRAM) stores the backup/startup configuration file and retains its content when the router is powered down or restarted.

pairs.term: Flash memory function
pairs.definition: Flash memory is erasable programmable read-only memory (EPROM) that holds the operating system image and microcode; allows software updates without removing chips; retains content when powered down; can store multiple versions of Cisco IOS Software.

pairs.term: ROM function
pairs.definition: Read-only memory (ROM) maintains instructions for POST diagnostics, stores a bootstrap program and basic operating system software; upgrades require replacing pluggable chips on the CPU.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Three basic connection types
pairs.definition: LAN interfaces, WAN interfaces, and management ports.

pairs.term: LAN interfaces
pairs.definition: LAN interfaces allow the router to connect to LAN media, usually some form of Ethernet, but could be Token Ring or ATM.

pairs.term: WAN interfaces
pairs.definition: WAN connections provide connections through a service provider to a distant site or the Internet; they can be serial connections or any number of other types, and may require an external device such as a CSU or a direct connection to the provider.

pairs.term: CSU role on WAN side
pairs.definition: With some types of WAN interfaces, an external device such as a CSU/DSU is required to connect the router to the service provider's local connection.

pairs.term: Interface configuration parameters
pairs.definition: Each interface is configured with its port number in the router, the specific transmission technology and bandwidth available on the connected network, and the types of protocols used through that interface.

pairs.term: Higher-end interface forwarding
pairs.definition: On higher-end platforms (7500 and 12000) the interfaces (VIP2 or line card) can forward packets without interrupting the main CPU.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Router main function 2 - switching
pairs.definition: The switching of packets to the proper outgoing interface.

pairs.term: Static route maintenance
pairs.definition: An administrator can maintain routing tables by configuring static routes.

pairs.term: Dynamic route maintenance
pairs.definition: Routing tables are generally maintained dynamically through the use of a routing protocol that exchanges network topology or path information with other routers.

pairs.term: Router OSI layers
pairs.definition: A router is an intelligent network device that operates predominantly at the first three layers of the OSI reference model but is capable of operating at all seven layers.

pairs.term: Four router functions
pairs.definition: Physical interconnectivity, logical interconnectivity, route calculation and maintenance, and security.

pairs.term: Router main function 1 - best path selection
pairs.definition: The selection of best paths for incoming data packets.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Interior router
pairs.definition: An interior router supports end systems accessing other end systems within the same network and supports no connections to any other network.

pairs.term: Exterior router
pairs.definition: An exterior router lies beyond the boundaries of any given network.

pairs.term: Border router
pairs.definition: A border router interconnects a network with other networks; it may denote the boundary between two autonomous systems rather than a private network and some other network.

pairs.term: Interior gateways
pairs.definition: Interior gateways are routers that specialize in learning about and distributing routing information within their domain.

pairs.term: Exterior gateways
pairs.definition: Exterior gateways are routers that specialize in collecting routing information about networks that lie beyond their domain.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Convergence criterion
pairs.definition: Convergence is the process of reaching mutual agreement after a topology change; a slow-converging protocol has greater potential to disrupt service.

pairs.term: Scalability criterion
pairs.definition: A network's scalability is its capability to grow; the selected routing protocol must scale upward to meet projected growth.

pairs.term: Hop count metric
pairs.definition: Hop count is the number of hops, or routers, that lie between the source and destination machines; one simple routing metric.

pairs.term: Routing protocol purposes
pairs.definition: Routing protocols identify potential routes to destination networks, perform a mathematical calculation to determine the best path, and continuously monitor the network to detect topology changes.

pairs.term: Distance-vector approach
pairs.definition: A distance-vector routing protocol makes decisions based on some measurement of the distance between source and destination machines.

pairs.term: Link-state approach
pairs.definition: A link-state protocol bases its decisions on various states of the links, or transmission facilities, that interconnect source and destination machines.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Default route definition
pairs.definition: A default route associates a specific router interface with all unknown destination addresses, allowing a router to forward a datagram to destinations it has not yet learned of.

pairs.term: Default route benefits
pairs.definition: Default routes can minimize the growth of routing tables and reduce the amount of traffic generated between routers as they exchange routing information.

pairs.term: Default route caution
pairs.definition: A default route should be considered carefully because it could potentially cause problems if not thoroughly thought out regarding traffic flow.

pairs.term: Routing table contents
pairs.definition: Routing tables correlate the port number of each interface with the network layer addresses that can be reached (directly or indirectly) via that port.

pairs.term: Learning network addresses
pairs.definition: Upon activation of a port, the router immediately monitors all packets on the attached network so it can learn about reachable network and host IP addresses.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: The Internet definition
pairs.definition: The Internet is the interconnection of thousands of large and small networks all over the world.

pairs.term: Four common WAN connection types
pairs.definition: Dedicated line, circuit-switching, packet-switching, and cell-switching are common WAN connection types.

pairs.term: WAN services requirement
pairs.definition: Many types of WAN services are available and the subscriber must know how to interface to the WAN provider's service.

pairs.term: WAN devices list
pairs.definition: WAN devices include routers, WAN switches, modems, CSU/DSUs, and access servers.

pairs.term: WAN physical layer protocols
pairs.definition: WAN physical layer protocols describe how to provide electrical, mechanical, operational, and functional connections for WAN services.

pairs.term: WAN data link layer protocols
pairs.definition: WAN data link layer protocols describe how frames are carried between systems on a single data link.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: LAPD
pairs.definition: Link Access Procedure on the D channel (LAPD) is used for signaling and call setup on an ISDN D channel.

pairs.term: LAPF
pairs.definition: Link Access Procedure for Frame-Mode Bearer Services (LAPF) is similar to LAPD and used with Frame Relay technologies.

pairs.term: X.25/LAPB
pairs.definition: X.25 (with LAPB) is an ITU-T standard defining how connections between DTE and DCE are maintained for remote terminal access; it is the predecessor to Frame Relay.

pairs.term: PPP multi-protocol support
pairs.definition: PPP is designed to work with several network layer protocols, such as IP and Internetwork Packet Exchange (IPX).

pairs.term: PPP built-in security
pairs.definition: PPP includes built-in security mechanisms: Password Authentication Protocol (PAP) and Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol (CHAP).

pairs.term: HDLC
pairs.definition: High-Level Data Link Control (HDLC) is an IEEE standard, the default encapsulation on point-to-point dedicated links and circuit-switched connections; Cisco HDLC is proprietary, bit-oriented, synchronous, and used between Cisco devices.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: WAN country distance
pairs.definition: About 100,000 m = 100 km (a country).

pairs.term: WAN continent distance
pairs.definition: About 1,000,000 m = 1000 km (a continent).

pairs.term: WAN planet distance
pairs.definition: About 10,000,000 m = 10,000 km (the planet).

pairs.term: WAN earth-moon distance
pairs.definition: About 100,000,000 m = 100,000 km (Earth and artificial satellites).

pairs.term: Definition of a WAN
pairs.definition: A wide-area network (WAN) is a data communications network that extends across a large geographic area and often uses transmission facilities provided by common carriers such as telephone companies.

pairs.term: WAN scale concept
pairs.definition: WANS span from 10 m (room LAN) up to 100,000 km (earth-moon) and carry traffic for widely separated sites.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Router WAN role
pairs.definition: Routers offer many services, including internetworking and WAN interface ports.

pairs.term: Switch WAN role
pairs.definition: Switches connect to WAN bandwidth for voice, data, and video communication.

pairs.term: Modem WAN interfaces
pairs.definition: Modems include interfaces to voice-grade services (analog dialup modems); CSU/DSUs that interface T1/E1 services; and terminal adapters/Network Termination 1s (TAs/NT1s) that interface ISDN services.

pairs.term: Communication server role
pairs.definition: Communication servers concentrate dial-in and dial-out user communication.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Factors affecting time between failures
pairs.definition: Ambient temperature ranges of the operating environment, cleanliness of the commercial electric power, and quality of handling of devices before and during operation.

pairs.term: Why availability is a poor metric
pairs.definition: Availability is vague because a router failure at one premise location makes the network unavailable only to users at that location while other locations remain unaffected, making a single aggregate measure nearly meaningless.

pairs.term: Peak volume
pairs.definition: The maximum volume that the network is expected to support; the greatest amount of traffic expected.

pairs.term: Average volume
pairs.definition: The traffic loads that can reasonably be expected during the course of a business day from any given work location.

pairs.term: Delay definition
pairs.definition: Delay is the total amount of time required by the network to transport a packet from its point of origin to its destination; it is the time that elapses between transmission and reception.

pairs.term: Satellite uplink/downlink delays
pairs.definition: Some transmission facilities are satellite-based, requiring the signal to be transmitted up to the satellite and back down, causing noticeable delays due to the great distances involved.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: DTE
pairs.definition: Data terminal equipment (DTE) is the device at the user end of a user-network interface that serves as a data source or destination; it connects to the network through a DCE and uses clocking signals generated by the DCE.

pairs.term: DCE
pairs.definition: Data circuit-terminating equipment (DCE) comprises network-end devices that provide a physical connection to the network, forward traffic, and provide a clocking signal to synchronize data transmission; modems and interface cards are examples of DCE.

pairs.term: Layer 2 encapsulation requirement
pairs.definition: To use the correct protocol, the appropriate Layer 2 encapsulation must be configured on the router; the choice depends on the WAN technology and communicating equipment being utilized.

pairs.term: EIA/TIA-232
pairs.definition: Common physical layer interface standard supporting unbalanced circuits at signal speeds up to 64 kbps; closely resembles the V.24 specification.

pairs.term: EIA/TIA-449
pairs.definition: A faster (up to 2 Mbps) version of EIA/TIA-232 capable of longer cable runs.
Physical layer interface between DTE and DCE; essentially the same as EIA/TIA-232.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does a Web bug do on a page?
pairs.definition: A small invisible third-party image used to track users.

pairs.term: What is a desirable front-menu browser feature per authors?
pairs.definition: Buttons to enable/disable Java, JavaScript, and ActiveX with visual feedback.

pairs.term: Browsing is generally not ___.
pairs.definition: anonymous.

pairs.term: Third-party cookies: authors say newer browsers can ___ them.
pairs.definition: block third-party cookies.

pairs.term: What can a tapped network reveal about users?
pairs.definition: Their interests and even sexual preferences.

pairs.term: Allow list concept best relates to controlling what?
pairs.definition: Cookies.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How does CSP allow secure inline JavaScript?
pairs.definition: Developers can tell browsers which inline code is trustworthy by using a nonce: Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'nonce-34fo3er92d'. Only script blocks carrying the matching nonce attribute are executed.

pairs.term: How can CSP rules be set?
pairs.definition: In the header of an HTTP response, or using a <meta> tag inside a web page. If the policy is the same for all pages, it can be set on the web server (e.g., Apache); if different pages need different policies or refreshed nonces, set it inside web applications.

pairs.term: What are the two ways to include JavaScript code inside an HTML page?
pairs.definition: The inline approach (placing code directly inside the page, e.g., <script>...</script> or an onclick attribute) and the link approach (putting the code in an external file and linking to it, e.g., <script src="myscript.js"></script>).

pairs.term: Why is the inline approach the culprit of XSS vulnerabilities?
pairs.definition: Because browsers do not know where inline code originally comes from — from the trusted web server or from untrusted users. Without that knowledge, browsers cannot decide which code is safe to execute.

pairs.term: What does the CSP rule 'Content-Security-Policy: script-src self' do?
pairs.definition: It disallows all inline JavaScript, and for external JavaScript it allows only code from the website's own origin (the meaning of 'self'). So only same-origin linked scripts can be executed.

pairs.term: How does CSP allow a whitelist of external script sources?
pairs.definition: By listing them in the policy, e.g., Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self' example.com https://apis.google.com allows code from self, example.com, and apis.google.com.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How is the CSP experiment HTTP server started?
pairs.definition: Run the Python program http_server.py, which starts an HTTPServer listening on port 8000 at 10.0.2.68 and serves static files with a Content-Security-Policy header.

pairs.term: Which URL is used to open the CSP test page in the browser?
pairs.definition: http://www.example32.com:8000/csptest.html (example32.com is mapped to 10.0.2.68, the address the Python server listens on).

pairs.term: What does the Python program http_server.py do?
pairs.definition: It runs a simple HTTP server that listens to port 8000 on 10.0.2.68; upon receiving a request, it loads a static file and sends a Content-Security-Policy header in the response.

pairs.term: What CSP policy is set in the Python experiment server?
pairs.definition: Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' *.example68.com:8000 'nonce-lrA2345' — only same-origin scripts, scripts from example68.com, or scripts with the nonce lrA2345 can execute.

pairs.term: What are the results of the CSP experiment?
pairs.definition: Inline with the correct nonce: OK. Inline with wrong nonce: Failed. Inline with no nonce: Failed. From self (script1.js): OK. From example68.com (script2.js): OK. From example79.com (script3.js): Failed — because example79.com is not on the whitelist.

pairs.term: In the CSP experiment, how are the three external script domains hosted?
pairs.definition: www.example32.com, www.example68.com, and www.example79.com are all mapped to the same IP address 10.0.2.68, so they are served by the same web server but have different origins.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: In the bank example, what does the URL http://www.bank32.com/transfer.php?to=3220&amount=500 do?
pairs.definition: It is a money-transfer service URL that transfers $500 from the logged-in user's account to Account 3220. The request must carry a valid session cookie or it will not be processed.

pairs.term: Why can't attackers transfer money by sending the forged request from their own computers?
pairs.definition: Because they do not have the victims' session cookies. Without a valid session cookie, the bank server will not process the transfer request.

pairs.term: Which two HTML tags can automatically trigger HTTP GET requests for CSRF attacks?
pairs.definition: The img tag and the iframe tag. When a browser loads a web page containing them, it automatically sends an HTTP GET request to the URL specified in their src attribute.

pairs.term: What is a same-site request?
pairs.definition: A request sent from a web page to the same origin/site it came from (e.g., a request from a page on www.example.com to another service on www.example.com).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Why is the referer header not a reliable CSRF countermeasure?
pairs.definition: It reveals part of a user's browsing history, causing privacy concerns, so some browsers, extensions, and proxies remove it. Using it may misclassify many legitimate requests as cross-site requests.

pairs.term: How was Elgg's CSRF countermeasure disabled in the lab?
pairs.definition: A 'return true' statement was added at the first line of the gatekeeper() function in ActionsService.php, forcing the function to always return true and let all requests pass the check.

pairs.term: What are same-site cookies?
pairs.definition: A special type of cookie with a SameSite attribute set by servers. The attribute tells browsers whether the cookie should be attached to a cross-site request or not.

pairs.term: Why does the CSRF attack fail after Elgg's countermeasure is turned back on?
pairs.definition: Attackers would need to know the secret token and timestamp values embedded in the victim's Elgg page, but browser access control (same-origin policy) prevents the JavaScript code in the attacker's page from accessing any content in Elgg's pages.

pairs.term: What does the SameSite attribute value Strict do?
pairs.definition: The cookie will not be sent along with cross-site requests; it is only sent with same-site requests.

pairs.term: In a CSRF attack, can the attacker's code read the victim's session cookies?
pairs.definition: No. In CSRF the malicious code runs on the attacker's third-party page, which cannot access Elgg's cookies. This differs from XSS, where injected code runs inside the Elgg page and is allowed to read the cookies.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is Elgg and why is it used in the CSRF lab?
pairs.definition: Elgg is a popular open-source web application for social networks. It has implemented CSRF countermeasures that were intentionally disabled in the lab VM to make it vulnerable to CSRF attacks.

pairs.term: How are the two lab websites hosted in the CSRF lab?
pairs.definition: Both www.csrflabelgg.com and www.csrflabattacker.com are hosted on localhost by mapping the hostnames to 127.0.0.1 in /etc/hosts and adding Apache VirtualHost entries in /etc/apache2/sites-available/000-default.conf.

pairs.term: What does DocumentRoot specify in an Apache VirtualHost configuration?
pairs.definition: The directory where the files of a website are stored, e.g., DocumentRoot /var/www/CSRF/Attacker for the attacker site and DocumentRoot /var/www/CSRF/elgg for the Elgg site.

pairs.term: Why can't the attacker hardcode the victim's session cookie value in a forged request?
pairs.definition: The cookie value differs for each user and each session, and the attacker cannot know it. However, the cookie field is set automatically by browsers, so the attacker does not need to set it at all.

pairs.term: What characters separate key/value pairs in a URL-encoded GET or form body?
pairs.definition: Parameters are separated by '&' (e.g., foo=hello&bar=world) and each key is joined to its value by '=' (e.g., to=3220).

pairs.term: Hostname mappings used in the CSRF lab (added to /etc/hosts):
pairs.definition: Entries mapping www.csrflabelgg.com and www.csrflabattacker.com to 127.0.0.1 (localhost), so both websites are hosted on the local machine.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Can a CSRF attack on an HTTP GET service be launched without JavaScript?
pairs.definition: Yes. GET requests attach all parameters in the URL, so they can be triggered simply by HTML tags such as img and iframe placed in the attacker's page.

pairs.term: What precondition must hold for the add-friend CSRF attack to succeed?
pairs.definition: The victim (Alice) must have an active session with the Elgg website; otherwise Elgg will simply discard the forged request.

pairs.term: What does an img tag expect as a response when loaded?
pairs.definition: The browser expects an image to come back and places it inside the tag area. From the attacker's perspective the response is not important; what matters is that the HTTP GET request is triggered.

pairs.term: How does Samy attract the victim Alice to the malicious web page?
pairs.definition: Inside the Elgg social network, Samy sends Alice a private message containing a link to his malicious web page. When Alice clicks the link, the page loads in her browser and the forged request is sent.

pairs.term: What does an iframe tag expect as a response when loaded?
pairs.definition: The browser expects a web page to come back and places the page inside the iframe. The response is irrelevant to the attacker, who only needs the HTTP GET request to be triggered.

pairs.term: How does an attacker investigate how a target web application sends requests?
pairs.definition: The attacker uses Firefox's HTTP Header Live extension to capture the HTTP request headers generated when performing the action, then reads the URL and parameters from the captured request.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Why are the form entries in the forged POST form set to type 'hidden'?
pairs.definition: So the entries are invisible to users and the victim does not see the parameters being submitted.

pairs.term: In the JavaScript forge_post() function, what do p.action, p.innerHTML, and p.method set?
pairs.definition: p.action sets the URL the form submits to; p.innerHTML fills the form's hidden input fields; p.method sets the request method (e.g., 'post').

pairs.term: What is the URL of Elgg's edit-profile service?
pairs.definition: http://www.csrflabelgg.com/action/profile/edit.

pairs.term: What does the accesslevel[description] parameter do and what does the value 2 mean?
pairs.definition: It sets the access level for the profile's description field, indicating who can view this field. Value 2 means public, so everybody can view the field.

pairs.term: What does the guid field in an edit-profile request indicate?
pairs.definition: It indicates which user's profile is to be updated. In the CSRF attack it must be set to the victim's GUID.

pairs.term: How can an attacker find the victim's GUID?
pairs.definition: By visiting the victim's profile page from any account and looking at the page's source for something like elgg.page_owner = {"guid": 39, "type": "user", ...}.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How does preparing a statement work in the database?
pairs.definition: The SQL statement template (with ? placeholders) is sent to the database, which parses, compiles, and performs query optimization on it, storing the result without executing it.

pairs.term: How is data bound and executed in a prepared statement?
pairs.definition: At a later time, values are bound to the parameters (bind_param), the statement is executed (execute), result columns are bound to variables (bind_result), and rows are fetched (fetch).

pairs.term: What do the type characters in bind_param mean?
pairs.definition: Each character in the type string specifies the data type of the corresponding data item: s for string, i for integer, d for double, and b for BLOB (Binary Large Object).

pairs.term: What are the three main approaches to protect against SQL injection?
pairs.definition: (1) Getting rid of code (filtering), (2) turning code into data (encoding), and (3) clearly separating code and data.

pairs.term: Why can prepared statements prevent SQL injection?
pairs.definition: Trusted code is sent via a code channel while untrusted user data is sent via a data channel, so the database knows the boundary; data from the data channel is never parsed, so code hidden in data is never executed.

pairs.term: What is the filtering approach against SQL injection?
pairs.definition: Before mixing user data with code, inspect the data and filter out any character that may be interpreted as code (for example the apostrophe).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does the Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded header indicate?
pairs.definition: That the request body contains form data with URL-encoded key=value pairs (e.g., foo=hello&bar=world), as used in POST requests for web form submission.

pairs.term: What is the role of the Content-Length header in a POST request?
pairs.definition: It specifies the byte length of the data carried in the request body, e.g., Content-Length: 19 for the body 'foo=hello&bar=world'.

pairs.term: Where are data attached in an HTTP GET request?
pairs.definition: Data are attached in the URL, e.g., GET /post_form.php?foo=hello&bar=world HTTP/1.1.

pairs.term: Where are data attached in an HTTP POST request?
pairs.definition: Data are attached in the body of the request (after the headers), e.g., POST /post_form.php HTTP/1.1 with Content-Length: 19 and body foo=hello&bar=world.

pairs.term: What is an HTTP GET service and an HTTP POST service?
pairs.definition: Most services in web applications are GET or POST services; to invoke them one sends an HTTP GET or HTTP POST request respectively. The main difference is where data are attached: GET attaches data in the URL, POST attaches data in the body.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What are the three main methods for PHP programs to interact with a MySQL database?
pairs.definition: (1) PHP's MySQL Extension, (2) PHP's MySQLi Extension, and (3) PHP Data Objects (PDO).

pairs.term: Which PHP MySQL extension is the most commonly used?
pairs.definition: The MySQLi extension, which allows PHP programs to access the functionality of MySQL 4.1 and above.

pairs.term: What arguments does new mysqli() take?
pairs.definition: Four arguments: the hostname of the database server, the login name, the password, and the database name.

pairs.term: Why is localhost used as the hostname in the getDB() example?
pairs.definition: Because the MySQL database runs on the same machine as the web application server; a separate hostname would be needed if the DB were on another machine.

pairs.term: What is the typical approach for executing a query with MySQLi?
pairs.definition: Construct the query string first, then use mysqli::query() to send the query string to the database for execution.

pairs.term: Why does user input become a security problem in getdata.php?
pairs.definition: Whatever data is typed in the form eventually becomes a part of the SQL string that is executed by the database.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Give a real-world example of reflective behavior in a web application.
pairs.definition: When you search Google for a non-existing word like 'xyz', the result page contains a phrase like 'No results found for xyz' — the input is reflected back into the response page.

pairs.term: What is the vulnerable reflective service used as an example in the book?
pairs.definition: http://www.example.com/search?input=word, where the user-provided word is reflected back in the response page.

pairs.term: What URL does the attacker send to the victim to exploit the reflective search service?
pairs.definition: http://www.example.com/search?input=<script>alert("attack");</script> (special characters in a URL must be encoded; the book omits the encoding for readability).

pairs.term: Why must the code-bearing input be sent from the targeted victim's machine in a reflected XSS attack?
pairs.definition: So the web page with the injected code is sent back to the victim's browser, where the injected code runs with the victim's privilege. If sent from the attacker's machine, the page would go to the attacker instead.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the parser in an attack on the system() function?
pairs.definition: system() actually executes a shell program (/bin/sh), which parses the string and runs the command identified from it; the shell program is the parser.

pairs.term: Which characters in a system() argument can alter the boundary, and what can a semicolon do?
pairs.definition: Special characters such as ';', '>', and '&' can alter the original boundary; in particular, a semicolon can introduce a new command.

pairs.term: What is the parser in a format string attack?
pairs.definition: A parser inside the printf() function (and similar functions) interprets format specifiers as 'code', deciding what action the parser should take.

pairs.term: Why do C programs in general clearly separate data and code?
pairs.definition: C source code is compiled before execution, so there is no user data during compilation; at runtime user data does not go through the C compiler again, so data stays data.

pairs.term: Why is code injection easier against web applications than against C programs?
pairs.definition: SQL and JavaScript are interpreted languages that need no compilation, so at runtime source code can be dynamically created and handed to the interpreter, opening a door for data and code to mix.

pairs.term: How can C programs still suffer code injection attacks?
pairs.definition: Via additional parsers — the external shell parser for system() and the format-string parser for printf() — and via buffer overflow, where the return address is stored in the data region (stack).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does the resulting query look like for the EID5002' # injection?
pairs.definition: SELECT Name, Salary, SSN FROM employee WHERE eid='EID5002' — everything after # is a comment, so the password check is removed.

pairs.term: What does the New Password injection paswd456', salary=100000 # accomplish?
pairs.definition: It turns the UPDATE into SET password='paswd456', salary=100000 # WHERE ... so the record's password AND salary are both changed even though the script only meant to change the password.

pairs.term: What is the resulting query for the a' OR 1=1 # injection?
pairs.definition: SELECT Name, Salary, SSN FROM employee WHERE eid='a' OR 1=1 — the predicate is always true, so all records are returned.

pairs.term: How does Alice reduce Bob's salary to 0 without knowing his password?
pairs.definition: In the EID box she types Bob's EID followed by ' # (EID5001' #) to comment out the old-password check, and in New Password she types paswd456', salary=0 # to also set salary to 0.

pairs.term: What did Alice type to attack Bob through the password-change form?
pairs.definition: EID: EID5001' # ; Old Password: anything ; New Password: paswd456', salary=0 # — this sets Bob's salary to 0 without knowing his password.

pairs.term: How can multiple SQL statements be included in one statement string?
pairs.definition: In SQL, multiple statements separated by semicolons (;) can be included in one statement string.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Why is the 'useless' 1=1 predicate important for this chapter?
pairs.definition: It looks useless in normal queries but becomes very useful in the SQL injection attack to make a WHERE predicate always true.

pairs.term: UPDATE employee SET Salary=82000 WHERE Name='Bob';
pairs.definition: Modifies an existing record, setting Bob's salary to 82,000.

pairs.term: What are the three comment styles supported by MySQL?
pairs.definition: (1) Text from the # character to end of line; (2) text from -- to end of line, where the second dash must be followed by at least one whitespace or control character; (3) text between /* and */ as in C.

pairs.term: Where does the user type SQL commands in the MySQL client?
pairs.definition: At the mysql> prompt, which appears after a successful login to the MySQL monitor.

pairs.term: What is SQL (Structured Query Language)?
pairs.definition: SQL is a special-purpose domain-specific language used in programming, designed for managing data held in a relational database management system.

pairs.term: What special requirement does the -- comment style have?
pairs.definition: The second dash must be followed by at least one whitespace or control character (such as a space or tab).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: curl -v http://10.0.2.69/cgi-bin/test.cgi
pairs.definition: curl with -v prints the HTTP request in addition to the response, showing headers such as GET line, Host, User-Agent, and Accept.

pairs.term: Why must the exploit output include 'Content-type: text/plain' followed by an empty line?
pairs.definition: Whatever the CGI program prints goes to Apache, which sends the data back to the client. Apache needs to know the content type (text, multi-media, etc.), so the exploit prints 'Content-type: text/plain' followed by an empty line before the command output.

pairs.term: curl -A "test" http://10.0.2.69/cgi-bin/test.cgi
pairs.definition: Sets the User-Agent header of the request to "test", which becomes the HTTP_USER_AGENT environment variable of the CGI process.

pairs.term: Under what user ID does a web server run, and what is its privilege?
pairs.definition: Web servers run with the www-data user ID, making their privilege quite limited. Using this privilege attackers cannot take over the server, but can read database passwords, steal files, or run a reverse shell.

pairs.term: curl -e "..." http://10.0.2.69/cgi-bin/test.cgi
pairs.definition: Sets the Referer header field using curl's -e option, an alternative field to carry the Shellshock payload.

pairs.term: What did the lab's curl -v experiment prove about the User-Agent field?
pairs.definition: It proved that HTTP_USER_AGENT in the CGI process gets its value directly from a remote user's User-Agent header, demonstrating a path to feed attacker data into bash via environment variables.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does the PHP putenv() function do in the vulnerable PHP example?
pairs.definition: It adds an argument (e.g. "ARG=$arg") to the process environment, so the user-supplied value becomes an environment variable ARG that is later passed to the bash process invoked by system().

pairs.term: Can Shellshock affect other server-side programs besides CGI scripts and PHP?
pairs.definition: Yes. The same analysis applies to Ruby, node.js, Java, C#, etc. The vulnerability requires two conditions: (1) invocation of bash, and (2) passing of user data as environment variables.

pairs.term: Why does the vulnerable PHP program use system("strings /proc/$$/environ | grep ARG")?
pairs.definition: To verify the attacker-supplied ARG env var reached the bash process, confirming the second Shellshock condition (user data passed as an environment variable to bash) is satisfied.

pairs.term: In the PHP attack, what do %20, %7B, %7D, and ';' represent in the URL encoding?
pairs.definition: %20 is a space, %7B is '{', %7D is '}', and the literal ';' separates commands. The decoded arg is: () { echo hello; }; /bin/cat /var/www/secret.txt.

pairs.term: What does getParam() do in the vulnerable PHP program?
pairs.definition: It reads the 'arg' parameter from the HTTP GET request ($_GET["arg"]) if it is set and non-empty, and returns it. This user-controlled string is then placed into the environment via putenv("ARG=$arg").

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Where do the parameter names and values in an HTTP request come from?
pairs.definition: The name comes from the form entry's name attribute and the value comes from whatever is typed into the form field.

pairs.term: What is the difference between HTTP and HTTPS when sending form data?
pairs.definition: HTTPS is the safe (encrypted) protocol; parameters are sent in the same way but over an encrypted communication channel.

pairs.term: How does a PHP script receive parameters from an HTTP request?
pairs.definition: Parameters are saved into the $_GET or $_POST array in PHP, depending on the type of the HTTP request.

pairs.term: What are the three major components of a typical web application?
pairs.definition: Web browser (client side), web application server, and database.

pairs.term: How do browsers and web servers communicate, and how do web servers and databases communicate?
pairs.definition: Browsers communicate with web servers using HTTP; web servers interact with databases using database languages such as SQL.

pairs.term: Why can't users attack the database directly in the three-tier architecture?
pairs.definition: Users do not interact with the database directly; the web application server provides the only channel for user data to reach the database.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is the countermeasure for confidentiality threats on the Web?
pairs.definition: Encryption and Web proxies. Confidentiality threats include eavesdropping on the net, theft of information from the server or client, and information about network configuration or which client talks to which server.

pairs.term: What is the countermeasure for denial of service on the Web?
pairs.definition: It is difficult to prevent. DoS includes killing user threads, flooding a machine with bogus requests, filling up disk or memory, and isolating a machine by DNS attacks.

pairs.term: What is the countermeasure for authentication threats on the Web?
pairs.definition: Cryptographic techniques. Authentication threats include impersonation of legitimate users and data forgery.

pairs.term: Why do Web usage characteristics suggest the need for tailored security tools?
pairs.definition: Web software is extraordinarily complex and may hide many security flaws; a Web server can be exploited as a launching pad into the entire computer complex; and casual, untrained users are common clients who lack security awareness and tools.

pairs.term: How are Web security threats classified by location?
pairs.definition: Web server, Web browser, and network traffic between browser and server. Server and browser security fall into computer system security; traffic security falls into network security.

pairs.term: What is the countermeasure for integrity threats on the Web?
pairs.definition: Cryptographic checksums. Integrity threats include modification of user data, a Trojan horse browser, modification of memory, and modification of message traffic in transit.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How do you find the _elgg_ts and _elgg_token values while viewing an Elgg page?
pairs.definition: Right-click the page, select 'View Page Source', and look for the JavaScript that assigns them, e.g., elgg = { ..., "security": {"token": {"_elgg_ts": 1543676484, "_elgg_token": "alg70Ivw5Md6iJbXFVgtDA"}} }.

pairs.term: Why does the attack code use Ajax (XMLHttpRequest) instead of a normal HTTP request?
pairs.definition: A normal HTTP request would cause the browser to navigate away from the current page, which may alert the victim. Ajax sends HTTP requests in the background, keeping the attack unnoticed.

pairs.term: Which Elgg profile field is chosen to inject the add-friend JavaScript, and why the 'Remove Editor' button?
pairs.definition: The 'About me' field. Because this field supports an editor that adds formatting data to the text (which can break the JavaScript), the attacker clicks the 'Remove Editor' button to switch to plaintext mode.

pairs.term: How could an attack still be launched if Elgg provided no plaintext editor for the field?
pairs.definition: The attacker could use a browser extension to remove the formatting data from HTTP requests, or send requests using a customized client instead of a browser; it would be slightly more difficult but still possible.

pairs.term: How does Alice end up viewing Samy's profile in the lab?
pairs.definition: Alice logs into her account, clicks 'More' and then 'Members' to find all users, then clicks on Samy. As soon as Samy's profile loads, the malicious code embedded in the 'About me' field is triggered.

pairs.term: What is the URL of Elgg's add-friend request in the XSS lab?
pairs.definition: http://www.xsslabelgg.com/action/friends/add, with the friend parameter specifying Samy's GUID (47 in the book example).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What does the term 'cross-site' mean in XSS, and how does it differ from CSRF?
pairs.definition: In XSS, the malicious code must 'cross' the target website to reach the victim. In CSRF, 'cross-site' means 'from another site'. Using the same term for both attacks causes confusion. In XSS the forged requests are actually 'same-site' requests.

pairs.term: What can injected XSS code do once it runs inside a page from the target website?
pairs.definition: If the user has an active session, the code can do whatever the user can do inside the session: access/change page content, read the website's cookies, and send requests to the website on the user's behalf.

pairs.term: What are the two typical ways attackers inject code into a victim's browser via the target website?
pairs.definition: Non-persistent (reflected) XSS and persistent XSS attacks.

pairs.term: What is a Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attack?
pairs.definition: A type of code injection attack that typically involves three entities: an attacker, a victim, and a target website. The attacker injects malicious code into the victim's browser via the target website, where it runs with the trust given to that website.

pairs.term: Why can't JavaScript placed on the attacker's own web page harm the victim's session with the target website?
pairs.definition: Because of the sandbox protection implemented by browsers, code from the attacker's page cannot affect pages from the target website or the user's interaction with it. The malicious code must come from the target website itself to have that privilege.

pairs.term: In XSS, why must the malicious code come from the target website?
pairs.definition: Code coming from a website S is considered trusted with respect to S: it can access and change content on S's pages, read S's cookies, and send requests to S on behalf of the user. Code from a third-party origin lacks these privileges.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How does the XSS edit-profile attack obtain the victim's GUID?
pairs.definition: From the page itself: the GUID is stored in the JavaScript variable elgg.session.user.guid, and the injected code reads it at runtime, so the attack is not limited to a particular victim.

pairs.term: How does obtaining the GUID in XSS differ from the CSRF chapter?
pairs.definition: In CSRF the attacker's code cannot access the victim's Elgg pages, so the GUID was hardcoded (only Alice could be attacked). In XSS the injected code runs inside Elgg pages, so it can read elgg.session.user.guid and attack any victim.

pairs.term: Why does the edit-profile worm code check if (elgg.session.user.guid != 47)?
pairs.definition: To avoid modifying Samy's own profile. Without this check, as soon as Samy puts the code in his profile the page loads and the code would overwrite Samy's profile with 'Samy is my hero', destroying the malicious JavaScript.

pairs.term: What is the URL of Elgg's edit-profile service in the XSS lab?
pairs.definition: http://www.xsslabelgg.com/action/profile/edit.

pairs.term: What message does the edit-profile XSS attack place in the victim's description field?
pairs.definition: 'Samy is my hero', with the spaces encoded as plus signs ('Samy+is+my+hero') in the form data.

pairs.term: Why must spaces be replaced with plus signs in the form data of the edit-profile request?
pairs.definition: Because with Content-Type application/x-www-form-urlencoded, the string sent in the form body is URL-encoded; each space is replaced by a plus sign so the server parses 'Samy is my hero' correctly.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: How is Elgg hosted in the XSS lab?
pairs.definition: At http://www.xsslabelgg.com, mapped to 127.0.0.1 (localhost) via /etc/hosts, with an Apache VirtualHost entry in /etc/apache2/sites-available/000-default.conf specifying ServerName www.XSSLabElgg.com and DocumentRoot /var/www/XSS/elgg.

pairs.term: What are the Elgg user accounts created in the XSS lab?
pairs.definition: Admin (admin/seedelgg), Alice (alice/seedalice), Boby (boby/seedboby), Charlie (charlie/seedcharlie), and Samy (samy/seedsamy).

pairs.term: Apache VirtualHost block added to /etc/apache2/sites-available/000-default.conf for the XSS lab Elgg site:
pairs.definition: <VirtualHost *:80> ServerName www.XSSLabElgg.com DocumentRoot /var/www/XSS/elgg </VirtualHost> — serves the vulnerable Elgg application used for XSS attacks.

pairs.term: Hostname mapping used to host the XSS lab on localhost (added to /etc/hosts):
pairs.definition: Map www.xsslabelgg.com to 127.0.0.1 (localhost).

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: What is self-propagation in an XSS worm?
pairs.definition: When victims' profiles are modified, they also get infected: their profiles carry a copy of the worm's JavaScript. When an infected profile is viewed by others, the code spreads further, propagating at an exponential rate.

pairs.term: What is a quine program?
pairs.definition: A non-empty computer program which takes no input and produces a copy of its own source code as its only output; also called self-replicating, self-reproducing, or self-copying program.

pairs.term: What are the two typical ways for a program to produce a copy of itself?
pairs.definition: 1) Get a copy of itself from outside, such as from the underlying system (files, DOM nodes) or the network. 2) Generate a copy entirely from the code, known as a quine program.

pairs.term: What are the two approaches to achieve self-propagation in JavaScript in the book?
pairs.definition: The DOM approach (get a copy of the code directly from the DOM tree via DOM APIs) and the link approach (include the code via a link using the src attribute of the script tag).

pairs.term: How does the DOM approach get a copy of the worm code?
pairs.definition: The script block is given an id (e.g., id="worm"); the code calls document.getElementById("worm").innerHTML to fetch the tag's content, then adds the surrounding <script id="worm"> and </script> tags to form an identical copy.

pairs.term: Why is the closing tag split into '</' + 'script>' in the worm code?
pairs.definition: If the string is written directly, Firefox's HTML parser treats it as the closing tag of the JavaScript code block, causing the rest of the code to be ignored. The split-and-then-merge technique fools the parser.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.definition: Wi-Fi 6, known as high efficiency (HE), supports data rates up to 1.2 Gbps per spatial stream with up to 8 spatial streams and 20, 40, 80, or 160 MHz channels. Designed to work on any band from 1 to 7 GHz.

pairs.term: Wi-Fi 6E
pairs.definition: The 6 GHz band version of 802.11ax; Wi-Fi 6 uses the 2.4 and 5 GHz bands only, while Wi-Fi 6E uses the 6 GHz band only.

pairs.term: OFDMA in 802.11ax
pairs.definition: Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access lets 802.11ax schedule and control access to the wireless medium, allocating channel air time as resource units so multiple devices can transmit simultaneously.

pairs.term: BSS coloring in 802.11ax
pairs.definition: Also called BSS marking, it avoids interference between neighboring BSSs along with better transmit power control.

pairs.term: 802.11ax vs 802.11ac throughput
pairs.definition: 802.11ax leverages even more complex and sensitive modulation and coding schemes, resulting in data rates roughly four times faster than 802.11ac.

pairs.term: AP-client standard compatibility
pairs.definition: An AP must support the same set of 802.11 amendments that its clients support. Most 802.11 amendments are backward compatible with previous ones that operate in the same band.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Sniffer mode
pairs.definition: The AP dedicates its radios to receiving 802.11 traffic from other sources, much like a packet capture device, and forwards the captured traffic to a PC running analyzer software such as Wireshark.

pairs.term: Rogue detector mode
pairs.definition: The AP dedicates itself to detecting rogue devices by correlating MAC addresses heard on the wired network with those heard over the air; rogue devices appear on both.

pairs.term: Bridge mode
pairs.definition: The AP becomes a dedicated point-to-point or point-to-multipoint bridge between networks; two APs can link two distant locations, and multiple APs can form a mesh network.

pairs.term: Flex+Bridge mode
pairs.definition: A mesh AP with FlexConnect operation enabled.

pairs.term: SE-Connect mode
pairs.definition: The AP dedicates its radios to spectrum analysis on all wireless channels; a PC running software such as MetaGeek Chanalyzer or Cisco Spectrum Expert connects remotely to collect and analyze spectrum data to find sources of interference.

pairs.term: Special-purpose modes vs local mode
pairs.definition: When an AP is configured for a special-purpose mode (anything other than local), the local mode and its BSSs are disabled.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: AP 360 View top information
pairs.definition: The top of the AP 360 View displays the AP's location, IP address, model, serial number, PoE status, country code, WPA3 capability, VLAN tag number, software version, and connection uptime.

pairs.term: AP Join Statistics tab
pairs.definition: Displays basic information about the last known events when the AP tried to join or leave the controller, including the reason it last rebooted or disconnected. A tag change typically causes the AP to disconnect and rejoin.

pairs.term: AP radio operational summary
pairs.definition: Scrolling down in the AP 360 View shows whether each radio is enabled, the number of wireless clients connected to each, the channel used, transmit power level, and channel/transmit/receive utilization indicators.

pairs.term: AP tag change behavior
pairs.definition: A change in an AP's tag causes it to refresh its connection to the controller or cycle its radios or WLANs to commit changes to its operation. This disconnect/rejoin is expected behavior.

pairs.term: High channel utilization meaning
pairs.definition: If channel utilization values are high, the channel is heavily used, likely slowing communication and making it difficult for wireless stations to get an opportunity to transmit.

pairs.term: AP 360 View
pairs.definition: Displays the AP's location, IP address, model, serial number, PoE status, country code, whether it is capable of WPA3, the VLAN tag number, software version, and connection uptime.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: router(config)# ip forward-protocol udp 5246
pairs.definition: Configures the router to forward broadcast CAPWAP Discovery Requests on UDP port 5246 toward the WLC addresses configured as IP helpers, enabling Layer 3 AP-to-WLC discovery.

pairs.term: WLC join state
pairs.definition: The AP selects a WLC from a list of candidates and sends a CAPWAP Join Request; the WLC replies with a CAPWAP Join Response.

pairs.term: WLC discovery step 5: reset
pairs.definition: If none of the discovery steps succeed, the AP resets itself and starts the discovery process all over again.

pairs.term: router(config)# interface vlan vlan-number
pairs.definition: Enters the VLAN interface under which the CAPWAP discovery relay helper-address is configured.

pairs.term: Download image state
pairs.definition: The WLC informs the AP of its software release. If the AP's release differs, the AP downloads a matching image from the controller, reboots to apply it, and returns to the boot state. If releases match, no download is needed.

pairs.term: WLC selection step 1: primed sequence
pairs.definition: If the AP was configured or primed with primary, secondary, and tertiary controllers, it tries to join those controllers in succession.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Patch antenna
pairs.definition: A flat rectangular directional antenna that can be mounted on a wall or ceiling, producing a broad egg-shaped pattern extending away from the flat surface. Typical gain is about 6 to 8 dBi in the 2.4 GHz band and 7 to 10 dBi at 5 GHz.

pairs.term: Yagi antenna
pairs.definition: A directional antenna (Yagi-Uda) made of several parallel elements of increasing length inside a thick cylindrical case, producing a focused egg-shaped pattern extending along its length. Gain is about 10 to 14 dBi.

pairs.term: Parabolic dish antenna
pairs.definition: A highly directional antenna that uses a parabolic dish to focus RF energy along one narrow elliptical, long and narrow pattern for long-distance line-of-sight paths. It has the highest gain of all wireless LAN antennas, between 20 and 30 dBi.

pairs.term: Client density
pairs.definition: The number of devices per AP. With many active clients contending for air time on a channel, less airtime is available to each, causing poor performance. Good design distributes users across APs to give more capacity to each.

pairs.term: Controlling client density with antennas
pairs.definition: You can limit the number of clients served by an AP by selecting an antenna with a more constrained coverage pattern where the clients are located.

pairs.term: Radiation pattern
pairs.definition: A plot that shows the relative signal strength around an antenna (usually drawn on a logarithmic scale). The isotropic antenna produces a perfect sphere.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Why authenticate wireless clients
pairs.definition: To control access: only trusted, expected devices should access corporate resources; guests should be confined to a guest WLAN; and rogue clients should not be permitted to associate at all.

pairs.term: Where wireless security is configured
pairs.definition: Wireless security is configured on a per-WLAN basis; all security configuration tasks for a WLAN occur in the WLAN > Edit Security tab.

pairs.term: Rogue client
pairs.definition: A rogue client is not expected or welcomed and is not affiliated with the corporate network; it is likely an unknown device within range of the network and should not be permitted to associate.

pairs.term: Guest access control
pairs.definition: Guest users, if permitted at all, should be joined to a separate guest WLAN where they can access nonconfidential or public resources.

pairs.term: Credentials presentation
pairs.definition: Wireless clients must identify themselves by presenting some form of credentials to the APs before being allowed to associate; authentication can use a static text string or interaction with a corporate user database.

pairs.term: Stolen device risk with static key
pairs.definition: With a static key string stored on a device, any user who possesses the stolen or lost device can still authenticate to the network. Username/password methods interact with a corporate database that a thief would not know.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Accessing Radioactive Trace
pairs.definition: Navigate to Troubleshooting > Radioactive Trace on the default WLC screen, or select the small wrench icon under the client's MAC address on the Monitoring > Wireless > Clients page.

pairs.term: Security Information contents
pairs.definition: The General > Security Information tab displays the client's wireless security parameters, such as WPA2, CCMP (AES), pre-shared key, whether EAP is used, and session timeout.

pairs.term: Radioactive Trace time intervals
pairs.definition: When generating the debug trace file, choose the time interval of logs to collect: the last 10 minutes, last 30 minutes, last one hour, or since the last WLC reboot. Check the Enable internal logs box to use the WLC's collected logs.

pairs.term: WLC GUI: search client MAC in the top-right search bar
pairs.definition: Authenticates nothing but returns a Client MAC Result for the entered wireless MAC address, from which the Client 360 View can be opened.

pairs.term: Radioactive Trace output
pairs.definition: After generating the trace, two small blue icons appear next to the client's MAC address: a downward arrow to download the file to your local machine, and a document icon to display the trace contents in the Radioactive Trace page.

pairs.term: WLC GUI: Troubleshooting > Radioactive Trace
pairs.definition: Opens the Radioactive Trace controls where you add client MAC addresses, Start/Stop collection, and Generate a debug trace file.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Centralized AP interface requirements
pairs.definition: Each AP connects to an access layer switch via an access link (not a trunk) and needs only a single IP address to terminate its CAPWAP tunnel, since multiple WLANs/VLANs are carried over the same tunnel.

pairs.term: Autonomous AP
pairs.definition: A self-contained, standalone AP that offers one or more fully functional basic service sets (BSSs) and is a natural extension of a switched network, connecting SSIDs to wired VLANs at the access layer.

pairs.term: Distributed wireless deployment
pairs.definition: Smaller, appropriately sized WLCs placed at each site/location. Distributed controllers are commonly smaller standalone models supporting up to 250 APs and 5,000 wireless clients.

pairs.term: Lightweight AP
pairs.definition: A Cisco AP that operates in lightweight mode and must join a wireless LAN controller (WLC) to become fully functional; it is not self-sufficient on its own.

pairs.term: Controller-less deployment (EWC)
pairs.definition: An embedded wireless controller (EWC), which is a regular AP that also runs WLC software. There is no discrete WLC; the controller is embedded in an AP. EWC typically supports up to 100 APs and up to 2,000 wireless clients.

pairs.term: Autonomous AP management
pairs.definition: An autonomous AP must be configured with a management IP address to enable remote management, normally on a dedicated management VLAN that is separate from the data VLANs.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: EAPOL
pairs.definition: EAP over LAN, used for wired and wireless networks to carry EAP authentication messages between the client and the network.

pairs.term: 802.1x limits access
pairs.definition: When 802.1x is enabled, it limits access to a network medium until a client authenticates. A client may associate with an AP but cannot pass data to any other part of the network until it authenticates successfully.

pairs.term: Pairwise Transient Key (PTK)
pairs.definition: The PTK is derived from the PMK during the four-way handshake and is used to secure unicast traffic between the client and AP.

pairs.term: PMK and GMK
pairs.definition: Pairwise Master Key and Groupwise Master Key are generated and distributed during EAP authentication. Pairwise keys protect unicast traffic; Groupwise keys protect broadcast and multicast traffic.

pairs.term: Open Authentication in 802.1x
pairs.definition: Even in an 802.1x WLAN, the client uses Open Authentication to associate with the AP first; the actual client authentication then occurs at a dedicated authentication server.

pairs.term: Groupwise Transient Key (GTK)
pairs.definition: The GTK is generated by the AP and derived using the PTK with the GMK; it is exchanged in Message 3 of the four-way handshake and is used to secure broadcast and multicast traffic.

prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.term: Signal bandwidth
pairs.definition: The width of frequency space required for a transmitted signal; for example, a signal with 22 MHz bandwidth is bounded at 11 MHz above and below the center frequency.

pairs.term: 2.4 GHz channel 14
pairs.definition: The 2.4 GHz band's 14 channels are spaced 5 MHz apart except for channel 14, which is set apart at 2.484 GHz.

pairs.term: Spectral mask
pairs.definition: A defined boundary that wireless devices use to ignore parts of a signal that fall outside the bandwidth boundaries.

pairs.term: Channel numbering benefit
pairs.definition: Channel numbers are easier to reference than specific frequencies, and standardized channel assignments can be used consistently in all locations.

pairs.term: Frequency
pairs.definition: The number of times a signal makes one complete up-and-down cycle in 1 second, measured in hertz (Hz).

pairs.term: 2.4 GHz channel overlap
pairs.definition: The 2.4 GHz band uses channels 5 MHz wide, but Wi-Fi signals have a 22 MHz bandwidth, so adjacent channel numbers overlap and interfere. Channels must be placed farther apart to avoid overlap.
