title: Implicit deny blocks everything
code:
R1(config)# access-list 101 deny ip host 10.0.0.5 any
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet 0/0
R1(config-if)# ip access-group 101 in
flaws: The list contains a single deny statement and nothing else, so every packet that does not match host 10.0.0.5 is dropped by the implicit deny any at the end of the ACL.
A final `access-list 101 permit ip any any` statement is missing, which is required if the intent was to block only host 10.0.0.5.
explanation: Every IP access list ends with an implicit deny any. Because the only explicit entry is a deny, all other traffic is silently discarded and the interface effectively blocks the entire network. Add an explicit `permit ip any any` after the deny so only 10.0.0.5 is filtered.

title: Deny statement unreachable
code:
R1(config)# access-list 101 permit ip any any
R1(config)# access-list 101 deny ip host 10.0.0.5 any
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet 0/0
R1(config-if)# ip access-group 101 in
flaws: The deny for host 10.0.0.5 is placed after `permit ip any any`, and ACLs are evaluated top-down with first match winning, so the deny is never reached.
Traffic from 10.0.0.5 is therefore still permitted — the block the admin intended simply does not happen.
explanation: IP ACLs are processed in order and the first matching statement wins. Since `permit ip any any` matches every packet first, the deny below it is dead code. Reorder the entries so the deny comes before the permit (deny first, permit last).

title: Subnet mask used instead of wildcard
code:
R1(config)# access-list 101 permit tcp 192.168.1.0 255.255.255.0 host 10.0.0.5 eq 80
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet 0/1
R1(config-if)# ip access-group 101 in
flaws: 255.255.255.0 is a subnet mask, but ACLs require wildcard masks; with this value only source addresses whose host bits are zero (192.168.1.0) can match.
Real hosts such as 192.168.1.50 never match the rule and are dropped by the implicit deny.
explanation: Wildcard masks mark ignored bits with 1, so the correct mask for a /24 range is 0.0.0.255. Entering 255.255.255.0 inverts the semantics and makes the rule match almost nothing useful. Replace it with 0.0.0.255.

title: ACL applied on the wrong interface
code:
R1(config)# access-list 101 deny ip 10.0.0.0 0.255.255.255 any
R1(config)# access-list 101 permit ip any any
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet 0/1
R1(config-if)# ip access-group 101 in
flaws: The access-group is bound inbound on gigabitethernet 0/1 (the LAN-facing interface), but the 10.0.0.0/8 traffic to be blocked arrives on the WAN-facing gigabitethernet 0/0.
Because the ACL inspects only packets entering gi0/1, WAN-sourced traffic passes through the router completely unfiltered.
explanation: An inbound ACL filters only packets that enter the interface it is attached to. To drop 10.0.0.0/8 traffic coming from the WAN, the access-group must be applied inbound on gigabitethernet 0/0, the interface that actually receives that traffic.

title: Network statement does not match the interface
code:
R1(config)# router ospf 1
R1(config-router)# network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
flaws: The neighbor link uses 10.0.1.0/24, but the network statement 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255 matches only 10.0.0.x, so the 10.0.1.1 interface is never enabled for OSPF.
Because the interface is not covered by any network statement, no hello packets are sent on it and the adjacency with the neighbor never forms.
explanation: An OSPF network statement enables OSPF on every interface whose address falls inside the matched range. The wildcard 0.0.0.255 with prefix 10.0.0.0 covers only 10.0.0.0/24, not the real 10.0.1.0/24 link. Change the statement to `network 10.0.1.0 0.0.0.255 area 0`.

title: Neighbors assigned to different areas
code:
R1(config)# router ospf 1
R1(config-router)# network 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
R2(config)# router ospf 1
R2(config-router)# network 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 area 1
flaws: Both routers enable OSPF on the same 192.168.1.0/24 segment but assign it to different areas: area 0 on R1 and area 1 on R2.
OSPF requires both ends of a shared segment to be in the same area; otherwise the adjacency never reaches FULL.
explanation: An area is a property of a link, not of a router. When the two routers claim the same segment belongs to different areas, their hello packets contain incompatible area IDs and the adjacency cannot form. Pick one area (for example area 0) and use it on both routers.

title: Hello and dead timers do not match
code:
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet 0/0
R1(config-if)# ip ospf hello-interval 5
R1(config-if)# ip ospf dead-interval 20
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet 0/0
R2(config-if)# ip ospf hello-interval 10
R2(config-if)# ip ospf dead-interval 40
flaws: R1 uses hello 5 / dead 20 while R2 uses hello 10 / dead 40, so the timer fields in their hello packets do not match.
A router rejects hello packets whose hello or dead interval differs from its own, so the neighbors stay stuck in the initial state and no adjacency forms.
explanation: OSPF neighbors must agree on the hello and dead intervals carried in every hello packet. The mismatch means neither side accepts the other's hellos. Set identical values on both routers, for example hello 10 / dead 40 on each.

title: passive-interface on an adjacency link
code:
R1(config)# router ospf 1
R1(config-router)# network 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
R1(config-router)# passive-interface gigabitethernet 0/1
flaws: gigabitethernet 0/1 is the 192.168.1.0/24 link to the OSPF neighbor R2, yet passive-interface is enabled on it.
A passive interface stops sending and receiving hello packets, so the adjacency with R2 can never be established.
explanation: passive-interface suppresses OSPF hellos on the interface, so the subnet can be advertised but no neighbor relationship is built. It is meant for interfaces facing end hosts. Remove the command, or use `passive-interface default` and then `no passive-interface gigabitethernet 0/1` to keep only the LAN interfaces passive.

title: Metric k-value mismatch blocks adjacency
code:
R1(config)# router eigrp 100
R1(config-router)# network 192.168.1.0
R1(config-router)# metric weights 0 1 1 1 0 0
R2(config)# router eigrp 100
R2(config-router)# network 192.168.1.0
flaws: R1 configures k-values 1 1 1 1 0 0 (k2=1, k4=1) via the metric weights command while R2 keeps the EIGRP defaults, so the k-values in their hellos differ.
EIGRP only forms neighbors with routers that advertise identical k-values, so the adjacency stays down.
explanation: The k-values (k1, k2, k3, k4, k5) are exchanged in hello packets and must match on both routers or the neighbor relationship is refused. R1's `metric weights 0 1 1 1 0 0` differs from R2's defaults. Remove the metric weights line, or configure identical values on both routers.

title: Discontiguous subnets collapsed by auto-summary
code:
R1(config)# router eigrp 100
R1(config-router)# network 10.1.0.0
R1(config-router)# network 10.2.0.0
flaws: auto-summary is still enabled (the default in classic EIGRP), so 10.1.0.0/16 and 10.2.0.0/16 are summarized to the single classful route 10.0.0.0/8 before being advertised.
Announcing only the 10.0.0.0/8 summary hides the two distinct discontiguous subnets, so traffic to them is routed incorrectly across the core.
The missing `no auto-summary` command is what would preserve the real /16 prefixes.
explanation: With auto-summary on, EIGRP collapses subnets at classful boundaries. Because 10.1.0.0/16 and 10.2.0.0/16 are discontiguous (separated by another network), summarizing them to one 10.0.0.0/8 breaks reachability. Configure `no auto-summary` under the EIGRP router to advertise the actual prefixes.

title: Subnet mask in EIGRP network statement
code:
R1(config)# router eigrp 100
R1(config-router)# network 192.168.1.0 255.255.255.0
flaws: EIGRP network statements take wildcard masks, not subnet masks; 255.255.255.0 matches only 192.168.1.0 itself and no interface with a nonzero host part.
The interface 192.168.1.1/24 is therefore not matched and EIGRP is never enabled on it, so the subnet is not advertised.
explanation: In `network prefix wildcard`, wildcard bits of 1 mean 'ignore'. Writing 255.255.255.0 flips the semantics and matches only the exact address 192.168.1.0. Use 0.0.0.255 so the whole 192.168.1.0/24 interface range is matched.

title: Lower-priority switch wins the root election
code:
SW1(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 4096
SW2(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 0
flaws: The bridge with the lowest priority value wins the election, so SW2 with priority 0 becomes root for VLAN 10 instead of the intended SW1 with 4096.
Setting priority 4096 on SW1 cannot win against a switch whose priority is 0, because 0 is lower than any other value.
explanation: STP elects the root by lowest bridge ID (priority first, then MAC). SW2's priority 0 beats SW1's 4096, so SW2 takes the root role. Raise SW2's priority (for example `spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 4096` on SW2 and keep 4096 on SW1, using MAC as tie-breaker), or configure `spanning-tree vlan 10 root primary` on the intended root.

title: PortFast on a trunk link to a switch
code:
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet 0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast
flaws: The trunk port connecting to another switch has PortFast enabled, which skips the STP listening and learning states and moves straight to forwarding.
If a loop exists in the cabling, the redundant port is never blocked during convergence, so a transient bridging loop can occur.
explanation: PortFast is intended only for access ports facing end hosts. On a trunk toward another switch it removes the STP convergence delay that prevents loops. Remove portfast from the trunk; inter-switch links should use normal STP timers.

title: Spanning Tree disabled for a VLAN
code:
SW1(config)# no spanning-tree vlan 1
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet 0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
flaws: The command `no spanning-tree vlan 1` disables STP for VLAN 1, removing all loop protection on that VLAN.
With redundant links present, every port can now stay in forwarding state, so broadcast frames circulate in a layer-2 loop and can saturate the network.
explanation: Disabling spanning tree for a VLAN turns off loop detection for the entire VLAN; any physical redundancy then forms a bridging loop. Re-enable it with `spanning-tree vlan 1` so STP elects a root and blocks the redundant port.

title: Root guard on the root port
code:
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet 0/1
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree guard root
flaws: gigabitethernet 0/1 is SW1's root port toward the legitimate root bridge, but root guard is enabled on it.

Root guard blocks a port as soon as it receives a superior BPDU, which is exactly what the legitimate root sends — so the root port is forced into the root-inconsistent (blocking) state and the uplink dies.
explanation: Root guard must be placed on ports where you never want a better root to be learned — typically ports toward other switches or access ports — never on the root port itself, which is supposed to receive superior BPDUs. Remove `spanning-tree guard root` from gi0/1 and enable it on the port facing the suspected rogue switch instead.

title: overload keyword missing
code:
R1(config)# ip nat pool PUBLIC 203.0.113.10 203.0.113.20 netmask 255.255.255.0
R1(config)# access-list 1 permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255
R1(config)# ip nat inside source list 1 pool PUBLIC
flaws: The translation statement lacks the `overload` keyword, so the pool is used strictly one-to-one and only as many inside hosts as there are pool addresses (11) can be translated at once.
The 12th concurrent inside host finds no free pool address and its traffic is not translated, breaking connectivity for everyone beyond the pool size.
explanation: Without overload, dynamic NAT performs a one-to-one mapping limited by the pool size. Appending `overload` turns it into PAT: all inside hosts share the pool addresses using source-port multiplexing, so hundreds of clients work with a handful of public IPs.

title: inside and outside interfaces reversed
code:
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet 0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# ip nat outside
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet 0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 203.0.113.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# ip nat inside
flaws: The LAN-facing interface (192.168.1.1) is marked `ip nat outside` and the WAN-facing interface (203.0.113.1) is marked `ip nat inside` — the exact opposite of the required assignment.
Because the inside/outside roles are swapped, the inside source translation rule never applies to the actual traffic flow and LAN clients are not translated at all.
explanation: NAT only translates traffic that crosses from an inside interface to an outside interface. With gi0/0 (LAN) marked outside and gi0/1 (WAN) marked inside, the flow direction is inverted and no translation occurs. Swap the two commands: `ip nat inside` on gi0/0 and `ip nat outside` on gi0/1.

title: local and global addresses swapped
code:
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet 0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# ip nat inside source static tcp 203.0.113.5 80 192.168.1.50 80
flaws: The command lists the public address 203.0.113.5 first and the private server 192.168.1.50 second, but the syntax requires the inside local address first and the inside global address second.
The resulting mapping (inside local 203.0.113.5 to inside global 192.168.1.50) is meaningless, so external users cannot reach the web server through the public address.
explanation: The correct order is `ip nat inside source static tcp 192.168.1.50 80 203.0.113.5 80` — inside local (private) first, inside global (public) second. Writing them reversed makes the router translate in the wrong direction and the static NAT fails.

title: Wrong default gateway handed to clients
code:
R1(config)# ip dhcp pool LAN
R1(dhcp-config)# network 192.168.1.0 255.255.255.0
R1(dhcp-config)# default-router 192.168.1.254
R1(dhcp-config)# dns-server 8.8.8.8
flaws: The pool hands out gateway 192.168.1.254, but the router's LAN interface is 192.168.1.1, so clients receive a default route to an address that does not exist.
All traffic that is not local then goes nowhere, because the configured gateway silently drops it.
explanation: default-router must point at the layer-3 address that actually routes for the subnet — the router's own LAN interface, 192.168.1.1. Setting it to 192.168.1.254 sends clients to a black hole. Change it to `default-router 192.168.1.1`.

title: ip helper-address on the wrong interface
code:
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet 0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# ip helper-address 192.168.2.10
flaws: gigabitethernet 0/0 is the interface toward the DHCP server's segment, while the clients needing relay are on gigabitethernet 0/1 — but the helper-address is configured on gi0/0.
The client broadcast on gi0/1 never enters gi0/0, so the relay never sees it and no client ever receives an address.
explanation: ip helper-address must be placed on the interface that receives the client's DHCP broadcasts — the client-facing interface, not the server-facing one. Configure `ip helper-address 192.168.2.10` on gigabitethernet 0/1, the interface toward the clients.

title: Overlapping DHCP pools
code:
R1(config)# ip dhcp pool LAN1
R1(dhcp-config)# network 192.168.1.0 255.255.255.0
R1(config)# ip dhcp pool LAN2
R1(dhcp-config)# network 192.168.1.128 255.255.255.128
flaws: The LAN2 scope 192.168.1.128/25 lies entirely inside the LAN1 scope 192.168.1.0/24, so the two pools may lease the same addresses.
Two pools handing out the same IP to different clients guarantees address conflicts on the LAN.
explanation: DHCP address ranges must not overlap: a given IP may belong to only one pool. Because LAN2 is nested inside LAN1, the server can double-assign addresses. Redefine LAN2 on a separate network (for example 192.168.2.0/24) or carve non-overlapping ranges.

title: Native VLAN not matched on both ends
code:
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet 0/24
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 99
SW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet 0/24
SW2(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
flaws: SW1's trunk uses native VLAN 99 while SW2's end still uses the default native VLAN 1, so the native VLANs do not match.
Untagged frames sent by SW1 are interpreted as VLAN 1 traffic on SW2 and vice versa, so hosts in the native VLANs cannot communicate and STP/CDP across the trunk misbehaves.
explanation: Both ends of a trunk must agree on the native VLAN (the VLAN carried untagged). With 99 on one side and 1 on the other, untagged traffic lands in the wrong VLAN on each switch. Set the native VLAN identically on both ends, either 99 on both or back to the default 1 on both.

title: VLAN 40 missing from the allowed list
code:
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet 0/24
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30
flaws: The allowed list contains VLANs 10, 20 and 30 only, but the requirement is that the trunk also carries VLAN 40.
Frames tagged for VLAN 40 are dropped at the trunk because that VLAN is not in the allowed list.
explanation: The `switchport trunk allowed vlan` list defines exactly which VLANs may cross the trunk; anything else is discarded. Since VLAN 40 is missing from the list, its traffic never reaches the other switch. Update the command to `switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30,40`.

title: Access/trunk mode mismatch on the inter-switch link
code:
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet 0/24
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet 0/24
SW2(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW2(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
flaws: SW2's side of the inter-switch link is configured as an access port in VLAN 10, so only untagged VLAN 10 traffic is accepted.
All other VLANs (20, 30, ...) that the trunk on SW1 is supposed to carry are discarded at SW2 because an access port never tags frames.
explanation: A link between two switches must be a trunk on both ends to carry multiple VLANs. With SW2's port in access mode, only VLAN 10 crosses the link. Configure `switchport mode trunk` on SW2's port as well so all VLANs are carried with 802.1Q tags.

title: Access port assigned to a VLAN that was never created
code:
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet 0/12
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 99
flaws: VLAN 99 does not exist on the switch: it was never created with the global `vlan 99` command before the port was assigned to it.
The port sits in an inactive VLAN, so hosts connected to it cannot communicate with anything, even if VLAN 99 is configured elsewhere.
explanation: An interface cannot function in a VLAN that does not exist in the switch's VLAN database. The `switchport access vlan 99` command is accepted, but the port stays inactive until `vlan 99` is created in global configuration mode. Create the VLAN first, then assign the port.

title: chmod 754 gives others no execute permission
code:
# make the script executable by everyone and writable by the group
$ chmod 754 /usr/local/bin/deploy.sh
flaws: 754 is rwxr-xr--: the group gets read and execute but no write, and others get read only.
If the script must be executable by the group and others (and writable by the group), 754 is wrong — the others bit 4 (r--) blocks execution for other users.
explanation: In chmod octal notation the three digits are owner, group, others: 7=rwx, 5=r-x, 4=r--. 754 therefore denies others the execute bit. If the intent is owner full, group read-write, others read-execute, use 775; for owner-only write use 755.

title: Missing colon after NOPASSWD
code:
# allow matthias to run systemctl without a password
matthias ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD /usr/bin/systemctl
flaws: The sudoers line is missing the required colon: the tag must be written NOPASSWD: followed by the command list.
As written, sudo reports a syntax error in the sudoers file and the entry is not applied, so matthias gets no passwordless sudo at all.
explanation: In sudoers, privilege tags such as NOPASSWD must be terminated with a colon: `matthias ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl`. Without the colon the line fails to parse. Fix the line and verify it with `visudo -c`.

title: Misused quantifier in grep pattern
code:
# find all hosts in the 192.168.1.x network in the log
$ grep "192\.168\.1\.*" access.log
flaws: In basic regular expressions the `*` applies to the preceding atom, which here is the escaped dot — so the pattern matches '192.168.1' followed by zero or more literal dots.
The pattern therefore also matches addresses like 192.168.10.5 or 192.168.15.9 (false positives) and never requires a final octet, so the intended filter for the 192.168.1.x subnet is wrong.
explanation: Writing `1\.*` means 'a literal 1 and any number of dots', not 'any last octet'. To match hosts in 192.168.1.0/24 use `grep "192\.168\.1\.[0-9]\+" access.log` (with the + quantifier) or simply `grep "192\.168\.1\." access.log`.

title: Mutable default argument shared across calls
flaws: The default argument `cart=[]` is a single list object created once at function definition time and shared by every call that omits cart.
Calling add_item('apple') then add_item('pear') returns ['apple', 'pear'] from the second call, so items from earlier calls leak into later results.
explanation: Default values are evaluated once, when the function is defined, so the mutable list is reused across all calls. The standard fix is `def add_item(item, cart=None):` followed by `if cart is None: cart = []` inside the function.

title: Single = in a condition
code:
if enabled = True:
    print("feature enabled")
flaws: The condition uses a single `=` (assignment) instead of `==` (comparison).
Python 3 rejects this as a SyntaxError, so the script does not even run; even in a context where it parsed, the value would always be truthy.
explanation: A single equals sign assigns a value and is not a valid condition in Python. The condition must be written `if enabled == True:` or, more idiomatically, `if enabled:`. Note that the same mistake would silently change logic in languages that allow it, which is why Python forbids it.

title: range(n) skips the upper bound
flaws: range(n) yields 0, 1, ..., n-1, so the number n itself is never added and a useless 0 is included instead.
For n=5 the function returns 10, but the documented behavior 'sum of 1..n' requires 15.
explanation: range() stops before the stop value, so summing 1 through n inclusive needs `range(1, n+1)`. The off-by-one hides at the boundary: any test with n at the limit reveals the missing n term.

title: bind() called with two arguments instead of a tuple
code:
import socket
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
s.bind("127.0.0.1", 8080)
s.listen(5)
flaws: bind() takes a single argument: a (host, port) tuple. Passing the address and port as two separate arguments raises TypeError: bind() takes exactly one argument.
The program crashes at startup, so the server never even reaches listen().
explanation: Python's socket.bind expects one tuple, `s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 8080))`. This is a classic mistake because many other languages take two parameters. Note the extra parentheses are mandatory — without them the call fails immediately.

title: return inside the loop
flaws: The `return None` is indented inside the for loop, so it executes on the very first iteration regardless of whether the first element is positive.
For input [-1, 5] the function returns None instead of 5, because it never gets past the first element.
explanation: The return that should run only after the whole loop finished is inside the loop body, changing the function's control flow. Dedent `return None` so it aligns with the `for` statement — then the loop scans all elements before giving up.

title: become_user without become
code:
- hosts: web
  tasks:
    - name: Install nginx
      apt:
        name: nginx
        state: present
      become_user: root
flaws: become_user: root is set without become: yes, so privilege escalation is never enabled and the task runs as the current (usually unprivileged) user.
The apt module then fails with a permission error when it tries to install the package.
explanation: become_user only defines which user to escalate to; the escalation must be switched on with become: yes at play or task level. Add `become: yes` (and optionally keep become_user: root) so the task executes with root privileges.

title: Module arguments misindented
code:
- hosts: db
  tasks:
    - name: Start postgresql
      service:
      name: postgresql
      state: started
flaws: The keys `name` and `state` are indented at the same level as `service`, so they are siblings of the module name instead of its arguments.
The service module is therefore called with no arguments at all and the task fails with a missing-required-argument error.
explanation: In YAML, indentation defines structure: module arguments must be nested under the module key. Here `service:` gets an empty mapping while name/state become new task keywords, which Ansible rejects. Indent both keys under service: so it reads service: name: postgresql, state: started.

title: Nonexistent restart module
code:
- hosts: all
  tasks:
    - name: Restart nginx
      restart:
        name: nginx
flaws: There is no `restart` module in Ansible — the task will fail with a module-not-found error.
Restarting a service must be done with the `service` (or systemd) module using state: restarted.
explanation: Ansible has no built-in restart module. The correct task is `service: name: nginx state: restarted` (or the systemd module). A student reaching for a convenient 'restart' keyword is a classic mistake — only real module names are accepted.

title: Unquoted 'no' becomes a boolean
code:
- hosts: all
  vars:
    force: no
  tasks:
    - name: Apply config
      template:
        src: nginx.conf.j2
        dest: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
      when: force == "no"
flaws: The unquoted value `no` is parsed by YAML as the boolean false, not the string "no".
The condition `force == "no"` compares a boolean with a string and is never true, so the template task never runs.
explanation: YAML 1.1 treats bare yes/no/on/off as booleans. To store the string "no", quote it: `force: "no"` — then the when-condition works — or, better, keep the boolean and compare with false. This pitfall silently disables tasks.

title: VTY accepts telnet instead of SSH only
code:
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# password cisco123
R1(config-line)# login
R1(config-line)# transport input telnet
flaws: The VTY lines are configured with `transport input telnet`, which permits insecure telnet sessions and leaves the router open to clear-text logins.
For secure remote management the line must use `transport input ssh` (after a hostname, domain name and crypto keys are configured) so only encrypted SSH sessions are accepted.
explanation: `transport input telnet` explicitly allows telnet onto the router, so passwords and sessions travel in clear text. Replace it with `transport input ssh` and generate crypto keys (hostname, `ip domain-name`, `crypto key generate rsa`) so SSH works and telnet is refused.

title: access-class applied out on VTY
code:
R1(config)# access-list 10 permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# access-class 10 out
flaws: To filter who may connect to the router, the access-class must be applied in the `in` direction; `out` only filters connections initiated from the router on that VTY.
A rogue host from 10.0.0.5 can therefore still establish an SSH/telnet session, because the outbound filter does not check incoming source addresses.
explanation: On VTY lines, `access-class <acl> in` evaluates the source address of every incoming connection attempt, while `out` applies to reverse connections leaving the router. Change the command to `access-class 10 in` so only 192.168.1.0/24 can connect.

title: login local without any local users
code:
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# login local
flaws: `login local` tells the router to authenticate against its local username database, but no `username ... secret ...` entry has been created.
With an empty database, every login attempt is rejected and nobody can access the router remotely.
explanation: login local requires at least one local user to be configured. Create a user first, for example `username admin secret Str0ngPass`, and keep login local on the VTY lines. Otherwise the router denies all remote sessions, locking administrators out.

setup: R1 has GigabitEthernet0/0 with 10.1.1.0/24 and GigabitEthernet0/1 with 192.168.1.0/24. The running config contains 'ip route 10.10.10.0 255.255.255.0 192.168.1.1' and the next-hop 192.168.1.1 is reachable.
question: What output do you expect for the 10.10.10.0/24 entry?

choices.label: C       10.10.10.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0

explanation: A configured static route is shown with the 'S' code. The bracket value [1/0] is the administrative distance (1) and metric (0) of a static route. Because the destination does not sit on a link local to R1, the route resolves through next-hop 192.168.1.1.

setup: R1 is an edge router with 'ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 172.16.1.1' configured and the upstream 172.16.1.1 is reachable.
question: How does the router display the candidate default route?

choices.label: C     0.0.0.0/0 is directly connected, FastEthernet0/1

expected_output:
S*    0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 172.16.1.1
Gateway of last resort is 172.16.1.1 to network 0.0.0.0
explanation: A static default route is installed with the codes 'S*', where the asterisk marks a candidate default. Its distance of 1 and metric 0 come from the static keyword defaults. The 'Gateway of last resort' line confirms packets are forwarded to next-hop 172.16.1.1 when no more specific entry matches.

setup: R1 (an ASBR) runs OSPF with 'default-information originate always' configured and has no static default route.
question: How does R1 advertise and show the default route?

choices.label: The default route is not shown in the table at all

explanation: Routes injected into OSPF via 'default-information originate' are type-2 external routes, shown with the O*E2 code. The O* marks the default candidate, and the distance 110 is OSPF's administrative distance.

setup: Router PE1 has a single eBGP session to the ISP at 10.1.4.2 (AS 65001). The session has been up about 2.5 hours and prefixes have been exchanged.
question: What does the neighbor column show in the BGP summary?

choices.label: Neighbor 10.1.4.2 is in state Down (Idle)
Neighbor 10.1.4.2 is Established and shows an Up/Down uptime
Neighbor is stuck in EXSTART because MTU differs
Neighbor hit max-prefix and dropped to a flapping state

expected_output:
Neighbor     V     AS     MsgRcvd   MsgSent    TQ  InQ  OutQ  Up/Down   State/PfxRcd
10.1.4.2     4   65001    1234      2356       0    0     0   02:31:45         5
explanation: A healthy eBGP session shows the State/PfxRcd column with 'Established' replaced by the peer uptime. MsgRcvd and MsgSent grow while InQ/OutQ stay at zero, and PfxRcd reports the number of prefixes learned from the peer.

setup: R2 has an iBGP peer configured at 10.0.0.10. The neighbor router's BGP process has been shut down, so the TCP session cannot be established.
question: What state does the neighbor show in the BGP table?

choices.label: State/PfxRcd = 0 and the session is in the Idle state
The pair stays Established but sends no messages
The peer reaches EXSTART and blocks waiting for the remote
The neighbor waits in a persistent shutdown state

expected_output:
Neighbor     V     AS     MsgRcvd   MsgSent    TQ  InQ  OutQ    Up/Down    State/PfxRcd
10.0.0.10    4  65000    0         3         0    0     0    00:00:00   Idle
explanation: When the peer cannot be contacted, BGP leaves the session in the Idle state with zero prefixes received. The session retries the TCP connection attempt and never reaches Established.

setup: R1 and R2 are directly connected and configured for OSPF area 0 with matching timers. The adjacency has fully formed.
question: What state does the neighbor column show?

choices.label: FULL/ - and the neighbor priority in the next column
2WAY/DR and the DR/BDR roles
EXSTART/ - because the MTU mismatches
DOWN/ - because the interface is passive

expected_output:
Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
2.2.2.2           1   FULL/ -         00:00:31     10.1.1.2        FastEthernet0/0
explanation: On a point-to-point link (or when neither router is DR/BDR), the adjacency state is FULL with the router ID of the neighbor. FULL means the two routers have exchanged databases and synchronized LSAs. On multi-access networks the second field shows DR or BDR.

setup: R1 and R2 are connected via a serial link where R1 has an MTU of 1500 but R2 has 1400 configured. The OSPF adjacency never becomes FULL.
question: Which state do the neighbors show?

choices.label: EXSTART/ - with the adjacency stuck
FULL/ - because MTU is irrelevant to OSPF
2WAY/DROTHER with a DR election ongoing
LOADING/ - because LSUs never complete

expected_output:
Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
2.2.2.2           1   EXSTART/ -     00:00:32     10.1.1.2        Serial0/0/0
explanation: An MTU mismatch on a link stops OSPF neighbors in the EXSTART state, because the Database Description (DBD) packets of one side cannot fit in the other side's interface MTU. Neighbors stuck in EXSTART are the classic symptom of MTU mismatch.

setup: R1 and R2 run EIGRP AS 100 over a directly connected link. The neighbor relationship has formed normally.
question: What does the neighbor table show for R2?

choices.label: An entry with R2's IP, hold time and uptime, queue counts of 0
An empty table because EIGRP needs a server
R2 listed with State/EXSTART and a partial MTU error
Only directly connected routes with no neighbor entries

expected_output:
H   Address                 Interface       Hold Uptime   SRTT   RTO  Q   Seq
0   10.1.1.2                Fa0/0            13  00:12:34     4   100  0  12
explanation: show ip eigrp neighbors lists each adjacency with the neighbor interface address, hold time remaining, uptime, SRTT/RTO timers, and the Q (queue) and Seq (sequence) counters. Q=0 means no packets are queued for the neighbor.

setup: Switchport GigabitEthernet0/1 is configured with 'switchport mode trunk' and native VLAN 1. VLANs 1, 10 and 20 cross the uplink and the port is trunking.
question: What does the report for the trunk show?

choices.label: Mode 'on', Status 'trunking', native VLAN 1, and allowed VLANs listed
Mode auto, Status not-trunking
VLAN1 with the port in shutdown mode
encapsulation dot1q with Mode 'access'

expected_output:
Port           Mode        Encapsulation  Status        Native vlan
Gi0/1          on          802.1Q         trunking      1

Port        Vlans allowed on trunk
Gi0/1       1-4094

Port        Vlans allowed and active in management domain
Gi0/1       1,10,20

Port        Vlans in spanning tree forwarding state
Gi0/1       1,10,20
explanation: A port in 'trunk' mode shows as trunking with 802.1Q encapsulation. 'Vlans allowed and active' lists the VLANs that actually exist (1,10,20). The last section shows the VLANs that are forwarding in STP.

setup: Switch A's GigabitEthernet0/2 is left in 'auto' mode, and the far end is also 'auto', so DTP does not bring up trunking.
question: What does the switch report for GigabitEthernet0/2?

choices.label: GigabitEthernet0/2 shows status not-trunking and native vlan 1
Status trunking with the VLAN 10 portion spanned
The command prints an 'invalid input' error
Trunking state with the interface administratively down

expected_output:
Port           Mode     Encapsulation     Status        Native vlan
Gi0/2         auto     802.1Q           not-trunking   1
explanation: Two ports in 'auto' never negotiate a trunk because DTP (Dynamic Trunking Protocol) requires at least one side to actively propose trunking. The port stays in access mode and is reported as not-trunking.

setup: A switch has VLAN 1 (default), VLAN 10 (LAN-IT), and VLAN 20 (LAN-IoT), each created with one access port assigned.
question: Which VLAN summary is correct?

choices.label: A table listing VLAN 1 default and created VLANs 10, 20 all Active
VLAN 10 and 20 reported with no ports
VLAN 1 shown as inactive until a host connects
Only VLAN 1 is listed because VLANs 10/20 have no name

explanation: show vlan brief lists each VLAN with its name, status, and the ports assigned to it. VLAN 1 is the default and always exists; created VLANs appear with the ports assigned to them.

setup: A user complains PCs on VLAN 30 have no access. The network team created VLAN 30 on both access switches, but the trunk between them carries only VLANs 1, 10, 20.
question: Why do VLAN 30 hosts fail to communicate?

choices.label: VLAN 30 exists locally, but the trunk does not allow VLAN 30, so frames are dropped
VLAN 30 cannot be created while it is not in the native VLAN
The switch must be rebooted after creating a VLAN
VLAN 30 requires a routed interface to exist

expected_output:
VLAN Name                             Status    Ports
---- -------------------------------- --------- -------------------------------
1    default                          active    Gi0/5, Gi0/6
10   LAN-IT                           active    Gi0/24
20   LAN-IoT                          active    Fa0/1
30   LAN-NEW                          active    Gi0/15
explanation: Creating a VLAN on the switches does not automatically add it to the trunks. The trunk must be configured with 'switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30' (or allowed-vlan lists including 30) for frames to cross between switches.

setup: A PC with MAC 0050.7966.6800 is connected to switchport Gi0/12 and has been sending traffic. No other host uses this MAC.
question: Which entry appears in the MAC address table?

choices.label: No entry, because the switch learns MACs only from BPDUs

explanation: The switch learns MAC addresses from the source addresses of received frames and records them as DYNAMIC entries on the ingress port. The entry ages out after the default aging time (300 s) of inactivity.

setup: SW1 has priority 4096 and SW2 has default priority 32768. Both are in the same VLAN and connected by a trunk.
question: Which switch is root, and what does SW1's output show?

choices.label: SW1 is root because its priority is lower; SW1 shows Root ID equal to its own Bridge ID
SW2 is root because 32768 is larger than 4096
Root election is decided by MAC address only
Both switches show themselves as root

expected_output:
Spanning tree enabled protocol ieee
Root ID    Priority    4097
           Address     0050.7966.0001
           This bridge is the root
Bridge ID  Priority    4097   (priority 4096 sys-id-ext 1)
           Address     0050.7966.0001
explanation: The root bridge is the switch with the lowest bridge ID (priority then MAC). With priority 4096 + system ID extension 1 for VLAN 1, SW1's effective priority is 4097, lower than SW2's 32769, so SW1 is root and its output confirms 'This bridge is the root'.

setup: A PC with inside address 10.0.0.10 has just opened a web session through R1's NAT, which uses the outside global pool 203.0.113.5 - 203.0.113.10.
question: What does the NAT translation entry look like?

choices.label: 10.0.0.10 mapped to one pool address (e.g. 203.0.113.5), inside global for the session
203.0.113.5 mapped to 10.0.0.10 with no outside global
The pool address appears as inside local
No translation appears until the session has been idle for 5 minutes

expected_output:
Pro  Inside global      Inside local       Outside local      Outside global
tcp  203.0.113.5:52113  10.0.0.10:52113    93.184.216.34:80    93.184.216.34:80
explanation: With dynamic NAT, the inside local (private) address is mapped to an inside global (public pool) address. The translation entry shows the mapping, and the outside addresses stay unchanged because the destination is public.

setup: A named ACL 'BLOCK_HTTP' has 10 lines and has been applied inbound on Gi0/0 for several hours. You suspect a specific permit line never matches.
question: How do you verify the suspect line's hit count?

choices.label: show access-lists displays each line with its match counter
The counters are cleared automatically every minute
Hit counts are visible only in the running config
A line with zero matches means the ACL is not applied

expected_output:
IP access list BLOCK_HTTP
    10 permit tcp any host 10.1.1.100 eq 443 (12345 matches)
    20 deny tcp any host 10.1.1.100 eq 80 (0 matches)
    30 permit ip any any (98765 matches)
explanation: show access-lists shows each ACE with its match count in parentheses. A line with 0 matches either matches nothing in practice or is shadowed by a preceding line — both are strong troubleshooting evidence.

setup: An administrator has just configured SSH on a router with a local username, RSA keys, and the vty lines set to 'transport input ssh' with 'login local'.
question: What does the vty section of the running config show?

choices.label: line vty 0 4 with login local and transport input ssh
line vty 0 4 with password cisco and transport input telnet
line vty 0 4 with login and transport input all
No vty lines because SSH uses a dedicated port

expected_output:
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh
explanation: Secure vty configuration restricts transport to SSH and authenticates against the local user database. The first line ranges over the five vty lines, and each vty line inherits the same settings.

setup: An IPSec tunnel between R1 and R2 has been up for two hours with both peers configured identically.
question: What does the IKE SA table show?

choices.label: QM_IDLE (IKEv1) or ACTIVE (IKEv2) state for the peer
The tunnel shows as DOWN until ESP traffic flows
Only the local peer address with no remote entry
The state column shows the transform-set name

expected_output:
IPv4 Crypto ISAKMP SA
Cnnct-id  Slot   Local Addr    Remote Addr   IKEv2 Role   State
    1      0     10.1.1.1      10.2.2.2      RESPONDER    ACTIVE
explanation: show crypto isakmp sa lists the IKE security associations. A healthy IKEv2 SA shows state ACTIVE. If phase 1 has not completed, the state remains CONNECTING or the SA is missing entirely.

setup: A DHCP server (the router) has just handed out an address from pool LAN-POOL to a host with MAC 0050.7966.6800. The lease is 24 hours.
question: What does the binding table show?

choices.label: IP, MAC, lease expiration, and binding type, e.g. Automatic
Only the pool name and total addresses
The host's hostname with no IP
The binding appears only after the lease expires

expected_output:
Bindings from all pools not associated with VRF:
IP address          Client-ID/              Lease expiration        Type
                     Hardware address/
                     User name
10.0.0.10           0050.7966.6800           Aug 06 2026 10:15:00  Automatic
explanation: show ip dhcp binding lists each active lease: the leased IP, the client's MAC, the lease expiration time, and the binding type (Automatic for dynamic leases). Manual bindings show as Manual.

setup: The LAN pool has a /24 (254 usable addresses) and 254 hosts are currently online; the 255th host tries to get an address.
question: What happens to the 255th client?

choices.label: It receives no address; show ip dhcp pool shows utilization 100%
It receives an address from the router's own interface range
The oldest lease is automatically stolen
It gets 10.0.0.1 because that address is reserved

expected_output:
Pool LAN-POOL :
 Utilization mark (high/low)    : 100 / 0
 Subnet size (first/next)        : 10.0.0.0 / 24
 Total addresses                 : 254
 Leased addresses                : 254
 Pending event                   : none
 1 subnet is currently in the pool
explanation: When a DHCP pool is exhausted, new clients get no address (the server sends no DHCPOFFER). show ip dhcp pool confirms exhaustion when Leased addresses equals Total addresses. The administrator must expand the pool or shorten leases.

setup: R1 has FastEthernet0/0 with 10.1.1.1/24. A host on the same segment is powered on and answers ICMP echo requests.
question: Which reply characters appear?

choices.label: !!!!! with Success rate 100 percent and round-trip times
..... with Success rate 0 percent
UUUUU with destination unreachable replies
!!... with 60 percent because the target drops UDP probes

expected_output:
!!!!!
Success rate is 100 percent (5/5), round-trip min/avg/max = 1/1/2 ms
explanation: Each '!' means one Echo Reply was received within the timeout. A 100 percent success rate indicates every probe returned, and the round-trip statistics give min/avg/max latencies.

setup: R1 has no route towards network 10.2.2.0/24 and no default route. The source interface FastEthernet0/0 is up.
question: What output follows when there is no route to the destination?

choices.label: !!!!! with 100 percent although the target is unknown
The packets queue and time out after 4 seconds
U..... with a network unreachable notification returned by the router itself
U!U!U with 60 percent partial reach

expected_output:
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 5, 100-byte ICMP Echos to 10.2.2.2, timeout is 2 seconds:
U....
Success rate is 0 percent (0/5)
explanation: Without a route, the router answers locally with ICMP Destination Unreachable coded as 'U' on the first probe, and the remaining probes time out. None of the packets leave the router, so the success rate is 0 percent.

setup: A host at 192.168.1.100 traces 10.6.6.6. The path hops through router1 at 192.168.1.1 and router2 at 172.16.1.1 before 10.6.6.6 answers.
question: What does each hop line display?

choices.label: Each hop with an IP and three per-probe delays; the destination answers at the last hop
Only hop 1 appears and later probes time out
All hops show only '* * *' because UDP probes are filtered
The trace prints one line with the destination name only

explanation: Traceroute sends probes with TTL 1, 2, then 3. The first two routers expire the TTL and send ICMP Time Exceeded replies, and the destination answers when TTL reaches it, completing the trace rows.

setup: The router at 172.16.1.1 drops ICMP Time-Exceeded replies but still forwards traffic toward 10.6.6.6.
question: What does the trace output show for the middle hop?

choices.label: The middle router shows '* * *' but the destination still answers
The whole trace stops with unsupported protocol errors
Each hop prints the destination name until the packet drops
The failing hop is skipped and replaced by the next router

expected_output:
Tracing the route to 10.6.6.6
  1  192.168.1.1  1 ms  1 ms  1 ms
  2  *  *  *
  3  10.6.6.6  8 ms  8 ms  9 ms
explanation: A router that filters ICMP Time Exceeded replies silently drops those responses, so traceroute marks its hop with '* * *'. Because traffic still transits, the final hop answers and the trace completes.

title: OSPF neighbors never reach FULL
intro: R1 and R2 are directly connected over a serial link. Both are configured for OSPF area 0, the link is up and interfaces have IPs, but the neighbor adjacency on R1 stays stuck and never reaches FULL.

start.text: You start by inspecting the OSPF neighbor state. What should you do first?

choices.label: Run show ip ospf neighbor and read the State column
Delete and reconfigure OSPF on both routers
Reboot both routers to reset the adjacency

check_state.text: show ip ospf neighbor shows the remote router stuck in EXSTART/ - for a long time. Which cause is most consistent with this?

choices.label: MTU mismatch between the two interfaces
Different OSPF process IDs on the two routers
Missing network statement on one router only

check_mtu.text: You suspect an MTU mismatch. How do you confirm it?

choices.label: Compare the MTU on both interfaces (show interfaces on each side)
Lower the OSPF hello/dead timers to force adjacency
Add OSPF authentication to speed up the state

mtu_mismatch.text: R1 has MTU 1500 and R2 has MTU 1400 on the link. MTU mismatch is confirmed. What is the correct fix?

choices.label: Set R2's interface MTU to match R1's (1500), or use ip ospf mtu-ignore so Database Description packets fit
Raise both interfaces to jumbo MTU 9000
Remove OSPF and use static routes instead

success.text: MTU must match on both ends of the OSPF link. After aligning the MTU (or enabling ip ospf mtu-ignore), the adjacency proceeds through EXSTART, EXCHANGE, LOADING and reaches FULL.

fail_1.text: That action does not address the root cause. An MTU mismatch prevents Database Description packets from being carried, so the adjacency stalls in EXSTART. Match the MTU or use ip ospf mtu-ignore.

fail_2.text: Different OSPF process IDs do not stop an adjacency (process IDs are local), and a missing network statement would prevent the neighbor from even appearing. Because the neighbor IS listed but stuck, the symptom points to the database exchange, i.e. MTU mismatch.

explanation: OSPF neighbors stuck in EXSTART almost always indicate an MTU mismatch on the link. During EXSTART the routers exchange Database Description packets; if one side's packet cannot fit in the peer's MTU, the exchange stalls. Verify equal MTU on both ends, or configure ip ospf mtu-ignore, and the adjacency proceeds to FULL.

title: Port keeps going err-disabled
intro: A switchport connected to an office PC was configured with port security (maximum 1 MAC). Every few minutes the port goes err-disabled and the PC loses connectivity. The port recovers after about 2 minutes.

start.text: The port becomes err-disabled periodically. What is the most efficient first step?

choices.label: Check show port-security and the violation counter on the port
Disable port security entirely to restore service
Increase the port's duplex speed

check_violation.text: show port-security shows a violation count greater than zero and the err-disable reason is port-security shutdown. That confirms a violation. What is the likely culprit?

choices.label: A second device with a different MAC (VoIP phone, hub, or new laptop) appears on the port
The switch CPU load is causing the port down
The link is flapping because of a duplex mismatch

recover.text: A second MAC is seen on a port configured for maximum 1 MAC. Decide the correct fix.

choices.label: If the extra device is legitimate, raise max-MAC (or use sticky); if it is rogue, remove it. Then re-attach the port or rely on errdisable recovery
Change the violation mode to 'restrict' so the port stays up while unknown MACs are dropped and logged
Reformat the switch and reload the configuration

success.text: When additional real devices belong on the port, either increase the max-MAC count (optionally sticky) or, if you only want visibility, change the violation mode to restrict so unknown-MAC traffic is dropped instead of the port being shut. If a rogue device was plugged in, it must be removed.

fail_1.text: That would disable security entirely or try to fix an unrelated physical-layer issue. Port-security violations log the err-disable state; identify the unexpected MAC, then adjust the maximum or violation mode on the port.

explanation: Port security with a max of 1 disables the port (shutdown violation) when a second MAC address is seen. The port goes err-disabled and is re-enabled only after the recovery timer. Inspect show port-security to identify the violating MAC, then increase the MAC maximum, use sticky/restrict mode, or remove the unsupported device.

title: Host gets no DHCP address
intro: A new PC in VLAN 20 cannot obtain an IP address via DHCP. The DHCP server is a router in another VLAN. Statically configuring the same IP works.

start.text: Static IP works but DHCP does not. The DHCP request must cross VLANs. What should you verify first?

choices.label: A DHCP helper (ip helper-address) on the VLAN 20 interface pointing at the DHCP server
The PC's cable and NIC
The switch firmware version

check_helper.text: You find the VLAN 20 SVI has no ip helper-address. Until it is set, broadcast DHCP discovery frames do not cross the router. What is the correct action?

choices.label: Configure ip helper-address <dhcp-server-ip> under the interface of the client's subnet
Add ip helper-address globally on the router only
Set the client's gateway to the DHCP server IP

success.text: Configure ip helper-address <server-ip> under the interface/SVI of the subnet where the DHCP clients live. The router then forwards the DHCP broadcast (UDP 67/68) as unicast to the server. Verify the client receives an address.

fail_1.text: That is not the operative fix. DHCP broadcasts do not cross subnets, so the layer-3 gateway must relay the request. ip helper-address on the interface facing the client subnet is the correct mechanism.

explanation: DHCP broadcasts stay in the local segment. When the server is on a different subnet, the client VLAN gateway must run ip helper-address pointing to the server. Without it, DHCPDISCOVER never reaches the server and the client gets no address.

topic: Router pings OK but host cannot
title: Router reachable, host not
intro: Administrators can ping the router's interface IP from a PC on the LAN, but cannot reach a management server behind the router at 10.1.1.100 via SSH. The routing table on the admin PC is correct. Pings to the host fail too.

start.text: The router answers ping from the LAN, but SSH to the management host fails. What best explains the symptom?

choices.label: An ACL that permits the router's own interface traffic but denies this specific host (applied inbound, or vty access-class)
The server's NIC is broken
The VLAN number is not registered

check_acl.text: show access-list shows the applied ACL has entries matching traffic to 10.1.1.100, and the deny line has matches. What is the root cause?

choices.label: An inbound access-list on the interface, or a vty access-class, denies the management host
A missing loopback on the server
NAT broke because the host uses a private IP

fix_acl.text: A deny ACE explicitly matching 10.1.1.100 drops its traffic, or an access-class on the vty lines blocks it. What now?

choices.label: Amend or reorder the ACL / access-class so the legitimate management host is permitted
Remove all ACLs on the router
Delete the vty lines

success.text: ACLs evaluate first-match. A deny ACE placed before the permit is the classic cause of a host being unreachable while the router interface stays reachable. Amend the allowed list or reorder the ACEs, then verify with ping and SSH.

fail_1.text: That does not match the symptom. The management traffic toward the specific host is being matched and dropped by the (first-match) ACL or vty policy.

explanation: When a router interface itself responds but a host behind it cannot be reached, inspect for an ACL applied to the path of that exact host, or a vty access-class restricting remote access. Cisco ACLs match in order, so a deny ACE before the permit drops the traffic silently.

title: Bridging loop in a LAN
intro: PCs on a flat L2 network suddenly get duplicate-IP conflict errors, CPU usage surges on some switches, and latency spikes across the LAN.

start.text: These symptoms strongly point to a Layer-2 loop. What should you do first?

choices.label: Check spanning-tree status and locate a port stuck in forwarding on both ends of a redundant link
Leave the network and observe for another day
Reboot the core router

investigate.text: show spanning-tree shows an interface forwarding on both ends of a redundant link (the loop). What is the correct fix?

choices.label: Block the redundant path (shutdown one end, or fix the STP mode so spanning-tree elects one forwarding and one blocking path)
Increase the network address range
Set every switch to half-duplex

success.text: Spanning Tree Protocol must elect a single root path and block all other paths per segment so frames cannot loop. Removing the loop (or re-establishing STP state so one path forwards while the other blocks) stops broadcast storms, duplicate-IP errors and CPU saturation.

fail_1.text: Waiting, rebooting, or random physical tweaks do not stop the frame loop. STP is disabled or a redundant port is forwarding, so broadcast frames circle endlessly. Restore STP so exactly one path forwards per segment toward the root.

explanation: A Layer-2 broadcast loop occurs when STP does not block a redundant path (wrong mode, disabled STP, or BPDU filtering). Frames duplicate, MAC tables flap and broadcast storms saturate CPUs. STP resolves the issue by electing a root and blocking one of the redundant paths per segment.

title: LAN hosts have no Internet
intro: Internal LAN hosts can reach each other and internal servers, but cannot ping the public Internet. The edge router R1 has a NAT configuration for web servers, the ISP interface is up, but normal hosts have no connectivity.

start.text: Internal resources work, the Internet does not. Which requirement is most likely missing on R1?

choices.label: A default route toward the ISP AND a PAT (overload) translation for host traffic
A new switch for the ISP segment
A larger memory order

route_nat.text: show run has neither a default route to the ISP nor the ip nat inside/outside mapping for host traffic. What must be configured?

choices.label: ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 <ISP next hop>; ip nat inside source list <ACL> interface <outside> overload; mark inside/outside on the interfaces
Default route only, do nothing for NAT
NAT only, no default route

success.text: Without a default route the router drops the packet (network unreachable), and without PAT the router does not translate private to public. Configure the default route and ip nat inside/outside plus overload on the outside interface; verify with ping to a public IP.

fail_1.text: LAN-to-ISP failures usually mean the edge lacks a default route (no destination) or NAT for host traffic. Everything on the inside is working; the problem is at the edge routing and translation.

fail_2.text: Both a default route and NAT are needed. With only a default route, private addresses are not translated and replies cannot be routed back. With NAT but no default route, R1 has no path to the Internet.

explanation: Two requirements hold at the edge: (1) a default route (0.0.0.0/0) to the ISP next-hop so the router knows where to send traffic; (2) NAT that PATs the inside source addresses onto the outbound interface (ip nat inside source list ... overload). Missing either one leaves LAN hosts without Internet while inside LAN communication still works.

title: SSH sessions drop early
intro: Administrators can open SSH sessions to a router, but the session disconnects after roughly 30 seconds of inactivity. The connection itself works.

start.text: SSH sessions terminate after about half a minute of idle time. What is the usual cause?

choices.label: The vty exec-timeout is set too short
The SNMP version is too new
The admin laptop battery is failing

check_vty.text: You review the vty configuration: transport input ssh, login local, and 'exec-timeout 0 30' on line vty 0 4. What is the issue?

choices.label: exec-timeout 0 30 disconnects idle sessions after 30 seconds; raise it (e.g. exec-timeout 30 0)
Disable SSH entirely
Raise the console baud rate

success.text: exec-timeout 0 30 means 0 minutes and 30 seconds of idle time before disconnect. Set exec-timeout to a larger value (e.g. exec-timeout 30 0 for 30 minutes), or configure exec-timeout 0 0 to never time out.

fail_1.text: That is unrelated. Sessions that drop at a fixed idle interval point to the vty exec-timeout, which controls how long a line survives without activity.

fail_2.text: Disabling SSH is not a fix for sessions being dropped by a timer. Change the vty exec-timeout instead.

explanation: The vty exec-timeout (default 10 minutes) disconnects idle sessions. If sessions drop after a shorter, fixed window, check the vty configuration: exec-timeout <min> <sec> is written as minutes then seconds. Fix by extending the timeout.

title: Web server missing after reboot
intro: An administrator configured nginx on a Linux server. It works after manually running 'systemctl start nginx', but after a reboot nginx is not running.

start.text: The service starts manually but not at boot. What is the most common root cause?

choices.label: The unit is not enabled, so systemd does not start it at boot
nginx does not support boot
The OS was installed today

check_enable.text: systemctl is-enabled nginx reports 'disabled'. What is the correct fix?

choices.label: Run systemctl enable nginx (creates the wanted symlink into the multi-user.target)
Run systemctl mask nginx
Delete the unit file

success.text: systemctl enable nginx makes the service start automatically at boot by symlinking the unit into the target (multi-user.target). Verify with systemctl is-enabled nginx and a reboot test.

fail_1.text: Starting manually works, which proves the unit file and binary are fine. The missing part is only that the service is never started at boot because it is not enabled.

fail_2.text: masking or deleting the unit makes things worse. systemctl enable is the correct operation to start a service at boot.

explanation: systemd distinguishes starting a service now (systemctl start) from enabling it to start at boot (systemctl enable). systemctl enable nginx creates the wanted symlink into multi-user.target so Linux boots the service automatically. systemctl disable removes it.

title: NTP clock never synchronizes
intro: A router is configured with NTP pool servers. The clock does not sync and 'show ntp status' reports 'clock is unsynchronized'. Ping to the NTP servers works.

start.text: NTP packets go out but the clock never syncs. What should be checked first?

choices.label: That NTP (UDP 123) is not filtered by an ACL/firewall in either direction, and the source interface is routable back
Replace the router's serial flash
Set the clock to local only

check_path.text: Ping to the NTP server works, but 'show ntp associations' shows the server is not reachable and the clock stays unsynchronized. What is the likely cause?

choices.label: UDP 123 is being filtered in one direction, or responses go to a source address that cannot be routed back (no ntp source set)
The NTP server pool address is a broadcast
The router needs a full factory reset

fix_and_verify.text: You confirm the path (permit UDP 123 both directions) and set 'ntp source <loopback-or-routable-interface>'. What happens next?

choices.label: Wait a few minutes, then check 'show ntp status' for 'clock is synchronized'
Reboot the router
Change the NTP server to an IP that does not exist

success.text: After fixing the UDP 123 path and the NTP source interface, NTP exchanges complete and show ntp status reports 'clock is synchronized'.

fail_1.text: That is not a time-protocol fix. NTP stays unsynchronized when UDP 123 is filtered or responses cannot return to the configured source. Verify reachability and set ntp source correctly.

explanation: NTP unsynchronized almost always means the exchange does not complete: a firewall/ACL blocking UDP 123 in either direction, or responses sourced from an address that cannot route back (fixed with ntp source). Use show ntp associations to see if the server is reachable; if not, the clock stays unsynchronized.

title: Hosts reporting duplicate IP
intro: Several users report 'There is an IP address conflict with another system' and suddenly cannot reach network resources. The address is also statically assigned to one PC.

start.text: A duplicate IP conflict is active. What is the first correct step?

choices.label: Check the ARP table and DHCP bindings to identify which two devices claim the same IP
Restart the domain controller
Remove the DHCP server from the network

find_dup.text: You confirm the address is leased by DHCP to one device while also statically assigned to a PC. What action resolves the conflict?

choices.label: Exclude the IP from the DHCP pool (or change the static device to a unique address) so only one device uses it
Wait for the conflict to disappear
Restart the DHCP server

success.text: A duplicate IP occurs when two devices use the same address: DHCP leased it while a static host uses the same address. Make the addresses distinct by excluding the address from the pool or changing one device. Verify conflicts stop.

fail_1.text: Those are destructive options, not fixes. The conflict persists until one device is moved to a different address.

fail_2.text: A duplicate IP conflict does not disappear by waiting or by restarting the server. You must make one of the two devices use a different address.

explanation: A duplicate IP conflict happens when two devices use the same address: DHCP leased it while a static host is configured with the same IP, or two static hosts share one. The fix is to exclude the address from the pool (or change one device), then verify the ARP/DHCP tables show a single owner.

title: Hosts on different VLANs cannot talk
intro: Hosts on VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 are connected to the same access switch. Each host has a default gateway configured, but hosts in different VLANs cannot ping each other.

start.text: Hosts on different VLANs cannot communicate even though they are on the same switch. What is the most common cause?

choices.label: There is no routing between the VLANs (no SVIs with IPs and ip routing, or no router-on-a-stick)
The switch cannot create VLAN 20
The hosts need a crossover cable

check_gw.text: Each VLAN SVI exists and has an IP, but hosts cannot reach the other VLAN. What should you check next?

choices.label: The hosts' default gateway matches the SVI IP of their own VLAN, and 'ip routing' is enabled on the switch
The switch must be in switchport mode on all ports
VLANs must be numbered consecutively

fix_gw.text: You find the host in VLAN 10 has the VLAN 20 SVI as its gateway. What is the correct fix?

choices.label: Set each host's gateway to the SVI IP of its own VLAN (VLAN 10 hosts use the VLAN 10 SVI), and enable ip routing for L3 switching
Delete both VLANs and create one
Swap the switchports

success.text: For inter-VLAN routing, each host must point at its own VLAN's gateway (the SVI IP), and the switch must route between SVIs (ip routing on a multilayer switch, or an external router with subinterfaces). After fixing the gateway and enabling routing, the hosts can ping each other.

fail_1.text: That is not the cause. Inter-VLAN traffic needs a layer-3 gateway per VLAN and routing between them. Wrong default gateway is the classic error.

explanation: Hosts on different VLANs need a layer-3 device to route between them: SVIs with IPs plus 'ip routing' on a multilayer switch, or an external router with subinterfaces (router-on-a-stick). Each host must use its own VLAN's SVI IP as default gateway. The classic mistake is pointing hosts at the other VLAN's gateway.

title: New service blocked by firewall
intro: A new internal application server listens on TCP 8443. Internal clients can reach it, but clients in a remote office (VPN users) cannot. The VPN tunnel is up and routing is correct.

start.text: The VPN tunnel is up and routes exist, but remote users cannot reach TCP 8443. What is the most likely cause?

choices.label: The firewall does not permit TCP 8443 from the VPN zone to the server zone (implicit deny)
The server cannot run on TCP 8443
VPN clients need a new network card

check_fw.text: The firewall logs show the connection attempts from the VPN pool being denied at the policy layer. What is the correct action?

choices.label: Add a security policy permitting the VPN zone to reach the server zone on TCP 8443 (and the return traffic), keeping everything else denied
Disable the firewall entirely
Change the server's port to 80

success.text: Stateful firewalls deny traffic by default. Adding a policy that permits only the needed service (TCP 8443 from VPN to server) restores access while preserving security. Verify the traffic appears as permitted in the logs.

fail_1.text: That does not address the security policy. The firewall logs clearly show the traffic denied by policy; the fix is a targeted permit rule, not disabling security or changing the port.

explanation: Firewalls (especially stateful ones) default to deny. When a tunnel and routing are fine but a new service fails for remote users, inspect the firewall logs: a denied session means a policy must be added to permit the specific source zone, destination zone, and port. Targeted rules keep the deny-by-default posture intact.
